translation: Well, what's the matter with me? - all do it; they glory in their illnesses, and I, perhaps, more than anyone else. Let's not argue; my objection is senseless. However, I am firmly convinced that not only is it a lot of consciousness that's a disease, but any consciousness is a disease at all. I stand by that. Let's leave it for a moment. Tell me this: why did it happen, as if on purpose, that, precisely when I was most capable of sensing all the subtleties of 'all that is beautiful and sublime' - as they used to say in our time - I would not be able to sense it, but rather engage in these unseemly actions, these, well, in a word, actions that, although everyone does them, but happened to me precisely at those moments when I most keenly sensed that they were completely unnecessary? The more I sensed goodness and all that 'beautiful and sublime', the deeper I plunged into my mire, and the more skilled I became at getting completely stuck in it. But the main trait was that it all seemed not to be a coincidence in me, but rather as if it was supposed to be so. As if this was my normal state, and not a disease or a defect at all, so that, finally, I lost the desire to struggle with this defect. It ended with me almost believing (and maybe I really did believe), that this, perhaps, was my normal state. And at first, in the beginning, how much I suffered in this struggle! I didn't believe that it could happen to others, and so I hid it from myself all my life like a secret. I felt ashamed (perhaps I still do), and I even got to the point of feeling a certain, abnormal, mean little pleasure in returning, occasionally, to another foul Petersburg night, to a corner of my room, and intensely sensing that I had done another awful thing, that it couldn't be undone, and secretly gnawing at myself for it with my teeth, chewing and sucking myself to the point where the bitterness turned into a shameful, accursed sweetness, and finally - into a resolute, serious pleasure! Yes, into pleasure, into pleasure! I stand by that. I said this because I must probably know: do others have such pleasures? I'll explain: the pleasure was precisely from the excessively vivid awareness of my own degradation; because you feel, that you've reached the bottom; that it's vile, but that it can't be otherwise; that you have no way out, that you'll never become a different person; that even if there was still time and faith to change, I wouldn't want to change; and if I did want to change, I wouldn't do it, because, in reality, it might be that there's nothing to change into. And, finally, the most important thing, that all of this happens in accordance with the normal and fundamental laws of intensified consciousness, and by inertia that directly follows from these laws, so that it's not only impossible to change, but you can't do anything at all about it. For example, as a result of intensified consciousness: I am right to be a scoundrel, as if this were a consolation for a scoundrel, since he already senses that he really is one. But enough... Oh, I've been rewarded, but I've explained nothing... What explains the pleasure? But I'll explain! I'll get to the end! That's why I picked up my pen...

So what am I to say?— they all do this; they take pride in their illnesses, and I, I suppose, am the worst of all. Let's not argue about it; my objection is frivolous. But I remain firmly convinced that it's not only excessive consciousness that's a disease, but consciousness itself is a disease. I stand firm on that point. Let's leave that aside for now. Tell me this: why is it that, precisely at the moments when I was most capable of appreciating the subtleties of the 'beautiful and sublime'— those were the words we used to say back then— I would find myself not being able to appreciate them, and instead engaging in such unseemly behavior, such behavior that, well, everyone does it, but in my case, it happened precisely when I was most aware that I shouldn't be doing it? The more I was aware of what was good and of all this 'beautiful and sublime,' the deeper I sank into my mire, and the more I was able to get stuck in it. The main characteristic was that it all seemed not to be a coincidence within me, but as if it was meant to be this way. As if this was my normal state, and not a disease or a defect, so that I eventually lost the desire to fight this defect. It ended with me almost believing— and perhaps I truly believed— that this was, in fact, my normal state. And at first, at the beginning, how much torment I endured in this struggle! I didn't believe it happened to others, and that's why I kept this secret to myself my whole life. I was ashamed (and maybe I still am ashamed); I got to the point where I felt a certain secret, abnormal, foul pleasure in returning, sometimes, to a dirty St. Petersburg night, to a corner of my room, and intensively feeling that I'd done another bad thing, that it couldn't be undone, and inwardly, secretly, gnawing, gnawing myself with my teeth, piling myself up, and sucking myself until the bitterness turned into some kind of shameful, cursed sweetness and finally— into a resolute, serious pleasure! Yes, a pleasure, a pleasure! I stand firm on that. I spoke up because I probably want to know for sure: do others experience such pleasures? I'll explain to you: the pleasure was precisely from the excessively sharp awareness of my own debasement; because you feel, yourself, that you've hit rock bottom; that it's nasty, but it can't be otherwise; that you're trapped, that you'll never become a different person; that if there was even still time and faith to change into something else, I probably wouldn't want to change; but if I wanted to change, I wouldn't have done anything here, because, in fact, it may be that there's nothing to change into. And most importantly, the ultimate conclusion is that all this happens in accordance with the normal and fundamental laws of intensified consciousness and as a direct consequence of these laws, so that you not only can't change, but you simply can't do anything. For instance, as a result of intensified consciousness: I'm right, I'm a scoundrel, as if that's consolation for the scoundrel, since he already feels that he is a scoundrel. But enough... Ugh, I've nagged on, and what have I explained? But I'll explain it further! I'll bring it to a close! I took up my pen for this reason...

After all, what's the point? They all do it - they boast of their illnesses, and I, perhaps, even more than anyone else. Let's not argue; my objection is absurd. Still, I'm firmly convinced that it's not just a lot of consciousness, but consciousness itself is a disease. I'm standing firm on that. Let's leave it aside for a moment. Tell me this: why was it, as if it were intentional, that in those very moments, those same moments when I was most capable of sensing all the subtleties of 'the beautiful and the lofty' as we used to say, I would often not be able to sense it, and instead do those repulsive acts, those, well, in a word, those that everyone else, perhaps, does, but which, as if intentionally, would always occur to me at those exact times when I was most aware of how they shouldn't be done? The more I was aware of what's right and all this 'beautiful and lofty' nonsense, the deeper I sank into my mire and the more capable I was of completely drowning in it. But the main trait was that it seemed as though it wasn't accidental in me, but as though it was supposed to be that way. As though it was my normal state, not a disease or a vice, so that I eventually lost the desire to struggle with this vice. It ended with me almost believing (and maybe I really believed) that this, perhaps, was my normal state. At first, in the beginning, how much suffering I endured in this struggle! I didn't believe it happened to others, and that's why I hid it from myself my whole life as a secret. I felt ashamed (and maybe I even still feel ashamed); to the point where I would feel a secret, unnatural, despicable little pleasure in returning, as it happened, to a wretched Petersburg night, and then intensively sensing that I had done something disgusting again, that I couldn't undo what had been done, and inwardly, secretly gnawing at myself over it with my teeth, torturing and sucking myself until the bitterness turned into a shameful, cursed sweetness, and finally - into a firm, serious enjoyment! Yes, in enjoyment, in enjoyment! I'm standing firm on that. I spoke up because I think I need to find out: do others have such enjoyments? I'll explain to you: the enjoyment was here precisely from the incredibly vivid sense of my own humiliation; from the fact that I knew I had reached the very limit; that it was wrong, but that it couldn't be otherwise; that there was no way out; that I would never become a different person; that if even there was still some time left and faith to change into something else, I probably wouldn't want to change; and if I did want to change, I wouldn't do it here because, in fact, there might not be anything to change into. And the main thing and the final point is that all this happens according to the normal and basic laws of intensified consciousness and by inertia directly flowing from these laws, so that you can't change it and simply can't do anything about it. It follows that because of intensified consciousness: I'm right to be a scoundrel, as if it's a consolation for the scoundrel that he already senses that he's indeed a scoundrel. But that's enough... Ugh, I rewarded myself with that, and what did I explain?... How is the enjoyment explained here? But I'll explain! I'll get it to the end! I picked up the pen for that reason...

However, what am I to do? They all do the same, and it's illnesses they glory in, while I, perhaps, am the worst of them all. Let's not argue about it; my objection is frivolous. Still, I firmly believe that it's not only a great deal of consciousness, but even consciousness itself that is an illness. I stand by that. Let's leave it for a moment. Tell me this: why is it that at the very same moments, yes, the very same moments when I was most capable of perceiving the subtleties of "all that's beautiful and sublime" – as we used to say – I would often find myself not perceiving anything of the sort, but instead committing such unpresentable actions, which... well, they're done by everyone, I suppose, but they were always an accident for me at those particular moments when I was most aware that I shouldn't be doing them? The more I was aware of what's good and all that's "beautiful and sublime," the deeper I would sink into my mire and the more adept I became at getting completely stuck in it. But the most striking feature was that it all seemed to happen in me by necessity, as if it was destined to be so. As if this was my normal state, not an illness or a deformity, so that I eventually lost the desire to struggle with this deformity. It all ended with me almost believing – and perhaps I did believe – that this, in fact, was my normal state. At first, at the beginning, how much suffering I endured in this struggle! I didn't believe it happened to others, and so I kept it to myself as a secret all my life. I was ashamed (perhaps I even am ashamed now); I felt a kind of secret, unnatural, and low pleasure in returning, now and then, to some foul Petersburg night to intensely be aware that I had done another nasty thing, that it couldn't be undone, and inwardly, secretly, to gnaw at myself for it with my teeth, to pick at myself and suck myself dry until the bitterness turned into some kind of shameful, accursed sweetness and finally into a resolute and serious pleasure! Yes, into pleasure, into pleasure! I stand by that. I brought it up because I'd like to know for certain: do others experience such pleasures? I'll explain: the pleasure came from the unusually vivid awareness of my own humiliation; from the fact that you feel you've reached the bottom; that it's disgusting, but it can't be otherwise; that there's no way out, that you'll never become a different person; that if there was still time and faith to change into something else, I wouldn't want to change, because I wouldn't even be able to change if I wanted to, because, in fact, there might not be anything to change into. And the main thing and the bottom line is that all this happens according to the regular and fundamental laws of intensified consciousness and inertia, directly stemming from these laws, so that you can't change it, and you can't do anything about it. For instance, it results from intensified consciousness: I'm right to be a scoundrel, as if that were a consolation for a scoundrel who already feels he's one in fact. But enough... Oh, I've rewarded myself, and what have I explained? But I'll explain myself! I'll get to the end! I took up the pen just for that.

But what of it, after all? They all do it; they make a show of their illnesses, and I, I suppose, am the greatest of them all. Let's not argue about it; my objection is ridiculous. Still, I firmly believe that it's not just a great deal of consciousness, but consciousness itself that's a sickness. That's what I stand on. Let's put that aside for now. Tell me this: why is it that, as if by design, it would happen to me, those very minutes, those same minutes, when I was most capable of grasping all the subtleties of "the beautiful and the sublime" as they used to say in our day, that I would not be able to grasp them at all, and instead I would be doing such unseemly deeds, such deeds as... well, to put it simply, such deeds as everyone does, but which, as if on purpose, would come to me precisely at those moments when I was most aware of how not to do them? The more I was aware of what is good and all that "beautiful and sublime" stuff, the deeper I sank into my mire, and the more I was able to entangle myself in it completely. But the main thing was that it seemed not to happen by chance in me, but as if it was meant to be; as if it was my normal state, and not a sickness or a flaw at all, so that eventually I lost the will to struggle against this flaw. It ended with me almost believing (and maybe I actually believed) that this was, in fact, my normal state. At first, in the beginning, how much anguish I endured in that struggle! I didn't believe that this could happen to others, and so I kept it to myself as a secret all my life. I felt ashamed (and maybe I still feel ashamed); to the point that I would even feel a certain secret, unnatural, base pleasure in returning, would you believe it, to some other vile Petersburg night to myself, and to strain myself to realize that I had done it all over again, that it couldn't be undone, and to gnaw at myself inwardly, secretly, with my teeth, to chew and savor myself to the point where the bitterness would finally turn into some kind of shamefaced, accursed sweetness, and then, finally, into a firm, serious pleasure! Yes, into pleasure, into pleasure! That's what I'm standing on. I started talking because I'm probably eager to know: do others experience such pleasures? I'll explain: the pleasure lay precisely in the stark awareness of my own degradation; in the fact that you can feel that you've hit the wall; that it's foul, but it can't be otherwise; that you have no way out, that you'll never become a different person; that even if there was still time and faith left to change into something else, you wouldn't want to change; and if you did want to change, you wouldn't do anything because, in reality, there might not be anything to change into. And, most importantly, and to put the matter to rest, this all happens in accordance with the laws of intensified consciousness and as a direct consequence of those laws, so that you can't change, and can't do anything about it at all. For example, as a result of intensified consciousness: I'm right, I'm a scoundrel, as if being a scoundrel was some kind of consolation to a scoundrel who feels it for himself. But enough... Ah, I've explained it, and what have I explained? But I'll explain it! I'll see it through to the end! I picked up the pen precisely for this...

K. waited throughout the next week from day to day for a new communication, unable to believe that his renunciation of interrogations had been taken literally, and when the expected communication did not arrive by Saturday evening, he assumed he was tacitly summoned again for the same time to the same house. He therefore went back on Sunday, this time going straight up the stairs and corridors; some people who remembered him greeted him at their doors, but he no longer had to ask anyone and soon came to the right door. On his knocking, it was opened immediately for him, and without looking around any further for the familiar woman who stood by the door, he wanted to head straight into the next room. "Today is no session," said the woman. "Why should there be no session?" he asked and wanted to believe it was a mistake. But the woman convinced him by opening the door to the next room. It was really empty and looked even more pitifully empty than it had last Sunday. On the table, which remained unchanged on the podium, some books lay. "Can I take a look at the books?" K. asked, not out of particular curiosity, but so as not to have been completely pointless here. "No," said the woman and closed the door again, "that is not allowed. The books belong to the examining magistrate."

Ether wafted from the crack in the door. I started walking back and forth. It came to me that I must have been directed here, among these people, to this overcrowded general consultation. It was, as it were, the first public confirmation that I belonged to the outcasts; had the doctor noticed me? But I had made a decent appearance for my visit, I had sent in my card. Still, he must have somehow found out, perhaps I had betrayed myself. Well, now that it was a fact, I didn't find it so terrible after all; the people sat quietly and did not pay attention to me. Some had pains and shifted their legs a bit to make them more bearable. Various men had their heads in their hands, others slept deeply with heavy, bearded faces. A stout man with a red, swollen neck sat huddled over, staring at the floor and from time to time spat with a splash onto a spot that seemed suitable to him. A child wept in a corner; it had pulled its long thin legs up onto the bench and now held them clasped and pressed to itself, as if it had to take leave of them.

As briefly as possible, please. For they have no time. It felt strange to me. The young people sat and looked at me with that superior, expert curiosity they had learned. The doctor I knew stroked his black goatee and smiled carelessly. I thought I would burst into tears, but I heard myself speaking in French: "I had the honor of providing you, sir, with all the information I can give. Do you think it necessary to brief these gentlemen, you will certainly be able to do so with a few words during our conversation, while it's very difficult for me." The doctor rose with a courteous smile, stepped up to the window with the assistants and spoke a few words, accompanied by a horizontal, wavering hand gesture. After three minutes, one of the young people, short-sighted and fidgety, returned to the table and said, trying to look at me sternly: "You sleep well, sir?" "No, poorly." On which he sprang back to the group. There, they still haggled for a while, then the doctor turned to me and informed me that I would be summoned. I reminded him that I was scheduled for one o'clock. He smiled and made a few swift, jerky movements with his small white hands, which meant he was incredibly busy. I thus returned to my hallway, where the air had grown much more oppressive, and began pacing back and forth again, although I felt dead tired. Finally, the damp, accumulated odor made me dizzy; I stood by the entrance door and opened it a little. I saw that it was still afternoon and there was a bit of sunlight outside, and that did me immeasurably good.

The doctor stood up with a courteous smile, stepped to the window with the assistants, and said a few words accompanied by a horizontal, wavering hand movement. After three minutes, one of the young men, nearsighted and fidgety, returned to the table and said, trying to look at me sternly: "Do you sleep well, sir?" "No, badly." Upon which he jumped back to the group again. There, they continued to discuss for a while longer, then the doctor turned to me and informed me that I would be summoned. I reminded him that I had been called for one o'clock. He smiled and made a few quick, jerky movements with his small white hands, meaning he was incredibly busy. I therefore returned to my corridor, which had become unbearably stuffy, and started pacing back and forth again, though I felt absolutely exhausted. Finally, the damp, heaped odor made me dizzy; I stood at the entrance door and opened it a little. I saw that there was still afternoon and some sunlight outside, and that did me unspeakably good.

When the World-Honored Buddha had exterminated the evil monkey, he summoned Shakya, Maha Maudgalyayana, and caused them to convert to the Western Paradise of Bliss. Just then, Tianpeng and Tianyou, emerging from the Palace of Precious Dharma in the Divine Apex, exclaimed: "We beg the World-Honored Buddha to delay his departure, our lord's majestic aura has arrived." The Buddha heard their words and turned to gaze in the rear. A brief interval elapsed, and indeed, an Eight-Trigrams Carriage of Auspicious Omens appeared, covered with a Nine-Light Ornamental Dome. Celestial music played a grand symphony of celestial melodies, chanting scriptures beyond reckoning. Flowers of treasure bloomed, wafting true fragrance to the very presence of the Buddha, who expressed gratitude and said: "It is my good fortune that I have practiced the great truth, annihilating evil spirits. I implore the World-Honored Buddha to delay his departure for one day, that the gods and immortals may gather to thank him in one grand banquet."

The World-Honored Buddha could not dare to disobey, and joined his palms to thank the gods, saying: "I am an old monk, who but a mere receptacle of the mandate from the Heavenly King, what power do I possess? It is the Heavenly King and the gods who are blessed with abundance, who have labored to pay their respects." The Jade Emperor decreed an edict, ordering the Cloud Department's retinue of gods to invite, in sequence, the Three Purities, the Four Celestial Attendants, the Five Officials, the Six Origins, the Seven Extremes, the Eight Extremities, the Nine Luminaries, the Ten Capitals, and the myriad saintly worthies to come to the assembly to offer their gratitude to the Buddha. He also commanded the Four Great Celestial Masters and the Nine Heavenly Maiden Immortals to open the Golden Gate of the Jade Capital, the Treasures Palace of the Ultimate Mysterious, and the Jade Pavilion of the Resplendent, to invite the Buddha to ascend the Seven-Jeweled Altar of Spiritual Response. They arranged the seating for each tier, prepared the dragon liver and phoenix marrow, the jade dew and the golden peaches.

As the Buddha Tathagata had just vanquished the demon monkey, He called upon Manjusri and Mahakasyapa to ascend to the Western Pure Land. Just then, the Heavenly Deities of Auspicious Cloud and Protective Blessing suddenly emerged from the Luminous Pavilion and exclaimed, "Please, Lord Buddha, tarry a while, the Jade Emperor is coming." Upon hearing their words, the Buddha turned back to glance behind Him. In a brief moment, behold, an eight-vaned heavenly palanquin appeared, adorned with a nine-rayed umbrella of treasures; divine music played a majestic and enchanting melody, eulogizing the infinite virtues of the Buddha; precious flowers scattered about, wafting the fragrance of truth, and immediately coming to a stop before the Buddha, they bowed in gratitude and said, "We are deeply grateful for Your great Buddhist teachings that have eliminated the wicked demons. We humbly implore the Buddha to stay for just one more day and allow the immortals to offer a feast to express our gratitude." The Tathagata, not daring to disobey the heavenly decree, joined his palms in thanks and said, "The old monk was summoned by the Jade Emperor's command to come here; what power of mine was there? It is the Jade Emperor and the multitudes of gods who possess great fortune, and we dare not presume to thank them." 

The Jade Emperor sent his edict, instructing the cloud department of the heavenly hosts to invite the Three Clarities, the Four Guardians, the Five Officials, the Six Primeval Spirits, the Seven Extremely Talismans, the Eight Extreme Energies, the Nine Planets, the Ten Captains, and the Myriad Sages to come to the gathering to express their gratitude to the Buddha. He also ordered the Four Great Heavenly Masters and the Nine Heavenly Maidens to open the gates of the Jade Capital's Golden Gate, the Supreme Treasures Palace, and the Jade Pavilion of the Sublime Void, and invite the Buddha to ascend to the seven-jewelled spirit altar. Each class was assigned its proper seating arrangement, and the dragon's liver and phoenix marrow were served, along with the nectar of jade and the immortal peaches.

The Buddha Sakyamuni, having annihilated the evil monkey, beckoned the Maitreya and Sariputra to transform and proceed to the Western Pure Land. At that time, Heaven's Imperial Seal, Heaven's Aid, suddenly flew out of the Divine Palace, saying, "Please, Great Buddha, wait a moment, I the Imperial Lord am coming." Upon hearing this, the Buddha turned his head and gazed back. A short while later, indeed a magnificent eight-dragon carriage appeared, adorned with nine-rayed treasure canopies; a heavenly orchestra was playing exquisite music of profound harmony, singing and chanting boundless sacred melodies; scattering precious flowers and wafting true incense, proceeding to offer thanks before the Buddha: "We are deeply grateful to your grand Buddhist law that annihilates evil demons. We beg the Great Buddha to stay for one day, and the gods and immortals to hold a banquet in gratitude." The Buddha dared not to defy, so he joined his hands in thanks, saying, "This humble monk receives the decree of the Supreme Emperor, what authority do I possess? It is the Emperor and the gods who are endowed with boundless blessings, and it is not for us to express gratitude." The Jade Emperor sent down his decree, ordering the Cloud Department and all the gods to separately invite the Three Clarities, the Four Worthy Ones, the Five Emperors, the Six Officers, the Seven Primes, the Eight Extremes, the Nine Celestial Radiance, the Ten Capitals, the Ten Thousand Saints, to come to the gathering to thank the Buddha's blessings. He also commanded the Four Great Heavenly Teachers and the Nine Skies' Goddesses to open the Jade Capital's Golden Gate, the Mysterious Treasure Palace, the Jade Valley Mansion, and invite the Buddha to sit on the seven-jewel sacred platform. He arranged for the seating arrangement, prepared dragon liver and phoenix marrow, jade liquor and peaches.

When the Buddha of the Past eradicated the demonic monkeys, he summoned Vimalakirti and Mahamoggallana to convert to the Western Pure Land. Just then, Taisui and Tianyou hurriedly emerged from the Spirits' Treasury Palace: "Please wait for a moment, Our Lord is coming." The Buddha heard this and looked back, gazing intently. After a brief moment, he saw a majestic sedan chair with eight auspicious clouds, adorned with a nine-glazed parasol; the sweet music of the heavenly qin resounded, singing celestial tunes without number; scattered flowers of precious jewels, exhaling true fragrance, came to the Buddha and said: "We deeply appreciate the great law of eradication of demonic evil. May the Buddha spare a day, and let us all assemble to pay our respects."

The Buddha, not daring to go against the will of Heaven, folded his hands and said, "The old monk was summoned by the Heavenly Emperor to come here; what is there that I can do? Is it not that the Heavenly Emperor and the multitude of gods are blessed with great good fortune, and dare to repay the Buddha's benevolence?" The Jade Emperor decreed an edict, ordering the cloud spirits and all the gods to, one by one, invite the Three Purities, the Four Observers, the Five Lords, the Six Administrators, the Seven Primal Ones, the Eight Co-Precursors, the Nine Stars, the Ten Capitals, and the Ten Thousand Saints to attend the gathering to thank the Buddha's benevolence. He also instructed the four Great Heavenly Masters and the nine Heavenly Maidens of the Nine Heavens to open the Jade Capital's Golden Barrier, the Treasure Palace of the Supreme Mystery, and the Jade Pavilion of the Sunlit Cave, to invite the Buddha to sit high upon the Seven Treasures Divine Dais. The seating arrangements for the various assemblies were prepared, and arrangements were made for dragon liver and phoenix marrow, and for yao-liquor and jie-fruit.

When the Tathagata had vanquished the demonic monkey, He summoned Vajra, Mahamoggallana to ascend to the Western Pure Land. At that time, a decree from the Heavens was issued from the Palace of Numinous Radiance, saying, "Please, the Tathagata, wait a moment, my Master has arrived." The Tathagata listened and turned his head to gaze. A brief while later, behold! A majestic sedan chair arrived, its eight dragons in bright array, with a canopy of nine radiant lights. A celestial melody of a sublime and mystic song resounded; incense dispersing divine scriptures; precious flowers blooming, fragrant scents wafting, came to the Buddha's presence to say, "We are deeply grateful to the great Dharma that has vanquished the demonic evil. We beg the Tathagata to wait a day, and all the immortals will gather for a grand feast to offer our gratitude." The Tathagata, not daring to disobey the celestial decree, clasped his hands together in gratitude and said, "This old monk is but obeying the command of the great Celestial Emperor to come here. What power of mine is worthy of being thanked? It is truly the Celestial Emperor and the multitude of gods who are blessed with good fortune. How could I presume to repay your kindness?" The Jade Emperor issued his edict, commanding the multitude of gods of the clouds to invite the Three Pure Ones, the Four Regency Gods, the Five Celestial Guardians, the Six Precepts, the Seven Palaces, the Eight Extremes, the Nine Mysterious Emissaries, the Ten Envoys, and the Thousand True Saints to gather here to offer their gratitude. He also ordered the Four Great Heavenly Teachers and the Nine Heavenly Maidens to open the Jade Capital's Golden Pass, the Pearl of the Great Ultimate, and the Cavern of Jade, to invite the Tathagata to take high seat on the Seven Precious Spirit Platform. The seating was arranged, with each group seated according to their respective order, the Dragon's liver and Phoenix marrow were prepared, and the Jade Elixir of the Peaches of Immortality were laid out.

The Jade Emperor, even as he was infuriated and furious, had the Eunuch left and right to speak on his behalf, to strip him of his crown and official title, and to cast him to the battlefield. It was thanks to the timely intervention of the barefoot Heavenly Immortal, who, while reviewing the candidates, rescued me. Although I was to meet with death and be sent to the Eastern Desolate Land, I happened to stumble upon this mountain and took refuge. When I was at my wit's end, I would go hungry and then skip along the waves in search of food. When the woodcutter encountered me, he had no expectation of seeing me again, and when the fisherman laid eyes on my appearance, he shook his head at my miserable condition. Coming and going, countless people devoured others, and rolling and rocking the boat caused me distress. You dare to launch a brutal attack on me, and today my belly has a glimmer of hope. Not knowing how to taste it, you grasp hold of me and say I'm coarse, and that you'll chop me up to make a relish. "You impudent creature, you've completely lost all sense of decorum! I, the old Hog, can still bring up water droplets, how dare you say I'm coarse and need to be chopped up to make a relish! You seem to have taken me for a wily and cunning fellow. Be careful, lest you offend me with your lack of decorum! Eat your ancestral blessings from me!" The monster, seeing the bronze ladle come, made a flapping motion with its wings to avoid it. The two splashed out of the water onto the surface, and each of them climbed up the waves. This battle was unlike the previous one, and look at it: the one wielding the Hanging curtain dagger, the one with the Heavens' Whiskers Standard, each revealed their magical powers, to be admired. That one with the descent-demon-beheading wand, that one with the nine-pronged bronze ladle that moved with incredible speed. Leaping over waves, shaking mountains and rivers, they pushed and turned the world around. The ferocity was as if the Great Year was crashing into the wind-bell, and the evil looked like a deceased person flipping over a treasure box. This one, with a steadfast heart, that one, a guilty one, wreaking havoc as a water monster.

The Jade Emperor may have been enraged, yet he ordered his trusted Minister of the Right to cashier me of my title and post, and cast my body to the execution grounds. Thanks to the timely intervention of the footless heavenly sage, I was pardoned and spared from death, and ended up being banished to the East Bank of the Desert. When I had passed the time and was bedridden in the mountains, I struggled with hunger, rummaging through the bushes for food to eat. Villagers who saw me believed I was a doomed man, fishermen who saw my looks thought I was dead. The more people who came and went, the more I got wounded and sickly. You dare to commit a heinous deed and come to my doorstep, and today I'm finally going to have my belly full. Don't speak with such crude and uncouth speech, and you will be chopped up and turned into pickled sauce!" Hearing this, Eighth Rice Bowl (Bully) flew into a rage and cursed, "You're such a wretch, utterly lacking in dignity! I, old Pig, still have the potency to produce water! How dare you call me crude and say I'll be turned into pickled sauce? It seems you're confusing me for an old long-stemmed garlic plant! Don't be so impolite! I'll deal with you, and it will be the same as chopping your ancestors down!" The fiend saw the sword and dodged with a phoenix-like movement, and then both of them splashed the water's surface, each one jumping onto the waves. This round of combat was different from the previous one – watch how the scroll of mighty powers and the Celestial General Fan each display their divine prowess. The fiend wielding the demonic-slaying rod, the other holding a nine-pronged spear, jump over the waves, send the mountains and rivers into chaos, as calamitous as a Geng Yin (a calamitous sign) tramples on a ceremonial banner, or as vicious as a yokel overturns the treasure cover. This one with his heart beating with righteousness is protecting the Tang Monk, that one wreaking havoc, pouring crimes, serves the water fiend.

The Jade Emperor, even when furious and enraged, ordered the Imperial Censor to remove his crown, strip off his official uniform, and throw him into the execution ground. Luckily, the fierce footless sage Shou Lao had my case taken up and submitted to the court. Although it was a capital offense, I was only exiled to the east coast. When I had spent my days hungry and sick, I took refuge in this mountain, and when I was even hungrier, I rummaged through the sea looking for food to eat. Woodcutters, upon seeing me, thought I was doomed to die, and fishermen, seeing me, thought I was a doomed corpse. People came and went, many eating away at my flesh, and I turned and turned, dodging their bites and trying to protect my life. You dare to come and intimidate me, and today I have a rumbling belly that has something to expect. Don't talk nonsense! If you catch me, I'll be sliced up and pickled in brine! " Upon hearing these words, Zheng Yeren (Monkey King) grew enraged and cursed, "You wretch, you have no sense at all! Even an old pig like me can send up water vapors! How dare you call me coarse and imply I'd be pickled in brine! You seem to think I'm just a coward! Don't be impudent! Eat my ancestral tablet!" The demon saw the tablet coming and dodged it with a phoenix-like gesture. The two of us battled in the water, creating a foamy splash as we each rode the waves onto the boat. This round of combat was unlike the previous one; observe how: the officers who wield the long banners, the heavenly general, each display their divine powers that are truly wonderful. The one wielding the miraculous cudgel has it bobbing on his head, and the other brandishes his nine-toothed iron staff with ease. Jumping over the waves and thrashing the mountains and rivers, stirring up the chaotic world. Fierce like a severe plague sweeping over the banners, treacherous like a demon flinging aside the treasure cover. That one fights with a pure heart, brimming with righteous intent, and this one does evil, recklessly causing chaos as a water demon.

Jade Emperor though angry and irate, sent off his Grand Minister: remove your cap, strip off your armor, and your title, and thrust your body onto the killing ground. Just in time, the barefooted Great Immortal from the Eastern Sea intervened, sending me to safety. Lest I die, be reborn, and incur an inauspicious punishment, I was banished to the eastern bank of the Drowning Sands. Hunger-stricken, I lay sick on this mountain, and starving, I went to the west to search for food to sustain myself. The woodcutter encountered me with my life in peril, and the fisherman saw that all I have is destruction and withered blight. To come and go, there are many who devour people. To stir and scoop, there is immense destruction of life. You dare to threaten me at my door, today I have hope for something in my stomach. Don't talk nonsense that is too crude to be endured. Take hold and give me a break and mince me into a savory sauce!" 

Hear this, Zhu Bajie blazed with anger, cursing: "You rascal, lacking any finesse whatsoever! My old boar can spit up water bubbles, how dare you say I'm crude, wanting to mince me into a savory sauce! Looking at you, I think you mistake me for some old fool. Do not be impertinent! I'll settle accounts with your ancestors right now!" 

That fiend saw the treasure glint, gave a nod with his phoenix head and dodged out of the way. The two of them plunged into the water and fought on the surface of the water, each one charging and landing on the waves. This fight was different from the previous one, you see: with this monk wielding the whisk of clouds and thunder, the virtues of the divine were manifest. That one grasped the staff of defeating demons, its head rotating rapidly; this one held the iron mace with nine prongs, swift and decisive. Jumping and stirring waves, pushing and bewildering the world. Fierce like a calamitous pestilence crashing into the solar umbra, wicked like the incursion of a defeated and desperate person upending a treasure canopy. That one's red heart blazed in fervent innocence, this one's deeds flowed with abundance, inciting chaos.

Jade Emperor, even if you grow angry and scold, still orders the Premier to hold a Censer in his left hand: take off my crown, remove my official robes, and push me into the execution ground. Thanks to the Red-Footed Heavenly Immortal, he recommends to beg the Emperor to spare my life. Not to be put to death, yet exiled to the East Bank of the Sandy Desert. When starving, I lie sick on this mountain, and when hungry, I search for food in the forest. Woodcutter meets me, a fisherman sees my body half-eaten, who come and go as if I were a piece of meat, flip-flop and scoot here and there to attack and wound me. You dare come to threaten me at my door, today my belly is full. Don't say it's coarse and not edible, don't let me be chopped into pickled relish!

Hear this, Monkey King becomes enraged, curses and says: "You this scoundrel, completely lack any decency! I, the old Pig, can even exorcise water vapor, how dare you say I'm coarse and want me chopped into pickled relish! You must think me an old painted tramp! Stop your impertinence! Eat your ancestors' pill!" That demon sees the Pole Star halberd, sidesteps with a nod. The two playfully dash the water surface, each tread on the wave and reach the shore.

This time's fight differs from the previous, look at this: Horses Man lets down the silk curtain, Heavenly Ranks shake heaven and earth, each shows the divine skill to be cherished. The one who wields the demon-capturing rod wears it as a crown, the other wields the Nine-Claw Halberd easily at his fingertips. Dancing on the waves, stirring the mountains and rivers, making the world go mad. Fierce like a bad year's cicada-bark axe, evil like a funeral gate knocking over a treasure casket. This one (Tang Seng) steadfastly and intrepidly guards the real Buddhists, the other criminal villainously wants to harm the Water Demon.

'Mr. Samsa,' the prokurist now called out in a raised voice, 'what's going on? You barricade yourself in your room, only answer with yes and no, cause your parents a great, unnecessary worry, and ignore – by the way – your business obligations in an unheard-of way. I speak in the name of your parents and your boss, and I seriously ask for a clear explanation right away. I'm astonished, I'm astonished. I thought I knew you as a calm and reasonable person, and now it seems you're about to start behaving strangely. Your boss did mention a possible explanation for your absences to me this morning – they concern the debt collection that's been entrusted to you lately – but I swear on my honor that this explanation can't be true. However, I see your inexplicable obstinacy and completely lose any desire to get involved with you in any way. And your position is by no means the most secure. I originally had the intention of saying all this to you privately, but since you're making me waste my time, I don't see why your parents shouldn't know about it. Your recent performance has been very unsatisfactory; we acknowledge that it's not the right time for special deals, we agree on that; but there is no season for not doing any business, Mr. Samsa, and there mustn't be.

"Mr. Samsa," called the procura, raising his voice, "what is going on? You are barricading yourself in your room, only responding with 'yes' and 'no,' causing your parents unnecessary and serious worry, and for some reason abandoning – I'm just mentioning this in passing – your business duties in an unheard-of manner. I speak on behalf of your parents and your boss, and I'm asking you in all seriousness for a clear and immediate explanation. I am stunned, I am stunned. I thought I knew you to be a calm and reasonable person, but now it seems that you are starting to act strangely with eccentric whims. Our boss hinted at a possible explanation for your absence today – it involved the collection work that has been entrusted to you lately – but I must swear that this explanation is impossible. Now, however, I see your inexplicable stubbornness and have lost all desire to put myself out for you in any way. Your position, after all, is far from secure. I had originally intended to have this conversation with you in private, but since you're making me waste my time here, I don't see why your parents shouldn't also know about it. Your performances in recent times have been very unsatisfactory; it's true that it's not the right season for special deals, we acknowledge that; but there is no season in which one should not make deals, Mr. Samsa, it simply cannot be."

'Mr. Samsa,' shouted the prokurist in a raised voice, 'what is the matter with you? Your recent performances have been very unsatisfactory; it's true that it's not the right time to make special deals, we acknowledge that; but there is no season for not making deals at all, Mr. Samsa, there must not be one.'

"Mr. Samsa," the procuraist called out loudly, "what is the matter with you? You're barricading yourself in your room, merely responding with yes and no, causing your parents unnecessary worry and – by the way – neglecting your business duties in an unheard-of manner. I'm speaking on behalf of your parents and your boss, and I'm seriously asking for a clear, immediate explanation. I'm astonished, I'm astounded. I thought I knew you as a calm, sensible person, but it seems you're suddenly starting to behave erratically. Our boss did hint this morning that he might have an explanation for your absence, but I genuinely swear that it couldn't be true – you've been entrusted with collecting debts, after all. Your performance over the past while has been very unsatisfactory; we acknowledge that it's not the right time for any special business deals, but there's no time for no business at all, Mr. Samsa; it simply cannot be the case."

"Mr. Samsa," the procurist called out now with raised voice, "what's going on? You're barricading yourself in your room, only answering with a yes or no, causing unnecessary worry for your parents and neglecting – this aside – your business duties in an altogether unheard of manner. I speak here in the name of your parents and your boss and ask you quite seriously for an immediate, clear explanation. I'm astonished, I'm astonished. I thought you to be a calm, reasonable man, and now it seems as if you're suddenly beginning to indulge in eccentric behavior. Our boss hinted at a possible explanation for your absences today – it concerns the debt collection you've been entrusted with recently – but I swear on my honor that this explanation cannot possibly be true. Now, however, I see your incomprehensible stubbornness and completely lose all desire to intervene on your behalf. And your position is by no means secure. Your performance in the past few days has been very unsatisfactory; it's true that it's not the season for making special deals, we acknowledge that; but there is no season for not making deals at all, Mr. Samsa, it cannot exist.

The stranger seemed to avoid speaking a lot, but when he did, he spoke in general terms with considerable modesty, and his conversation took on a somewhat bookish tone: that he was an insignificant insect of this world and not worthy of much attention, that he had experienced a great deal in his life, endured much on his service, and had many enemies who had even sought to take his life; and that now, desiring to calm down, he was seeking to find a place to live and, upon arriving in this city, felt it his duty to pay his respects to its highest officials. This was all that was known about this new man in the city, which soon proved itself on the governor's social gathering. The preparations for this gathering took over two hours, and in the guest, there was a fastidiousness with regards to his attire that was rarely seen elsewhere. After a short post-dinner nap, he ordered to be brought a washbasin and, for an incredibly long time, wiped his cheeks with soap, first with the back of his tongue, and then, taking a towel from the shoulder of a tavern servant, he wiped his entire face with it, starting from behind his ears and before giving the tavern servant two hearty slaps in the face. Then, in front of a mirror, he put on a crawat, plucked out two hair from his nose and, immediately after, found himself in a brick-red frock coat with an embroidered scythe. Having thus dressed, he rolled in his own carriage through the city's excessively wide streets, illuminated by the faint light of occasional lamps. However, the governor's house was well-lit, even for a ball; the carriage with lanterns, the two gendarmes at the entrance, the stable lads' cries in the distance – in short, everything was as it should be. Entering the ballroom, Chichikov had to close his eyes for a moment because of the bright light from the candles, lamps, and the ladies' dresses. Everything was illuminated. The black coats flitted and swirled around, here and there, like flies on a white sugar loaf during a hot summer when an old maidservant splits it up into sparkling fragments in front of an open window; children gather around her, watching with curiosity as her stiff hands raise the hammer, while the aerial squadrons of flies, lifted by the gentle breeze, fly in boldly, as though they were the masters, and, taking advantage of the old woman's near-sightedness and the sun, which bothers her eyes, showering her with sugary pieces in a scattered or dense heap. Sated with the summer's abundance and already scattering sugary treats at every step, they flew not to eat, but to show themselves, fly back and forth across the sugar heap, knock their hind or fore legs against each other, scratch them under their wings, or, stretching out their front legs, scratch their heads with them, turn and fly away, and then fly back with new cloggy squadrons. Before Chichikov could take a good look around, he was grabbed by the hand by the governor, who introduced him to the governor's wife immediately. The guest did not waste any time and said a polite remark suitable for a man of middle age with not too high, not too low rank. When the established couples pressed everyone to the wall, he, with his hands clasped behind his back, looked at them for two minutes with great attention. Many ladies were well-dressed and in the latest fashion, while others had dressed as they pleased in the provincial town. The men, as everywhere, were of two kinds: some were thin and spent all their time near the ladies; some of them were so similar to those from St. Petersburg that it was difficult to distinguish them, with well-combed, tidy beards or simply well-shaven, well-rounded faces, speaking French as they laughed at the ladies just like in St. Petersburg. The other kind of men were fat or, like Chichikov, not too fat, but not thin either. These men, on the contrary, looked around suspiciously at the ladies and glanced around to see if the governor's servant had set up a green table for whist. Their faces were full and round, and some had warts; some were gray-haired; they did not have either queues, side-locks, or locks 'pour l'amour de l'art', as the French say; their hair was either low-cut or combed; their facial features were more rounded and strong. They were the esteemed officials in the town. Alas! The fat ones can do their business better in this world than the thin ones. The thin ones serve more on special assignments or only hold positions and flit about here and there; their existence is somehow too easy, airy, and unstable. The fat ones never take indirect positions, but all direct ones, and if they sit down somewhere, they sit firmly and sturdily, so that the place will creak and bend under them, and they won't be tossed away. They do not like external show; their frock coat is not as well-cut as the thin ones', but in the stockroom, there is a divine gift. A thin man won't have any soul in a pawn shop after three years; a fat one will quietly glance around, and there, in the end of the town, will be a house bought in his wife's name, then another one in another part of the town, then a village near the town, and then a village with all its property. Finally, a fat one, having served God and the State, having earned the universal respect, leaves service, moves on, and becomes a landed proprietor, a glorious Russian landowner, a breadwinner, and lives and lives well. And then, in accordance with the Russian custom, the thin heirs of the deceased often squander their father's fortune on the couriers. The traveling guest did not disappoint; he said some compliment, very suitable for a man of middle years, not too high in rank and not too low. When the pairs of dancing couples crowded everyone against the wall, he, placing his hands behind his back, looked at them for two minutes with great attention. Many of the ladies were well-dressed and à la mode, while others were dressed as fate had seen fit in the provincial town. The men, as everywhere, were of two kinds: some were thin and always hovered around the ladies; some were of the kind that it was hard to distinguish from Petersburg men, with their hair well-groomed, combed, and evenly cut, and their beards immaculately trimmed or simply well-groomed, just as carelessly sitting with the ladies, talking French, and amusing them just like in Petersburg. The other kind of men consisted of fat ones, or those like Chichikov – not too fat, but not thin either. These, on the other hand, glanced and sidled away from the ladies and looked around to see if the governor's servant had not set up the green table for whist somewhere. Their faces were full and round, with some even having warts, and some were streaked, with none wearing their hair in topknots, braids, or à la Gott mit uns, as the French say; their hair was either cut low or trimmed, and their facial features were more rounded and robust. These were the honored officials in the town. Alas! Fat men are more skilled at their affairs on this earth than thin ones. Thin men serve more as special emissaries or are simply listed and run back and forth; their existence is somehow too easy, airy, and completely unreliable. Fat men never occupy secondary positions, but take the main ones, and if they sit down, they sit firmly and steadily, so that the place creaks and bends under them, and they do not get up. They do not like outer show; their coats are not tailored as neatly as those of thin men, but they have the blessings of the Lord in their strongboxes. A thin man does not have even a soul in a pawnshop after three years; a fat man is calmly there – and lo and behold, he has appeared somewhere in the end of the city with a house bought in his wife's name, then another house in the other end, then a village near the town, then a village with all the outbuildings. Finally, the fat man, having served God and the state, having earned universal respect, leaves his service, settles in, and becomes a noble landowner, a worthy Russian barin, a breadwinner, and lives, and lives well. And after him, the thin successors come, in accordance with Russian custom, and dissipate their father's estate on the couriers. It cannot be hidden that almost such thoughts occupied Chichikov at the time when he observed the society, and the result was that he finally joined the fat men, where he encountered almost all the familiar faces: the prosecutor with his very thick, dark eyebrows and his left eye slightly squinting, as if saying, 'Come on, brother, let's go to the next room, I'll tell you something there,' – a serious and taciturn man, in any case; the postmaster, a short man, but a witty and philosophical one; the chairman of the court, a very prudent and affable man – who all greeted him as an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov returned their greetings with a somewhat awkward inclination of his head, but not without pleasure. He also made the acquaintance of the very courteous and polite landowner Mihailov and the somewhat awkward-looking Sobakevich, who, from the very start, accidentally stepped on his foot, saying, 'Please forgive me.' He was also handed a card for whist, which he accepted with a similarly polite bow. They sat down at the green table and did not get up until dinner. All conversation came to a complete halt, as always happens when they finally get to a meaningful occupation. Although the postmaster was very talkative, but as soon as he took the cards in his hands, he immediately showed a thoughtful expression on his face, covered his lower lip with his upper one, and kept this position for the whole game. When he left the table, he struck the table with his hand, saying, if a lady was playing: 'Be gone, old hag!' and if a king: 'Go to Tambov!' The chairman exclaimed, 'And I'll get you by the ears! And I'll get you by the ears!' Sometimes, when the cards hit the table, there were outbursts: 'Oh, she didn't have it! There was nothing to take, so she took it with a windmill!' or simply exclamation: 'Damnation! Cheater! Pidzhok!' or 'Pidzhindras! Pidzhrushka! Pidzhu!' and even simply 'Pichuk!' – names with which they had baptized the suits in their company. After the game, they argued, as usual, quite loudly. Our traveler also argued, but in a most extraordinary manner, so that everyone saw that he was arguing, and yet argued agreeably. He never said, 'Go away!' but: 'You deigned to leave!' 'I had the honor of covering your double!' and the like. In order to agree even more with his opponents, he offered them his silver snuffbox with finery, which had two forget-me-nots on it, placed there for a scent. The attention of the traveler was particularly drawn to landowners Mihailov and Sobakevich, whom he had mentioned above. He immediately inquired about them, asking the chairman and postmaster a few questions. The questions he asked showed not only curiosity, but also thoroughness, because he first asked how many peasants each of them had, and in what condition their estates were, and then inquired about their names and patronymics. He managed to win them over completely in a short time. Landowner Mihailov, who was not too old, with eyes as sweet as sugar, and who would wrinkle them whenever he smiled, was in love with him. He shook his hand for a long time and begged him to visit him at his estate, which, according to his words, was only fifteen versts from the city's outposts. To which Chichikov replied with a very polite inclination of the head and a sincere handshake that he not only eagerly agreed to do so but even considered it his sacred duty. Sobakevich also said it succinctly, 'And come to me, too,' – tapping his foot with his shoe, which was of a size that it would be difficult to find a matching leg, especially in these times when even on Russia's soil, giants are being brought out.

– Murderer! – the old man shouted at the top of his voice, but he was only able to shout that one word before he suddenly fell, struck as by lightning. Mitya jumped down from the garden again and bent over the fallen man. In his hand, Mitya held a metal pestle, and he automatically tossed it aside into the grass. The pestle fell two steps from Gregory, but not into the grass, onto the path, in a very conspicuous place. For several seconds, he gazed at the man lying before him. The old man's head was all bloody; Mitya extended his hand and began to feel his head. He remembered later on very clearly that at that moment he had a terrible desire 'to make quite sure' whether he had cracked the old man's skull or 'just knocked him on the head' with the pestle. But the blood was flowing, flowing terribly, and in an instant it poured a hot stream over Mitya's trembling fingers. He remembered that he had pulled out of his pocket a white new handkerchief, which he had prepared for going to Khokhlaikova's, and he applied it to the old man's head, futilely trying to wipe away the blood from his forehead and face. But the handkerchief quickly became soaked with blood. 'Lord, what's the point of this? – suddenly came to Mitya, – if I did kill him, how can I ever tell? – and what's the difference now? – he added suddenly in despair – I've killed him, so I've killed him... – I must confess, Smerdyakov said, with a pedantic calmness, that there's a secret I share with Fyodor Pavlovich. They, as you are well aware (if you are aware, that is), have been locking themselves in for days, sometimes even for the evening. Each time you would return to your rooms early, and yesterday they didn't even go out, so perhaps you don't know that they've taken to locking themselves in for the night. Even if you were to summon Grigory Vasilyevich, they would probably only open up if they recognized your voice. But Grigory Vasilyevich doesn't come, and so I've been the only one tending to their rooms – they decided that from the very moment they started this business with Agrafena Alexandrovna, and I've been instructed, under their orders, to leave their quarters each night to a separate wing of the house and sleep there, so as not to sleep till midnight, but to keep watch, get up, patrol the yard, and wait for Agrafena Alexandrovna to arrive – they've been waiting for her for several days, as if they were possessed. They reason that she must be afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovich (they call him Mitya, for short), and that's why she'll come through the rear door to me later at night. You, they say, are to watch over her until midnight, and if she comes, then you're to rush to my door or window from the garden and tap softly two times: tap-tap, and then quickly three times: tuk-tuk-tuk. They've instructed me that when I hear that, I'll know that she's arrived, and I'll quietly open the door for you. We've established another signal in case of an emergency: first two quick taps: tuk-tuk, and then, after a brief pause, a louder knock. That way they'll understand that something unexpected has happened and that I should come to see them, and they'll open up for me, and I'll go in and report. All this is in case Agrafena Alexandrovna doesn't come herself, but sends a message; or in case Dmitri Fyodorich arrives nearby – they're afraid of him so much that even if Agrafena Alexandrovna has already come and locked herself in with her, and Dmitri Fyodorich turns up nearby, I'll have to inform them right away, tapping on the door three times, so that the first signal, five taps, means: "Agrafena Alexandrovna has arrived," and the second signal, three taps, means "they're in a hurry, that is, you're expected." They've explained and shown me these signs several times as an example. As it happens, in the whole universe, only I and they know these signs, so they unlock without a moment's hesitation, without a single shout – they're very afraid of shouting aloud – and open the door for me. And these very signs have now become known to Dmitri Fyodorich.

The crowd that saw them clapped their hands and laughed loudly, all saying, "What a fine monkey! What a fine monkey!" Their laughter and noise disturbed the Patriarch, who rushed out of his room, staff in hand, asking, "Who is making such a commotion here?" The crowd, upon hearing the Patriarch's voice, quickly composed themselves, tidied their clothes, and stepped forward. The Monkey King revealed himself, blending into the crowd and saying, "Honor to the venerable master, we are merely a group gathering here and will not disturb the outside world." The Patriarch was enraged and shouted, "You all cry out and make a racket, acting like none of you are cultivating your discipline! A cultivator must be disciplined in speech, maintain a dignified demeanor, and not stir up trouble with your tongues. How can you make such a ruckus here?" The crowd replied, "We dare not deceive the master, but the Monkey King just now performed a transformation and became a pine tree, and indeed it was a real pine tree. The disciples were all praising and applauding him, and that's why they were making so much noise and startling the venerable master. We beg for your pardon." The Patriarch said, "You all go away. You, Monkey King, come over here and tell me, what inspired you to transform into a pine tree? To show off your abilities to the people at this moment? If someone else has a similar ability, don't you demand it from them? But if they have it, they will definitely ask you. If you teach them, they will bring you harm, and if you don't, they will still cause you trouble: your life will be at risk." The Monkey King kowtowed, saying, "I beg for the master's pardon!" The Patriarch said, "I won't punish you, but just get out of here." The Monkey King heard this and his eyes welled up with tears as he said, "Master, where should I go?" The Patriarch said, "You came from somewhere, so go back there." The Monkey King suddenly had a moment of clarity and said, "I came from the East Victory Demon Country's Boastful Country, Flower Fruit Mountain Water Curtain Cave." The Patriarch said, "Quickly go back, and spare your life. If you stay here, you will be utterly eliminated." The Monkey King acknowledged his guilt, saying, "I respectfully report to the venerable master, I have been away from home for twenty years, and though I may cherish the memories of the past, I have yet to repay your benevolence, so I dare not go." The Patriarch said, "What benevolence and duty? You just don't cause any trouble and don't bring any trouble back to me and you're fine."

He called out: "Monkey King, come here! I ask you, what possessed you to turn yourself into a pine tree? Why show off in front of people? If someone else does something like that, you don't ask them to teach you. But when someone sees you do it, they'll certainly ask you. If you're afraid of trouble, you should teach them; if you don't teach them, they'll surely harm them, putting your own life at risk." Monkey King bowed and said: "I humbly ask for your forgiveness, Master." The Master of the Mountain replied: "I won't punish you, but I tell you to leave." Monkey King heard this and began to cry, his eyes welling up with tears: "Master, where am I supposed to go?" The Master of the Mountain said: "You came from somewhere, so you should go back to that place." Monkey King suddenly woke up to the realization: "I came from the East Sea God's domain, from the State of Bear Country on the Peach Blossom Tree Mountain, from the Cave of the Water Curtain." The Master of the Mountain said: "Quickly return. Give your life back. If you stay here, you won't be able to survive." Monkey King acknowledged his mistake and said: "I have been away from home for twenty years, and I long to see my old home, but I'm reluctant to leave without repaying my Master's kindness." The Master of the Mountain said: "What kindness? You just avoid causing trouble and staying out of my affairs, that's all."

There wasn't a bit of the Monkey King's magic, but all the branches were frost-weathered and enduring snow. When the crowd saw it, they applauded and laughed aloud. They all exclaimed: "Good monkey! Good monkey!" Unbeknownst to them, they had raised a commotion that roused the venerable Patriarch. The Patriarch rushed out with his staff and asked, "Who is making such a commotion here?" The crowd, hearing his voice, hastily composed themselves, straightened their clothes and stepped forward. The Monkey King then revealed his true form and mingled in with the crowd and said, "Honorable Patriarch, we are here to perform a gathering, and have no intention to disturb outsiders." The Patriarch scolded him, "You disciples are shouting and making a ruckus, totally unlike proper ascetics! People practicing the way should keep a dignified demeanor and not cause trouble with their words. How dare you cause such a ruckus here?" The crowd said, "We dare not hide it from the master. We just watched as Monkey King performed a transformation and did some antics. He actually turned into a pine tree, and the disciples all applauded and cheered for him, so we raised our voices in joy and startled the Patriarch, begging for pardon." The Patriarch said, "You go." He called out, "Monkey, come here! I ask you, what inspired you to make such a pine tree, and how good is it to show off in front of people? If you see others have the ability, you don't ask them for it? If others see you have it, they are sure to ask you for it. If you fear harm, you should pass it on; if you don't, you will invite harm upon yourself, and your own life will be forfeit." Monkey bowed and said, "I only beg for the master's pardon." The Patriarch said, "I won't punish you, but you'd better be off." Monkey heard these words and shed tears in his eyes and said, "Master taught me to go to where?" The Patriarch said, "You came from somewhere, so go back there." Monkey suddenly came to his senses and said, "I came from the East Ocean's Heaven-bestowing Island's Louts' Pride Mountain's Water Curtain Cave." The Patriarch said, "You hurry back; it's no place for you to be. You'd better not stay here." Monkey acknowledged his wrongdoing, "I have been away from home for twenty years, although I sometimes recall the old place and my relatives, I still have not repaid the master's kindness, so I dare not go back." The Patriarch said, "What kindness or justice is there? You only have to avoid getting into trouble and not bring it to my doorstep, and that's all."

K. was interrupted by a scream from the back of the hall, he shaded his eyes to see what was happening, as the dim daylight made the fog look milky and blinding.  It was the laundress, whom he had immediately recognized as a major disturbance upon his entrance. Whether she was guilty or not was impossible to tell. K. only saw that a man had pulled her into a corner by the door and was holding her there. But it wasn't she who was screaming, it was the man, who had his mouth wide open and was staring at the ceiling. A small circle had formed around the pair, and the gallery viewers nearby seemed delighted that the seriousness K. had brought to the gathering was being broken in this way. K. wanted to rush down under the first impression, and he thought that everyone would want to restore order and at least have the pair removed from the hall, but the rows of people in front of him remained frozen, no one moved, and no one let K. through. On the contrary, they blocked his way, old men held their arms in front, and some hand – he didn't have time to turn around – grabbed him by the back of the neck. K. wasn't thinking about the pair anymore; he felt as if his freedom was being restricted, as if they were serious about arresting him, and he jumped recklessly off the podium. Now he was face to face with the crush. Had he misjudged the people? Had he given his speech too much effect? Had they pretended to listen to him while he was speaking, and now that he was drawing conclusions, had they had enough of the pretence? What faces were all around him! Small, black eyes darted back and forth, the cheeks hung low like those of the drunk, the long beards were stiff and thin, and if you reached into them, it was as if you were grasping claws, not beards. But under the beards – and this was the real discovery K. made – insignia shone on the lapel pins in different sizes and colors. Everyone had these insignia, as far as one could see. Everyone belonged together, the apparent parties to the right and left, and as he suddenly turned around, he saw the same insignia on the lapel pin of the investigating judge, who sat with his hands in his lap and gazed calmly down. "So," K. cried out, throwing his arms up in the air, "you're all officials, as I see it, you're the corrupt clique I was talking about, you've packed yourselves in here as listeners and snoops, formed apparent parties, and one of them applauded to test me, you wanted to learn how to entrap the innocent! Now, you weren't completely useless here, I hope you've either talked among yourselves about how someone expects the defense of the innocent from you, or – let me or I'll strike –" he said to an elderly man who was pressed particularly close to him – "or but you've actually learned something. And with that, I wish you good luck in your trade." He quickly picked up his hat, which lay on the edge of the table, and pushed his way through the complete and utter silence, at least the silence of complete surprise, to the exit. The investigating judge, however, seemed to have been faster than K., for he awaited him at the door. "Just a moment," he said. K. stopped, but he didn't look at the investigating judge, he looked at the door, which he had already grasped. "I just wanted to draw your attention to," he said, "that you – it may not have become clear to you yet – have deprived yourself of the advantage that an interrogation always means for the arrested." K. laughed at the door. "You scoundrels," he exclaimed, "I'll give you all the interrogations you want," opened the door and rushed down the stairs. Behind him, the noise of the revived assembly arose, which likely began to discuss the events in the manner of students.
