As the great saint arrived at the entrance to the river, he transformed himself in an instant into the likeness of the venerable Elder Lao Gong, and by pressing down on his head, walked straight into the temple. The ghostly officers, unable to recognize him, bowed their heads in greeting one by one. He sat in the center and scanned the incense offerings: he saw Lee Hu's three offerings, Zhang Long's vows for blessings, Zhao Jia's written petitions, and Qian Bing's good wishes for good health. Just then, someone reported, "Another elder has arrived." The ghostly officers looked at each other in surprise. True Lord said, "Is there a Big Saint here?" The ghostly officers replied, "We've never seen a Big Saint; there's only an elder checking things in there." The True Lord then rushed into the hall, and when the Great Saint saw him, he suddenly revealed his true appearance, saying, "Don't make a fuss; the temple's master is now surname Sun." True Lord immediately brandished his triple-edged sword with divine sharpness and struck him in the face. The Monkey King dodged with a clever technique, allowing the sword to pass, and then drew out the embroidered needle, making a 'flop-flop' sound as it turned thick and coarse. He chased up to the front to face True Lord, and the two shouted and tussled. They burst out of the temple gate, half-hidden in mist and clouds, continuing to fight as they went, and eventually fought all the way to Flower Fruit Mountain. This alarmed the four heavenly kings and the multitudes, who all watched out even more closely. The Officials Kong and Zhang met True Lord, joining their efforts and striving together to surround the beautiful Monkey King.

But it so happened that the Great Sage had arrived at the entrance to the river, and with a wave of his hand, he transformed himself into the likeness of Erlang the Grandfather, and, tapping the clouds, he entered the temple. The ghost officials, unable to recognize him, each bowed their heads in greeting one by one. He sat in the middle, inspecting the incense: he saw the three sacrificial animals presented by Li Hu, the offerings made by Zhang Long in exchange for blessings, the documents sought by Zhao Jia on behalf of his son, and the good wishes expressed by Qian Bing for his illness. Just as he was looking on, someone reported, "Another grandfather has arrived." The ghost officials looked on in amazement, their hearts racing. The True Lord said, "What of this Quan Tian Great Sage, has he arrived here?" The ghost officials replied, "We have not seen any Great Sage, but there is a grandfather inside examining things." The True Lord rushed into the temple. The Monkey King saw him, and, reverting to his true form, said, "No need to shout, the temple belongs to the Sun family now." The True Lord, meanwhile, grasped his three-edged divine blade and struck a blow at the Monkey King's face. The Monkey King executed a move, dodging the blade, and pulled out a embroidered needle, fluttering it about, swinging back and forth, with a thickness that matched the blade, and approached him, parrying the blow. The two of them shouted and struggled, fighting out the temple gates, and amidst a haze and mist, they continued to fight, making their way to the Flower Fruit Mountain, where the four Heavenly Kings and the others were watching with even greater vigilance. The Lord, and the Marshals Kong and Zhang, rushed towards the True Lord, uniting their efforts to try and surround the beautiful Monkey King.

Just then the Great Sage arrived at the Ganjiang River Mouth, transforming himself instantly into the likeness of Erlang's grandfather, descending from the clouds straight into the temple. The demonic officers did not recognize him, each and every one of them lowering their heads in greeting. He sat in the middle, inspecting the incense: he saw the three sacrificial animals offered by Li Hu, the felicitous vow made by Zhang Long, the written petition of Zhao Jia, and the good wishes of Qian Bingshi who had reported illness. Just as he was taking a look, someone reported: "Another Grandfather has come." The demonic officers all looked over in a panic. The True King said: "Has there been a Great Sage who has come here?" The demonic officers said: "We have not seen any Great Sage, only a Grandfather inside checking things." The True King charged in, the Great Sage seeing him, revealing his true self: "The Grandfather should not have made such a commotion, the temple already belongs to the Sun family." This True King at once drew out the three sharp edges of his divine sword, slicing him right across the face. The Monkey King employed a martial art, dodging the divine sword's edge, drawing out the embroidered needle, and with a "Whoosh, whoosh," struck through it fine and coarse, charging forward to face him. The two of them shouted and fought, and out of the temple door, amidst haze and cloud, and still fighting, they clashed over to Flower Fruit Mountain, frightening the four heavenly kings and their entourage, and their vigilance grew even tighter. As they went, Kang, Zhang, the two Imperial Censors, came forward to meet the True King, and with combined effort, they set out to encircle the Great Monkey King.

It was said that the Great Sage soon arrived at the mouth of the Dongting Lake, where he suddenly transformed into the guise of the Heavenly Lord Erlang, descended from the clouds, and entered the temple directly. The ghostly judges could not recognize him, and one by one, they bowed down to welcome him. He sat in the middle, examining the incense: he saw the three animals offered by Li Hu, the blessings wished for by Zhang Long, the documents requested by Zhao Jia, and the good wishes for recovery made by Qian Bing. Just as he was examining, someone reported, "Another grandfather has arrived." The ghostly judges all looked at each other in shock. The Holy King, however, said, "Is there a Great Sage just coming here?" The ghostly judges replied, "We have not seen any Great Sage, but there is a grandfather inside checking things." The Holy King rushed into the room, and the Great Sage saw him and immediately revealed his true form, saying, "Don't make a fuss, the temple is now in the Sun family." The Holy King unsheathed his three-pronged spear with its sharp edges, and immediately hacked at the Great Sage's face. The Monkey King employed a technique and dodged the spear's blade, pulled out a flower-patterned needle, and waved it up and down. The needle was swift and sure, and rushed forward to counterattack. The two of them shouted and struggled, and as they fought, they came out of the temple, amidst fog and clouds, and continued to battle as they went, and arrived at Flower Fruit Mountain, causing the four Heavenly Kings and the crowd to become increasingly wary. Then Kang and Zhang the military marshals rushed to welcome the Holy King, joining forces to attack the Monkey King and encircle him.

It was said that the Great Sage had already arrived at the entrance of the river and transformed himself into the appearance of Erlang, and pressed down his head into the clouds and entered the temple directly. The ghostly judges were unable to recognize him and one after another knelt down to greet him. He sat in the middle, checked the incense: he saw the three victims offered by Li Hu, the scriptures left by Zhang Long for good fortune, the documents sought by Zhao Jia on behalf of his son, and the good wishes submitted by Qian Bing on account of his illness. Just as he was looking, someone reported: "Another old master has arrived." All the ghostly judges watched in alarm, none without a start. The True Lord asked: "Is there some heavenly Grand Sage come?" The ghostly judges replied: "We have not seen any Grand Sage; there is only an old master inside checking things." The True Lord barged in, and the Great Sage saw him and revealed his true self: "The young lord need not shout; the temple already belongs to the Sun family." The True Lord instantly raised the three sharp blades of his divine knives and struck his face. The Monkey King employed a move, dodged the divine knife, drew out the embroidery needle, flicked it, and suddenly became as thick as a bowl, arriving at the front and facing the other party. The two clashed and struggled, and they fought their way out of the temple gates, half-fog, half-cloud, advancing and retreating as they fought, and then clashed to Flower Fruit Mountain, causing the four Great Heavenly Kings and others to be all the more vigilant. The Kang and Zhang Marquises rushed towards the True Lord, united in their efforts, and surrounded the beautiful Monkey King.

He was still free. "Allow," he said, and quickly walked between the guards into his room. "He seems reasonable," he heard someone say behind him. In his room, he immediately opened the drawers of the desk, everything was in order, but in the excitement he couldn't find the identification papers he was looking for right away. Finally, he found his bicycle license and was about to take it to the guards when he seemed to deem the paper too insignificant and kept searching until he found his birth certificate. As he returned to the adjacent room, the door opposite him just opened and Mrs. Grubach was about to enter. One could only see her for a moment because as soon as she recognized K., she seemed to feel embarrassed and apologized before she vanished and very carefully closed the door. "Come in," K. had just been able to say. Now he stood in the middle of the room with his papers, looked at the door, which did not open again, and was only roused by a call from the guards who sat at the small table by the open window and were, as K. now recognized, eating his breakfast. "Why didn't she enter?" he asked. "She's not allowed to," said the big guard. "You're arrested." "How can I be arrested, and in this manner?" "Well, let's start all over again," said the guard, dipping a buttered bread into the honey pot. "We won't answer such questions." "You will have to answer them," said K. "Here are my identification papers, show me yours now and especially the arrest warrant." "Good heavens!" said the guard. "That you can't accept your situation and that it seems to you to have tried to provoke us, who are probably the closest people to you among all your fellow men, in vain!" "It's so, believe it," said Franz, holding the coffee cup he was holding not to his mouth but looking at K. with a long, probably meaningful but incomprehensible glance. K. let himself be drawn into a dialogue of glances with Franz, but then slapped his papers and said, "Here are my identification papers." "What business do we have with them?" cried the big guard now. "You're acting like a child. What do you want? Do you want to bring your great, cursed trial to a quick end by discussing identification papers and arrest warrants with us? We are lowly employees who hardly know our way around an identification paper and who have nothing to do with your case other than to stand watch here for ten hours a day and get paid for it. That's all we are, and yet we are capable of realizing that the high authorities we serve must inform themselves very precisely about the reasons for the arrest and the arrested person before they issue an arrest warrant. Believe it or not, I'm convinced he managed to get his hands on Aglaya! And if he didn't, he'll take them. Rogozhin has gotten in touch with him too. How the prince doesn't notice this is beyond me! And how he'd love to catch me off guard now! He considers me a personal enemy, I've long figured that out, and why on earth should he care, when he's going to die anyway? — I'll just feed his illusions; you'll see, it's not he who's got the upper hand, it's I.

—Ippolit, you ask? I know him myself. You can't even imagine the cunning of the man; what a gossip, what a nose he has for sniffing out all the scandal, all the dirt. Whether you believe it or not, I'm convinced that he's already got hold of Aglaya. If he hasn't, he'll get her. Rogozhin's gotten mixed up with him, too. How does the prince not notice? And how he's itching to get the better of me now! He takes me for a personal enemy, I've long since realized that, and I still can't fathom what's gotten into him. But I'll play along; you'll see, it's not he who'll catch me, but I who'll catch him.

— Hippolyte, did you find out?  You can't even imagine to what extent he's a sly creature; what a gossiper he is, what a nose he has to sniff out all the scandalous things, all that's bad. Whether you believe it or not, I'm convinced that he's already got his hands on Aglaya! If not, he will. Rostanev's gotten in touch with him too. How the prince doesn't notice it! And how he's dying to corner me now! He takes me for his personal enemy, I've known it for a long time, and what's he doing here, anyway, he'll die – I don't understand it at all! But I'm leading him on; you'll see, it's not him who's going to corner me, it's me who'll corner him.

Thousands of imperial officers stood in order, their halberds arrayed before and behind, their long banners aligned to the sides. Golden halberds and war axes stood in pairs, and bright silk candles and incense burners stood in pairs. The dragon and phoenix danced in the air, and the sacrificial lambs were prepared. The sage and mighty emperor sat above, his great ministers loyal and just below. Our dynasty shall last for a thousand years like Shun and Yu, and our era of peace shall surpass that of Yao and Tang.

Then, behold the imperial umbrella with its dragon-shaped handle, the golden brocade robe, and the dazzling radiance it emitted. The jade pendant and the feather fan with its plumage of auspicious birds fluttered and danced in the air. The imperial crown, the jade belt, and the gold seal shone brightly. A thousand troops guarded the emperor's carriage, and the attendants formed two rows on either side.

This emperor bathed in piety and reverence, devoutly worshiping the Buddha, surrendering to the teachings of merit and rejoicing in the scent of incense. The Tang king's imperial carriage arrived early at the temple, and he ordered the music and instruments to be stopped, dismounted from his carriage, and led by many officials to pay respects to the Buddha and take incense. After three circuits, he raised his head to look, and indeed, the temple was a grand assembly hall, and behold: the flagpoles fluttered and danced in the air, and the parasols shone with radiance.

The flagpoles fluttered and danced in the air, casting a kaleidoscope of colors, and the parasols shone with radiance, reflecting the sun's fiery rays. The Buddha's golden image appeared serene, and the bodhisattvas' jade faces shone with grandeur. Vases held lotus flowers, and the incense burners released the fragrance of sandalwood. The vases held lotus flowers, casting a blaze of colors over the sacred mountain, and the incense burners released the fragrance of sandalwood, wafting a mist of pure fragrance to the heavens. Fresh fruits were arranged in a jade plate, and a colorful pastry was piled on the table. High-ranking monks recited the true scriptures, wishing to free a lone soul from suffering. The emperor of great virtues, both military and civil, together took incense, paid respects to the Buddha's golden body, and paid homage to the bodhisattvas.

Then, behold that renowned monk, Tripitaka, with his staff, led a procession of monks to pay homage to the Tang king. After the ceremony, the monks took their seats in order, and the monk presented a scroll with an edict to the emperor. The scroll read: "The virtue of benevolence is far-reaching and profound, and the teaching of the Chan school is extinct. The clarity of the mind is like a radiant spirit, circulating through the three worlds. The endless transformations and changes are brought under one unified principle. The true essence is ever-present and without bounds. Upon beholding this lone soul, we must feel compassion and pity. I hereby order: select monks to participate in Chan lectures and propagate the teachings. Open the gates of convenience, and let the boat of compassion sail widely, to rescue a multitude of living beings from the sea of suffering and to liberate them from the cycle of birth and death. Lead them back to the path of truth, and let them revel in the depths of the spiritual realm. Let them abandon all action and stillness, and merge into pure essence. By relying on this righteous cause, invite the blessings of the capital city and the gate of the crimson palace. Take advantage of this auspicious moment to escape the hells and the realms of the mundane world. May you ascend to the heavens of bliss and wander freely in the West. The poem says: One pot of eternal incense burns, and a few scrolls of liberation scripts. The wondrous teachings have no bounds, and the blessings of the heavens are poured upon us. The karma of revenge is exhausted, and the lone souls are all freed from prison. May our country enjoy eternal peace and prosperity."

The emperor, filled with joy, read the edict, and then addressed the monks: "You monks have firmly upheld the true meaning, and do not tire of the task of the Buddha. Wait until your work is completed and accomplished, and each of you shall have a place to return to. I shall reward you heavily, and I shall not let your efforts be in vain." Then the thousand two hundred monks bowed their heads in unison, expressing their gratitude.

Thousand officials in ceremonial attire march in procession, in front and behind, five imperial guards with their banners held to the left and right, double and pair by pair. They bear golden halberds and wields axes, while red silken lanterns and ritual incense swirl with pomp and ceremony. Dragons soar, phoenixes dance, phoenix banners and imperial pennants flutter in the air. The divine and wise Emperor rides in majesty, accompanied by loyal and righteous ministers.

Forth from the royal carriage comes a canopy, a dragon robe, and a radiance that shines like lightning. A jade-linked pendant and a colored phoenix fan flutter in the breeze. The imperial crown, the jade sash, and the golden seal adorn his majesty's person. Thousands of guard troops escort the imperial carriage, with bearers walking alongside.

The Emperor, devout and reverent, immerses himself in worship, embracing the true virtues of compassion and joy as he sniffs the incense. The Grand Duke arrives early in his imperial carriage, ordering the music and instruments to be silenced and alighting from the chariot. He leads a multitude of officials, and they pay homage to the Buddha, snatching incense from the burner.

After three circuits, he lifts his head to look around and is pleased to see a thriving place of enlightenment. He gazes and sees: pennants and banners dancing and fluttering in the air, while jewel-adorned parasols shine like beacons. The pennants and banners dance and flutter, casting a colorful rainbow across the void; the parasols shine, illuminating the red lightning of the sun. The Buddha's golden form shines resplendent, the arhats' jade-like countenance magnificent and awe-inspiring. On the tables are rare fruit arranged in jade plates, and sugar pastries piled on colorful platters.

High-ranking monks line up to recite the sutras, praying to free a lonely spirit from suffering. The Emperors of Text and Warfare each grasp incense sticks, pay homage to the Buddha's golden body, and pay respects to the arhats. They see that the Great Master Xuanzang leads the crowd of monks in paying respects to the Grand Duke. Having finished their formalities, the monks take their seats in order, the master presents a scroll of the sacred texts to the Emperor to read, and the scroll reads:

"The virtue of the Emperor is profound and far-reaching, the Chan school is extinct. The mind is clear and the spirit is free; the three realms are harmonized. The thousand changes and the myriad forms are unified, the harmony of yin and yang is complete. The essence is eternal and constant, and has no end. In the face of the lonely spirits, we should feel compassion and pity. By the Emperor's sacred command, I select and gather the monks, to expound the teachings of Chan. I open the gates of ease and convenience, operate the boat of compassion, and guide the masses out of the sea of suffering. I bring them back to the true path, and lead them to delight in the original Mind. In this way, we attain non-action and become pure and simple. With this good cause, we seek the blessings of the capital city and the imperial throne; with our triumph, we escape the suffering of hell and the prison of the mundane world. We soon ascend to the heavens of bliss and become carefree. The poem says: 'The eternal fragrance of the incense burner is always fragrant; a few pages of the sacred texts exceed human life. The boundless teachings of the Buddha are declared, and the countless blessings of heaven are bestowed upon us. The karma is eradicated, and the spirits are released from prison.'

The Emperor reads the scroll with a happy heart and addresses the monks, saying, 'You uphold the true doctrine and should not be idle or remiss in your reverence for the Buddha. Wait until your work is accomplished and complete, and each of you shall have a place to return to; then I will reward you generously and not let your efforts go to waste.' The twelve hundred monks simultaneously bowed their heads and expressed their gratitude.

The imperial processions, numbering in the thousands, approached from the front and rear, their pennants fluttering like a symphony of color and sound. The eunuchs, with golden goblets in hand and axes in possession, stood in pairs; the imperial maidservants, bearing crimson silk lanterns and incense, radiated a serene ambiance. Dragons and phoenixes danced, their mythical forms majestically unfolding; a myriad of eunuchs and courtiers stood in line, their arrayed silk ribbons fluttering in the wind. The emperor, enthroned in imperial grandeur, shone like a brilliant star; the grand ministers, stately and virtuous, stood by his side, evoking the bliss of a golden age spanning a thousand years, eclipsing the era of Yao and Shun.

He beheld the purple parasol, the dragon embroidered robe, and the halo of glory; the jade cord, the imperial fan, and the auspicious pennant floating in the air; the imperial crown, the jade sash, and the golden seal, symbolizing the divine majesty. The imperial guards, with a thousand men, marched in formation, escorting the emperor's carriage, two lines of eunuchs accompanying the imperial carriage. The emperor, devout and reverent, took a bath in the offerings to the Buddha, renouncing his worldly attachments and seeking refuge in the divine.

When the Tang emperor's imperial carriage arrived early at the temple, he commanded the musicians to start playing their instruments and alighted from the imperial carriage, accompanied by numerous officials. He offered incense to the Buddha. Having completed three rounds of circumambulation, he looked up and marveled at the serene atmosphere of the hall, where: vermilion pennants and banners fluttered and danced, and golden parasols radiated their light; vermilion pennants and banners fluttered and danced, with purple wisps of cloud aglow, as if encased in a celestial aura; golden parasols radiated their light, illuminating the red electric radiance of the morning sun. The Buddha's majestic countenance shone like a radiant jewel, the patriarchs' jade faces exuding an aura of awe-inspiring majesty. Lotus flowers were inserted into vases, while sandalwood incense burned in the censers; the lotus flowers in the vases emitted a radiant glow, as if illuminating the halls of the sacred precincts; the sandalwood incense filled the air, its fragrance permeating the heavens. Fresh fruits and sweets were arranged on a red platter, an assortment of colorful confections in a mosaic pattern. The venerable monks sat in rows, reciting the sutras with devotion, seeking to free the isolated spirits from their suffering.

The emperor and his empress, joined in prayer, together burning incense before the Buddha's golden body and paying homage to the patriarchs. He saw that the venerable Master Xuanzang, accompanied by a multitude of monks, invited the Tang emperor to prostrate himself in reverence. After the ceremony, the monks took their seats in formation, and the master presented to the emperor a scroll of blessings, which read: "The virtue of the enlightened is boundless, the pure truth is silent. The sacred spirits flow unobstructed through the three realms. A myriad transformations, endless and infinite, contain within them the harmony of yin and yang. The authentic essence is unchanging, without bounds. Behold the isolated spirits, deserving of compassion and pity. By the imperial edict of the great emperor: Gather together the wise monks, that they may expound the teachings and propagate the dharma. Open the gate of benefits and the gates of wisdom, spreading the sail of compassion and the anchor of benevolence, rescuing the multitude of suffering beings, freeing them from the six paths. Leading them back to the true path, allowing them to experience the bliss of the Western heaven. This poem says: One censer of fragrant incense will guarantee eternal life, a few volumes of sutras will bring salvation. The wondrous dharma has no bounds, nor does the divine grace showered upon us. The karma of suffering is forever eradicated, and all isolated spirits are released from their prison."

The emperor, with a heart full of joy, gazed at the monks and said, "You noble monks have devoted yourselves to the Buddha's teachings, never wavering in your commitment. When the task is completed and all is accomplished, each of you shall receive the reward that is due to you, and I shall show my appreciation and gratitude, with no regrets or disappointment." The one thousand two hundred monks then bowed their heads in unison, expressing their gratitude.

A thousand officials in ranked order, their badges of office arranged in order of precedence, the five regiments with their banners arrayed on either side. They carried golden gourds and axes, paired in perfect harmony; the crimson silk lanterns and fragrant incense rising in dignified procession. Dragons soared and phoenixes danced, eagles and falcons were swept along. The wise and sagely emperor, the faithful and righteous ministers, were standing in their places. I have seen the glory of emperors through the ages, from Shun and Yu on, and the prosperity of dynasties that rivalled the Sage-Kings Yao and Shun. And then I saw that resplendent parasol, the dragons wrapped in swirling clouds, and the radiance intermingling with each other; the jade necklace and the jade fan with its vibrant plumes; the imperial cap and the golden seal. A thousand troops escorted the carriage, with two rows of attendants following. This emperor paid his respects with sincere reverence and devotion to the Buddha, renouncing all attachments and delighting in the fragrance of incense. The Tang emperor arrived early at the temple, ordered the musicians to play the instruments, and then alighted from his chariot, leading many officials. He bowed before the Buddha, fumigated incense. After three circuits, he lifted his head to look around, and indeed, the place was a most excellent site for a Buddhist shrine: the parasols and banners fluttering about, the pagodas shining with brilliant lights. The parasols and banners fluttered about, with rainbow-coloured clouds rippling through the air; the pagodas shone brightly, reflecting the sunbeams that danced about. The Buddha's golden body, majestic and serene, stood out amidst the roshis' jade-like countenances, resplendent with great dignity. The porcelain vases held lotus flowers, the incense burner was ablaze with sandalwood smoke. The porcelain vases held lotus flowers, shining with an array of jewels; the incense burner was ablaze with sandalwood smoke, with clouds of fragrance wafting up to the heavens. New fruits were arranged in a red dish, and the colourfully decorated tables were piled high with sugar cookies. The high-ranking monks chanted the scriptures, seeking to liberate the solitary spirits from their suffering. Emperor Taizong, both as a military leader and a literati, went to the Buddha and participated in the ritual, then bowed before the golden body of the Buddha and consulted with the roshis. I have seen the Master Xuanzang, leading the crowd of monks, paying homage to the Tang emperor. After the ritual was complete, the monks took their positions, with Master Xuanzang presenting a decree to Emperor Taizong. The decree reads: "The virtue of benevolence is vast and deep, the Dharma gate is empty and vast. The truth is manifest and pure, and permeates the three realms. The ten thousand transformations and ten thousand changes are all encompassed by this one principle. Its essence and function are eternally true, and beyond all limits. Observing the solitary spirits, it is fitting to show them pity and compassion. By my imperial decree, I order the selection of the monks to lecture on the Dharma, and to open the doors of convenience and compassion, to sail the boats of loving-kindness, to rescue the crowds of beings lost in the ocean of suffering, and to free them from the hells and the realms of the unenlightened. May they return to the path of reality, and indulge in the bliss of the great liberation. When I rise to the highest position, I will reward them richly, and invite them to the pure imperial court, and free them from the cycles of birth and death. Come and go as you please in the Western Land of Bliss." The scriptures say: "A single wisp of incense can bring eternal life, a few volumes of scriptures can bring transcendence from birth and death. There is no limit to the wondrous Dharma, and no boundary to the blessings of the heavens. All karmic affinities will be eradicated, and all solitary spirits will be freed from prison." Emperor Taizong, having read the decree, was deeply delighted, and said to the monks, "You have upheld the true mind, and should not be remiss in your devotion to the Buddha. Wait until your efforts are completed and your accomplishments are realized, then you will each return to your rightful place, and I will reward you richly, and not see your toil go in vain." All one thousand two hundred monks, in unison, bowed their heads in gratitude.

Thousand officials arranged their official seals in front and behind, and the Five Guards arrayed their flags on the sides. They bore the golden gourd, the halberd, and axe, in pairs; they carried the crimson silk lanterns, the imperial censer, and fragrant smoke wafted and rose. Dragons flew and phoenixes danced, the officials raised and presented; the virtuous Emperor reigned, and the loyal officials were virtuous.

Interjecting the era of thousands of years beyond Shun and Yu, and the reign of tens of thousands of years surpassing Yao and Tang; seen that noble parasol and the roll of the dragon robe, radiance and splendor intermingled; jade pendant and colorful feather fan fluttered and danced; jasper crown and ruby sash, golden insignia, surrounded the Imperial carriage; the army of a thousand troops escorted, the bearers of the imperial litter marched on either side.

This Emperor bathed in sincere and reverent worship of the Buddha, renouncing attachments, and received blessings, and respectfully took incense. The Tang Emperor, in his grand carriage, arrived early at the temple in front; he ordered the music to begin and the ritual objects to be set up, and alighted from the carriage; the multitude of officials were led in. They paid homage and took incense. Having made three circumambulations, and raising his head to look, indeed it was a beautiful site; but seen: pennants and standards fluttered and danced, the precious umbrella flew with brilliance. Pennants and standards fluttered and danced, and colorful rainbow clouds shook in the empty space; the precious umbrella flew with brilliance, and reflected the sunbeams dancing in red lights. The sage Buddha's countenance was as golden as gold, and the faces of the Arhats were as jade-like, solemn and majestic. The vase held lotus flowers, the censer was burning sandalwood incense. The vase held lotus flowers, and the jade trees sparkled with brilliant jewels, covering the holy mountain; the censer burned sandalwood incense, and fragrance wafted upwards to the clear heavens.

The newly-brought offerings were piled into the vermilion plate; the weird sugar pastry piled high on the colorful table. The venerable monks stood in line to chant the true scriptures, and wished to rescue the lone souls from suffering. Emperor Taizong and his virtuous officials each respectfully took incense, and paid homage to the Buddha's golden body, and kowtowed to the Arhats. Seen was the great translator Xuanzang, who introduced the multitude of monks to pay respects to the Tang Emperor. After the rites were concluded, the monks took their seats in formation, and the Master presented the text for saving the solitary souls to Emperor Taizong to peruse, and the text read: "The Virtue of Benevolence is vast and profound; the Chan school is extinct, and the Pure Land is empty. The spirit realm is tranquil and clear, and the three worlds flow through. In a myriad transformations, one controls yin and yang. The true and constant, has no bounds. Looking at those solitary souls, it is deeply fitting to pity them. This is in compliance with the imperial edict of Emperor Taizong: to select the good monks, lecture the teachings of Chan, open the gate of Expediency, and extensively promote the Dharma-boat of compassion, save all living beings from suffering, liberate them from the sufferings of the six realms. Lead them to the path of truth, and let them enjoy the bliss of the Western Heavens; in movement and stillness, there is no dharma; the dharma is primordial, and its essence is pure. With this excellent cause, I invite blessings from the capital city of the Empyrean; I take advantage of my winning, and escape from the hells of the worldly realm. Early I shall ascend to the blissful realm and roam freely, and move about the Western Heavens as I please." A poem says: "One furnace of eternal incense, countless rebirths transcended; no bounds of the wonderful dharma proclaimed, the vast and mysterious heaven's grace showered upon. The accumulated offenses are completely eradicated, and the lone souls are all freed. I pray that I may preserve my country, and grant peace and blessings for ten thousand years."

Emperor Taizong, having read it, was full of joy, and said to the multitude of monks: "You, in solemn assembly, have upheld the Buddhist dharma with sincerity, and must not be lax. Wait until the task is completed and perfected, and each of you shall have a destination for your merits; I shall reward you, and not be a wasteful labor."

The one thousand two hundred monks, simultaneously bowed their heads, expressing their thanks.

"So, let her be your mistress," said Leni, "but you wouldn't really miss her if you were to lose her or exchange her for someone else, for example, me." "Of course," said K, smiling, "that's conceivable, but she has an advantage over you - she knows nothing about my lawsuit, and even if she did know, she wouldn't think of it. She wouldn't try to persuade me to yield." "That's no advantage," said Leni. "If she had no other advantages, I wouldn't lose my courage. Does she have any physical flaws?" "A physical flaw?" asked K. "Yes," said Leni, "I have a tiny one, you see." She stretched out her middle and ring finger, between which the web of flesh reached almost up to the top joint of her little fingers. K didn't immediately notice what she wanted to show him in the darkness, so she guided his hand to let him feel it. "What a natural wonder," he said, and added as he looked at the whole hand, "What a lovely nail!" With a kind of pride, Leni watched as K, astonished, repeatedly spread her fingers apart and closed them again, until he finally lightly kissed them and let go. "Oh!" she cried, however, "You've kissed me!" She quickly climbed up to his lap with her knees, her mouth open. K looked at her almost in alarm, now that she was so close, a bitter, enticing odor like pepper wafted from her, and she took his head in her arms, leaned over him, and bit and kissed his neck, bit into his hair. "You've traded me in!" she exclaimed from time to time, "see, now you've traded me in!" Her knee slipped out, and with a small scream, she almost fell onto the carpet; K caught her to hold her, and was pulled down to her. "Now you belong to me," she said.

Already on the first day, the father laid out the entire state of the family's finances and prospects, both the mother's and the sister's. He would stand up from the table every now and then to fetch some receipt or other from his small savings box, which he had saved from the collapse of his business five years earlier. One could hear how he struggled with the complicated lock and relocked it after taking out the document. These explanations by the father were among the first pleasant things that Gregor had heard since his confinement. There he is, our Pavel Ivanovich! Allow me to grasp you, Pavel Ivanovich! Come here, let me kiss him more ardently, my dear Pavel Ivanovich!" Chichikov felt himself enveloped in several sets of arms. Hardly had he managed to extricate himself from the official's arms when he found himself in the arms of the police master; the police master handed him over to the sanitary inspector; the sanitary inspector to the tax collector; the tax collector to the architect; and so on and so forth. The governor, who at that time was standing near the ladies and held a fancy ticket in one hand and a little dog in the other, upon seeing him, flung the ticket and the dog down, and let out a shriek of the little dog; in short, he diffused an extraordinary joy and merriment. There was not a face on which there was no sign of pleasure or, at least, a reflection of general pleasure. This is how it is on the faces of officials during the inspection by the newly arrived chief of their subordinated places: after the initial fear had passed, they saw that many things pleased him, and he even decided to make a joke, that is, to utter a few words with a pleasant smile. They laughed twice as much in response to this at the officials surrounding him, the ones who, however, had only partially caught the words he spoke, and, finally, some distant police officer, who had never laughed in his whole life and had only just shown the crowd his fist, and who, according to the unchanging laws of reflection, displayed on his face some kind of smile, although this smile looked like someone was about to sneeze after a strong cigar. Our hero responded to all and everyone and felt an extraordinary ease: he bowed to the right and to the left, as was his custom, a bit to the side, but completely freely, and captivated everyone. The ladies immediately formed a dazzling garland around him and brought with them a whole cloud of various scents: one was exhaling roses, another was exhaling spring and violets, and a third was completely permeated with musk. Chichikov raised his nose up and sniffed. In their outfits, there was a marvelous mismatch: muslins, silks, and poplins were such pale fashionable colors that one could hardly name them (to such an extent had the taste gone); there were braided ribbons and flower bouquets fluttering around the dresses in the most picturesque disorder, although a respectable head had been working on this disorder. A light hat was perched only on the ears, and it seemed to say, "Oh, I'll take off, only it's a shame I won't take the beauty with me!" Waists were tightly tied and had the strongest and most pleasing forms (it should be noted that all the ladies of city N were somewhat plump, but they were so skillfully belted in and had such a pleasant demeanor that their plumpness was not noticeable at all). Everything was thought out and provided with extraordinary consideration; necks, shoulders were revealed to just the right extent, no more and no less; each one had exposed their possessions up to the point they felt they could do so in good conscience, and the rest was carefully hidden with exquisite taste: either a lightweight bow tie made of ribbon, or a scarf as light as a well-known pastry called a kiss, ethereally hugged the neck, or small, toothed pleats made of fine batiste were let out from under the dress, known as "modesties." These "modesties" concealed in front and behind what could no longer harm a person, but at the same time, they caused suspicion that that very thing was the thing most capable of causing harm. Long gloves were worn only up to the sleeves, but intentionally left the stimulative parts of the hands above the elbow exposed, which were exuding a tempting plumpness; some even had cracked gloves, induced to move further, and so it seemed as if it were written everywhere: no, this is not a province, this is the capital, this is Paris itself! But then suddenly a hairstyle or even a slightly ostrich feather would poke out in opposition to all fashions, to their own taste. But it's impossible without this, this is the nature of the governor's city: it must somewhere burst out. Chichikov, standing before them, thought, "Which, then, is the author of this letter?" and poked his nose out, but it was pulled back by a whole row of elbows, sleeves, cuffs, ends of ribbons, and fragrant chemisettes and dresses. He galloped headlong into the void: the postmaster's wife, the captain of inspectors, the lady with the blue feather, the lady with the white feather, the Georgian prince Chikhpilidze, the official from St. Petersburg, the official from Moscow, the Frenchman Kukulka, Perkhunovskiy, Berendovskiy – all rose and swept away.

It required unimaginable caution to live with this blood. The Duke was contained within himself, and at times he cowered and grew dark when it swirled around him. It could be gruesomely alien to him, this nimble, half-Portuguese blood that he hardly knew. Often, it terrified him that it might seize hold of him in his sleep and tear him apart. He made an effort to master it, but he stood always in its fear. He never dared to love a woman, lest it become jealous, and so pining was it that wine never crossed his lips; instead, he soothed it with rosewater. Yet, once he drank, in the camp near Lausanne, after Granson was lost; then he was ill and withdrawn and drank much pure wine. But at that time his blood was asleep. In his senseless final years, it would sometimes fall into this heavy, animal sleep. Then it showed how completely he was its slave; for when it slept, he was nothing. Then no one from his surroundings was allowed to enter; he didn't understand what they were saying. He couldn't show himself to the foreign envoys, as desolate as he was. Then he sat and waited for it to wake.

But little comfort could Dounia and her husband derive from these tidings, especially at first. Sonya ceaselessly reported that he remained constantly glum, uncommunicative, and even almost entirely uninterested in the news she brought him from her letters; that he sometimes asked about his mother; and when she, seeing he already intuited the truth, finally told him of her death, he was surprised by how little effect the news of his mother's death had on him, at least outwardly. She reported, among other things, that, despite his appearance of being deeply absorbed in himself and isolated from all around him, he reacted to his new life in a very straightforward and simple way; that he clearly understood his situation, did not expect anything better nearby, and had no naive hopes (which is common in his position) and was hardly surprised by anything in the new surroundings, which bore so little resemblance to anything in the past. She said his health was satisfactory. He went to work, from which he did not shirk and to which he did not ask to be excused. He was almost indifferent to food, but since the food was so bad on all days except Sundays and holidays, he finally agreed to accept a few rubles from Sonya to buy himself a daily tea. As for everything else, he asked her not to worry, assuring her that all these troubles on his behalf were a nuisance to him.

Sonya also reported that he was housed in the same block as all the others in the bastille, and she had not seen the interior of their barracks, but she concluded that it was cramped, dirty, and unhealthy; that he slept on a pallet, covered with a sheepskin, and that he wanted nothing else for himself. But that he lived so crudely and poorly not by any preconceived plan or intention, but simply out of carelessness and external indifference to his fate. Sonya wrote bluntly that, especially at first, he was not only not interested in her visits, but almost resented them, was uncommunicative and even coarse with her, but that by the end these meetings had become a habit and almost a necessity, so that he even suffered when she was sick for a few days and couldn't visit him.

She would visit him on holidays at the bastille gates or in the governor's lodge,[95] where he was summoned to her for a few minutes; on weekdays, she would go to him at work, in the workshops, on the brickworks, or in the warehouses by the Irtysh. Sonya reported to herself that she had managed to make some acquaintances and connections in town, and she occupied herself with needlework, and since there was almost no seamstress in town, she had become necessary in many homes; she did not mention that she had also obtained protection for Raskolnikov from the authorities, that his work was eased, and other things.

Finally, she received news (Dounia even noticed a special agitation and anxiety in her latest letters) that he was repelled by everyone, that the convicts in the bastille did not like him; that he would spend whole days in silence and became very pale. In her last letter, Sonya wrote that he had fallen seriously ill and lay in the prison hospital, in the convict ward…

But little comfort could Dunya and her husband derive from this news, especially in the beginning. Sonya went on to report that he was constantly gloomy, uncommunicative, and hardly at all interested in the news she brought him from her letters, which she read to him every time; that he sometimes asked about his mother; and when she, seeing that he had already guessed the truth, finally told him of her death, he was, to her surprise, hardly affected by the news at all, at least that's how it seemed from the outside. She told Sonya that, despite his apparent deep immersion in himself and his complete withdrawal from the world, he reacted to his new life very straightforwardly and simply, that he clearly understood his position, did not expect anything better nearby, did not harbor any idle hopes (which was characteristic of his situation), and was hardly surprised by anything in his new surroundings, which bore little resemblance to anything else. She reported that his health was satisfactory. He went to work and did not shirk it or seek to be excused from it. He was almost indifferent to food, but that the food, apart from Sunday and holiday days, was so bad that, finally, he eagerly accepted some money from Sonya to get himself a daily cup of tea; as for the rest, he asked her not to worry, assuring her that all these concerns about him only troubled him. Further, Sonya reported that his accommodation in the prison was shared with everyone else, she had not seen the inner workings of their barracks but concluded that it was cramped, disgusting, and unhealthy; that he slept on a plank bed, using a fur to cover himself, and wanted nothing more for himself. But he didn't live so poorly and miserably out of some preconceived plan or intention, but simply from a lack of attention and external indifference to his fate. Sonya wrote quite straightforwardly that he, especially at first, did not only show no interest in her visits but almost resented them, was uncommunicative and even rough with her, but that, eventually, these meetings became a habit and almost a necessity, so that he even missed her when she was absent for a few days due to illness and could not visit him. She saw him on holidays at the prison gates or in the guardhouse, where they summoned him to see her for a few minutes; on weekdays, she visited him at work, in the workshops, or on the brickworks, or in the storehouses by the Irtysh River. Sonya confided to herself that she had managed to gain some acquaintances and patronage in the city; that she took up sewing, and as there was almost no seamstress in the city, she became necessary in many households; she did not mention, however, that it was through her that Raskolnikov had gained patronage from the authorities, and that his work had become easier, and so on. But Dounia and her husband could hardly derive any comfort from these tidings, especially at first. This was the third time Ivan Fyodorovich was going to speak with Smerdyakov upon his return from Moscow. The first time after the catastrophe he saw him and spoke with him on the very first day of his arrival, and he visited him again two weeks later. But after that second meeting, he stopped seeing him altogether, so that it had been almost a month since he had last seen him and almost heard nothing about him. However, it was on the fifth day after the death of his father that Ivan Fyodorovich returned to Moscow, and he missed the funeral, which had taken place the day before his arrival. The reason for Ivan Fyodorovich's delay was that Alyosha, not knowing exactly where he lived in Moscow, had resorted to Katerina Ivanovna to send a telegram, but she too was in the dark about his address, and so she telegraphed to her sister and aunt, counting on Ivan Fyodorovich visiting them as soon as he arrived in Moscow. However, it was on the fourth day after his arrival that he paid them a visit and, having read the telegram, immediately rushed off to us. He found Alyosha there, but after talking to him he was greatly surprised that Alyosha did not even suspect Mitya of the crime, and, on the contrary, pointed a direct finger at Smerdyakov as the murderer, which ran counter to the views of everyone else in our town. After seeing the police inspector and the prosecutor and learning the details of the indictment and the arrest, he was even more astonished by Alyosha and attributed his opinion to the brotherly love and compassion he felt for Mitya, which Ivan knew Alyosha felt deeply. By the way, a few words to dispel the notion forever: Ivan had not loved his brother Dmitry Fyodorovich and had often felt a sort of pity for him, but mixed with a great contempt, which often turned to outright disgust. Mitya was extremely unlikable to him, even in his very appearance. Ivan regarded Katerina Ivanovna's love for him with indignation. He did see Mitya, however, on the very first day of his arrival, and that meeting did not weaken his conviction of Mitya's guilt, but rather strengthened it. He found him in a state of distress, a state of painful agitation. Mitya was loquacious, but rambling and incoherent, spoke very sharply, accused Smerdyakov and got himself utterly entangled. What he said most of all was about the three thousand rubles which the deceased "stole" from him. "Those were my money, they were mine," he kept repeating, "even if I had taken them, I would be right." He almost did not dispute the evidence that stood against him and, when he did try to spin facts in his own favor, he did so in a disjointed and ridiculous manner – in fact, as if he did not want to defend himself at all, on the contrary, he became indignant, haughtily dismissed the accusations, scoffed and raged. He simply laughed contemptuously at Grigory's testimony about the open door and swore that it was the devil who opened it. He offered no coherent explanation for this fact. He even managed to insult Ivan in this first meeting, sharply telling him that he was wrong to suspect and question him, as he was the one who said "everything is permitted." In general, Mitya was very unfriendly to Ivan on this occasion. And it was then that Ivan Fyodorovich went to see Smerdyakov.

It was as if there was nothing to do. I walked around the city and noted that it had changed. It was pleasant to step out of the hotel I had been staying at and see that it had now become a city for adults that took itself together, almost like a stranger. Everything seemed a little smaller, and I strolled along the Langelinie to the lighthouse and back. If I came to the area of the Amaliengade, it was possible that something might emerge from somewhere that had been acknowledged for years and was trying to exert its power once again. There were certain corner windows or archways or lanterns that knew a lot and threatened with it. I looked at them and made them feel that I was a guest at the 'Phönix' hotel and could leave at any moment. But my conscience wasn't at ease with this. A suspicion arose within me that none of these influences and connections had truly been overcome. They had been left behind one day, unfinished as they were. Childhood would have to be tended to, in a sense, if it wasn't to be lost forever. And while I grasped how I was losing them, I felt at the same time that I would never have anything else to call upon.

Just as the hubbub was subsiding, the True Lord arrived, inquiring, "Brothers, where did they vanish?" The gods replied, "We were right here, surrounding them, and then they vanished." Erlang widened his eyes, observing the Grand Sage transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree. He put away his staff, discarded his gods' feathers, took off his bow, and in one transformation changed into a sparrow hawk. He flapped his wings and took off to pounce. The Grand Sage saw him and instantly transformed into a large old cormorant, soaring into the heavens. Erlang saw him and in haste shook his plumage, transforming himself into a large sea crane, soaring into the clouds to snatch it. The Grand Sage pressed his body down and plunged into the ravine, transforming into a fish. Erlang rushed to the edge of the ravine but saw no sign of him. He thought to himself, "This imp must have gone into the water as well. He must have transformed into something like a fish or a shrimp. I'll just transform once more and catch him." Indeed, in a flash he transformed into a fish hawk and floated on the surface of the ripple. He waited for a moment, and the Grand Sage transformed into a fish, swimming smoothly along. He suddenly saw a bird flying above, resembling a blue kite, its feathers not a deep blue; resembling a grey heron, lacking a crest on its head; resembling a crane, but its legs not red: "Is this Erlang changing his form to await me?!" He hastily turned his head and flew away. Erlang watched, "A fish with a blossom-like appearance, its tail not red; a fish with flower-scales invisible; a black fish, no star on its head; a fish with a red carp-like body, no dewdrop on its cheek. Why did it see me and fly away so quickly? It must be that the monkey has changed." He gave chase, beak snapping. The Grand Sage popped out of the water, transformed into a water snake and swam near the shore, then slid into the grass. Erlang could not catch him, and then saw a water snake slither out of the water. Recognizing it was the Grand Sage, he quickly turned around and transformed into a red-brocade topped crane, with a long beak, similar to a sharp-pointed iron pincer, and flew directly to eat this water snake. The water snake jumped into the air, and then transformed into a flower pigeon, listlessly standing on the rushes in the reeds. Erlang saw that it had degraded itself, that the flower pigeon was the most base and most promiscuous of all birds, regardless of its relationship to peacocks, phoenixes, hawks, or crows – so he did not pursue it, but instead appeared in his true form and walked away, taking out his bow and drawing an arrow. With one shot, he struck it so it fell with a [loud] thud.

As they chattered, a True Ruler arrived, asking, "Brothers, where have you gone?" The gods replied, "We were just here, surrounding him, and then he vanished." Second Brother opened his eyes wide, looked and saw the Big Saint transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree, so he sheathed the law seal, tossed aside the celestial blade, and unslung his bow. With a shake of his body, he transformed into a sparrow hawk, flapped his wings, and flew to attack. The Big Saint saw him, startled, flapped one wing and took off, changing into an old goose and soaring into the sky. Second Brother saw him, shook his feather quills, and transformed into a great swan, swooping up into the clouds. The Big Saint pressed his body back down, plunged into the ravine, transformed into a fish, and submerged into the water. Second Brother arrived at the ravine, but saw no sign of him. He thought to himself, "This little monkey must have gone into the water; he must have transformed into something like a fish or a shellfish. I'll wait for a moment and transform myself into something to catch him." And so he transformed into a fish hawk, drifting on the ripples on the water's surface.

For a moment, the Big Saint transformed into a fish, swimming smoothly in the water, when he suddenly saw a flying bird, green as an oriole, but with no streak on its feathers; like a heron, but with no fillets on its head; like an old crane, but with legs that were not red; "Could it be that Second Brother has transformed himself to wait for me?" He hastily turned his head and took flight. Second Brother saw him, and said, "The fish with its fins spread wide, like a carp, its tail not red; like a scalloped fish, its scales not visible; like a black fish, its head with no star; like a weevil fish, its cheek without whiskers. Why does it see me and fly away? It must be that the Monkey King has transformed himself." He chased after him, and gave him a snap of his beak. The Big Saint then plunged out of the water, transformed into a water snake, swam near the shore, and slithered into the grass. Second Brother couldn't hit him, but he heard the splash in the water and saw a snake shoot out, recognized it as the Big Saint, hastily turned around and transformed into a gray crane with a crimson adornment on its head, with a long beak that was similar to a pair of sharp-toothed pincers, and flew straight to eat the water snake. The water snake jumped up, but then transformed into a flowering pheasant, listlessly standing on the water's edge. Second Brother saw that he had transformed into a lowly creature – a pheasant was the lowest, most despicable of all birds, not associating with either a roc, a phoenix, an eagle, or a crow – and so he didn't go after him, but instead transformed back to his original form, walked away, took out his bow and strung an arrow, and shot him dead with a shot that hit him with the power of a dragon.

Just then, the Patriarch arrived, asking, "Brothers, where did the fugitive disappear to?" The gods said, "We were all standing here surrounding him, and suddenly he was gone." Erlang's eyes widened in a circle as he looked around and saw the Great Sage transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree. He collected his spirit sword, sheathed his divine whiskers, removed his bow, shook his body, and transformed into a falcon, spreading his wings and flying off. The Great Sage saw him and raised a wing in flight, transforming into a big old swan, soaring into the heavens. Erlang saw him and quickly shook his feathers, transforming into a big sea crane, diving into the clouds to strike. The Great Sage again transformed, entering the ravine, changing into a fish. Erlang ran to the edge of the ravine and couldn't see any sign of him. He thought to himself, "This monkey must have dived into the water, and he must have transformed into a fish, shrimp, or something like that. I'll just wait a bit and transform again to catch him." After a while, the Great Sage transformed into a fish, swimming along the water, when suddenly he saw a bird flying above, which looked like a blue kite, but its feathers were not blue; it looked like a heron, but had no crest; it looked like an old owl, but its legs were not red: "I bet Erlang has transformed into a bird to wait for me!" The fish quickly turned its head and swam away in a splash. Erlang saw the splashing fish and said, "This fish looks like a carp, but its tail is not red; it looks like a mandarin fish, but it has no scales; it looks like a black fish, but it has no star on its head; it looks like a crucian carp, but it has no whisker; how did it see me and swim away so quickly? It must be that monkey transformed." Erlang chased after and struck the fish with a beak, but the fish swam out of the water, transforming into a snake and slithering into the grass. Erlang couldn't catch him, but then he saw the commotion in the water, and a snake was swimming out, which he recognized as the Great Sage, so he quickly transformed into a scarlet-painted crane with a long beak, similar to an iron tongs, and flew over to eat the snake. The snake jumped out and transformed into a painted stork, standing listlessly in a reed bed. Erlang saw that he had become lowly and base, and a painted stork was the most base and lustful creature among birds, not even associating with sacred birds like the phoenix or pheasant, so Erlang didn't bother to catch him and appeared in his original form, walking away. He picked up his bow, drew the string, and shot an arrow, hitting the snake and killing it.

And it's clear to me that they are the discarded, not just beggars; no, they are not beggars at all, one must make a distinction. They are refuse, shells of people, spewed out by fate. Sticky with the spit of fate, they cling to a wall, a lamppost, a poster column, or trickle slowly down an alley with a dark, dirty trail behind them. What in the world did that old woman want from me, who had crawled out of some hole with a dresser drawer containing a few buttons and needles? Why did she keep following me and watching me as if she was trying to recognize me with her runny eyes, which looked as if a sick person had spat green mucus into her bloody lids? And how did that grey, small woman come to stand in front of a shop window next to me for a quarter of an hour, showing me an old, long pencil slowly coming out of her bad, clenched hands? I pretended to look at the things laid out and paid no attention, but she knew I had seen her; she knew I was standing there thinking about what she was actually doing. For the fact is, in a society that values the right things, those who are neglected are not people at all.

Zhu Bajie cursed, "You devil! Come on up! What a grand spot to fight, with solid ground beneath my feet!" The monster retorted, "You tricked me into coming up, and now you're calling in reinforcements. Get down here and fight it out with me!" It turned out the monster was too cunning, unwilling to climb up any further, and only continued to quarrel with Zhu Bajie along the riverbank.

Because the Queen Mother holds the Peaches of Immortality, she has invited all guests to a grand banquet at the Jasper Pool. At that time, being drunk and half-asleep, he staggered about, crashing into the Jade Cavern, where he was greeted by a group of beautiful immortals. Seeing him's appearance took people's souls, his past mortal heart was hard to erase completely. He didn't distinguish between high and low, and grabbed Chang'e, wanting her to rest together. Despite being begged to leave several times, he didn't comply and dodged left and right with an unhappy heart. His boldness was like thunder, nearly knocking down the heavenly gate. The celestial officer who supervised the matter reported to the Jade Emperor, "On that day, I'll have to be responsible for his fate." The Jade Cavern was sealed off with no wind passing through, and he had no escape route. It was only that the gods caught him, and there was still the wine in his heart, which didn't frighten him. He was led to the Spirit Realm to meet the Jade Emperor, who asked in accordance with the law: "He shall be sentenced to execution." Fortunately, Tai Bai, Li Jin Xing, stepped forward and kowtowed to speak up on his behalf. His punishment was commuted to being struck with 2,000 hammers, his flesh torn, skin split, and bones almost broken. He was pardoned and exiled to the World below, and settled at the foot of the Fuxing Mountain. I committed a crime and was reincarnated, and people now call me Pig-headed Jiangzuo.

When the Wayfarer heard this, he said, "You're actually the Heavenly Pond Water God who descended to the mortal realm; I've been wondering why I know your name." The fiend spoke up, "Ah! You're that crooked old Taoist, in the past you caused trouble and brought calamity upon us, and now you come here and deceive others again! Don't be impolite, let me take revenge on you!" The Wayfarer wouldn't yield, raised his rod and hit him on the head. They fought in the darkness of the mountain midway, their two figures swirling about. The Wayfarer's golden eyes flashed like lightning, the fiend's ringed eyes glimmered like silver flowers. One emitted a misty cloud, the other breathed a crimson glow. The crimson glow dazzled people, the misty cloud radiated brilliant light. Gold collar rod, nine-clawed halberd – the two heroes are indeed deserving of praise: one is the Saint descending to the mortal realm, one is the General descending to the far corners of the heavens. That one was turned into a monster because of his loss of dignity, this one, having escaped calamity, took refuge in a monk's household. The halberd went swiftly, like a dragon stretching its claws, the rod approached, like a phoenix piercing flowers. One said to you: "You've ruined people's relationships, just like killing a father!" They fought until almost dawn, and the fiend felt his limbs ache. They fought from the second watch until the east became light. The fiend couldn't withstand the enemy, and fled in defeat, once again turned into a whirlwind, directly returning to his cave, and locked the door tightly, not daring to come out again. The Wayfarer stood before the cave entrance, seeing a stone stele with the inscription "Cloudy Tower Cave" on it. Seeing that the fiend didn't come out, the sky was now bright, and he thought, "Perhaps Master is waiting for me; I'll go back and see him, then come back to catch this fiend." With a step on the cloud, he was soon at the doorstep of Master Lao.

Because the Queen Mother attended the peaches banquet, she invited numerous guests to the Yutiao Pool. At that time, they were drunk and sloppy, staggering this way and that, behaving wildly. What a ferocious sight! The Monkey King's golden pupils flashed like lightning, and the fiend's ringed eyes shone like silver flowers. One of them spat out a colorful mist, and the other exhaled a crimson glow. The crimson glow illuminated the dark place, and the colorful mist radiated a celestial light. The iron rod, with its nine iron knobs, and the axe, clashed with each other in a heroic display: one was the Great Sage who descended to the mortal realm, and the other was the Heavenly General who descended to the edge of the sky. The one who had lost his dignity had become a monster, and the other had narrowly escaped misfortune and taken refuge in the Buddhist faith. The axe sliced through the air like a dragon extending its claws, and the rod approached with the ferocity of a phoenix darting through flowers. That fiend said to me, 'You broke the heart of a person by deceit, just like killing one's father!' This fiend said to me, 'You had your way with a young girl, and you certainly deserved to be caught!' Idle chatter and commotion filled the air as the two of them swung their rod and axe at each other. Looking at it, they fought until nearly dawn, when the other party's two arms were numb with fatigue. The two of them fought from the second watch until the east turned white. The fiend could no longer withstand the enemy's attacks, and he fled in defeat, but he immediately turned into a whirlwind and returned to his cave, locking the door and hiding inside. The Monkey King stood outside the entrance of the cave and saw an inscribed stele, which read 'Cloud Platform Cave.' Since the fiend didn't come out, the day grew brighter, and the Monkey King thought to himself, 'I fear that my master may be waiting for me, so I'll return to see him and then come back to catch this fiend another time.' With one step on the cloud, he soon arrived at the Old Ox Mountain.

Idle talk and tumult, frequently coming and going with staff and saber. They fought until almost dawn, and the monster felt his arms and legs numbed. Because the Queen Mother attended the Peaches of Immortality Banquet, she invited numerous guests to the Yutong Pool. The Golden Arhat staff, and the Nine-toothed Hammer, were two heroes worthy of praise: one was the Sage of the Age, sent to the mortal world; the other was the General of the Heavenly Army, sent to the mortal realm. One of them lost his dignity and became a monster, while the other escaped great hardships to join the Buddhist order. The hammer glided through the air like a dragon stretching its claws, and the staff moved swiftly like a phoenix flying through the flowers. One of them said, "You ruined the love of a family!" Seeing the fiend did not emerge, the sun was shining brightly in the sky, and the Monk thought to himself, "I fear that my Master may be waiting for me, so I'll go back to see him, and then return to catch this fiend another day." He tapped his foot on the clouds and, in an instant, arrived at the Xiaolaozhuang.

You, Sir Burial Master, when you were in trouble, you dragged me and others down with you, but now you come here and deceive people! You should be punished!" The Monkey King wouldn't forgive him and lifted his staff to hit him. The two of them fought in the dark of night in the middle of a mountain. What a spectacle: the Monkey King's eyes shone like lightning, and the fiend's eyes glowed like silver flowers. This one breathed out a swirling mist, and that one spat out a fiery glow. The fiery glow was blinding, and the misty breath was like the stars shining at night. The Golden Hoop Staff and the nine-taloned hammer, these two heroes, were truly deserving of praise: one was the Great Sage who descended to the mortal realm, and the other was the General who descended to the end of heaven. That one was the fiend who had lost his dignity and become a monster, and this one had escaped from the abyss and sought refuge under the Bodhi tree. The hammer went flying like a dragon's claw, and the staff met him like a phoenix flying through flowers. The fiend said, "You destroyed people's relationships like killing one's own father!" They fought until dawn was about to break, and the fiend's two arms felt numb. The two of them fought from midnight until the east grew light. The fiend couldn't resist, and the Monkey King's army retreated, defeated. But the fiend didn't give up and transformed into a whirlwind, and returned to his cave, closing the door tightly and not coming out. The Monkey King stood in front of the cave, looking at a stone stele with the characters "Cloud Platform Cave" inscribed on it. Seeing the fiend did not come out, the sun had already risen high in the sky, and his heart thought: "Perhaps my Master is waiting for me, I'll go back to see him and then come back to catch this fiend." He stepped on the cloud and touched the ground, and soon arrived at the old patriarch's hermitage.

Then Fräulein Montag said, with her head held unusually erect as always, 'I don't know if you know me.' K. looked at her with his eyes narrowed. 'Of course,' he said, 'you've been living at Frau Grubach's for a while now.' 'But,' she said, 'I believe she doesn't really take much interest in the boarding house.' 'No,' said K. 'Would you like to sit down?' Fräulein Montag asked. They both silently pulled two armchairs from the far end of the table and sat facing each other. But Fräulein Montag stood up again at once, because she had left her handbag on the window sill and went to get it; she trailed through the whole room. You'll excuse her and hear me instead. She wouldn't have been able to say anything to you that I won't say, and in fact I think I can tell you even more, since I'm relatively uninvolved. Don't you believe that too?'

It seemed to Razumikhin that the clerk had become even more carefree and contemptuous towards him after his confession - but a strange thing - he suddenly no longer cared about the opinion of anyone, and this change had occurred as suddenly, in a single moment, in one minute. If he had only thought for a moment, he would have been surprised at how he had spoken to them just a minute ago, and even forced his feelings upon them. And where did these feelings come from? On the other hand, if the room were suddenly filled with his most esteemed friends, he wouldn't have found a single human word for them, his heart felt so empty. A dismal feeling of anguished, endless isolation and alienation suddenly became conscious to his soul. He had never before experienced such a strange and terrifying sensation. If he wanted to think a bit more, he would probably have been surprised at how he could have spoken with them a minute ago and even gone out of his way to share his feelings. And where did these feelings come from? On the other hand, if the room were suddenly filled with the first friends of his, he would seem to have no single human word for them, so suddenly had his heart become empty. A gloomy feeling of anguishing, endless solitude and isolation suddenly became manifest to his soul. It was not the baseness of his heart's outpourings to Alyona Ivanovna, nor the porfiry's triumph over him that turned his heart upside down suddenly. Oh, what was his concern now about his own baseness, about all these ambitions, Porfiry, Germans, quests, offices, and the rest, and the rest. If he had been sentenced to be burned in this very minute, he would not have stirred, hardly even listened to the sentence attentively. Something new, unknown, sudden, and unexperienced was taking place with him. He didn't understand it, but he clearly felt with the full force of the sensation that he could not any longer address these people in the district office with the sentimental expansiveness as he had the day before, and even if they were his own brothers and sisters, not district clerks, then he wouldn't have any business addressing them, even in any case in life; he had never experienced a similar strange and terrible sensation in his life before. And what was most tormenting was that it was more of an experience than a conscious awareness, more a sensation than a thought; a most agonizing sensation of all those that he had experienced up to this moment.

One day, the four heavenly generals arranged a grand feast at the cave, inviting the Six Kings to dine, slaughtering a bull and a horse to sacrifice to the heavens and the earth. The whole gang of demons danced and sang in delight, all getting drunk and extremely intoxicated. After sending the Six Kings off, the four heavenly generals then rewarded the big and small officers, leaning against the iron bridge under the shade of the willows. In no time, they fell asleep. The four heavenly generals led the crowd to protect them, not daring to make any noise. Just then, the Monkey King was seen in his dream being taken by two men who held a scroll with the words "Monkey King Sun" written on it. They approached him without hesitation, bound him with a rope, and spirited him away, dragging him straight to a city. The Monkey King gradually woke up, only to find a sign above the city reading "The Underworld". Suddenly he realized the truth, "The Underworld is the abode of King Yama, what am I doing here?" The two men said, "Your time has come to an end, and we have orders to bring you here." The Monkey King replied, "I, the Old Monkey, have transcended the three realms and am no longer within the Five Elements, why should I be brought here?" The two spirit officers just dragged and tugged at him, determined to pull him inside. The Monkey King grew angry, producing a precious item from his ear and, with a flick of his hand, transformed it into a giant club. With one swing, he struck the two spirit officers into minced meat. After untying himself, he shook them off his hands, took up a staff, and marched into the city. The ox-headed ghost fled to the east, the horse-faced ghost fled to the south, the group of ghostly guards scurried up to the Sumeru Heaven Palace, shouting, "Your Majesty! Disaster! Disaster! A hairy-faced divine official is coming!"

One day, the four heavenly generals arranged a grand banquet and invited the six kings to attend. They slaughtered oxen and horses, offered sacrifices to heaven and earth, and the various demons danced and sang with joy. They all drank to the point of intoxication and passed out. As they sent the six kings away, they again rewarded the heads of the smaller demons, and the four heavenly generals leaned against an iron-plank bridge under the shade of the pines. In a moment, they fell asleep. The heavenly generals surrounded them, afraid to make a sound. Just then, the Monkey King, who was drunk, saw two figures approaching with a warrant in their hands, bearing the characters "Sun Wukong" on it. The Monkey King got no chance to say a word; they bound him with ropes and took him away, dragging him to the edge of a city. The Monkey King gradually came to his senses, and, looking up, saw a large iron plaque on the wall with the three characters "Yue Ming Jie" – the Realm of Hell. The Monkey King was startled awake, exclaiming, "The Realm of Hell is where the King of Hell resides; why have I been brought here?" The two men replied, "You have reached the end of your earthly life; we have received orders to fetch you." The Monkey King heard this and said, "I have transcended the three realms and am no longer subject to the Five Elements; how can I be summoned again?" The two men, however, only continued to pull and drag him, determined to take him in. The Monkey King, infuriated, took out a magical bead from his ear and snapped it, producing a glow. It turned into a club, and with a slight movement of his hand, he struck the two men, reducing them to a pulp. The Monkey King freed himself from his restraints, threw away the rope, and brandished a stick, pounding his way into the city. The ox-headed ghost scurried about, dodging left and right, the horse-faced ghost ran off in all directions, and the cohort of demons rushed up to the Heavenly Gate to report, "Great King! Disaster! Disaster! A man with a monkey face has come charging in!"
