Cattle and horses were slaughtered, and sacrifices were made to heaven and earth. In attendance were a multitude of strange creatures who danced and sang in joy, all becoming intoxicated and drunk. Upon sending off the Six Kings, the Four Heavenly Kings rewarded their attendants, a great and small heads of the crowds, and leaned against an iron bridge under the shade of trees, falling asleep at the same time. Just then, the Monkey King, who was fast asleep, saw two people approaching with a scroll in hand, inscribed with the characters "Sun Wukong". The Monkey King got up without hesitation, and the two men quickly bound him with ropes. They dragged him away, stumbling and staggering, straight to the edge of a city. As the Monkey King gradually recovered from his intoxication, he suddenly lifted his head to look around and saw an iron sign hanging above the city gate, inscribed with three characters that read "Mystery and Darkness Realm". The Monkey King was suddenly enlightened and said, "The Mystery and Darkness Realm is where King Yama resides. Why have I been brought here?" The two men said, "You have exhausted your lifespan and are due to depart, we've been sent to bring you." The Monkey King heard this and said, "I have long surpassed the limits of the three realms and am no longer subject to the jurisdiction of the Five Elements. How can they possibly dare to come for me again?" The two spirits merely continued to tug and pull, determined to drag him inside. The Monkey King's temper flared up, and from his ears came out a precious treasure, a jewel emitting a loud noise that was like thunder; it shook everything. With a wave of his hand, the two spirits were reduced to mincemeat. He freed himself from the ropes, tossed them aside, and with a sturdy staff in hand, entered the city. The cow-headed ghost ran east and west, the horse-faced ghost fled south and north, and the multitude of ghostly attendants rushed to the registers of the Eight Trigrams, reporting to King Yama, "Great King! Disaster! Disaster! Outside, a fierce and mighty being, with a hairy face, has come to attack!"

I'm warning you, my dear, that a truly wretched event occurred at our place, one truly deserving of our pity. Today, at five o'clock in the morning, little Gorshkov passed away. I don't know from what, possibly scarlet fever or something; the Lord only knows. I paid a visit to the Gorshkovs. Well, Mother, how poor they are! What a mess! And no wonder, they all live in one room, partitioned off with some screens for decency's sake. They've already got a tiny coffin; they bought it ready-made for the boy, who was nine years old, they say, and was showing such promise. It's heartbreaking to look at them, Varinka! The mother isn't crying, but she's so sorrowful, poor thing. Maybe it's even easier for them that it's one less to worry about; they've still got two more kids left, one who's still in diapers and a little girl who's six years old and growing. What a pleasant thing to see, in all earnest, a sick child and a dear little creature, and you can't even do them any good! The father sits in an old, soiled frock coat, on a broken-down chair. He's crying, and maybe it's not even grief, but just habit, his eyes are just running. What a ridiculous sight! He blushes and gets all flustered whenever you talk to him, and doesn't know what to say. The little girl, their daughter, is standing by the coffin, leaning against it, such a poor little thing, so dull and thoughtful! I don't like it, Mother, Varinka, when children are brooding; it's unpleasant to look at! Some sort of doll is lying on the floor near her, made of cloth; it's not playing; it's got a finger on its lips; stands there stiff as a board. They gave her a candy; she took it, but didn't eat it. It's sad, Varinka – isn't it?

What a pleasure it is to see a child suffer, a child of their own, when they can't even help! The father sits there in his old, stained frock coat on a worn-out chair. Tears are streaming down his face, perhaps not because he's grieving, but just because it's become a habit for his eyes to get all watery. He's a remarkable sight! He blushes and gets flustered whenever you talk to him, and he's at a loss for words. The little girl, the daughter, stands against the coffin, looking so sad and thoughtful. I don't like it when children get lost in thought, Varinka; it's unpleasant to watch! There's a rag doll lying nearby on the floor, but it's not playing; it's got a finger on its lips; it's just standing still, not even twitching. The owner gave it a lollipop, but it didn't even eat it. It's heart-wrenching, Varinka – isn't it?

Fear was the beginning, fear and lust and a horrified curiosity at what was to come. Night reigned, and his senses listened; for in the distance drew near a tumult, a din, a mix of noise: rattling, booming, and a dull thudding, shrill shouting alongside and a certain howl in the drawn 'u' sound, all cut through and hauntingly sweetly overlaid by a deep, assiduously persistent flute-like tone, which on shamelessly intrusive terms entranced his entrails. But he knew a word, dark, yet naming what came: 'The foreign God!' Smoldering embers glowed: he recognized mountainous land, similar to his summer cottage. And in torn light, from forest-covered height, between tree trunks and moss-covered rock formations it rolled and careened swirling down: humans, animals, a swarm, a frenzied rabble, and it overflooded the slope with bodies, flames, tumult and spinning dance. Women, stumbling over their excessively long fur cloaks, which hung from their belts, shook sheil drums over their groaning thrown-back heads, waved blazing torches and naked daggers, held grasping snakes in the middle of their body or carried their screaming breasts in both hands. Men, horns on their foreheads, with fur-worked fur and coarse skin, bent their necks and lifted arms and legs, let resounding copper bellows boom and beat angrily on drums, while smooth youths with garlanded wands gored buck, whose horns they clung to and from whose springs they leapt wildly laughing. And the ecstatic ones let out a call from soft vowel sounds and drawn 'u' cry at the end, sweet and wild at once, such as never heard before: there it resounded on, in the air boomed, like that of stags, and there they gave it back, multi-voiced, in wild triumph, urged each other to dance and toss their limbs and let it never cease. But all was permeated and dominated by the deep, alluring flute-like tone. Did it not also lure him, the resistive experiencer, shamelessly persistently to the feast and measure of the most extreme sacrifice? Great was his revulsion, great his fear, sincere his will, until the very end to protect himself against the foreigner, the enemy of the captured and worthy spirit. But the noise, the howl, amplified by echoing mountain wall, grew, took hold, swelled into compelling madness. Mists pressed on the senses, the pungent scent of bucks, the breath of panting bodies, and a hint of decaying water, along with another, familiar: of wounds and spreading disease. With the drumbeats his heart thundered, his brain whirled, rage seized him, confusion, numbing lust, and his soul yearned to join the dance of the God. The obscene symbol, gigantic, made of wood, was revealed and raised: then they howled without restraint the watchword. Foam foamed at their lips, they teased each other with lewd gestures and enticing hands, laughing and groaning,—they thrust the spiky wands into each other's flesh and licked the blood from their limbs. But with them, in them was the dreamer now and belonged to the foreign God. Yes, they were himself, as they hurled themselves onto the animals, tearing and murdering, and devoured smoking shreds, as on the trampled moss-ground an endless mixture began, for the God's sacrifice. And his soul savored excess and the madness of destruction.

He again heard a loud noise, and the gate swung open. Monkey King flew in, his heart pounding, and saw that the old devil ordered the guards on the various doors to be on their guard and that one side was busily gathering their arms, saying, "I fear that yesterday's gust of wind did not blow Sun Wukong to death; today he will certainly come, and I will give him a death sentence when he comes." Monkey King heard this and flew past the hall to the rear. He saw a tiered gate that was very tightly shut. Monkey King slid through the narrow gap between the gates and found that it was a big empty courtyard on the other side. There was a pole with a rope tied to it, and Sun Wukong bound to it was Master Tang. The Master was in a daze, shedding tears and thinking only of Wukong and Monkey, but not knowing where they were. Monkey King folded his wings and buzzed on the Master's head, calling out "Master." The old Master recognized his voice and said, "Wukong, you want to kill me too! Where are you calling me from?" Monkey King said, "Master, I'm right on your head. You shouldn't be worried, and don't be bothered. We must catch the devil first before we can save your life." Master Tang said, "Disciple, when can we catch the devil?" Monkey King said, "We've already caught that tiger-like creature belonging to you; Hunkwon had beaten it to death. But the devil's magic is very treacherous, so I guess he'll show up today. Don't be anxious, stop crying, I'll go and scare him."

He heard another branch snap, and the second gate creaked open. Monkey King flew in, his footsteps light as a feather, and saw that the old demon was giving orders to his men, at the same time, instructing them to be on their guard: "The array of wind we sent yesterday may not have killed the monkey, and he's sure to come today, I'll make sure to get rid of him the moment he arrives." Hearing these words, Monkey King flew over the hall again, and went straight to the rear. He saw a corridor with doors tightly shut. He squeezed through the crack in the door, and to his surprise, it led to a spacious courtyard on the other side. He saw a rope wrapped around a pole on the wall, holding up the White Bone Demon monk. The venerable master was shedding tears, and his mind was filled with thoughts of Guanyin and Wujing, wondering where they were. Monkey King stopped flying, landed on the master's head, and called out "Master." The old master recognized his voice and exclaimed: "Wukong, you think you're going to kill me! Where are you calling me from?" Monkey King replied: "Master, I'm right on your head! Don't be anxious, don't worry, we must first capture the demon, then we can save your life." The master said: "Disciple, how are you going to capture the demon?" Monkey King said: "I've already killed the tiger demon for you, it was beaten to death by Eight Immortals, but the old demon's array of wind is too powerful. I think it will come today, and we'll seize him then. Master, please calm down and don't worry, I'll go deal with him."

A second time came the sound of footsteps, and the gate was opened. Monkey King flew in, his eyes scanning the place. The old demon ordered the guards to be vigilant, and at the same time, he ordered the soldiers to pick up their arms: "Fearing that the wind that blew yesterday did not kill Monkey King, he is bound to come today, and when he does, I shall put an end to his life for good." Monkey King overheard this and flew past the hall, directly making his way to the back. There he saw a courtyard, its gates shut very tightly. Monkey King managed to squeeze through a small gap in the gate and found himself in a large empty courtyard. On the other side, on a pillar hung a rope tied to the neck of the Tang Monk, causing the old master's tears to fall profusely, his heart only thinking of Guanyin and Wukong, but not knowing where they were. Monkey King alighted, tapping his staff on the master's head, calling out "Teacher!" The old master recognized the voice, saying, "Monkey, do you come to kill me! Where are you?" Monkey King replied, "Teacher, I am right on top of your head. Do not worry, be calm, we must capture that evil spirit before we can save your life." The Tang Monk said, "Disciple, when will you be able to catch the evil spirit?" Monkey King replied, "I have already caught that tiger spirit for you, and it was beaten to death by Eight Immortals. But that old demon's attack was most treacherous. I reckon he will only show himself today. You have nothing to worry about, stop crying, I'll go to silence him."

Just then, another sound was heard, and the second gate swung open. The Monkey King flew in with a "gab-gab-gab" and saw the old demon giving orders to each of the guards, also instructing them to be on the lookout, one side of him collecting the arms: "Perhaps that gust of wind yesterday didn't kill the Monkey King; he will certainly come today, and when he does, I will finish him off once and for all." The Monkey King overheard this and flew back through the hall, going directly to the back. There he saw a door, which was locked very tightly. The Monkey King wriggled through the narrow slit between the door and its frame, and it turned out to be a big empty courtyard. On the other side, a rope tied to a windlass was bound to the Bodhisattva of Great Mercy. The venerable patriarch's eyes welled up with tears, and he thought of Guanyin and his own disciple Wukong, not knowing where they were. The Monkey King folded his wings, tapped gently on his master's head, and called out, "Master." The elder recognized his voice and said, "Wukong, you want to kill me, I see! Where are you calling me from?" The Monkey King said, "Master, I'm on your head." "Don't worry and be anxious, let's catch the demon first and then save your life," he said. The Bodhisattva of Great Mercy asked, "Disciple, when will we catch the demon?" The Monkey King said, "The beast that was tied to you has already been killed by my brother, Eight Rules, but the old demon's powers are cunning and treacherous. I'm sure he'll be caught today. Just be calm and don't cry, I'll deal with him."

Again he heard a sound, and the second gate opened. The Monkey King flew in, making a whirring sound as he went. He saw that the old demon was issuing orders to the various attendants, at the same time collecting up his arms, saying, "I fear that the gale of yesterday did not blow the Monkey King to death; he is sure to come today, and I'll see to it that he meets his end then." When Monkey heard this, he flew over the hall and made his way to the rear. There he saw that a door was locked tight, so he slipped through the crack and discovered that it was a large empty courtyard. To one side, a rope was coiled round a post, binding the Tang Monk. The old monk was weeping and calling to mind his disciples, not knowing where they were. Monkey stopped flying, tapped him on the head, and called out, "Father." The old monk recognised his voice and said, "Ah, Monkey, you're after me too! Where are you?" Monkey said, "I'm right on your head, Father. Don't worry, don't be anxious. We must certainly capture the demon before we can rescue you." The old monk said, "Disciple, when can we capture the demon?" Monkey said, "We've already caught your tiger demon. Only the old demon's blow is powerful. I reckon he'll be here today. We'll be sure to catch him. Don't cry, Father, I'll go and scare him off."

– It's a long story, Avdotia Romanovna. Single-minded evil is the only obstacle to a thousand good deeds! It's also quite hurtful for a young man with virtues and an immoderate sense of pride to know, for example, that he could have been among those three thousand, and his entire career, his whole future, was shaped in a different way, and yet those three thousand were not there. Add to that the irritation of hunger, the cramped apartment, the beggarly circumstances, the acutely felt awareness of one's social standing, and the standing of one's sister and mother. And above all, one's pride, conceit, and ambition – or who knows, perhaps even with a good disposition... I'm not blaming him, please don't think I am; it's not my business anyway. There was also one of his own little theories – a theory of sorts, really – that people are divided, you see, into raw material and exceptional people, that is, people of high standing, for whom the law isn't written, but who make laws for the rest of humanity, for the raw material, the rabble. No, it's just a theory; that's it, another theory. Napoleon fascinated him terribly, I mean, specifically, it was what many great people didn't think about single-minded wickedness, but simply stepped over, without a second thought. He seems to have thought that he was a great man, too, that is, for a time, he was convinced of it. He suffered, and still suffers, from the thought that he was able to concoct the theory, but not step over, without a thought, and therefore is not a great man. And that's especially humiliating for a young man with an inflated sense of pride in our era...

It is said that the monk took the Fire-Resisting Cloak and with one somersault leaped up to the Southern Gate of Heaven, handing it over to the Broad-Eyed Heavenly King and saying, "Thank you for lending! Thank you for lending!" The king took it back, saying, "The Great Sage's sincerity is genuine. I was worried that I would never see my precious item again, so I had no choice but to have it sent back. What a relief!"

The Great Sage said, "Is the old monkey capable of deceiving people in person? This is truly good lending and good repaying. I won't need to borrow it again."

The Heavenly King said, "I haven't seen you in a long time, please come into the palace and rest for a while. What do you think?"

The Great Sage said, "The old monkey is unlike his former self, full of hot air, talking nonsense. Now I'm taking care of the Tang Monk, and I don't have any free time. Wait a bit longer! Wait a bit longer!"

Quickly he bid farewell and jumped off into the clouds, then saw the sun rising in the sky and flew straight to the temple in front, transforming himself into a bee and flying inside. When he appeared in his true form, he saw that the Patriarch was still fast asleep. The Great Sage called out, "Master, it's dawn, wake up!"

The Patriarch was just starting to wake up, rolled over and said, "Just so." He got dressed, opened the door and came out, then suddenly looked up and saw that the walls were red, with no towers or halls to be seen, and was greatly startled:

"What happened to our temple?"

It is said that the Monkey King took the Fire-Resisting Cap, and with a single somersault, he went up to the Southern Heavenly Gate, where he handed it over to the Broad-Eyed Heavenly King, saying, "Thank you for lending it! The Monkey King replied, "Old Sun is not a person who would deceive others in the face. This is what's called good borrowing and good returning. It's easy to lend, but hard to return." The Heavenly King said, "It's been a long time since we've met. Please come and sit in the minor courtyard for a while, how about that?" Wait a moment, please wait a moment!" And with that, he hastily bid farewell and jumped into the clouds, then saw the sun shining above and flew straight to the Zen hall, shedding his transformation and changing back into his original form, whereupon he saw that his Master was still fast asleep. The Monkey King called out, "Master, it's daybreak, get up!" The Tang Monk was just waking up, rolled over and said, "Just so!" He put on his clothes, opened the door and came out, but just looked up and saw that the wall in front of him was upside down and the red walls, but there were no halls or pavilions in sight, and he was greatly startled:

"You must be dreaming, this can't be! Where have all the halls and pavilions gone? Where have all the buildings gone? The trees, the rocks, the forests, the rivers, and the mountains are all unfamiliar! What should I do? I've got to find a way back! I've got to make a pilgrimage! There must be someone who can guide me! The door, the windows, the gate, the walls, the trees – all of them are all upside down! This can't be! This can't be! The monk then took the Fiery Palm, shot up to the Southern Gate, handed it to the Broad-Eyed Heavenly King and said, "I thank you for the loan! I thank you for the loan!" The king said, "Please excuse my long absence and visit the young master in the palace. Sit down for a moment, how about it?" Mother never came at night – or did she, once? I had screamed and screamed, and Mademoiselle had come and Sieversen, the housekeeper, and Georg, the coachman; but that hadn't helped. And so they had finally sent the carriage to fetch my parents, who were at a big ball, I think at the Kronprinz's. And all of a sudden I heard it pull into the courtyard, and I became quiet, sat still and looked at the door. And then there was a bit of a rustling in the other rooms, and Mother came in wearing the grand housecoat she never bothered with, and ran in almost and left her white fur cloak behind and took me in her bare arms. And I felt, amazed and enchanted as never before, her hair, and her small, well-groomed face, and the cold stones in her ears, and the silk at the edges of her shoulders, which smelled of flowers. And we stayed like that and tenderly cried and kissed each other, until we felt that Father was there and that we had to part. "He has high fever", I heard Mother whisper softly, and Father reached out and took my hand and felt my pulse. He was wearing the Jaegermeister uniform with the beautiful, wide, watery blue sash of the elephant. "What nonsense to summon us", he said into the room without looking at me. They had promised to return if it was nothing serious. And serious it was nothing. But on my blanket I found Mother's dance card and white carnations, which I had never seen before and which I put on my eyes, as I noticed how cool they were.

As evening drew near, the old firs rustled more loudly. A powerful wind swept in, rushing and roaring through the dense foliage. The sound was so enchanting that it went straight to Heidi's ears and into her heart, and she was completely cheerful, skipping and leaping among the firs as if she had experienced an unheard-of joy. Grandfather stood under the cattle shed and watched the child. Just then a shrill whistle pierced the air. Heidi stopped her jumping, Grandfather stepped out. It came bounding down from above, goat after goat, like a hunt, and Peter in the middle. With a cry of joy, Heidi shot straight into the group and greeted the old friends from this morning, one by one. As the hut came into view, everything fell silent, and two beautiful, slender goats – a white one and a brown one – came out of the herd and ran to Grandfather, licking his hands, because he held a little salt in them, as he did every evening to greet his two little animals. Peter vanished with his flock. Heidi stroked the one goat tenderly, then the other, and jumped around them to stroke them from the other side as well, and was completely full of joy and happiness at the sight of the little animals. "Are they ours, Grandfather? Are they both ours? Will they come into the stall? Will they stay with us forever?" Heidi asked in rapid succession, her joy bubbling over, and Grandfather could hardly fit a steady "Yes, yes!" into the gaps between her questions. When the goats had licked the salt from his hands, the old man said, "Go and get out your little dish and the bread."

"Are they ours, Grandfather? Are both ours? Do they come into the stable? Will they always stay with us?" Heidi asked in its delight, one question after the other, and the Grandfather could hardly fit his steady "Yes, yes" between the one and the other question. When the goats had licked their salt, the old man said: "Go and fetch your little bowl and the bread."

Maybe some readers will think that my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, impoverished, poorly developed nature, a pale dreamer, a frail, liquorish wretch. On the contrary, Alyosha was at that time a sturdy, ruddy-cheeked, bright-eyed nineteen-year-old youth, brimming with health. He was even very handsome then, well-built, of medium height, dark-haired, with a correct, albeit slightly elongated, oval face, with bright, dark-gray, wide-set eyes, very thoughtful, and seemingly very calm. Perhaps it will be said that ruddy cheeks do not contradict fanaticism or mysticism; and to me it seems that Alyosha was even more of a realist than anyone. Oh, of course, in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but, in my opinion, miracles never confuse a realist. Realism is not inclined to faith by miracles. A true realist, if he is not a believer, always finds within himself the strength and ability not to believe in a miracle, and if a miracle becomes an inescapable fact before him, he will rather not believe his feelings than admit the fact. If he does admit it, then he will admit it as a natural fact, but one that was previously unknown to him. In a realist, faith is not born from a miracle, but a miracle from faith. If a realist believes, then he must necessarily admit the miracle precisely because of his realism. Thomas the Apostle declared that he would not believe until he sees, and when he saw, he said: "My Lord and my God!" Was a miracle what led him to believe? It is more likely that not, and he believed only because he wanted to believe and, perhaps, already believed entirely in the depths of his being, even when he said: "I will not believe until I see."

A few years later, after the strange night in the gallery at Urnekloster, I spent days trying to confide in little Erik. But after our nighttime conversation he had shut himself up completely from me, avoided me; I think he scorned me. And precisely because of that, I wanted to tell him about the 'Hand'. I thought I could win him over (and I longed to do so for some reason), if I could explain to him that I really had experienced it. But Erik was skilled at evading, so it didn't come to that. One day, the Patriarch and his many disciples were frolicking in the evening at Three-Star Grotto. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, has your task been accomplished?" Monkey replied, "Thanks to my benevolent father's guidance, I have completed my training, and can now soar into the clouds and ascend into the air." The Patriarch said, "Let's see you fly and lift me." Monkey employed his skills, puffed out his chest, pulled his hair back, and jumped high, landing a distance of five or six zhang. He strode on the clouds for a while and then returned, landing a mere three li away, and sat down before the Patriarch, clasping his hands together and saying, "Father, this is flying and soaring in the clouds." The Patriarch laughed and said, "This does not count as flying and soaring in the clouds; it merely counts as climbing onto the clouds. From ancient times it has been said, 'In the morning he wanders north of the sea, and in the evening he sojourns in southern Wuyue.' You've only managed to climb up halfway, and that is still not yet worthy of the title of flying and soaring in the clouds." Monkey said, "What is the meaning of 'morning he wanders north of the sea and in the evening sojourns in southern Wuyue'?" The Patriarch replied, "All those who can fly and soar across the seas depart early in the morning from the north sea, travel to the east sea, the west sea, and the south sea, and then return to Wuyue, which is the name of a region north of the Lingling River in the north sea. Only when one has traversed the four seas and returned, does one truly fly and soar." Monkey said, "This is indeed difficult, this is indeed difficult!" The Patriarch said, "In this world there is no task that cannot be accomplished, except that those who have a strong will are the only ones who can accomplish it." Monkey heard these words, bowed and worshiped, and then said, "Father, 'one must thoroughly cultivate oneself as a person.' So, let me beg a great mercy from you, and you can grant me the method for flying and soaring in the clouds, and I will never forget the favor." The Patriarch said, "All sages who fly and soar in the clouds tumble and fall, and then rise up. But you, the moment I see you, are able to leap high. I will only pass on to you the technique for 'striking the cloud with a somersault'." Monkey again bowed and begged, and the Patriarch transmitted the secret phrase, saying, "Grip this cloud, grasp the technique, recite the true words, clench your fists tightly, shake your body, and then jump up – you will cover a distance of ten million or eight hundred thousand li in a single somersault!" The crowd heard this and all laughed in amazement, saying, "Monkey's good fortune! If he can master this technique, he can go wherever he pleases, accepting invitations to dine, sending written communications, and delivering documents, and no matter where he goes, he will never go hungry!" Each of the disciples returned to his own grotto. That very night, Monkey employed his divine energy and refined his technique, mastering the technique of striking the cloud with a somersault. From then on, he was free from any constraints and spent his days in carefree, joyous abandon, basking in the beauty of this long life.

One day, the Patriarch and his disciples were playing at the West Pagoda. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, have you mastered your accomplishments?" The Monkey King replied, "Thanks to my venerable Master's kindness, I have made great progress and am now capable of floating and rising into the air." The Patriarch said, "Try lifting me up and see." The Monkey King practiced his technique and suddenly tensed his body, then gave himself a whiplash crack and leapt five or six yards into the air, reached out and plucked a cloud, staying aloft for about the time it takes to eat a meal, and then came down three or four li away, landing before the Patriarch, clasping his hands in a bow and saying, "Master, this is the art of floating and rising." The Patriarch laughed and said, "This can be called rising no more than climbing a cloud. In the past, people have said, 'The gods visit the Northern Sea in the morning and the South of Xiang in the evening.' You take half a day, going no farther than three li, and can only be said to have climbed a cloud!" The Monkey King asked, "How is it 'visiting the Northern Sea in the morning and the South of Xiang in the evening'?" The Patriarch said, "Whenever one acquires the ability to rise into the clouds, he starts at dawn from the Northern Sea, touring the Eastern Sea, the Western Sea, the Southern Sea, and then goes back to the South of Xiang; and the South of Xiang is a phrase used to describe the Northern Sea. To have toured the four seas and their surroundings in one day is what it means to rise into the clouds." The Monkey King said, "This is difficult! How difficult!" The Patriarch said, "The world is not full of impossible things, only that people may not be of a determined mind." The Monkey King, upon hearing this, bowed his head and worshiped, then said, "Master, one must be thorough in one's nature; I will give up a great deal of compassion and beg you to hand down this art of rising into the clouds to me, and I will never forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "All the immortals rise into the clouds by the method of hopping. You are not like that. I just came to you and you were just able to jump up with a slight pull of your arms. I shall give you the technique of 'Monkey Cloud Leap' this one time." The Monkey King again bowed his head and begged, the Patriarch gave him an oral transmission, saying, "Grasp this cloud by this principle, recite the true word, make fists and shake your body, and leap up. One leap can cover eighty thousand or ninety thousand li." The assembly heard this and all burst out laughing, saying, "Monkey is a wonder! If you can master this technique, you can use it to deliver goods, send letters, or run errands, and won't have to worry about finding food anywhere." The Master and his disciples went back to their respective caves. On that night, the Monkey King cultivated his divine power and practiced the technique, mastering the art of Monkey Cloud Leap. From then on, he was no longer bound by anything and roamed freely, enjoying this beauty of a long life.

One day, the Patriarch and the multitude of his disciples were playing in the evening at the Three Star Grotto. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, have you accomplished your tasks?" Monkey replied, "Thanks to my venerable Father's blessings, I have completed my endeavors and can now ascend to heaven with a single leap." The Patriarch said, "You try flying and leaping for me to see." Monkey practiced his arts, stood up straight, and, with a violent motion, suddenly sprang into the air, pulling off a tuft of his hair as he leapt six or seven paces high, disappearing into the clouds and reappearing after a whole meal's time, falling to the ground about three miles away, and then landing in front of the Patriarch, crossing his arms and saying, "Father, this is my flying and leaping." The Patriarch laughed and said, "This doesn't count as flying; it's only crawling on the clouds. From ancient times, it's said: 'The gods amuse themselves in the North Sea at dawn, and return to Mount Cangwu at dusk.'" You're like that, only able to go a few miles in half a day; even crawling on clouds isn't something that's worth bragging about!" Monkey said, "How is that like the saying 'amusing oneself in the North Sea at dawn, and returning to Mount Cangwu at dusk'?" The Patriarch said, "Those who can truly fly the clouds start their journey at dawn in the North Sea, and then travel across the East Sea, West Sea, and South Sea before returning to Mount Cangwu; Mount Cangwu itself is a region in the North Sea, and it refers to having traversed all four seas in a day." Monkey said, "This is truly difficult! Truly difficult!" The Patriarch said, "There are no difficult tasks in the world, except perhaps for those with a determination to achieve them." Monkey heard these words and bowed his head in reverence, and then said, "Father, 'be a man and be thorough', I'll give up my merciful heart, and accept this method of flying the clouds and hand it down to me. I won't forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "All sages who fly the clouds take a great fall before rising up; you, however, jumped up after a brief pause. I'll only give you this technique, the 'nine-yards cloud somersault,' from your current momentum." Monkey again knelt down in supplication, and the Patriarch then taught him a secret rhyme, saying, "Take this cloud in your fist, and recite the True Word; draw tight your fist and shake your body, and with one somersault, you can cover ten million eight thousand li of distance!" The assembly heard this and all laughed with joy, saying, "Monkey's potential is vast! If he masters this technique, he can be a wandering swordsman, a postal messenger, or a merchant who delivers contracts, and no matter where he goes, he'll be able to find food to eat!" The Patriarch and his disciples returned to their respective abodes, each lost in their own thoughts. That night, Monkey cultivated his spirit and practiced the technique, mastering the nine-yards cloud somersault. From then on, he moved freely without constraint, living a carefree life in his long journey of immortality.

One day, the Patriarch and the numerous disciples were leisurely strolling in front of the Trifling Star Cave at dusk. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, has your business been accomplished?" Monkey said, "Thanks to my master's great mercy, your disciple's accomplishments are complete, and I am already able to soar and ascend." The Patriarch said, "Try flying and ascension for me to see." Monkey displayed his skills, raised his body suddenly, pulled his hair and tail together, leapt away six to seven yards from the ground, stepped onto the clouds for a moment, and returned within a few miles, landing before the Patriarch. He clasped his hands and said, "Master, this is called soaring and ascending." The Patriarch smiled and said, "This does not count as soaring and ascending; it is merely climbing clouds at most. In ancient times, it was said, 'Celestial beings roam the North Sea in the morning and go to the Cangwu region in the evening.' A fellow like you, unable to reach three miles in half a day, can hardly be counted as soaring and ascending!" Monkey said, "What does 'roaming the North Sea in the morning and going to the Cangwu region in the evening' mean?" The Patriarch said, "All beings who soar the clouds start from the North Sea in the morning, visit the Eastern Sea, the Western Sea, and the Southern Sea, and then return to the Cangwu region. The term 'Cangwu' is a phrase used by those who reside in the western part of the North Sea. It means to travel all the seas in a single day, only then can it be considered soaring and ascending." Monkey said, "This is indeed a difficult feat! This is indeed a difficult feat!" The Patriarch said, "In the world, there is no task impossible, only those with a courageous heart." Monkey heard these words and bowed in worship, then asked, "Master, a person must be thorough, and so I beg you, out of great compassion, teach me this method of soaring and ascending, so I will never forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "All celestial beings who soar the clouds all jump up from a standing position; you, however, jumped up after taking a few steps. Today I will teach you this one move, 'The Cloud-Somersault'." Monkey bowed in worship, begging, and the Patriarch taught him a secret phrase, saying, "This cloud, grasp this phrase, recite the authentic mantra, tighten your fists, shake your body, and jump up with a somersault – you will soar ten million eight thousand li in a single jump!" The crowd heard the news and burst out laughing, saying, "Monkey is indeed blessed! If you master this technique, you can be a delivery boy, a messenger, and a porter, and you will never lack food anywhere!" The master and disciples each returned to their caves, one by one. That night, Monkey practiced his divine energy and mastered the Cloud-Somersault technique. From then on, he was free from all constraints and enjoyed a life of carefree freedom, a beautiful and eternal existence.

One day, the Patriarch and his disciples were playing at dusk in front of the Three Stars Cave. The Patriarch said, "Monkey, have you completed your tasks?" Monkey said, "Thanks to the benevolence of the Patriarch, the disciple has fulfilled his duties and can now effortlessly ascend to heaven." The Patriarch said, "Try to fly up and show me." Monkey displayed his skill, stood up straight, pulled a handful of hair, jumped a distance of five or six zhangs, stepped on clouds and crossed rivers in an instant, and returned in a moment, landing not even three li away, before the Patriarch. He clasped his hands and said, "Master, this is flying and ascending to the clouds." The Patriarch smiled and said, "This can hardly be called ascending to the clouds. It's only climbing the clouds at best. As the saying goes: 'Morning, I stroll north of the sea, and in the evening, I gaze at the misty hills of the south.' You've been out for half a day and haven't even covered three li; you're still just climbing clouds. It's not worth talking about!" Monkey asked, "What's the meaning of 'morning I stroll north of the sea, and in the evening, I gaze at the misty hills of the south'?" The Patriarch said, "As for those who can ascend to the clouds, they rise from the north sea at dawn, visit the east sea, the west sea, the south sea, and then turn back to the misty hills of the south. The phrase 'misty hills of the south' actually refers to the north sea's Lingling dialect. They've traversed all four seas and spent a whole day traveling; only then can one be said to ascend to the clouds." Monkey said, "This is indeed difficult, it's indeed difficult!" The Patriarch said, "There are no impossible tasks in the world, it's just that people lack the heart to do them." Monkey heard these words and bowed his head in reverence, then asked, "Master, 'be thorough in one's dealings,' you might as well give up on that bit of compassion and give me the method for ascending to the clouds right away, and I'll never forget the debt of gratitude." The Patriarch said, "All the immortals ascend to the clouds by falling back and rising up. You, however, just jumped up when I came over. I'll only teach you this 'corkscrew cloud' based on the momentum you've achieved so far." Monkey again bowed and implored, and the Patriarch transmitted an incantation to him, saying, "This cloud, grasp the key, recite the true words, clench your fists tightly, shake your body, and jump up with a corkscrew motion, and you'll cover a distance of tens of thousands of li in an instant!" The disciples all heard this and burst into laughter, saying, "Monkey is marvelous! If he learns this technique, he can travel anywhere to bring goods, deliver documents, or convey messages, and he'll never go hungry!" The master and disciples all returned to their respective dwellings in a daze. That night, Monkey practiced his spirit and refined his technique, and soon mastered the corkscrew cloud. From then on, he was completely unencumbered and free, enjoying this long life of carefree bliss.

"Mother, Mother," Gregor said softly and looked up at her. The commercial agent had momentarily slipped his mind; instead, he couldn't help but snap his jaws open several times at the sight of the flowing coffee. The mother shrieked and ran away from the table, throwing herself into the arms of the rushing father. But Gregor didn't have time for his parents now; the commercial agent was already on the stairs; his chin resting on the banister, he looked back one last time. Gregor took a running start to catch up to him as quickly as possible; the commercial agent must have sensed it, because he leaped over several steps and vanished; "Huh!" he shouted, the sound echoing through the entire hallway. 

Unfortunately, it seemed that the commercial agent's flight now completely threw the father off, who had been relatively composed so far. Instead of pursuing the commercial agent or at least not hindering Gregor in his pursuit, he grabbed the commercial agent's cane, which he had left with his hat and overcoat on a chair, took a large newspaper from the table with his other hand, and set about driving Gregor back into his room with a swinging motion of the cane and the newspaper. No amount of begging from Gregor helped; no begging was even understood; Gregor could twist his head as humbly as he wanted, the father only stomped his feet harder. On the other side of the house, the mother had thrown open a window despite the cold weather, and, leaning out into the wind, pressed her face far beyond the windowpane into her hands. A strong draft arose between the street and the hallway, the curtains flew open, the newspapers on the table rustled, and individual sheets were blown across the floor. The father was relentless and let out hisses like a wild animal. 

But Gregor had still had no practice in backing up, it was really going very slowly. If only he could have turned around, he would have been in his room in no time; but he was afraid of making the father impatient with the time-consuming turning, and every moment threatened him with the deadly blow from the father's cane on his back or head. In the end, however, there was nothing left for him to do, as he realized with horror that he couldn't even keep the direction in his backwards walking; and so he began to turn around as quickly as possible, glancing anxiously over at the father all the while. Perhaps the father noticed his good intentions, because he didn't interfere with him, but instead even guided his turning from a distance with the tip of his cane. If only this unbearable hissing of the father's hadn't been there! Gregor completely lost his head over it. He was almost all the way turned around when, still listening intently for that hissing, he even stumbled and turned himself back a little. 

But when he finally made it successfully with his head into the doorway, it became apparent that his body was too wide to pass through without further ado. The father didn't even remotely think of opening the other door leaf to make a suitable passage for Gregor in his current state; his fixed idea was that Gregor had to get back into his room as quickly as possible. He would never have allowed the complicated preparations that Gregor needed to stand up and perhaps in this way pass through the door. Perhaps he was driving Gregor, as if there were no obstacles, forward with special noise; it didn't even sound like the voice of a single father anymore; now there was no more play, and Gregor pushed himself – let what would happen – into the doorway. One side of his body was lifted, he was lying awkwardly in the doorway, one flank was severely rubbed raw, ugly marks remained on the white door, and he became stuck and couldn't move on his own anymore; his legs hung dangling in the air on one side, and the other were pressed painfully to the floor – then the father gave him a truly liberating strong push from behind, and he flew, heavily bleeding, deep into his room. The door was slammed shut with the cane, and then it was finally quiet.

Perhaps the father noticed his good intentions, as he did not interrupt him, but rather directed the turning movement from a distance with the point of his cane. If only the unbearable hissing of the father hadn't been there! Gregor lost his head completely over this. He was almost entirely turned around when, listening intently for the hissing, he even strayed and turned himself back a bit. But when he finally managed to get his head past the doorway, it became apparent that his body was too wide to pass through without difficulty. It was not even remotely apparent to the father in his current state that he might open the other door to create a sufficient passage for Gregor. His fixed idea was that Gregor had to get into his room as quickly as possible; he would never have granted the complicated preparations that Gregor needed to stand up and perhaps in this way get through the door. As if there were no obstacle at all, the father seemed to be driving Gregor forward with especial loudness; it wasn't just the voice of one father anymore, it was clear that there was no fun anymore; and Gregor pressed himself – whatever might happen – into the doorway. One side of his body lifted, he lay at an angle in the doorway; his flank was badly scraped, ugly marks remained on the white door; he got stuck and couldn't move on his own anymore; his legs hung trembling on one side in the air, while those on the other were painfully pressed down to the floor – at this point the father gave him a strong push from behind, and he flew, heavily bleeding, far into his room. The door was then slammed shut with the cane, and it was finally quiet.

At the same time, he thought to himself, "Not good, not good! This calamity is greater than heaven; if the Jade Emperor finds out, it's hard to survive. Let's go! Let's go! Let's go! It's better to be a king in the underworld!" He fled out of the Rotating Heavens Palace, not taking the old path, but going out through the Western Heavenly Gate, using the Veiled Body Art to escape. He suddenly turned into a cloud and flew back to the Fruit and Flower Mountain border. Suddenly, he saw that the banners and standards were shining brightly, the halberds were radiating a luster, and it was found that the Four Heavenly Generals and the 72 Heavenly Kings of the Heavenly Passages were practicing their martial arts there. The Great Sage shouted loudly, " Servants, I'm here!" The demons all dropped their weapons and knelt down, saying, "Great Sage, please calm down! You've been gone for a long time, not paying attention to us!" The Great Sage said, "Not long, not long!" Then he walked, directly entering the depths of the Heavenly Passages. The Four Heavenly Generals finished cleaning up and settling down to kneel down and worship, and said in unison, "Great Sage, how many years have you been in heaven?" The Great Sage laughed and said, "I remember it's just half a year or so, why are you talking about a hundred years?" The Generals said, "A day in heaven is equivalent to a year on the earthly realm." The Great Sage said, "I'm glad that the Jade Emperor loves me so much that he has bestowed upon me the title of 'All-Under-Heaven Great Sage', established the 'All-Under-Heaven Prefecture', and set up the offices of An Qing and Ning Shen. Since then, I see that there's no trouble, I'm in charge of the Fruit and Fruit Garden. Later, because the Queen Mother set up the 'Great Peach Gathering', I was never invited, so I went to the Jade Pool first, and I ate all the Heavenly Peach and Heavenly Wine. Leaving the Jade Pool, I carelessly stumbled into the Old Master's palace, and I also ate the five jars of Golden Elixir. Fearing that the Jade Emperor will see me as guilty, I just came out of the Heavenly Gate."

A moment later, Tang Sanzang woke up with a full belly, and to himself, he thought: "It's no good, it's no good! This calamity is even greater than heaven; if I alarm the Jade Emperor, my life won't be spared. Let's go! Let's go! Let's go! It's better for me to go to the lower realm to be the king than to stay here!" He rushed out of the Crouching Tiger Heavenly Palace, took the old road, and went out through the Western Heaven Gate using the art of invisibility to escape. He then held onto a cloud and returned to the territory of Flower Fruit Mountain. There he saw that the banners were flashing and the halberds were shining brightly, and it turned out that the Four Heavenly Steeds and the 72 Guardian Kings of the Caves were practicing martial arts there. The Great Sage shouted loudly, "Little ones! I'm here too!" The demons dropped their weapons and knelt down, saying, "Great Sage, please be at ease! You've been absent for such a long time, why haven't you come to visit us?" The Great Sage said, "Not long, not long." He continued to walk, straight into the depths of the heavenly realm. The Four Heavenly Steeds cleaned up, made themselves comfortable, and bowed to greet him. They all said, "Great Sage, in the heavens for a hundred or so years, what duty have you actually fulfilled?" The Great Sage laughed and said, "I remember it was only half a year ago, why are you saying a hundred or so years?" The Heavenly Steeds said, "A day in heaven is equivalent to a year on earth." The Great Sage said, "This is a joyous occasion for the Jade Emperor to have liked me, and indeed he has bestowed upon me the title of 'Almighty Sage,' established the Almighty Court, and set up the Two Offices of Anxi and Ning Shen, and established the heavenly clerks and guards. Since then, seeing that I was idle, he ordered me to manage the Garden of the Golden Peaches. Lately, the Mother of the West arranged for a 'Gathering of the Golden Peaches,' and since I wasn't invited, I went to the Jade Pond on my own, and ate all of her immortal foods and immortal wine. After leaving the Jade Pond, I stumbled and staggered into the Abode of the Prime Heavens, and also ate the five golden elixirs of the old Lord. But fearing the Jade Emperor will see my offense, I've just left the heavenly gate."

Just then, when he had drunk all the wine and had regained consciousness, he muttered to himself, "How terrible! How terrible! This calamity is greater than the heavens; if it stirs up the Jade Emperor, my life will be hard to survive. Go! Go! Go! It's better to go to the mortal realm to become a king." He then ran out of the Cavern of Replenishment, not taking the old path, but through the Western Heaven Gate, using the art of invisibility to escape. He flew in the clouds and returned to the border of Flower Fruit Mountain. He saw that the pennants were shining, and the halberds were glowing, and it turned out that the four strong warriors and the 72 Netherworld Demons were practicing their martial arts there. The Great Sage shouted loudly, "You rascals! I'm here!" The demons dropped their weapons and knelt down, saying, "Great Sage, please calm down! You haven't come to visit us for a long time, not to mention send us a thought." The Great Sage said, "It's not been long, not been long!"  As he said, he continued on his journey, straight into the depths of the heavens. The four strong warriors finished cleaning and resting, knocking their heads in respect and worship. They said in unison, "Great Sage, how have you served in heaven for a hundred or so years?" The Great Sage laughed and said, "I remember it's only been half a year, how come they say it's a hundred or so years?" The strong warriors said, "A day in heaven is equivalent to a year below." The Great Sage said, "And I'm happy that the Jade Emperor has favored me so much, actually bestowing upon me the title of 'Universal Sage', creating a Heavenly Capital, setting up the departments of Yanjing and Ningshen, and appointing heavenly officials and guards. Afterward, since I've been idle, I was put in charge of the Peony Garden. Lately, because the Queen Mother set the Peach Banquet, I wasn't invited, so I went to the Jade Pool of her own accord, and ate her magical elixir and magical wine. I came out of the Jade Pool and stumbled and staggered and mistakenly entered the Palace of the Old Lord, and even ate the five jade gourds of elixir of the Old Lord. Afraid that the Jade Emperor would see this as a transgression, I just came out of the heavenly gate."

In a moment, it dawned on Tang Sanzang that he had had too much to drink, and then he thought to himself, "Oh no! Oh no! This calamity is greater than the Heavens; if the Jade Emperor finds out, my life will be forfeit. Run! Run! Run! It's better for me to become the king of the underworld!" So he dashed out of the Sumeru Heaven Palace, not taking the old path, and slipping through the western gate, he cast a transformation spell to escape. He turned into a cloud and flew back to the area of Flower Fruit Mountain. And behold, those fluttering banners shone like blazing fire, and the glittering halberds shone like rays of light. It turned out that the four Heavenly Guards and the 72 Goblin Kings were practicing martial arts. The Great Sage loudly exclaimed, "Little guys, I'm here!" The supernatural beings dropped their weapons and knelt down, saying, "Great Sage, we've been waiting for you for so long; why haven't you come to see us?" The Great Sage said, "Not long, not long!" He went ahead and entered the innermost part of the Heavens. The four Heavenly Guards cleared the way and knelt in a row, worshiping him and then asked, "Great Sage, it's been a hundred or so years since you ascended to heaven, what responsibilities have you held?" The Great Sage laughed and said, "I only remember it's been half a year or so, how come you mention a hundred years?" The Heavenly Guards replied, "A day in heaven is a year below." The Great Sage said, "Then I'm happy that the Jade Emperor favors me, and he has bestowed upon me the title of 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven' and set up the Zhitian Palace and the offices of Anqing and Ningshen, and appointed heavenly officials and guards. Since then, seeing that I have no tasks, he has tasked me with overseeing the Peony Garden. Lately, because the Queen Mother set up a grand feast at the Peony Garden, and I wasn't invited, I went to the West Chamber, and I ate all of the heavenly foods and drinks. I came out of the West Chamber, and stumbled into the Old Master's palace, and I also ate all of the Old Master's five golden elixirs. I was afraid that the Jade Emperor would discover my crime, so I ran out of the heavenly gates just now."

In the blink of an eye, the drunken Tang was back to his senses, and he thought to himself: "No good, no good! This calamity is greater than heaven itself; if it were to awaken the Jade Emperor, my life would be at stake. Walk, walk, walk! It's better to be a king of the underworld than to be a spirit!" He then ran out of the Lingxiao Palace, did not take the old road, and instead, through the Western Heaven Gate, made a figure of himself disappear, and fled away. He then floated on a cloud's head and returned to the territory of the Peach Garden.

As he approached, he saw that the pennants flashed brightly, and the spears shone radiantly. It turned out that the four valiant generals and the seventy-two kings of the 72 Cave had come to the spot to practice their martial arts. The Great Sage loudly shouted: "My younger generations, I have arrived!" The demons all dropped their tools and knelt down, saying: "The Great Sage, you must calm down! I've been missing you for a long time, and I haven't had the chance to pay my respects!" The Great Sage said: "It's not long, it's not long!"

He then continued on, straight into the depths of the heavens. The four valiant generals swept away the dust, rested, knocked their heads, and paid their respects. They all said: "How many years have you been the Great Sage in the heavens, actually taking on what position?" The Great Sage laughed and said: "I remember it's just half a year, how come it's talked about as one hundred years?" The generals said: "One day in heaven is equal to one year on earth." The Great Sage said: "It's fortunate that the Jade Emperor loves me, he has actually promoted me to 'Heaven's Great Sage,' set up the Heavenly Court, and established the Departments of Pacification and Serenity, and appointed divine officials and guards to serve.

Later on, seeing that I had nothing to do, he told me to take care of the Garden of the Peach. Recently, the Queen Mother had held a 'Peach Banquet,' and I wasn't invited. I went to the West Mountain and stole some of her divine foods and divine wine. As I walked out of the West Mountain, I tripped and stumbled, accidentally entering the Throne of the Old Master of the Teachings, and I also stole his five golden elixirs. In fear of the Jade Emperor seeing my transgressions, I've only just come out of the heavens."

But I was afraid even earlier. For instance, when my dog died. The same one who accused me utterly. He was very sick. I knelt beside him the whole day, when suddenly he barked, jerkily and briefly, as he used to when a stranger entered the room. A barking of that kind had been tacitly agreed upon in this case, and I looked involuntarily towards the door. But it was already within him. Unsettled, I searched for his gaze, and he searched for mine too; but not to bid farewell. He looked at me sternly and strangely. He reproached me for having let it in. He was convinced that I could have stopped it. Now it became clear that he had overestimated me all along. And there was no time left to clarify anything to him. He looked at me strangely and alone until it was over.

But I had been afraid even before that. For instance, when my dog died. The same one who, once and for all, accused me. He was very ill. I had knelt beside him the whole day when suddenly he barked abruptly and briefly, as he was wont to do whenever a stranger entered the room. Such a bark was between us a kind of agreed-upon signal, and I involuntarily looked toward the door. But it was already within him. Agitated, I searched his gaze, and he too searched mine; not to take leave of each other. He looked at me harshly and with a sense of distance. He reproached me for letting it in. He was convinced that I could have stopped it. Now it was shown that he had overestimated me. And there was no more time to explain it to him. He looked at me with a sense of distance and loneliness until it was over.

But I was scared even back then. For example, when my dog died. The same one who had me in his sights forever. He was very ill. I knelt beside him all day, when suddenly he let out a short, jerky bark, the way he always did when a stranger entered the room. Such a bark was agreed upon between us in this instance, and I looked involuntarily towards the door. But it was already there. I frantically searched his gaze, and he searched mine too; not to bid each other farewell. He looked at me hard and detachedly, accusing me of letting it in. He was convinced I could have stopped it. It now became apparent that he had overestimated me all along. And it was too late to set him straight. He looked at me detachedly and alone until the end.

But I was scared even before that. For instance, when my dog died. The same one who had blamed me for everything. He was very ill. I knelt beside him all day, and then suddenly he barked sharply and briefly, just as he usually did when a stranger entered the room. A barking like that was more or less what we had agreed on in that case, and I involuntarily looked towards the door. But it was too late already. I searched his gaze anxiously, and he too searched mine; but not to take leave of each other. He looked at me with a hardness and a distance in his eyes. He accused me of having let it in. He was convinced I could have prevented it. It then became clear that he had always overestimated me. And there was no more time to set him straight. He looked at me with distance and loneliness in his eyes until it was over.

But I was already afraid back then. For example, when my dog died. The one who accused me definitively, to be sure. He was very ill. I knelt beside him the whole day, when suddenly he barked on, jerkily and short, as he was accustomed to do when a stranger entered the room. Such a barking had been tacitly agreed upon for this case, and I looked involuntarily at the door. But he was already gone. I searched for his gaze, and he searched for mine too; but not to say goodbye. He looked at me sternly and with suspicion; he reproached me for letting it in. He was convinced that I could have stopped it. Now it turned out that he had overestimated me all along. And it was no longer possible to enlighten him. He looked at me with suspicion and loneliness until it was over.

— No, Constant wasn't there then; he was traveling with a letter... to Empress Josephine then; but instead of him, two ordinaries, a few Polish lancers... well, that was the entire entourage, of course, minus the generals and marshals, whom Napoleon brought along to survey the area, troop dispositions, and confer... Mostly Dau was with him, as I now recall: a huge, full, phlegmatic man in glasses, with a strange gaze. He consulted with him most often. Napoleon valued his thoughts. I remember they were conferring for several days; Dau came in the morning and evening, often even arguing; eventually Napoleon seemed to be agreeing. They were alone in the cabinet, and I was nearly invisible to them. Suddenly Napoleon's glance falls on me by chance, a strange thought flashes in his eyes. "Child!" he says suddenly, "how do you think: if I were to accept Orthodoxy and liberate your slaves, would the Russians follow me?" — "Never!" I shouted in indignation. Napoleon was taken aback. "In the eyes of this child, blinded by patriotism," he said, "I have read the opinion of the entire Russian people. Enough, Dau! It's all fantasies! Present me with your other plan."

— Ah, morality! I'm just a boy, I know it myself, — Ganya interrupted warmly, — and just that conversation with you is proof of it. I, a prince, am not going into this darkness out of calculation — I would have erred, probably, for the very reason that I'm still not strong-headed enough in my character and youth. I'm going in out of passion, out of impulse, because I have a substantial goal. You think I'd get seventy-five thousand and start buying carriages right away. No, I'd still be wearing the shabby old coat of a third-year student and would have thrown in the towel on all my club acquaintances. We have so few people with backbone, even though they're all usurers, and I want to have backbone. The main thing is to see this through to the end — that's the whole task! Pticyn was fifteen on the streets, selling matches with a pocket knife, starting from a copper piece; now he's got sixty thousand, but only after such a struggle. That's exactly the struggle I'll cut through and start with a capital; in fifteen years they'll say: 'There's Ivolgin, the king of the Jews.' You tell me I'm not an original person. Mark this to yourself, kind prince, there's nothing more mortifying for a person of our time and lineage than to be told they're not original, weak-willed, without special talents, and an ordinary person. You didn't even consider me a good scoundrel, and, you know, I wanted to eat you alive for it just the other day! You've offended me more than Epanchin, who considers (without hesitation, without enticement, in the simplicity of his heart, note that) me capable of selling him his wife! That's what's been bugging me for ages, and I want money. Once I make some money, you know — I'll be a man of the highest degree of originality. Money is the most contemptible thing of all, and it's even worse that it gives people talents. And it'll keep giving them until the end of time. You'll say it's all childish or perhaps poetic — well, it'll be more fun that way, and the deed will still be done. I'll see it through and stand my ground. Rira bien qui rira le dernier! 1 You've been offended by Epanchin because of malice, or why not? Never. Simply because I'm too insignificant. Well, then... However, I'm done, and I'm off. Kolya's already stuck his nose out twice: he's inviting you to dinner. And I'm going out. I'll sometimes drop by to visit you. You'll get on all right with us; now you'll be accepted as part of the family straight away. Just be careful not to blow our secret. I think we'll either be friends or enemies. And how do you think, prince, if I'd kissed your hand the other day (as I genuinely wanted to), would I become your enemy for it afterwards?

"Ah, morality! What I'm still a child, I know that myself, — Ganya interrupted hotly, — and you only had to have this conversation with me to prove it. I, a prince, did not come to this darkness for calculation, — he continued, wounded in his own self-esteem as a young man, — I would have erred, probably, if I came for calculation, being as unsteady both in my head and character as I am. I came from passion, from impulse, because I have a great goal. You think that I'll get seventy-five thousand and immediately buy a carriage? Pticyn, at seventeen, used to sleep on the street and traded with pocket change, starting from nothing; now he has sixty thousand, but at what cost! His sleep was fleeting; the deliciously uniform days were separated by short nights filled with happy unrest. Although he withdrew early, for by nine o'clock, when Tadzio had vanished from the scene, the day seemed to be over to him. But at the first light of dawn, a gentle and piercing fright awoke him, his heart recalled his adventure, it no longer allowed him to rest on his pillows, he rose, and lightly wrapped against the shivers of the morning, he sat by the open window, awaiting the rising of the sun. The wonderful event filled his soul consecrated to sleep with reverence. The sky, earth, and sea still lay in a ghostly, glassy dawn-blaze; still a passing star swam in the void. But a trembling came, a report of unreachable dwelling places, that Eos was rising from the side of her husband, and that first, sweet blushing of the remotest heavenly and marine zones took place, by which the sensuality of creation reveals itself. K. stopped and looked down at the floor. He was still free, he could still continue on and slip through one of the three small, dark wooden doors in front of him. It would only mean that he hadn't understood, or that he had understood but didn't care. If the priest had called out again, K. would certainly have gone, but since everything remained silent as long as K. waited, he did turn his head a little, since he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He stood still on the pulpit, just as he had before, but it was clear that he had noticed K's head movement. It would have been a childlike game of hide-and-seek if K. hadn't turned completely around. He did and was beckoned closer by the priest with a flick of his finger. Since everything could now be openly done, he walked – he did it out of curiosity and to cut the matter short – towards the pulpit with long, flying strides. He stopped at the first pews, but the priest thought the distance was still too great, so he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply pointed finger at a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. followed him in this too, he had to bend his head back far to see the priest at that spot. "You are Josef K.," the priest said and raised a hand on the railing in an indefinite movement. "Yes," K. said, thinking about how openly he had always had his name mentioned, and how it had become a burden for him lately; now people he met for the first time knew his name, how nice it was to introduce himself first and then be known. "You are accused," the priest said particularly quietly. "Yes," K. said, "I have been informed of it." "Then you are the one I'm looking for," the priest said. "I am the prison chaplain." "Ah, so," K. said. "I summoned you here," the priest said, "to speak with you." "I didn't know it," K. said. "I came here to show an Italian the cathedral." "Let's not bother with trifles," the priest said. "What do you have in your hand? Is it a prayer book?" "No," K. replied, "it's an album of the city's sights." "Put it down," the priest said. K. threw it so violently that it opened and dragged its crushed pages across the floor. "Do you know that your case is going poorly?" the priest asked. "It seems to me that way," K. said. "I've made a great effort so far, but without success. I'm still working on the petition, though." "How do you envision the end?" the priest asked. "I used to think it would end well," K. said, "but I doubt it now sometimes. I don't know how it will end. Do you?" "No," the priest said, "but I fear it will end badly. They consider you guilty. "Sometimes and often I might agree with you," K. said, "but not always. Women have great power. If I could persuade some women I know to work together for me, I'd get through. "You are accused," said the clergyman especially quietly. "Yes," said K., "I've been informed about it." "Then you are the one I'm looking for," said the clergyman. "I am the prison chaplain." "Oh, so that's it," said K. "I called you here to speak to you," said the clergyman, "to talk to you." "I didn't know that," said K. "I came here to show an Italian the cathedral." "Leave the trivialities," said the clergyman. "What's in your hand? Is it a prayer book?" "No," replied K., "it's an album of the city's sights." "Put it down," said the clergyman. K. threw it so violently that it opened up and with crumpled pages slid a piece across the floor. "Do you know that your case is in a bad state?" the clergyman asked. "It seems to me so too," said K. "I've made a lot of effort so far, but without success. I'm still working on the application, though." "How do you see the end?" asked the clergyman. "Earlier I thought it would end well," said K., "now I sometimes doubt it myself. I don't know how it will end. Do you?" "No," said the clergyman, "but I fear it will end badly. You're considered guilty. Your case may not even make it out of the lower court. At least, your guilt is considered proven for the time being." "I'm not guilty," said K., "it's a mistake. How can a man be guilty at all? We're all human beings, one as another." "That's true," said the clergyman, "but the guilty usually talk like that." "Do you have a prejudice against me?" K. asked. "I have no prejudice against you," said the clergyman. "I'm grateful to you," said K., "but everyone else involved in the proceedings has a prejudice against me. They instill it in the uninvolved as well. My situation is getting more complicated." "You're misunderstanding the facts," said the clergyman, "the verdict doesn't come all at once; the proceedings gradually lead to the verdict." "So that's it," said K. and lowered his head "What do you plan to do in your case next?" asked the clergyman. "I want to seek help," said K. and raised his head to see how the clergyman judged him. "There are certain possibilities I haven't yet used." "You're seeking too much outside help," said the clergyman disapprovingly, "and especially from women. Don't you realize that it's not true help?" "Sometimes and often I could agree with you," said K., "but not always. Women have great power. If I could convince some women I know to work together for me, I might get ahead. Especially in this court, which is almost entirely composed of hunting women. Show the examining magistrate a woman from afar, and he'll run to get here on time, and jump over the court table and the accused." The clergyman leaned his head towards the railing; now the roof of the pulpit was pushing down on him. What kind of storm must be outside? It was no longer a gloomy day; it was already deep night. None of the large windows' glass paintings was able to break the dark wall even with a glimmer. And just now, the church server began to extinguish the candles on the main altar, one by one. "Are you angry with me?" K. asked the clergyman. "You might not know what court you serve." He got no answer. "It's just my experience," said K. Above, it was still quiet. "I didn't mean to offend you," said K. Then the clergyman shouted to K. from below: "Can't you see two steps ahead?" It was a shout in anger, but at the same time like someone who sees someone fall and, because they are frightened themselves, cry out unintentionally and involuntarily.

Frau Margarete Brigge had always, as far as I can recall, been a tall, unapproachable elderly woman. I can hardly imagine her being any younger than the chamberlain. She lived her life right in the middle of us without paying any heed to anyone. She wasn't reliant on any of us and always had a somewhat aging countess Oxe, whom she had, through some act of charity, bound herself to without limit. This must have been an exception, for charity wasn't her style. She didn't love children and animals weren't allowed near her. I don't know if she loved anything else. It was said that as a young girl she had been betrothed to the handsome Felix Lichnowski, who then died a terrible death in Frankfurt. And indeed, after her death, there was a portrait of the prince that, if I'm not mistaken, was returned to the family. Perhaps, I think now, she missed, above this confined rural life that Ulsgaard had become with each passing year, another, shining one - her natural one. It's hard to say if she regretted it. Maybe she despised it for not having come to be, for having missed the chance to live with skill and talent. She had taken all this into herself and sealed it with many, stern, slightly metallic glinting shells, each of whose uppermost layers parted anew and coolly. Occasionally, however, she gave herself away by a naive impatience to be noticed enough; during my time, she could suddenly become engrossed in some clear and complicated way at table, securing the attention of everyone and, for at least a moment, making herself appear as sensational and captivating as she might have been in the grand style. Nevertheless, I suspect that my father was the only one to take these frequent mishaps seriously. He watched her, leaning forward in polite attention, and one could see how he offered her, in thought, his own, proper windpipe, and made it entirely available to her. The chamberlain had stopped eating, too; he took a small sip of wine and kept to himself.

He looked at her with a courteous inclination, one could see how he mentally offered her his own orderly trachea, so to speak, and placed it at her disposal. The chamberlain had naturally stopped eating by then; he took a small sip of wine and held back from any opinion.

Mrs. Margarete Brigge was, as far as I can recall, always a tall, unapproachable old woman. I can hardly imagine her as anything younger than the chamberlain. She lived among us, living her life without giving anyone the slightest consideration. She didn't rely on any of us and always had a sort of companion, the aging Countess Oxe, who had somehow tied herself to her with an unlimited debt of gratitude. This must have been an isolated exception, for showing benevolence was not her usual manner. She didn't love children and animals were forbidden to be near her. I don't know if she loved anything else. It was said that as a young girl she was betrothed to the handsome Felix Lichnowski, who then met a terrible end in Frankfurt. And indeed, after her death, there was a portrait of the prince, which, if I am not mistaken, was returned to the family. Perhaps, I thought to myself now, she regretted that in her life in the country, which Ulsgaard had become more and more rustic from year to year, a different, brilliant one had not come her way: her natural one. It's hard to say if she regretted it. Perhaps she even scorned it for having missed its chance, for not being lived with skill and talent. She had taken all this in and had coated it with layers, many of them, harsh, a little metallic, shimmering, with the topmost one of each layer emerging new and cool. Occasionally, however, she betrayed herself with a naive impatience, not being noticed enough; at my time, she would then suddenly choke on some striking, complicated way, which ensured the attention of everyone and made her, for at least a moment, seem as sensational and captivating as she might have been on a grand scale. Nevertheless, I suspect that my father was the only one who took these frequent mishaps seriously. He looked at her, bending over her, respectfully, and one could tell that he offered her his own, orderly airway in his thoughts, almost making it available. The chamberlain had, of course, stopped eating; he took a small sip of wine and kept to himself.
