Fathers and teachers, I ponder: "What is hell?" I reason thus: "Pain is that which cannot be loved again." Once, in an infinite existence unmeasurable by time or space, a spiritual being was given the ability, upon its appearance on earth, to say: "I am, and I love." Once, and only once, was given to it a moment of active, living love, and with it earthly life, and with life, time and dates; and what happened: this blessed being rejected the priceless gift, did not value it, did not love it, sneered at it and remained unfeeling. Thus, one who has departed from the earth beholds Abraham's bosom and converses with Abraham, as is indicated in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, and beholds paradise, and may ascend to God, but precisely because of this he is tormented: that he shall ascend to God having not loved, having slighted the love of those who loved. For he sees clearly and says to himself now: "Now I have knowledge and although I longed to love, there will be no impetus for my love, no sacrifice, because earthly life is at an end and no drop of the living water of life (that is, the earthly life given anew) will come to quench the flame of the spiritual thirst for love which now consumes me, since I slighted it on earth; there is no life, and there will be no more time! Although I would have been willing to give my life for others, but it is too late, because that life which could be offered as a sacrifice of love has passed, and now a chasm yawns between that life and this existence." They speak of the material hellfire; I do not investigate this mystery and I am afraid, but I ponder that if there was material fire, they would indeed rejoice at it, because, I imagine, in material suffering for a moment the most grievous pain of this spiritual suffering would be forgotten. And it is impossible to take away from them this spiritual pain, because this suffering is not external, but within them. And if it were possible to take it away, I imagine they would become even more wretched, because the righteous in paradise, beholding their pain, would forgive them and call them to themselves, loving them boundlessly, but in doing so they would increase their torments even more, because they would stir within them an even stronger flame of a responsive, active, and grateful love which is now impossible. In the timidity of my heart, I ponder, however, that this consciousness of impossibility might finally serve as a means of relief, because, accepting the love of the righteous with the impossibility of repaying it, in submission to this and in the action of this humility, they will finally find a kind of likeness to that active love which they slighted on earth, and some kind of action similar to it. I sorrow, brothers and friends, that I am unable to express this clearly. But woe to those who have annihilated themselves on earth, woe to suicides! I ponder that no one could be more wretched than they. We are told that we should pray to God for these, and the Church outwardly rejects them as it were, but I ponder in the secrecy of my soul that it would be possible to pray for them. Christ will not be offended by love, I confess to you, fathers and teachers, that I inwardly prayed for such throughout my life, and now every day I pray for them.

Zhang sighed, "Li Ding, these two lines of mine are just a trifling tune, not worth sharing with a lyre and a jade cup. Let's just read them out, and I'll see how well they match our fisherman's and woodsman's chat."

Li Ding replied, "Zhang brother, your words are most ingenious. Please, brother, recite them first."

"The boat stays in green water amidst the waves of smoke,
At home, I reside in the deep mountainous wilderness.
I especially love the willow bridge in the spring water,
And begrudge the rocky peak at dawn under the misty clouds.

The dragon gate's fresh carp are when cooked,
The insects' gnawing on dry wood scorched by the day's fire.
The fishing net can support me for many a day,
The burden of the pole for all my years to bear.

In my small boat, I lie back and watch the flying geese,
On the grass path, I slantingly listen to the lamenting wild ducks.
In the court of words, I have no niche,
In the ocean of right and wrong, there is little trace of me.

The silk on the riverbank is as if it's embroidered with brocade,
The stone axe on the stone surface, like a sharp blade.

Every autumn evening, I'm alone fishing, 
The spring mountain is quiet, without a soul meeting.

I trade the fish for wine and drink it with my wife,
The leftover firewood is sold, the pot is shared among the children."

The Master said: "Within the door of the Tao, there are three hundred and sixty auxiliary doors, all with their own correct fruit. Which one do you learn?" The Monkey said: "I rely on Your Reverence's intention. This disciple will incline my heart and listen." The Master said: "I will teach you the method of the door of the character 'Shu', what do you think?" The Monkey said: "How do you say it is the method of the 'Shu' door?" The Master said: "In the 'Shu' door, it is some that beguile sages to descend to fetch the phoenix, and ask for divination with the milfoil, to know the principles of seeking good luck and avoiding calamity." The Monkey said: "May one gain immortality by such means?" The Master said: "Cannot! Cannot!" The Monkey said: "Then I will not learn! I will not learn!"

Master: "In the gate of the 'way', there are three hundred and sixty sub-gates, and each sub-gate has a proper outcome. Do you not know which sub-gate you have studied?"

Monkey: "Relying on your honor's intentions. Your disciple will follow wholeheartedly."

Master: "I will teach you the way of the 'technique' gate. How is it?"

Monkey: "What is the way of the technique gate?"

Master: "In the technique gate, they are merely seeking to seek the aid of immortals, seeking the presence of benevolent beings, inquiring of diviners and reading stalks of divination grass to know the ways to seek good fortune and avoid calamity."

Monkey: "Will this kind of thing lead to longevity?"

Master: "It cannot! It cannot!"

Monkey: "I will not learn it! I will not learn it!"

The Patriarch said, "The door of the 'dao' has 360 subsidiary doors, and each has its own direct reward. I don't know which door you wish to study?" The Monkey said, "As for this, I rely on Your Holiness' will. Your disciple will listen with an open heart." The Patriarch said, "I'll teach you the way of the 'shu' door. How will that be?" The Monkey said, "How is the way of the 'shu' door?" The Patriarch said, "The 'shu' door contains some who summon celestial beings to fetch the divine birds, or ask to divine with the divining stalks, and are able to discern the principles of moving towards fortune and avoiding calamity." The Monkey said, "Can one gain eternal life by this way?" The Patriarch said, "No, one cannot! No, one cannot!" The Monkey said, "Not studying it, not studying it!"

Master Teacher said, "The door of the Tao has three hundred and sixty lesser doors, and each lesser door has its proper fruit.  Which one do you study?" The Monkey asked, "I'll follow your honored intention, master. Your disciple will listen with an open heart." Master Teacher said, "I'll teach you the way of the 'shu' door within the Tao. What do you say?" The Monkey asked, "How is the way of the 'shu' door?" Master Teacher said, "The 'shu' door is about asking the immortals to descend and asking the diviners to read the milfoil, knowing the principle of seeking fortune and avoiding calamity." The Monkey said, "This can get me eternal life?" Master Teacher said, "It can't! It can't!" The Monkey said, "I won't learn! I won't learn!"

The Patriarch said, "The door of 'the Way' has three hundred and sixty subsidiary doors, each with its own direct cultivation. Don't you know which one you're learning?" The Monkey King said, "I rely on the Master's meaning. I will wholeheartedly follow." The Patriarch said, "I will teach you the way of the 'skill' door. What do you think of it?" The Monkey King said, "How is the way of the 'skill' door described?" The Patriarch said, "The 'skill' door way involves going to seek immortals and requesting a phoenix to ride on, consulting a diviner and divining with an oracle bone to understand the principles of seeking good fortune and avoiding evil." The Monkey King said, "Will this sort of thing allow for eternal life?" The Patriarch said, "No, it won't! It won't!" The Monkey King said, "Then I won't learn it! I won't learn it!"

Aschenbach tried to intimidate him with his finger. "But I advise Kritobulos," he thought, smiling, "go on a year-long journey! You will at least need that much time to recover." And then he ate large, ripe strawberries, which he bought from a vendor. It had grown warm, although the sun was unable to pierce the haze that shrouded the sky. Lethargy ensnared the mind, while the senses indulged in the immense and numbing entertainment of the stillness of the sea. Guessing, inquiring as to which name it might be, one that sounded approximately like "Adgio," seemed to the serious man an appropriate and completely filling task and occupation. And with the help of some Polish memories, he deduced that "Tadzio" must be what was meant, the diminutive of "Tadeusz" and, in the call, "Tadziu" sounding. Tadzio was bathing. Aschenbach, who had lost sight of him, spotted his head, his arm with which he was pulling, far out in the sea; for the sea may have been shallow far out. But already concern for him was evident, already women's voices called out to him from the huts, again and again pronouncing this name, which almost dominated the shore like a rallying cry, and with its soft consonants and drawn-out, diphthonged "u" at the end, had something both sweet and wild about it: "Tadziu, Tadziu!" He obeyed, he ran, with legs splashing the retreating water and head thrown back, back into the tide; and to see the living figure, before-mannered and gentle, with dripping locks and beautiful as a delicate god, emerging from the depths of heaven and sea, and freeing itself from the elements: this sight gave mythological conceptions, it was like the lore of primordial times, of the origin of form, and of the birth of the gods. Aschenbach listened with closed eyes to this singing within him; and again he thought that it would be good here and that he wanted to stay.

"If we must bear the responsibility for carrying the luggage, then we must endure hardships and toil to be worthy disciples." Eight said, "Brother, look at how heavy this luggage is." Tang monk said, "Brother, since you and Sandy monk have been with me, I have not had to carry it myself, I don't even know how heavy it is." Eight said, "Brother, look at the tally: four wraps of yellow cloth, eight strands of twine, and three or four layers of waterproof covers. Not to mention the wooden shoulder pole, both ends of which have nails in. The walking stick is made of copper and iron, with nine rings, wrapped in rattan and woven fibers. Considering the weight of all this luggage, it's hard for an old pig like me to carry it every day, and yet I'm following the master, and you're doing labor for me!" Tang monk laughed and said, "Fool, who are you talking to?" Eight said, "Brother, I'm talking to you." Tang monk said, "It's a mistake to talk to me. Old Monkey only thinks about the master's welfare, and you and Sandy monk just have to worry about the luggage and the horses. But if you slack off even a little, the master will give us a good beating with a thick stick!"

"You are such a devout practitioner, you have to endure hardships and hardships to become a disciple." Eight said, "Brother, look at how heavy this baggage is." Sanzang said, "Brother, ever since you and Sha Monk joined me, I've never carried it myself, so I don't know how heavy it is." Eight said, "Elder brother, just count it with your eyes: four yellow silk pieces, eight-meter long ropes. And we have to be prepared for rain, there are three or four layers of cloth coverings. The bamboo pole is slippery, and we have to nail the handles. The copper-inlaid iron ring pole, the rattan string wraps a large bundle of goods. Like this, it's such a lot of luggage, how can Old Pig, one person, carry it every day, and you follow the master as a disciple, while I'm here to do the hard labor for you!" The Monkey King laughed and said, "Fool, who are you talking to?" Eight said, "I'm talking to you, big brother." The Monkey King said, "I've misunderstood you. The old monkey only worries about the master's comfort, while you and Sha Monk, just take care of the luggage and horses. But if you are even a bit careless, the master will give you a severe beating!"

"When it comes to carrying a heavy load of the Master of the Law, we must endure hardships and sufferings before we can become disciples." Eight Rules said, "Brother, look at how heavy this load is!" The Monk Sha Wujing said, "Brother, since you and the Vulture Transformation Heavenly King joined me, I have never had to carry it myself, I don't know how heavy it is." Eight Rules said, "Big Brother, count them for me: there are four sheets of yellow cloth, eight strings of varying lengths. We also need to prepare for rain, so we wrap it with three to four layers of leather. The poles are slippery, so we hammer nails on both ends. There's a copper-bound iron ringed staff and a rope woven with rattan and wicker. With so much luggage like this, it's hard for an old boar like me to carry every day, yet you're the disciple, and I'm the servant – following the Master around, and you rely on me for all the luggage and horses." The Monkey King laughed and said, "You simpleton, who are you talking to?" Eight Rules said, "Brother, I'm talking to you." The Monkey King said, "I see you said it to the wrong person. As for me, I only care about the Master's well-being, you and the Vulture Transformation Heavenly King are responsible for the luggage and horses. But if you're careless and neglect your duties even a little bit, it's the Master who'll take the rough end of it!"

It is no easy matter to be a disciple, let alone a master monk, you must be willing to endure hardships and difficulties. “It's a heavy load you're carrying,” Eight Rules said, pointing to the luggage. Monkey King said, "Brother, since you and Sanzang have joined me, I haven't had to carry a load myself, so I don't know how heavy it is." Eight Rules said, "Brother, take a look at the count: four strips of yellow cloth, eight lengths of rope, and three or four layers of oilcloth. And on top of that, the wooden pole is slippery, and we've got iron nails at both ends. And we've got a copper-joined iron shaft, wrapped with a bundle of woven reeds and a big cloth canopy. With so many heavy things to carry, it's hard enough for an old pig like me to take on each day, yet you've managed to find a master, and I'm the one doing the hard labor." Monkey King laughed and said, "Fool, who were you talking to?" Eight Rules said, "To you, brother." Monkey King said, "Oh, you were talking to me. Later Nikolaj Kusmitsch always assured everyone that on that Sunday evening, although he was understandably in a rather depressed mood, he had not drunk anything. He was therefore completely sober as what followed, if one can even call it that, took place. Perhaps he just dozed off a bit in his corner; one could think that. This short sleep initially brought him a sense of relief. I got mixed up with the numbers, he told himself. Well, I don't understand numbers. But it's clear that one mustn't assign them too much significance; they're basically just a setup by the state, for the sake of order. No one had ever seen them anywhere but on paper. It was inconceivable that, for example, a seven or a twenty-five would be encountered in a society. They just didn't exist there. And then there was this little mistake that occurred through mere absent-mindedness: mixing up time and money, as if they couldn't be told apart. Nikolaj Kusmitsch almost laughed. It was good when one got on to such a trail, and in good time, that was the important thing – in good time. Now it should be different. Time, yes, that was a painful thing. But did it affect him alone, didn't it also go like that for the others, the way he had found out, in seconds, even if they didn't know it?

When the Great Sage heard this, he chuckled to himself and said, "Good heavens! I, the Old Sun, can leap a distance of eighty thousand li with one somersault. How could I possibly be confined by such a small hand?" Suddenly he blurted out, "If you say so, may I take the lead?" The Buddha replied, "I agree! I agree!" He stretched out his right hand, and it expanded to the size of a large lotus leaf. The Great Sage put away his Ruyi staff, puffed out his divine might, and sprang upwards, landing on the palm of the Buddha's hand, saying, "I've gone out too!" You see him disappearing into the clouds, leaving no shadow behind. The Buddha looked on with his wise eyes and saw that the Monkey King moved forward like a whirlwind, never faltering. As the Great Sage traveled, he suddenly saw five scarlet pillars supporting a blue aura. He said, "This is the end of the road. When I return, I will have the Buddha bear witness that the Throne of the Palace of Sages is mine to occupy." He pondered for a moment and said, "Wait! Let me leave some signs first so I can negotiate with the Buddha." He plucked out one of his whisker hairs, blew on it, and said, "Transform!" It turned into a thick brush made of two horsetails, and he used it to write a line of large characters on the central pillar, saying, "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven has come and gone." Having finished writing, he retrieved his whisker hair. Then he unzipped his flies and let loose a stinky monkey pee at the base of the first pillar. He flipped a somersault in mid-air and returned to his starting point, standing on the palm of the Buddha's hand and saying, "I've gone out, and now I've returned. Tell the Jade Emperor to ask the Heavenly Palace to let me in."

That great saint heard the words, smiled knowingly in the darkness, and said, "This Great Buddha is truly quite dense! I, Old Sun, can leap ten million eight thousand li with a single somersault. How could he, with a palm no more than a circle of less than a foot, possibly not jump out?" He suddenly shouted, "If it's like this, can you make the decision?" The Buddha said, "I can! I can!" Spreading out his right hand, it looked like a large lotus leaf. The great saint retrieved the Heaven-Sent Staff, shook off his divine energy, and with a bound, stood on the Buddha's palm, saying, "I'll go out too!" You see him go one stretch of cloud light, with no shape or form, gone. The Buddha looked on with his wise eyes and saw the Monkey King moving like a wheel of wind, not stopping for a moment, just going forward. While the Monkey King was traveling, he suddenly saw five red pillars of flesh, supporting a green gas. He said, "This is the end of the road. On the way back, the Buddha can serve as witness; the Hall of the Spirit Heaven will be my throne seat." Again, he thought and said, "Wait! Let me leave some marks behind, so I can talk to the Buddha later." He plucked out a single strand of hair and blew a mouthful of divine breath, calling out, "Change!" and it turned into a thick black brush with two fine hairs, writing a line of large characters on the middle pillar: "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven, a journey to this place." After writing, he retrieved the hair strand. Then, without warning, he poured a splash of monkey urine at the base of the first pillar. He turned over and somersaulted and, in a straight line, returned to the place and stood on the Buddha's palm: "I've gone, and I've come back. You, tell the Jade Emperor to allow the Heavenly Palace to give me the throne."

Upon hearing this, the Great Sage sneered and said, "Your Maitreya is quite ridiculous! I, Old Monkey, can leap an incalculable distance with a single somersault. How could his palm, not even one foot square, not be able to jump out?" He then suddenly exclaimed, "If you say so, will you put it to the test?" The Buddha replied, "Agreed! Agreed!" Spreading out his right hand, which appeared as large as a lotus leaf, the Great Sage retrieved the Golden Rod, shook out his divine aura, and sprang upward, landing in the Buddha's palm, where he declared, "I shall leave too!" One could see that he vanished without a trace, leaving behind a trail of cloud light.

The Buddha, with his keen insight, observed that the Monkey King resembled a wind-swept chariot, ceaselessly moving forward. As the Great Sage moved along, he suddenly spotted five crimson pillars supporting a column of green qi. He said, "This is the farthest point on this road. On my return, the Buddha will bear witness, and the Hall of Elysium shall be my throne." Pondering for a moment, he then said, "Wait! I shall leave some marks so that I can discuss this with the Buddha." He plucked out a single hair and blew a mouthful of divine breath, saying, "Transform!" The hair transformed into a heavy, double-edged brush, with which he wrote a line of large characters on the middle pillar, reading, "Great Sage Equalling Heaven, once visited this place." Upon completing the writing, he retrieved the hair. Then, turning a somersault, he spat a piece of monkey urine onto the base of the first pillar. He turned over and leapt back to where he was standing before, in the Buddha's palm, saying, "I have gone and now I have returned. Teach the Jade Emperor to instruct the Heavenly Palace to grant me an audience."

The Great Sage heard this and, with a subtle smile, said, "The Lord Buddha is quite amusing! I, old Monkey King, will jump ten million, eight thousand li with one somersault. My palm, which is less than a foot in diameter, how can I not jump out?" He then exclaimed, "If it's really so, can you make a decree?" The Buddha replied, "It can be done, it can be done!" He stretched out his right hand, which looked like a palm-sized lotus leaf. The Great Sage put away the Magic Staff, puffed out his divine might, jumped up with a single bound, and stood on the Buddha's palm, saying, "I am going out too!" As he flew off, his path resembled a whirlwind, with no form and no shadow.

The Buddha, with his wise eyes, saw that the Monkey King looked like a windmill, moving steadily forward without stopping. As the Great Sage flew, he suddenly saw five red pillars, held up by a greenish-blue column of air. He said, "This must be the end of the road. From now on, I'll go back. I'll let the Lord Buddha bear witness, and I'll definitely be appointed to sit in the Palace of the Firmament." He then thought for a moment and said, "Wait a minute! I'll leave a few signs first, so I can have something to discuss with the Lord Buddha." He pulled out a single hair, blew a mouthful of divine breath, and called out, "Change!" It changed into a thick, dark, double-edged brush, writing a row of big characters on the middle pillar: "The Great Sage Equalling Heaven, made a passing visit." Having finished writing, he put away the hair. Then, without bowing, he urinated on the root of the first pillar. He flipped a somersault and came back straight to the Buddha's palm, saying, "I've gone, I'm back now. You teach the Jade Emperor to let the Heavenly Palace hand over to me."

The Great Sage heard this and smiled in secret, saying: "This Jade-Eyed One is very stubborn! My old Sun can jump ten million eight thousand miles with one somersault. How could his palm, not exceeding one foot in circumference, not come out?" Suddenly he spoke up, saying: "If you say so, then decide it!" The Buddha said: "Decided! Decided!" Spreading out his right hand, it looked like a lotus leaf in size. The Great Sage tucked away the divine staff, shook his mighty aura, and with one leap, stood on the Buddha's palm, saying: "I'm going out too!" One saw him gliding away in the clouds, leaving no shadow or form. The Buddha looked closely with his keen eye, seeing that the Monkey King resembled a whirlwind, rushing forward unceasingly. The Great Sage moving along, suddenly saw five vermilion pillars holding up a blue streamer. He said: "This is the end of the road. When I return, the Tathagata shall bear witness that I shall sit in the Celestial Palace." After some thought, he said: "Wait! I'll leave some marks here to talk with the Jade-Eyed One later." He pulled out one strand of hair, blew a breath of divine air, calling out: "Transform!" It transformed into a brush made of ink and two hairs, and he wrote a line of large characters on the middle pillar: "Great Sage Equal to Heaven, came to visit once." Having finished writing, he retrieved the hair. He then stood respectfully at the base of the first pillar and urinated. Folding his body, he performed a somersault in the clouds, returning to his former place, standing before the Buddha's palm: "I have gone, now I have come. Teach the Jade Emperor to let the Heavenly Palace grant me a place."

The heavenly edict arrived, and the Jade Emperor took it outside the Southern Heavenly Gate, and pressed down on the auspicious cloud, all the way to the Water Curtain Cave on Flower Fruit Mountain.  To the group of little monkeys, he said, "I am a heavenly messenger, with a heavenly edict in hand.  I have come to invite you, great king, to come out quickly!" The little monkeys passed the message layer by layer until it reached the deepest part of the cave, and said, "Great king, there is an old man outside with a document under his arm, saying that he is a heavenly messenger come from above, inviting you to come out as well." 

The Monkey King heard this and was greatly delighted, saying, "I was just thinking about going up to heaven a couple of days ago, and now there is a heavenly messenger here inviting me!"  He called out, "Quickly bring him in!"  The Monkey King hurriedly put on his attire, and the door was greeted with a warm welcome.  The Gold Star (Jade Star, the name for the star that is actually the planet Venus) directly entered the middle and stood facing south, saying, "I am the Venus from the Western Olympus, bearing a heavenly edict from the Jade Emperor, ordering you to ascend to heaven, to accept the heavenly register." 

The Monkey King laughed and said, "What a delightful surprise to see an old star arrive."  He ordered, "You, my attendants, arrange for a grand banquet to entertain him."  The Gold Star said, "The edict is in my possession, and I dare not stay long.  I ask you, great king, to come with me, and we'll wait until we are promoted to a higher rank before we explain it in detail."  The Monkey King said, "Accept my gratitude, sir!  I shall withdraw."  He immediately called his four martial heroes and entrusted them with, "You are to instruct the younger generation to be cautious and watchful.  Wait for me to go up to heaven and take a look at the road, then bring the others up to live with me as well."  The four martial heroes agreed to this. 

The Monkey King and the Gold Star took to the cloud tops and ascended into the emptiness, at that very moment: they achieved a high celestial position, a top-rank position in the Heavenly Register, listed among the Celestial Guard of the Clouds.  It is hard to say what rank or title they were given, let's wait and see how it unfolds in the next chapter.

The heavenly decree was received, so the Monkey King went out through the Southern Heavenly Gate, pressed down on the auspicious cloud, and headed straight for the Jade Screen Cave of the Peach and Fruit Mountain. Addressing the little monkeys, he said, "I am a heavenly emissary, bearing an imperial edict. Please inform the Great King at once!" The little monkeys relayed the message, one layer at a time, down to the deepest part of the cave. "Great King," they said, "there's a gray-haired old man outside, carrying a staff of authority, who says he's a heavenly emissary with an imperial edict, asking you to pay your respects." The Monkey King heard the news with great joy and exclaimed, "I've been thinking of going up to heaven for the past two days, and now there's a heavenly emissary to summon me." He ordered, "Bring him in at once!" The Monkey King hastily straightened his attire and attire, to receive the guest. The Golden Star stepped inside, stood facing south, and declared, "I am the golden star of the Western Heavens, sent by the Jade Emperor to bring an imperial edict of amnesty, summoning you to go up to heaven and receive the Register of Immortals." The Monkey King chuckled and said, "I'm deeply moved by the arrival of the celestial dignitary." He ordered, "Minions, prepare a banquet to entertain our guest!" The Golden Star replied, "The imperial edict is in my possession; I won't tarry. Please come along with me, and we'll discuss the details after the ceremony is complete." The Monkey King replied, "Thank you for the honor! Farewell! Farewell!" He called upon his four stalwart generals, assigning them to "cautiously instruct our descendants, wait for me to go up to heaven to take a look at the route, and then we'll all ascend together to reside in heaven." The four generals took note of the order. The Monkey King and the Golden Star shot up on a cloud, ascending into the emptiness, exactly that moment being: a high-ranking heavenly official, entering the ranks of the highest among the Immortals, and inscribed in the Roll of Honorable Clouds. But what official title he would receive is yet to be known; let's wait for the next installment to find out.

The Jade Star received the edict, went out of the South Gate of Heaven, pushed down the auspicious cloud, and came straight to the Water Curtain Cave on Flower Fruit Mountain. He said to the throngs of monkeys: "I am a heavenly emissary, bearing an imperial edict here. Please tell the King to come forth quickly!" The outside monkeys, one layer by layer, transmitted the news to the depths of the cave, saying: "The King, outside there's an old man carrying a scroll, saying he's a heavenly emissary who came from above, bearing an imperial edict asking you to come out too." The Monkey King heard the news and was overjoyed, saying: "I was just thinking of going to Heaven these two days, and it's the emissary who comes to ask me to go." He called out: "Quickly bring him in!" The Monkey King hurried to tidy up his clothes and welcomingly received the emissary outside.

The Jade Star immediately entered the center and stood facing south, saying: "I am the Western Star, the great white Jade Star, sent by the Jade Emperor with a decree of peace, inviting you to ascend to Heaven, to receive the Heavenly Register." The Monkey King laughed and said: "How wonderful that the elder star descended!" He ordered: "You little ones, arrange a feast to entertain him." The Jade Star said: "I bear the imperial edict, I dare not linger; let us please the King to go with me, and we'll discuss the details after we've been promoted." The Monkey King said: "I receive your gracious visit; I retire!" Immediately, he called the four bravest generals, saying: "Be cautious and teach my descendants; wait for me to ascend to Heaven and take a look at the road, then bring them up to live with me." The four generals agreed.

The Monkey King and the Jade Star leapt up into the cloud head, rose into the sky, and were just that: elevated to the high-ranking celestial position, inscribed in the List of Treasure in the Clouds. I do not know what official title he was given; let's hear it in the next chapter.

The Immortal handed down the edict, departed from the South Heavenly Gate, and descended upon the auspicious cloud, proceeding to the Water Curtain Cave on Flower Fruit Mountain. To the multitudes of monkeys he said, "I am the Heavenly Agent, bearing an imperial edict. I beg Your Majesty to hasten to receive the news!"

The news was relayed from one monkey to another, layer by layer, reaching the deepest part of the cave. They told Monkey King, "A gentleman has arrived outside. He is carrying an imperial decree and says he is a Heavenly Agent, come to invite Your Majesty to ascend to heaven."

Monkey King heard the news and was overjoyed, saying, "I have been thinking of ascending to heaven these two days, and now a Heavenly Agent has come to invite me. I am to be summoned!"

"Quickly bring him in!" he ordered. Monkey King hastened to straighten his clothes and attire. The Heavenly Agent promptly entered the middle, stood facing south, and declared, "I am the Western Celestial Jade Star, bearing the heavenly edict from the Jade Emperor to summon you, Monkey King, to ascend to heaven and receive the Saintly Records."

Monkey King laughed and said, "I am deeply grateful for the esteemed Star's visit." He ordered, "Young ones, make preparations for a feast to receive our guest."

The Heavenly Agent said, "The edict is in my person, I dare not tarry; I beg Your Majesty to accompany me. Let us ascend first, and only then discuss the details." Monkey King said, "Accept my thanks, I bid you farewell!" He immediately called his four loyal generals and entrusted them with these words: "Take good care of the younger generations, let me ascend to heaven and take a look at the road ahead, so I can bring you all along to reside in the heavens too."

The four generals acknowledged the order. Monkey King and the Heavenly Agent took to the clouds, ascending into the vast expanse above. At that moment, he was in the midst of the High Ascension's upper rank of Immortal Realm, with his name recorded in the Rolls of the Heavenly Ranks. He did not yet know what official rank he would be granted; we will know only in the next chapter.

The Golden Star received the imperial edict, went out of the South Heaven Gate, descended onto a cloud, and then onto the Water Curtain Cave of the Flower Fruit Mountain. He said to the numerous small monkeys: "I am a heavenly messenger, bearing a heavenly mandate; I beg you, King of the Monkeys, to hasten the announcement!" The small monkeys passed on the news, layer by layer, deep within the cave. "The King, there's an old man outside, carrying a deified document, saying that I am a heavenly messenger, bearing a heavenly mandate, come to invite you as well."

The Monkey King, hearing the news, was overjoyed, and said: "I've been thinking of going up to heaven for the past two days, but it seems there's a heavenly messenger come to invite me." He shouted, "Quickly bring him in!" The Monkey King hastily tidied up his attire and welcomed the visitor at the door.

The Golden Star stepped forward into the center, standing facing south and said: "I am the Western Pole Star of Gold, coming from the Jade Emperor to bring an edict of imperial mandate, ordering the Netherworld to send you to heaven to receive a scroll of sacred records." The Monkey King laughed and said, "What a grand occurrence it is for a great star to descend upon me."

He ordered: "My attendants, prepare a feast to receive our guest!" The Golden Star said, "The mandate on my person means I shouldn't tarry; I beg you, King, to go with me now, and after the promotion, we can take our time to discuss the details as well."

The Monkey King said: "I thank you for your honor, I take my leave! I take my leave!" He immediately called upon his four brave generals, saying, "Be cautious and convey the news to our sons and descendants, I'll go up to heaven to take a look at the route; then, I'll bring all of you up with me to live there as well." The four brave generals acknowledged their instructions.

The Monkey King and the Golden Star mounted a cloud and rose into the air, arriving at the heavenly realm, which is none other than the high-ranking position of the Heaven Immortals, recorded in the Cloud-rank List. It remains unknown what title or position the Monkey King would be granted; to be continued in the next chapter.

In the doorway of the conference room stood a young man, he was small, had not quite straight legs, and was trying to give himself dignity by means of a short, thin, reddish beard, in which he constantly ran his fingers around. K. looked at him with interest; after all, he was the first student of unknown jurisprudence to whom he had, as it were, spoken as a human being, a man who would probably also rise to higher official positions. Bodhidharma recounted to Tripitaka his three sons' dream words, and Tripitaka was pleased. He served them a meal of vegetarian food and gave Bodhidharma one silver ounce as a gift. Tripitaka declined the gift, saying, "It is you who has shown me mercy and agreed to escort me, so I am deeply grateful."  Bodhidharma and his mother wife could not persuade him to accept the gift, so they hastily made some coarse noodles and roasted bread, which they called Bodhidharma to eat and bid him farewell. Tripitaka was delighted to receive them.

With his mother's orders, the Heavenly Guardian led three family servants, each equipped with hunting gear, to accompany Tripitaka along the main road. They gazed at the endless wilderness and the wondrous vistas of the mountains. They journeyed for half a day, and soon came upon a massive mountain that really was as high as the blue heavens and steep and rugged as the towering clouds. Tripitaka did not take long to reach the mountain's edge. The Heavenly Guardian climbed this mountain as if he were walking on flat ground. As he walked halfway up, Bodhidharma turned around, standing at the foot of the mountain, saying, "Senior, you go ahead, I'll be returning."

Tripitaka heard this and dismounted his horse, saying, "I implore you, Guardian, don't be a bother to escort me further!" Bodhidharma said, "Senior, you don't know, this mountain is called Two-Junction Mountain, with the eastern half belonging to the Great Tang Empire, and the western half belonging to the Tujue territory. There are wolves and tigers in that area that do not submit to our rule. I also cannot cross the border. So you should continue on." Tripitaka was shocked, his hand and sleeve dripping with tears. As they were about to part, they heard a loud shouting from the foot of the mountain: "My master is coming! My master is coming!" This startled Tripitaka, who stood there in a daze, and Bodhidharma rushed to comfort him. However, they still did not know who it was shouting, and so the story will continue in the next chapter.

Buddha's disciple, Triangular, related to Tri-calm Buddha, the visions of his dream, and Tri-calm Buddha was pleased. He provided a vegetarian meal and gave Buddha one two-ounce piece of white silver in gratitude. Tri-calm Buddha did not accept the gift. The family once again implored and implored, and Tri-calm Buddha, ultimately, did not accept the gift, saying, "It is you who kindly showed compassion and took me on a journey; this has touched me deeply." 

Being left with no choice, Buddha's disciple and his mother and wife hastily prepared some coarse flour biscuits, ordered Buddha's disciple to go see him off, and Tri-calm Buddha happily accepted the offerings. Grand Guardian then received the order from his mother, called upon three house servants, each armed with hunting gear, and set off on the grand road, beholding the endless wild scenes and mountain vistas. They traveled for half a day, and on the opposite side, there was a great mountain, truly connecting the blue sky, steep and precipitous. Tri-calm Buddha did not take long to arrive at the edge of the mountain. That Grand Guardian ascended the mountain as if walking on flat ground. As he was walking halfway up the mountain, Buddha's disciple turned around and stood on the path below, saying, "Elder, you go ahead, I'll head back." 

Tri-calm Buddha heard this and slid off his horse, saying, "Don't go to the trouble, Grand Guardian, to see me on one more stretch!" Buddha's disciple said, "Elder, you don't know that this mountain is called the Two Frontier Mountain, the eastern half belongs to the territories of our Great Tang Empire, and the western half belongs to the territory of the Daxia people. Over there, the wolves and tigers are not subject to my authority, and I also cannot cross into their territory, so please proceed." Tri-calm Buddha's heart was filled with fear, and he grasped the disciple's sleeve and executed his hands, as tears streamed down his face. 

At the moment of farewell and entreaty, just as the two were parting, a loud shout like thunder echoed at the foot of the mountain, saying, "My master has come! My master has come!" This sent Tri-calm Buddha into a trance, and Buddha's disciple also stirred. However, they didn't know who was calling out, and the story will continue in the next chapter.

Master Xuanzang retold to Master Shishi his three mouths' dream words, and Master Shishi was pleased. He early provided a vegetarian repast and gave one tael of white silver as a thank-you gift. Master Shishi refused no gifts. His householder father again and again begged him to accept, but Master Shishi still refused no gifts, saying, "If you're willing to pityingly escort me for a while, that would be a great kindness." Master Xuanzang and his wife were at a loss and hastily prepared some coarse steamed buns and dry provisions to send him off, and Master Shishi was pleased to accept. The Guardian Master took his mother's orders and again called for the two family slaves, each carrying their hunting gear, to accompany him on the main road and view the endless wild scenery and magnificent views of the mountain ridges. After half a day's journey, they saw a great mountain opposite, truly towering up to the sky, precipitous and rugged. Master Xuanzang did not take long to reach the edge. That Guardian Master ascended the mountain as if walking on level ground. As he walked halfway up the mountain, Master Xuanzang turned around, standing by the road below, saying, "Master, you go on ahead, I'll go back." Master Shishi heard the words, leapt from his horse, and said, "I beg you, Guardian Master, not to trouble yourself to escort me further!" Master Xuanzang said, "Master, you don't know this mountain is called the Two Realm Mountain, with the eastern half under our Great Tang's jurisdiction, and the western half part of the Tangut territory. Over there, there are wolves and tigers that don't submit to our rule; I wouldn't dare to cross the boundary myself. You go on your way." Master Shishi was frightened, brandished his hand, grasped his garment, and shed tears he could hardly hold back. At the moment of urgent entreaty and parting, he suddenly heard a loud cry from the foot of the mountain, saying, "My master is coming! My master is coming!" It startled Master Xuanzang into a daze, and Master Xuanzang was shocked. It is still unclear who it is that's shouting; let's see how the story unfolds in the next chapter.

Buddhist Master Buddha-lantern told Tang Sanzang his three-day dream, and also reported it to Tang Sanzang, who was delighted. Early, he provided a simple vegetarian meal, and then gave a white silver ounce as a thank-offering. Tang Sanzang refused to accept any payment. The mother and wife of Bajin, all the more begged to be excused, but to no avail; Tang Sanzang just said, "As long as you're willing to show kindness and send me on my way, it's enough to show your great affection." Bajin and his wife had no choice, so they quickly prepared some coarse steamed buns to pack some provisions, and called Bajin to bid farewell to Tang Sanzang. Tang Sanzang was overjoyed and accepted the provisions. 

The Tower Guardian received the mother's order, and then called out two young servants, each of whom brought their hunting gear, and went along with him on the main road. The scenery of the mountains and wilds stretched far and wide, and the grandeur of the mountain peaks was sublime. After traveling for half a day, they saw a great mountain opposite them, one that truly touched the blue sky and was majestic and precipitous. Tang Sanzang took a little time to arrive at the foot of the mountain. The Tower Guardian ascended the mountain as if he were walking on flat land. Just as they were halfway up the mountain, Bajin turned around and stood at the roadside, saying, "Master, please proceed ahead, I'll return." 

Tang Sanzang heard these words, dismounted and said, "A thousand times thank you for the Tower Guardian's trouble, please do send me a bit further!" Bajin said, "Master, you don't know, this mountain is called the Two-Frontiers Mountain; the eastern half belongs to our great Tang, and the western half is part of the territory of the Tatars. On their side, wolves and tigers don't submit to our rule, so I won't be able to cross over; you must go your own way." Tang Sanzang was shocked, extended his hands, and with a sad voice pulled Bajin's sleeves, welling up tears. In the midst of their urgent entreaties to bid farewell, a loud shouting echoed from the foot of the mountain: "My Master's come! My Master's come!" It so terrified Tang Sanzang that he stood there in a daze, and Bajin struck him. In the end, they didn't know who was shouting and, therefore, the story will continue in the next chapter.

Monk Sanzang was at a loss, so he quickly made some coarse steamed buns and rice to take with him and bid farewell to Monk Tripitaka. After walking for half a day, they saw a great mountain across from them, truly a lofty peak that touched the sky and rose steeply into the air. Monk Tripitaka soon arrived at the foot of the mountain. The Captain of the Guards climbed the mountain as if he were walking on flat ground. When they were halfway up, Monk Tripitaka turned around, standing on the path below and said, "Elder, you should go ahead, I'll return." Monk Tripitaka heard him and rolled down from his horse, saying, "Please, Captain, don't put yourself out to see me any further!"

Monk Tripitaka said, "Elder, you don't know, this mountain is called the Mountain of the Two Frontiers. I too cannot cross the boundary. You should go on your way."

Monk Tripitaka's heart trembled and his hands shook. He grasped Monk Tripitaka's sleeve and collar, shedding tears uncontrollably. At the moment when they were about to bid each other farewell, a loud cry echoed from the foot of the mountain, "My teacher is here! My teacher is here!" Monk Tripitaka was dumbfounded, and Monk Tripitaka twitched. They were both unsure who was shouting and were left hanging in suspense, to be continued in the next chapter.

All these are the consequences of each individual's karma; do not attribute them to him.

The Saṃgha heard this and said, "Brother, is this dragon?" The Monkey said, "It is a dragon." The Ox said, "I've heard that in ancient times, dragons were said to have the power to spew out clouds and mists, scatter earth and scatter sand. They have the ability to traverse the mountains of Ba and cross the passes, and to stir up the ocean and churn up the sea. Why is it that this dragon walks so slowly today?" The Monkey said, "If you want it to walk fast, I'll teach it how to walk fast, you watch." Great Sage, the Monkey cracked his whip and the golden ring on the end flashed with thousands of colors. The horse saw the whip and was afraid, its four legs trembling like lightning, and it fled at a speed that left the old monk in the dust. The old monk, whose grip was weak, was unable to hold the reins, and the horse ran up the cliff, nearly falling to its death. Only when the monk finally caught his breath did he look up and see a cluster of pine trees in the distance, their branches shady and serene. A few houses stood hidden among them, their roofs leaning against the sky, the entrance shaded by a verdant cypress tree, and the surroundings dotted with green hills and bamboo groves.

I once carried a tray, some Bohemian crockery, what's this, smooth floors, slippery – so I'd slip right down! Suddenly my legs parted, the tray fell to the floor, and I fell down too: oh, and I was chased out! Suddenly a venerable-looking old countess took a liking to me: "the man looks respectable," she said, and she took me as a door attendant. It's a fine, ancient position: just sit loftily on a chair, put your foot on your knee, rock back and forth, and don't answer right away when someone comes; first spit out a loud phrase, and then let them pass or push them off the way you need; and for good guests, just click the tongs: that's it! – Zachar made a gesture with his hand like that. – It's nice to say so! But the lady turned out to be a disagreeable one – God be with her! She once peered into my little room, spotted a bedbug, jumped away, started screeching, as if I had invented the bedbugs! When a household is without bedbugs! In another instance, she passed by me and thought she caught the scent of wine from me – the fact is! And she fired me.

— Ah, so he settled in, as one would expect, a German, a merchant, to sit in the anteroom; everything was going smoothly, and he sent me to the buffet to serve: is that any of my business? I once carried out some fine, Bohemian-style dishes, or whatever you'd call them, with smooth, slippery tables – they almost had me fall! Suddenly my feet got tangled, all the dishes went flying off with the tray, and they crashed to the floor: ah, and they dismissed me! Suddenly a gray-haired countess happened to take a liking to my appearance: "He looks respectable," she says, and took me as a valet. A good job, an old position: just sit more importantly on the chair, put your foot on your other foot, swing back and forth, and don't answer anyone right away when they come in, but first snort and then either let them pass or push them out in the throat, as it suits you; and to good guests, I know, you need only nod with your finger – Zahar mimed a nod with his finger. – It's pleasant, of course! "How you all sit here!" exclaimed Leni, who had returned with the cup and stopped in the doorway. They were sitting very close together, and at the slightest movement, their heads would knock against one another. The merchant, who, aside from being small, also had his back crooked, forced K. to bend low in order to hear everything. "Just a little while longer!" K. called out to Leni in a warning, waving his hand impatiently, which was still resting on the merchant's hand. "He wanted me to tell him about my case," the merchant said to Leni. "Tell him, tell him," she said. She spoke to the merchant with affection, but also with a certain condescension, which K. did not like; he had just come to realize that the man had a certain value, at least he understood how to share his experiences well. Leni probably judged him incorrectly. He watched irritably as Leni now took the candle from the merchant, wiped his hand with her apron, and then knelt down beside him to scrape off the wax that had dripped onto his pants from the candle. "You wanted me to tell him about the itinerant lawyers," said K., and gently pushed Leni's hand away without saying another word. "What do you want?" "Perhaps he doesn't want to talk about it in front of Leni," thought K., mastered his impatience and forced himself not to interrupt him further.

K. turned around, just as the merchant noticed him, as he was about to get up. "Sit down," said K. and pulled a chair next to him. "Are you already an old client of the lawyer?" asked K. "Yes," said the merchant, "an extremely old client." "How long has he been representing you?" asked K. "I don't know how to say it," said the merchant, "in business legal matters – I have a grain business – the lawyer has been representing me since I took over the business, that is, about twenty years; in my own case, on which you are probably hinting, he has been representing me since the beginning, it has been longer than five years, yes, far longer than five years," he added, and pulled out an old wallet, "here I have everything written down; if you want, I'll tell you the exact dates; it's hard to remember everything. My case has probably been going on for a long time, it started shortly after my wife's death, and that is longer than five and a half years." K. leaned in closer to him. "The lawyer also takes ordinary civil cases, then?" he asked. This connection between the courts and law seemed to calm K. greatly. "Certainly," said the merchant, and then whispered to K.: "They even say he is more skilled in these cases than in the others." But then it seemed he regretted what he had said; he laid a hand on K.'s shoulder and said: "Please don't tell me." K. patted him on the thigh to calm him down and said: "No, I'm not a blabbermouth." "He's actually vengeful," said the merchant. "Against a client as loyal as you, he won't do anything, I'm sure," said K. "Oh, but he will," said the merchant, "if he's excited, he knows no distinction; by the way, I'm not actually very loyal to him." "Why not?" asked K. "Should I tell you?" the merchant asked hesitantly. "I think you can," said K. "Well," said the merchant, "I'll tell you partly; you have to tell me a secret, so that we can hold each other back against the lawyer." "You're very cautious," said K., "but I'll tell you a secret that will completely calm you down. What's the disloyalty to the lawyer, then?" "I have," said the merchant hesitantly, and in a tone as if he were confessing something dishonorable, "besides him, I also have other lawyers." "That's not so bad," said K., a bit disappointed. "Here, yes," said the merchant, who had been gasping heavily since his confession, but after K.'s remark felt more trusting. "It's not allowed. And it's least of all allowed to take on shadow lawyers alongside a real lawyer. And I did just that; I have besides him five shadow lawyers." "Five!" exclaimed K., the number astonished him, "five lawyers besides this one?" The merchant nodded: "I'm negotiating with a sixth one right now." "But why do you need so many lawyers?" asked K. "I need all of them," said the merchant. "Don't you want to explain that to me?" asked K. "I'd be happy to," said the merchant. "First of all, I don't want to lose my case, that's self-evident. As a result, I can't afford to leave anything that could help me out; even if the chance of success is quite small in a particular case, I can't rule it out either. I've therefore used up everything I possess on the case; so I've taken all the money away from my business; previously, my office staff filled almost a floor; now a small room in the attic is enough, where I work with a young apprentice. This decline wasn't just caused by the removal of the money, but also by the removal of my own labor force. When you want to pursue a case, you can only deal with very little else. "Do you work at the court yourself, then?" asked K. "Just that's what I'd like to hear more about." "I can only tell you a little," said the merchant, "at first, I think I even tried it, but I soon gave it up. It's too exhausting and doesn't lead to much success. Even just sitting and waiting is a great strain. You know the heavy atmosphere in the law offices yourself." "How do you know that I've been there?" asked K. "I was just in the waiting room when you walked by," said the merchant. "What a coincidence that is!" exclaimed K., completely taken aback and having completely forgotten the previous absurdity of the merchant. "You saw me, then! You were in the waiting room when I walked by. Yes, I did walk by once." "It's no great coincidence," said the merchant, "I'm there almost every day." "I'll probably have to go there more often myself now," said K., "but I'll hardly be welcomed as honorably as I was that time. Everyone stood up; they probably thought I was a judge." "No," said the merchant, "we greeted the court clerk. We knew you were the accused. Such news spreads quickly." "You already knew, then," said K., "so my behavior may have seemed arrogant to you. Did you people talk about it?" "No," said the merchant, "on the contrary. But that's just nonsense." "What nonsense?" asked K. "Why are you asking?" said the merchant irritably. "You seem not to know the people there and might misunderstand them. You have to consider that in this case, many things come up again and again that are beyond the understanding, people are simply too tired and distracted for a lot of things, and so they rely on superstition instead. I'm talking about the others, but I'm not better myself. One such superstition is that many people want to predict the outcome of the case from the accused's face, especially from the shape of their lips. These people claimed that, judging by your lips, you would certainly and soon be condemned. I repeat, it's a ridiculous superstition and in most cases, it's completely disproven by the facts, but it's hard to get away from such opinions when you live among those people. Just think how strongly such a superstition can influence you. You did talk to someone there, didn't you? He could hardly answer you. There are, of course, many reasons for confusion there, but one of them was the sight of your lips. He later told me that he thought he could also see the sign of his own condemnation on your lips." "My lips?" asked K., pulled out a pocket mirror and looked at himself. "I don't notice anything special about my lips, and you?" "I don't notice anything either," said the merchant, "not a thing." "How superstitious those people are!" exclaimed K. "Didn't I say so?" asked the merchant. "Do they have a lot of contact with each other and exchange their opinions?" asked K. "I've kept myself apart until now," said the merchant. "In general, they don't talk to each other," said the merchant, "that wouldn't be possible; there are just so many of them. There are also few common interests. When a common interest occasionally arises in a group, it soon turns out to be a misconception. We can't achieve anything against the court together; each case is carefully examined individually. So we can't achieve anything together; only an individual occasionally achieves something secretly; only when it's achieved do the others find out; no one knows how it happened. There is no unity, we do meet occasionally in the waiting rooms, but we don't talk much there. The superstitious opinions have been around for a long time and are even spreading on their own." "I saw the gentlemen in the waiting room," said K., "their waiting seemed so pointless to me." "The waiting isn't pointless," said the merchant, "the pointlessness is only in independent action. I said that I have now besides this lawyer five other lawyers. One should think, now I can hand the whole thing over to them; that would be entirely wrong. I can give them less, than if I had only one. You don't understand that, do you?" "No," said K., and laid a calming hand on the merchant's hand, "I'd just ask you to speak a bit more slowly, it's all very important to me, and I can hardly follow you." "Good that you reminded me," said the merchant, "you're a newcomer, a young man. Your case is half a year old, isn't it? Yes, I've heard of it. Such a young case! But I've been thinking about these things countless times, they're the most natural thing in the world to me." "Are you happy that your case is so far advanced?" asked K., not quite asking how the merchant's affairs stood. He didn't get a clear answer, however. "Yes, I've been dragging out my case for five years," said the merchant, and bowed his head, "it's no small accomplishment." He then fell silent for a moment. K. listened out for Leni, wondering if she might come. On the one hand, he didn't want her to come, because he still had many questions to ask and didn't want to be caught in this confidential conversation with the merchant; on the other hand, he was annoyed that she stayed at the lawyer's for such a long time, much longer than was necessary for delivering the soup. You look at this Monkey King, who, having parted the waters, went back to Iron Board Bridgehead, leaped up with a flourish. Just then, he saw four old monkeys, leading the rest of the monkeys, waiting by the bridge's edge. On seeing Monkey King jump out of the water, not a single drop on his body, shining gold, and walking up to the bridge, the monkeys were all taken aback and knelt down, exclaiming in unison: "Great King, you are resplendent! Great King, you are resplendent!" Monkey King's face beamed with joy as he ascended to the throne, placed his iron staff in the center. Those monkeys, not knowing what to do, all came to grab the treasure, but like a cicada bumping into an iron tree, they could not even budge it. One after another, they bit their fingers and stuck out their tongues, saying: "Grandpa! This is heavy! How did you manage to carry it?" Monkey King stepped forward, extended his hand, and gave a big wave, chuckling and said: "Each thing has its owner. This treasure has been sealed within the Ocean of Treasures for several thousand or hundreds of years, and only now, with the current year shining brightly, the Dragon King thought it was just a piece of black iron, and called it the Treasure of the Divine Bottom of the Heavenly River. They all couldn't carry it, so I went there personally to fetch it. At the time, this treasure was over two yards long and thick as a load; I gave it a wave, and it seemed a bit smaller; I gave it a wave again, and it seemed even smaller; I gave it another wave, and it was even smaller still; I glanced up at the heavens, and on a line of characters, it read: 'The As-You-Please Golden Lock Staff, one million three thousand five hundred jin.' You all stand aside, wait for me to change it again for you to see." He flipped the treasure around in his hand and said, "Small! Small! Small!" It immediately transformed into something resembling a tiny needle with embroidery, small enough to be inserted into one's ear. The monkeys were amazed and shouted: "Great King! Take it out to play some more!" Monkey King took it out of his ear and placed it on his palm, saying: "Big! Big! Big!" And it suddenly expanded to the original size, over two yards long and thick as a load. He was in high spirits and jumped up onto the bridge, then stepped out of the cave, holding the treasure in his hand, employing the celestial-like divine power, he bent his waist and said, "Long!" It instantly grew as tall as ten thousand feet, his head like Mount Tai, his waist as steep as a mountain ridge, his eyes like lightning, his mouth like a bloody cauldron, his teeth like a scimitar; the iron staff in his hand stretched to the 33 heavens above and reached the 18th layer of hell below, striking awe into all the tigers, leopards, wolves, and other demons, who were hiding in the mountains and the 72 caves, as well as all the 72 grotto-heaven kings, so they all bowed down in submission, trembling and frightened, their spirits shattered and souls flying away. He then stored away the divine form, and turned the treasure back into a needle with embroidery, which he then hid in his ear, and returned to his lair. The various grotto-heaven kings all came to congratulate him.

"First of all, whence came the possibility of such a suspicion?" began Ippolit Kirillovich, addressing himself to this question. "The first person to shout that he had killed Smerdyakov was the accused himself in the very moment of his arrest, and yet he had presented not a single fact from the first cry to the present moment of trial, not only a fact, but even some kind of reasonable hint at a fact. Then three people confirm the accusation: both the accused's brothers and Madam Svetlova. However, the elder brother of the accused declared his suspicion only today, in a state of incontestable frenzy and delirium, and until now, for two months as we know, he had absolutely shared the conviction of his brother's guilt and did not even think of contradicting this idea. But we'll delve into this later. Then the younger brother of the accused announced yesterday that he had not the slightest facts to confirm his opinion of Smerdyakov's guilt, but only concluded thus from what the accused had said and 'from the expression on his face' – yes, that was a colossal proof that was twice stated yesterday by his brother. And Madam Svetlova expressed herself even more colossally: "Whatever the accused says, believe it, he is not the kind of person to lie." These are all the factual evidence against Smerdyakov from these three people who are too interested in the accused's fate. And yet the accusation against Smerdyakov has been going on and holding up – can this be believed? Can one imagine it?"

The Great Saint took a sip, and then exclaimed with a yawn, "Not good! Not good!" The generals Crank and Bash both said, "The Great Saint was in the Heavenly Palace, drinking elixir and feasting on divine dishes. It's natural that the coconut wine wouldn't be to his taste. As the saying goes, 'Beauty is relative; what's pleasing to one may not be pleasing to another.' What you locals like or dislike is a matter of personal taste."

The Great Saint said, "You are all 'people from the hometown,' the same hometown, so you share a liking for what's native to it. This morning when I was dining at the Jade Pool, I saw rows of jugs and vats of jade liquid and jujube wine under a long corridor. You haven't even tasted any of it. Wait for me to sneak some back, and we'll each have a half cup, and you'll all live forever young." The monkeys were overjoyed.

The Great Saint stepped out of the cave entrance, somersaulted, and made himself invisible with a puff of cloud, then directly arrived at the Peach Garden. He entered the Jade Pool palace gates, but saw that the craftsmen who brewed the wine, the waiters who served the intoxicants, the ones who drew water, and the firewood collectors were all fast asleep, still in a snore. He took two large ones from underneath each of their arms and carried two in each hand, and then flipped back with a change of cloud direction, returning to the monkey gathering in the cave. He held an impromptu "Elixir Feast" with the monkeys, and they each had a few cups, rejoicing beyond measure.

They laughed and, of course, baptised the poor little boy. Grigory prayed at the font fervently, but his opinion of the newborn hadn't changed. For several years, the Indian cholera had shown an intensified tendency towards spreading and wandering. Bred in the warm marshes of the Ganges Delta, having risen with the mephitic breath of that luxuriant but untouristed primordial wilderness and island wilderness, whose interior was shrouded in bamboo thickets where the tiger lairs, the disease had been raging all over Hindustan, exceptionally violent, persisting. It had already extended east to China, west to Afghanistan and Persia and, following the main caravan routes, had brought its terrors as far as Astrakhan, yes, even to Moscow. But while Europe shuddered at the specter of it and of its arrival on land, it had, almost simultaneously, emerged in several Mediterranean ports, was spotted in Toulon and Malaga, revealed itself several times in Palermo and Naples, and seemed from Calabria and Apulia not to be willing to yield at all. The northern part of the peninsula was spared, however. Yet in the middle of May of this year, one found in Venice, on the same day, the frightful Vibrio in the emaciated, blackened corpses of a waterman and a silk merchant. The cases were hushed up. But after a week, there were ten, twenty, thirty of them, scattered throughout different quarters. A man from the Austrian province who had stayed in Venice for his own amusement died back in his hometown, after unmistakable symptoms, and so it came to pass that the first rumors of the plague's arrival in the lagoon city reached German newspapers. The authorities of Venice claimed that the city's health situation had never been better and took the necessary measures to combat it. But probably foodstuffs had been infected. Vegetables, meat or milk, for denied and concealed, death devoured itself in the narrow alleys, and the early onset of the summer heat, which warmed the water in the canals soothingly, was particularly favorable to its spread. Yes, it seemed as if the disease had recovered its strength, as if the tenacity and fertility of its germs had doubled. Cases of recovery were extremely rare; eighty per cent of those infected died and did so in an agonizing way, for the illness manifested itself with utmost ferocity and often took on its most deadly form, which is known as "dry" cholera. In this case, the body was unable to expel the copious fluid mass released from the blood vessels; within a few hours, the patient dehydrated and suffocated in spasms and hoarse cries, heaving. Fortunate him if, as occasionally happened, the onset followed mild initial suffering in the form of a deep faint, from which he did not wake up anymore, or hardly at all. By early June, the isolation barracks of the Ospedale civico were filled in silence, and it was starting to be short on space in the two orphanages, and a ghastly busy traffic dominated the quay of the new foundations and San Michele, the cemetery island. But the fear of general harm, the consideration for the recently opened art exhibition in the public gardens, the massive scale of the collapses that would be threatened if panic and the resulting bad reputation hit hotels, businesses, and the entire diverse foreign trade, proved to be more powerful in the city than truthfulness and respect for international agreements; it enabled the authorities to obstinately maintain their policy of concealment and denial. The chief sanitary official of Venice, a man of merit, was outraged and stepped down from his post and was quietly replaced by a more complaisant personality. The people knew that, and the corruption of the ruling elite, combined with the prevailing uncertainty, the state of emergency into which the impending death had cast the city, produced a certain loosening of morals among the lower classes, an encouragement of the more questionable and antisocial inclinations that manifested themselves in excessive drinking, shamelessness, and growing criminality. In the evenings, one often noticed many drunken men; according to rumors, villainous ruffians made the streets unsafe at night; there were repeated instances of robbery and even murder, for it had already been proven twice that people allegedly succumbed to the disease were actually poisoned by their own relatives, and the rampant lewdness took on an impudent and profligate form that was unknown in this place and only to be found in the south of the land and the Orient.

He had already taken a step towards the stairs, when suddenly new footsteps were heard.

I spent a few hours a day at Dronningens Tværgade, in the cramped rooms that looked as squalid as all the rental flats where someone has died. I went back and forth between the desk and the large white tile oven, burning the huntsman's papers. I had begun to toss the envelopes, as they were bound, into the fire, but the small packages were too tightly wrapped and only blackened at the edges. It took me an effort to untie them. Most of them had a strong, convincing scent that impinged on me, as if it wanted to stir memories in me as well. I had none. It could happen that photographs slipped out, which were heavier than the rest; these photographs burned unbearably slowly. I don't know how it came to pass, but suddenly I imagined it could be Ingeborg's picture among them. But each time I looked, they were ripe, magnificent, unmistakably beautiful women, who put me on other thoughts. It turned out that I wasn't completely without memories after all. Exactly such eyes were the ones in which I sometimes found myself when, at the time when I was growing up, I walked with my father across the street. Then they could surround me with a gaze from within a car interior, from which it was hard to escape. Now I knew that they compared me to him back then and that the comparison didn't go in my favor. Certainly not, the huntsman didn't have comparisons to fear.

Sometimes he thought she was holding back too much, restraining herself too much, and this frightened him. Indeed, he had tried not to think about it all these days, chasing away those heavy thoughts, but what lay hidden in her soul? This question had long been tormenting him, although he believed in her soul. And now all this had to be resolved and revealed right this very day: a terrible thought! And again – 'this woman'! Why did he always think that this woman would turn up at the very last moment and tear apart his whole fate, like a rotten thread? He was so convinced of it, and this was something he was willing to swear to, although he was almost in a delirium. If he tried to forget her lately, it was only because he was afraid of her. Someone must have denounced Josef K., for without his having committed any crime, he was arrested one morning. The housekeeper of Frau Grubach, his landlady, who always brought him his breakfast at eight o'clock in the morning, failed to appear this time. This had never happened before. K. waited a little while, peeked from his pillow at the old woman who lived across from him and who observed him with a curious look, one that was completely uncharacteristic of her, then, simultaneously puzzled and hungry, he rang the bell. It knocked immediately, and a man he had never seen before entered. He was slender but sturdy, wore a tightly fitting black suit that was similar to traveling suits, with various folds, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, and therefore seemed practical without it being immediately clear to what purpose it was meant. "Who are you?" K. asked, and sat up half-reclined in bed. But the man ignored the question, as if one had to accept his presence, and merely said, "Did you ring?" "Anna is supposed to bring me my breakfast," K. said, and, initially silently, attempted through attention and contemplation to determine who the man actually was. But this man did not let himself be scrutinized for long, and instead turned towards the door that he slightly opened, in order to tell someone who was apparently standing just behind the door, "He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast." A small laugh from the adjacent room followed, it was not clear whether it was not several people involved. Although the foreign man did not learn anything from this that he hadn't already known, he nonetheless told K. in a tone of reporting, "It is impossible." "That would be new," said K., "and sprang out of bed and quickly put on his trousers. "I want to see what kind of people are in the next room and how Frau Grubach is going to account for this disturbance." It occurred to him that he shouldn't have said this out loud and that he was in effect acknowledging the foreigner's oversight of him, but it didn't seem important to him now. Still, the foreigner took it that way, for he said, "Would you not rather stay here?" "I will neither stay here nor be spoken to by you as long as you do not introduce yourself." "It was done in good faith," the foreigner said, and opened the door freely now. In the next room, into which K. entered more slowly than he wanted, it looked almost exactly like it had the evening before. It was Frau Grubach's living room, perhaps there was a little more space in this room filled with furniture, curtains, china, and photographs than usual, one could not tell, especially as the main change in the presence of a man was best understood, who sat with a book at the open window, looking up from it. "You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you so?" "Yes, what do you want?" K. said, and looked from the new acquaintance to Franz, to whom he had been referred, and then back again. Through the open window one could see the old woman again, who had taken a position by the window on the opposite side in order to see everything still further. "I want to see Frau Grubach –" said K., made a movement as if he were tearing himself loose from the two men, who stood far away from him, and wanted to continue. "No," said the man at the window, threw his book onto a small table and stood up. "You're not allowed to leave, you're under arrest." "It looks that way," said K. "And why?" he asked then. "We're not authorized to say that," said the other. "Go into your room and wait. The procedure has been initiated, and you will learn everything in due time." "I'm going beyond my instructions," he continued, "if I speak to you so kindly. But I hope that only Franz hears it, and he is already friendly to you in defiance of all procedure. If you continue to have as much luck as you had in choosing your warders, then you may be confident." K. wanted to sit down, but now he saw that there was no place to sit in the whole room, except for the armchair by the window. "You'll see soon enough how true that is," said Franz, and walked along with the other man towards K. The latter towered significantly over K. and patted him on the shoulder frequently. Both examined K.'s nightshirt, and said that he would have to put on a much worse shirt, that they would keep this one as well as the rest of his laundry, and if his case turned out well, they would return it to him. "It is better if you give the things to us than to the depot," they said, "because in the depot there are often embezzlement and besides, after a certain time, people sell everything without regard for whether the relevant case has been concluded or not. And how long do these kinds of cases drag on, especially in recent times!
