Still at the beginning of the proceedings, Mrs. Rascolnikov fell ill. Dounia and Razumikhin decided it would be possible to take her out of St. Petersburg for the duration of the trial. Razumikhin chose a town along the railway line and close enough to St. Petersburg to keep an eye on everything and visit Avdotya Romanovna as often as possible. Mrs. Rascolnikov's illness was a strange, nervous one, accompanied by something like madness, or, at the very least, partly madness. When Dounia returned from her last visit with her brother, she found her mother already in a terrible state, burning with fever and raving. On that same evening, she agreed with Razumikhin that he would respond to her mother's questions about her brother, and they even concocted a whole story together about Rascolnikov's departure to a distant border of Russia, supposedly on a private commission that would bring him both money and fame. But they were surprised that at that time or later, Mrs. Rascolnikov did not ask them anything about it. On the contrary, she had her own story about her son's sudden departure; she told it with tears, describing how he had come to say goodbye to her, giving hints that she alone knew about many very important and mysterious circumstances, and that Rodion had many very powerful enemies, and he had to hide. As for his future career, she seemed to be convinced that it was inevitable and dazzling, once some hostile circumstances had passed; she assured Razumikhin that her son would be a man of the state, that his article proved it, and his literary talent shone brightly. She read that article constantly, sometimes even aloud, almost went to sleep with it, and yet she did not seem to be curious about where Rodion was now – despite the fact that they clearly avoided talking about it with her, which in itself was enough to set her imagination aflame. They began to fear the strange silence of Pul'heria Alexandrovna on certain points. For instance, she didn't even complain about not receiving any letters from him, whereas before, living in her provincial town, she had lived in nothing but hope and expectation of receiving a letter from her beloved Rodion as soon as possible. The last circumstance was too inexplicable and greatly troubled Dounia; it seemed to her that her mother perhaps sensed something terrible in her son's fate and was afraid to ask, so as not to learn something even more terrible. At any rate, Dounia saw clearly that Pul'heria Alexandrovna was not in her right mind.

One need not concern oneself with a high-ranking position to live in peace, for one's nature is as unyielding as a ten-li city wall. A ten-li city's high walls repel the barbarian invaders, a high-ranking position's words command reverence. It's rare to come across places that bring joy both to the eyes and the ears; I've experienced such places and repented, grateful to the heavens, the earth, and the divine. 

The two of them recited verses and made joint poetic allusions, then parted ways at some turn in the road, bowing their heads in farewell. Zhang said, "Li, you be careful on your journey! Look out for tigers on the mountain. If you encounter any danger, perhaps we'll see less of each other on the streets tomorrow!" Li Deng was incensed and said, "You wretched man, you're lucky I consider you a good friend, or else you wouldn't even think of messing with me. If I get injured by a tiger, I'll be the one to make sure you get swept away by the waves!" Zhang said, "I'll not be swept away by the waves for a lifetime." Li Deng said, "Heaven can unleash unpredictable storms, and fate can bring temporary good fortune or misfortune. How can you be so certain of avoiding harm?" Zhang said, "Even if you say what you say, you still can't fathom my circumstances. Unlike yours, which are beset with countless dangers, I can see what lies ahead and know what will happen. 

Li Deng said, "Your business is a gamble on the surface of the water, full of perils and risks, hidden and obscure – what could you possibly know for sure?" Zhang said, "You just don't understand. In the city of Chang'an, on the West Gate Street, there's a diviner who sells prophecies. I give him a gold-colored fish every day, and in return, he teaches me a technique, basing it on the stars and their movements. Today I went to see him, and he taught me to cast my net at the east bank of the Jingle River and cast my line on the west bank. I'm sure to haul in a full load of fish and shrimp by the time I return. Tomorrow I'll come back to the city and earn some money by selling it, then meet up with you, old friend." From that day on, they bid each other farewell.

Amongst the eight mountains, one disports himself at will; in the four seasons of the lake, he lets himself go to his emotions.  When chopping wood, it's the spirits that get excited; when fishing, there's no worldly thought. The wildflowers outside the gate are fragrant and resplendent; the waters are serene with the waves calm at the bow of the boat. No need to talk about the three higher positions; one's nature is as strong as a ten-li-long city wall. The ten-li-long city wall guards off danger and keeps out evil; the three higher positions proclaim joyful sounds.  It's rare to see a place as pleasant as Mountain Lu and Water Shu. He is grateful to heaven, grateful to the earth, and grateful to the divine. 

Two men each spoke their words and then linked verses together.  Wherever they walked, they bowed and bid farewell. Zhang said, "Li Brother, take care on the way! Be careful of tigers on the mountain. If you encounter any danger, it's not to be seen on the street tomorrow!" Li then heard and became enraged, saying, "You idler! How can a good friend curse my life for me? If you meet a tiger and get hurt, I'll have to deal with the calamity of capsizing the boat!" Zhang said, "I won't have to deal with capsizing the boat for the rest of my life." Li said, "Heaven has unpredictable winds and clouds, people have changing fortunes and misfortunes. How can you be sure of avoiding danger?" Zhang said, "Li Brother, though you talk this way, you still don't understand; I, however, know the direction of events. My livelihood is out on the water, extremely perilous and mysterious. Why can I be sure?" Li said, "You don't know. In the Chang'an city, at the west gate street, there is an astrologer who sells divination. I give him a gold carp every day and he gives me a lesson in a small corner of his sleeve.  According to the direction, he has predicted a hundred or a hundred and one things. Today I went to buy divination again, and he instructed me to fish at the eastern head of Jing River and to cast a hook at the west shore, and I'll surely catch a full load of fish and shrimp to bring back. Tomorrow I'll go to the city, sell my goods, and drink, then meet with you again." After that, the two men bid each other farewell.

On Mountain Path Eight we indulge our natures, by Four Season Lake we give free rein to our moods. Picking firewood has the succor of the Fairy clan, fishing in the whole lake has none of the worldly forms. Outside the gate, wild flowers fragrance is vibrant and beautiful, the boat's bow glides smoothly over the green waves. To rest easy, one wouldn't care about the Three Official's positions, as unyielding as a city wall ten li around. 

Ten-li city walls stand firm and tall, blocking off invaders, the Three Official positions reflect the grandeur of their voices. Mountains and waters in harmony are rare, to be grateful for heaven, the earth, and divine beings.

They had exchanged poetic phrases separately, as well as associated poems, when they reached that point where they parted ways, they bowed to each other as a sign of good-bye. Zhang said, "Lee brother, be cautious on your way! On the mountain, watch out for the tiger. If there is any danger, I'll see you less on the streets tomorrow!" Lee listened to these words and his face reddened with anger, saying, "You idle good-for-nothing! How could you, a true friend, curse me to death? If I get attacked by a tiger, you must certainly encounter a shipwreck!" Zhang replied, "I won't have a shipwreck for the rest of my life."

Lee said, "The heavens have unforeseen changes, and people have transient good and bad fortune. How can you ensure no accidents?" Zhang replied, "Lee brother, though you say such things, I still haven't grasped your intentions; rather, my livelihood is something I can grasp. So, I won't fall victim to such a thing." Lee said, "Your livelihood on the water's surface is very perilous and treacherous. It's hard to grasp anything." Zhang said, "You don't know this. In Chang'an city, at the Western Gate Street, there's a Mr. geomancer selling fortunes. I give him a golden carp each day, and he shares a lesson with me, using the [hexagrams] for both predicting the future and pinpointing benefits. Today I went to buy a reading, he taught me to cast my net at the east bank of the Jing River Bayhead and to fish on the west shore. I'm sure to catch a full load of fish and shrimp to sell and make a profit to drink with you when I come up to the city tomorrow." From that point on, they parted ways.

I inserted six rubles into the letter, sealed it and asked Apollo to deliver it to Simonov. As soon as he found out there was money in the letter, Apollo became more deferential and agreed to go. In the evening, I went out for a walk. My head still ached and swirled with yesterday's turmoil. But the closer it got to evening and the thicker the twilight grew, the more my impressions became jumbled and unclear, and the thoughts behind them grew increasingly confused. Something inside me refused to die, deep in my heart and conscience, and it manifested as a searing longing. I walked along the most crowded and industrial streets – Mещанские, Садовая, past Юсупов's garden. I particularly enjoyed strolling along these streets in the twilight, when the crowds of working people, with worried and angry faces, scurried off to their homes after a day's work. I was drawn to this everyday commotion, this sordid prosaicness. This time, however, the throngs of people on the street only irritated me further. I couldn't collect myself, couldn't find the end to it all. Something was constantly rising up in my soul with pain, and refused to calm down. I returned home, completely discombobulated. It was as if some sort of crime weighed heavily on my conscience.

Well, good, my angel, good! You decided that it's not a disaster that I couldn't get the money. Well, good, I'm calm, I'm happy on your account! Even glad that you don't leave me, the old man, and will stay in this apartment. Well, if you really want to know, my heart is overflowing with joy when I saw that you wrote so kindly about me in your little letter and paid me due tribute to my feelings. I'm not saying this out of pride, but because I see how much you love me, how you worry about my heart. Well, good; what do I need to talk about my heart now? My heart is on its own; but you, my mother, you scold me not to be timid. Yes, my angel, I'll admit myself that I don't need that timidity; and yet, at the same time, please decide for yourself, my mother, in what boots I'll go to work tomorrow. That's the thing, my mother; but the thought of such a kind of death can completely destroy a person. And most importantly, my dear one, I'm not crying for myself, not suffering for myself; it's all the same to me, whether I go around in piercing cold without a greatcoat and boots or in boots; I'll endure it all, I'll take it, nothing bothers me; I'm just a simple, ordinary man, but what will people say? My enemies, those wicked tongues, will all speak when I go without a greatcoat? After all, I'm walking around for the people too in a greatcoat, and I wear boots, probably, for their sake too. In such a case, my dear mother, these boots are necessary for me to support my honor and good name; in worn-out boots, however, both are lost – believe me, dear mother, believe my long experience; listen to an old man who knows the world and people, and not to some dirty gossipmongers.

A call from the next room startled him so that he slammed his teeth against the glass. "The warden is calling for you," it said. It was only the screaming that startled him, that short, abrupt, military screaming that he wouldn't have suspected from the warden Franz. The command itself was very welcome. "At last!" he exclaimed, locked the wardrobe and immediately hastened into the next room. There the two warders were waiting and herded him, as if it were only natural, back into his room. "What are you doing?" they shouted. "You want to appear in your undergarments before the warden? He will thrash you and us too!" "Leave me alone, the devil!" K. cried, already being pushed back to his wardrobe. "If you overpower me in bed, don't expect to find me in a suit and tie." "It won't do any good," said the warders, who always, whenever K. shouted, grew completely calm, yes, almost sorrowful, and thereby confused or, in a way, brought him to his senses. "Futile ceremonies!" he grumbled, but already lifted a coat from the chair and held it for a moment in both hands, as if he were holding it out for the warders' judgment. They shook their heads. "It has to be a black coat," they said. K. then threw the coat to the floor and said – he didn't even know in what sense he said it –: "But it's not the main hearing yet." The warders smiled, but stuck to their: "It has to be a black coat." "If that speeds things up, I'm fine with it," said K., opened the wardrobe himself, searched for a long time among the many clothes, selected his best black suit, a jacket coat that had almost caused a stir among his acquaintances because of its cut, now pulled out another shirt and began to dress carefully. In secret, he thought he had achieved a acceleration of the whole proceedings by making the warders forget to force him to take a bath. He observed them, whether they would perhaps remember it after all, but that never occurred to them, and on the other hand, Willem did not forget to send Franz with the message to the warden that K. was dressing.

"No use," said the guards, who became calm, yes, almost sorrowful, whenever K. shouted, thus confusing or rather bringing him to his senses. "Futile ceremonies!" he grumbled, but had already lifted a coat from the chair and was holding it for a moment with both hands, as if offering it to the verdict of the guards. They shook their heads. "It has to be a black coat," they said. K. then threw the coat to the ground and said – he didn't know in what sense he said it – "It's not the main trial yet." The guards smiled, but stuck to their: "It has to be a black coat." "If I hasten the process by doing so, it will be fine with me," said K., opened the closet himself, searched for a long time among the many clothes, chose his best black suit, a jacket suit that had almost caused a commotion among his acquaintances because of its cut through his waist, and now pulled out another shirt as well, and began to dress carefully. In secret, he believed he had achieved a shortening of the whole process by making the guards forget to force him to take a bath. He observed them, whether they might remember it anyway, but that didn't occur to them, whereas Willem didn't forget to send Franz with the message to tell K. to get dressed and send him to the overseer.

He was so startled by a shout from the next room that he slammed his teeth against the glass. "The guard is calling for you!" it said. Here, Hippolyte Kirillovich unfolded the entire picture of the accused's doomed passion for Grushenka. Here we have her own admission: "I – I laughed at both of them," she says. The old man, who revered money like God, immediately prepared three thousand rubles, just to have her visit him in his hermitage, and soon he was brought to the point of being willing to put his name and all his fortune at her feet just to become her lawful wife, if only she agreed to be his legitimate spouse. And here, in this month of hopeless love, moral falls, betrayal of his fiancée, and appropriation of his father's money, entrusted to his honor, the accused comes close to frenzy, to madness, driven by ceaseless jealousy – and at whom, at his own father! And most importantly, the mad old man lures and entices the object of his son's passion with the very same three thousand rubles, which his son considers to be his family inheritance, which his mother left him, and in which he reproaches his father. Yes, I agree, it was hard to bear! Even madness could have presented itself at that moment. It wasn't about the money, but with the fact that the happiness of the accused was shattered with such repulsive cynicism with these very same funds!"

A staff-bearing banner stands outside the cave entrance, inscribed with four characters: 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' It is a decree that bestows upon him that official title, and if we are not granted permission, we will have to assault the Palace of Supreme Treasure itself!" The Jade Emperor, upon hearing this, was astonished and exclaimed: "This monkey spirit dares to be so presumptuous! Order the multitude of generals to immediately put him to death forthwith." Just as he was speaking, a eunuch from the side stepped forward, saying: "The Monkey King only knows how to speak, but not how to gauge the size of the situation. If we launch a military campaign against him, we will not be able to capture him in one go, and instead will be incurring unnecessary losses. I beg Your Majesty to grant Your benevolence, and issue a decree calling for his submission. Let him be given the official title of 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' but only in name, without any actual power or authority; he can then be kept in custody to keep his wickedness in check, so as to prevent his conduct from becoming more audacious, thus bringing peace to heaven and earth, and tranquility to the nine seas." The Jade Emperor said: "How do you propose to call this 'having an official title without any power or authority'?" The eunuch replied: "The official title is indeed 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' but he won't be in charge of anything, nor will he receive any stipend. Let him be kept in confinement, and his rebellious heart can be tamed, thus preventing him from becoming more arrogant. Thus, the harmony of the universe can be maintained, and the seas and oceans can be kept clear." The Jade Emperor said: "I will follow your suggestion." He then ordered the edict to be issued, and once again entrusted the eunuch to convey it.

The Imperial Commander Li and the Third Prince led the army to the Hall of Elysium. The Imperial Commander Li presented the report, saying: "We were dispatched by imperial order to subjugate the rebel, Sun Wukong. But unexpectedly, his supernatural abilities are far-reaching, and we are unable to defeat him. We hope Your Majesty will increase our troops to destroy him."

The Jade Emperor responded: "You think this evil monkey has how many skills? We need to increase troops?"

The Third Prince approached forward and presented his petition: "I humbly request Your Majesty to pardon my death penalty. This evil monkey wields a iron rod and first defeated the Powerful God, then struck and injured my arm. A banner with the inscription 'Great Saint of Heaven' has been erected outside the gates. It is a formal announcement of his appointment to this office, and he will cease fighting and surrender; if not, he will attack the Palace of the Heavenly Jewel as well."

The Jade Emperor heard this and was astonished, exclaiming: "This evil monkey dares to be so arrogant! Order the generals to kill him at once."

Just then, the former Grand Marshal Tai Bai made an appearance and presented his petition: "The evil monkey only speaks bold words, but does not know what is trivial and what is significant. If we launch an attack and try to subjugate him, we may not be able to do so immediately, and our troops will only be wasted. It would be more merciful if Your Majesty would graciously issue an amnesty edict, and let him take on the title of Great Saint of Heaven. We can just confer on him the empty title, and let him live without a salary or benefits, letting him bask in the fields and mountains, so as to calm his evil thoughts, and thus bring peace and tranquility to the universe."

The Jade Emperor heard this and agreed: "How would you have him called the Great Saint of Heaven?" Tai Bai replied: "His title is Great Saint of Heaven, but without any actual powers, and without a salary or benefits, he can live in the fields and mountains, and his evil thoughts will be calmed, and peace will be restored to the universe."

The Jade Emperor issued a decree, which was then entrusted to Tai Bai to deliver.

It was then said that Emperor Li and the Third Prince, accompanied by the countless officials, proceeded straight to the palace of the Heavenly Sage. They presented their petition, saying, "We have been sent by the Imperial Decree to descend to the mortal realm, to subdue the demonical Monkey King, Son of the Heavens. Unbeknownst to us, his supernatural powers are boundless, and he has not been vanquished. We therefore beseech Your Majesty to command the dispatch of more troops to eliminate him." The Jade Emperor replied, "You mean that one mischievous monkey has such great abilities that we need to send more troops to suppress him?" The Third Prince approached closer and petitioned, saying, "We beg Your Majesty to pardon our past transgressions! That mischievous monkey brandished a steel rod, defeated the Great Sage of the Immortals, and even struck my arm. A flag was erected outside the gate, bearing the inscription 'Heaven's Supreme Sage.' It is a warning that he has been granted this title and is thus willing to surrender; if not for this title, he would even dare to strike the palace of the Celestial Treasure." The Jade Emperor heard his words, shocked, and said, "This mischievous monkey dares to be so arrogant! Command the officials to execute him at once." Just as they were speaking, the Star General White Star suddenly appeared from among the assembled officials and petitioned, saying, "That mischievous monkey knows only how to boast, but is unaware of the right and wrong. If we were to engage him in battle, we might not be able to subdue him, and would only be expending troops in vain. I beg Your Majesty to exercise compassion and benevolence, and send a benevolent edict to summon him. Let him be appointed the Heaven's Supreme Sage, but strip him of any power or position, and confine him in the open space between heaven and earth. This would keep his evil heart from concealing its malice and spare us from further anxiety. This would bring peace and tranquility to the world and purify the universe." The Jade Emperor heard his words and replied, "I shall follow your proposal." He immediately issued a decree and ordered White Star to deliver it.

Speaking of Li Tianwang and the Third Prince leading the generals to the Palace of the Gods, the officials in attendance reported: "We were dispatched by the Imperial Decree to descend into the mortal realm and capture the demonic Monkey, but to our surprise, he was powerful beyond measure, and thus we were unable to overcome him. We humbly request that the Emperor augment our troops in order to eradicate him." The Jade Emperor replied, "How could a demonic monkey possibly have such great abilities? Do we need to augment our troops?" The Prince stepped forward and reported, "I humbly beg for forgiveness for my transgressions! That demonic monkey wields a magical iron rod, and first defeated the Great Spirit, and then injured my arm. A banner stands outside the entrance with the four characters 'Zǐ Tiān Dà Shèng,' saying that he has been conferred this title, and that we should stop our troops and let him surrender; if not, we will batter down the Palace of the Heavenly Treasure." 

The Jade Emperor was shocked and said, "This demonic monkey dares to be so audacious! Order the generals to immediately put him to death." Just then, Tai Bai Jin Xing, from the ranks, suddenly appeared and reported, "The demonic monkey only knows how to boast, but does not comprehend the situation. To deploy troops to fight him would only lead to an unremitting struggle, and our forces would not be able to subdue him in the short term. It would be wise for the Emperor to show mercy and benevolence, and to issue a decree summoning him to submit. Let us just confer on him the title 'Zǐ Tiān Dà Shèng,' but strip him of his authority and not grant him official emoluments. Then, let him live in the void, and let his wickedness be stilled, so that the world may be peaceful and the heavens be clear and serene." The Jade Emperor said, "How should one call him 'with official title but no emoluments'?" Tai Bai Jin Xing replied, "He is called 'Zǐ Tiān Dà Shèng,' but he does not actually have any authority or emoluments, and is simply left to reside in the void. This way, his wickedness will not grow arrogant, and the world will be at peace." The Jade Emperor said, "This is as you have advised. I hereby issue a decree." He then commanded Tai Bai Jin Xing to take it away.

Just as they were drinking and celebrating, someone came to report: "Great King, there are two horned ghost kings waiting outside to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let them in." That ghost king straightened his clothes and rushed into the cave, bowing down on the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "Why have you come to see me?" The ghost king replied, "I have long heard of the Great King calling for the talented, but never managed to meet him; today I see the Great King conferring the Heavenly Canon, and I am overjoyed to return with great honor; I have specially presented a piece of cinnabar-yellow robes to the Great King to celebrate. I dare not be rejected as a humble person; if I am taken in, I can render the service of an ass or a horse." The Monkey King was greatly pleased, put on the cinnabar-yellow robes, and the others were delighted to form a line and bow in reverence; he then appointed the ghost king as the Commander-in-Chief and the Vanguard. After the ghost king had expressed his gratitude and finished speaking, he said, "The Great King has been in heaven for a long time, what office has he been entrusted with?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor favors the talented and has appointed me to the position of what 'Equine Servitor'!" The ghost king listened and then said, "The Great King has such divine power, how can he care for horses? Why not be appointed as the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven'?" The Monkey King heard this and was overjoyed beyond measure, exclaiming repeatedly, "Good! Good! Good!" He instructed his four brave generals: "Hurry and make a pennant with the four characters 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' set up the pole and hang it up. From now on, I am only to be called the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and not to be called the Great King. This decree should also be sent to all the ghost kings of the various caves, so that they know about it."

As they were drinking and feasting together, someone came to report, "The Great King, there are two horned kings of ghosts at the door, asking to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let them come in." The horned king came in, hurriedly removing his coat and bowing to the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What brings you here to see me?" The horned king replied, "I have long heard that the Great King is recruiting talent and haven't had the chance to meet him. Today, having been granted the Heavenly Classic, I've returned in triumph and come to offer a piece of cinnabar-colored robes as a gift, to celebrate with the Great King. Would you deign to take in a humble man, and allow me to render my services like a dog or a horse?"

The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the cinnabar-colored robes. The assembly stood in line and bowed respectfully to pay their homage. Thereupon, the Monkey King promoted the horned king to the position of Commander-in-Chief and Vanguard. The horned king expressed his gratitude, and then asked, "Great King, it's been a long time since You've been in heaven, what position were You given?" The Monkey King replied, "The Jade Emperor has slighted You and gave me the title of 'Protector of Horses'!" The horned king then said, "With Your supernatural abilities, how could You possibly tend horses? Why not just give Yourself the title of 'Supreme Sage of Heaven'?" The Monkey King heard this and was overjoyed, saying "Good! Good! Good!" and ordered the four sturdy generals, "Quickly set up a banner with the four characters 'Supreme Sage of Heaven,' and raise it on a pole to hang there. From now on, I'll be known as the Supreme Sage of Heaven and won't be called the Great King again. You may also spread this to the various cave-dwelling demons, so that they'll all know."

Just as they were drinking and feasting together, someone came to report: "Great King, there are two Horned Goblin Kings outside who want to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let them in." The goblin king hastily ran into the cave, and then bowed on his face to the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What business do you have with me?" The goblin king said, "For a long time I've heard of the Great King's call for the talented, yet I've never had the chance to see him; today I see that the Great King has taken possession of the Heavenly Script, and I'm full of joy and gratitude. I'd like to offer a cassia yellow robe to the Great King, to express my congratulations. If you don't reject this lowly person, and instead receive me, I'll be able to repay your kindness by performing the labor of a dog or a horse." 

The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the cassia yellow robe. All the others greeted him with reverence and lined up to pay their respects, and the Monkey King then appointed the goblin king as the Front Commander-in-Chief Vanguard. The goblin king finished his thank-yous, then asked, "Your Majesty, the Heavenly Script has been bestowed on you for a long time. What position has Your Majesty been given?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor has promoted me to some insignificant 'Arhat-protecting-the-horses.'" The goblin king heard this and then added, "Your Majesty has such divine abilities, how could you be in charge of raising horses? Why not just call yourself 'Equal to Heaven Great Sage' instead?" 

The Monkey King heard this and was filled with joy beyond words, and several times said "Excellent! Excellent! Excellent!" He ordered his four mighty generals, "Quickly set up a pennant for me, and on it write the four characters 'Equal to Heaven Great Sage.' Plant the pole and hang it up. From now on, I'll only be known as 'Equal to Heaven Great Sage.' Don't ever call me Great King again. You can also inform all the goblin kings in the other caves to be aware of this."

As the wine feast was in full swing, someone came to report: "The Great King, there are two yakssha princes wanting to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let him come in." The yaksha prince ran in, prostrating himself on the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What business do you have with me?" The yaksha prince said, "I have long heard that the Great King is inviting virtuous ones to serve him, but I had no opportunity to meet him; now that I have seen the Great King granting the heavenly book, I have great occasion for joy, so I offer this one cassia-colored robe to the Great King to celebrate the occasion. If the Great King is willing to accept this lowly person, I shall be able to work as hard as a horse or dog." The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the cassia-colored robe. Everyone stood in line to pay their respects to him. The yaksha prince was immediately enfeoffed as the Commander-in-Chief of the vanguard. The yaksha prince thanked him and then asked, "For so long, Great King, what appointment did the heaven grant to you?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor favors virtue and bestowed on me the title of 'Who-Knows-What-Is-Helpful-to-the-Horse.'" The yaksha prince heard this and then said, "The Great King has such divine powers, how could he take care of horses? Let's just call him 'The Sage Equal to Heaven.' What's wrong with that?" The Monkey King heard this and was overjoyed, repeatedly saying "Good! Good! Good!" and told his four vigorous generals: "Quickly get me a flag, write 'Sage Equal to Heaven' on it, and set it up. From now on, don't call me Great King anymore; call me Sage Equal to Heaven instead. You can also inform all the kings of the various demon realms to be aware of it."

As the banquet was in full swing, a servant came to report, "The Great King, there are two horned devil kings outside who wish to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Invite them in." The devil king straightened his clothes and rushed into the cave, prostrating himself on the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What business do you have with me?" The devil king replied, "For a long time I have heard that the Great King attracts talents, but never had the chance to meet him; now that the Great King has been granted the heavenly records and returned with honor, I specially bring a piece of vermilion robe to celebrate with the Great King. If you deign not to despise this lowly person, would you take him in and let him serve you like a dog or a horse?" The Monkey King was overjoyed, put on the vermilion robe, and all the others welcomed him with pleasure, lining up to pay their respects. Then the Monkey King invested the devil king as the Commander-in-Chief of the vanguard. The devil king finished his thanks and said, "The Great King has been in heaven for a long time; what office has he been given?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor favors virtuous individuals and granted me a position of what's-it-called 'the one who takes care of the horses'!" The devil king heard this and added, "The Great King has such divine abilities; how could he care for horses? Why not give him a title of 'He Who Equals Heaven' instead? Is there anything wrong with that?" The Monkey King heard this and was so pleased that he exclaimed several times, "Good! Good! Good!" He ordered his four loyal generals, "Quickly, set up a flag with the four characters 'He Who Equals Heaven' on it. From now on, no one is to address me as the Great King anymore; call me He Who Equals Heaven instead. Also, let it be known to all the king spirits of the other caves."

He walked for a long time down the long and narrow corridor, finding no one, and he was about to shout loudly when, in a dark corner between the old wardrobe and the door, he noticed some strange object, something that seemed to be alive. He bent down with a candle and saw a child - a girl no more than five years old, soaked, like a torn rag, in her dripping dress, shuddering and crying. She didn't seem to be frightened by Svidrigailov, but looked at him with dull amazement in her big black eyes, and occasionally sobbed like a child who has cried for a long time, has stopped, and then suddenly starts sobbing again. Her little face was pale and exhausted; she was numb from the cold, but 'how did she end up here? Probably she hid herself here and didn't sleep all night.' He started to question her. The girl suddenly perked up and quickly, rapidly babbled something to him in her child's language. There was something about 'mama' and that 'mama will beat' and some cup she 'shattered' (broke). The girl spoke without stopping; one could somehow guess from all these stories that this was a neglected child, whom a mother, probably a permanently drunk cook from the local inn, had beaten and intimidated; that the girl had broken her mother's cup and that she was so scared that she had run away the evening before; that she had probably hidden somewhere in the yard, in the rain, and finally slipped in here, hiding behind the wardrobe, and sat there in the corner all night, crying, shuddering from the dampness, from the darkness, and from fear that they would now punish her severely for it. He picked her up, went to his room, put her on the bed, and started undressing her. Her holey little shoes, on her bare foot, were so wet as if they had lain all night in a puddle. Undressing her, he put her in bed, covered and wrapped her up completely in a blanket. She fell asleep at once. Having finished, he again became gloomy and pensive.

He walked a long time down the long and narrow corridor, not finding anyone, and was about to call out loudly when he suddenly spotted something strange in a dark corner, between the old cabinet and the door. It looked like something alive. He bent down with the candle and saw a child - a girl, not more than five years old, shivering and crying in a soaking-wet, torn dress. She didn't seem to be frightened of Svidrigailov, but looked at him with a dull, blank stare from her big black eyes, and occasionally let out a stifled sob, like children who have been crying for a long time but are now somewhat comforted, yet still suddenly break into a sob. The girl's face was pale and worn; she had frozen with cold, but 'how did she get here? It means she was hiding here and didn't sleep all night.' He started questioning her. The girl suddenly came to life and rapidly babbled away in her childish language. It was something about 'mama' and 'mama will beat' and 'the cup she broke', 'the one she shattered' (broke). The girl talked without stopping; from all these stories, one could somehow guess that it was an unwanted child, a child whose mother, some drunk old cook, probably from this very hotel, had beaten and terrified; that the girl had broken her mother's cup and was so scared that she ran away even before dinner; for a long time, she probably hid somewhere in the yard, in the rain, and then crept in here, hid behind the cabinet, and sat here in the corner all night, crying, shivering with the cold, the darkness, and the fear that they would now really punish her. He took her in his arms, went to his room, put her on the bed, and began to undress her. Her boots, which she was wearing without socks, were so wet as if they had lain in a puddle all night. Undressed, he put her on the bed, covered her, and wrapped her up with her head completely in a blanket. She fell asleep right away. Having finished, he brooded darkly once more.

He walked along the long and narrow corridor for a long time, finding no one, and was on the point of calling out loudly when he suddenly spotted a strange object in the dark corner, between an old wardrobe and a door. He picked her up, went to his room, put her on the bed, and started undressing her. Her worn-out little boots were so wet as if they had lain in a puddle all night. After undressing, he put her to bed, covered her, and wrapped her all the way up in the quilt. She fell asleep at once. After that, he again became gloomy and lost in thought.

He walked down the long, narrow corridor for a long time, but couldn't find anyone, and was just about to shout loudly, when in the dark corner, between the old wardrobe and the door, he spotted some strange object that seemed to be alive. He bent down with the candle and saw a little girl, a girl of five years old, no more, in a soaked and tattered dress, trembling and crying. She didn't seem to be scared of Svidrigailov, but looked at him with dull amazement in her big, dark eyes and occasionally let out a sniffle, like children do when they've been crying a long time but have almost stopped and almost gotten themselves together, but suddenly let out a sniffle again. He walked down the long and narrow corridor for a long time, finding no one, and was just about to call out loudly, when, in a dark corner between the old wardrobe and the door, he noticed something strange - something that seemed alive. An hour went by before he appeared. People had arrived and were there, yet they had no hurry and were driven by impatience. The young Polish officers, patriotically dressed, and probably also stirred by the military bugle calls echoing from the direction of the public gardens across the water, had come on deck, and, carried away by their enthusiasm for the Asti, were cheering on the Bersaglieri exercising on the opposite side. But it was repulsive to see how their false community with the youth had reduced him to this state. His old head had been unable to keep pace with the wine like the youthful, robust men; he was miserably drunk. With a dazed look, a cigarette between his shaking fingers, he swayed, struggling to maintain his balance, back and forth under the rush, as if drawn by the din. Afraid to take a step and fall, he didn't dare to move from the spot, yet he showed a miserable recklessness; he grabbed anyone who came near him by the lapel, grinned, blinked, giggled, lifted his wrinkled, ringed index finger to absurd jesting, and with an abhorrent, ambiguous gesture licked his lips with the tip of his tongue. Aschenbach watched him with a frown, and once again he felt a sense of dizziness, as if the world was inclining towards something strange and grotesque; but he was held back by the circumstances, as the machine's pounding activity began anew and the ship resumed its interrupted journey through the San Marco canal, close to its goal. So he saw him again, that most astonishing landing place, that dazzling composition of fantastical architecture, which the Republic presented to the reverent gaze of approaching sailors: the Palace's light grandeur and the Seufzerbrücke, the columns with lions and saints at the shore, the proudly advancing flank of the fairy-tale temple, the view of the Torg and Riesenuhr, and, gazing upon it, he thought that to land on the mainland, to enter a Palace by a back door, and that one should not get there any differently than as he, as to ships, as over the high sea to reach the most unlikely of cities.

An hour passed before she appeared. One was there and not there; one had no haste and was driven by impatience nonetheless. The young Polishmen, patriotically dressed, and doubtless inspired by the military bugle calls that echoed from the direction of the public gardens across the water, had come on deck, and, their spirits inflamed by Astarte, cheered on the Bersaglieri drilling over there. But it was disgusting to see how their company with the young people had reduced this elderly man to a sorry state. His old brain, unable to keep up with the wine like the youthful and vigorous others, had him drunk to a pathetic degree. With a vacant gaze, a cigarette between his trembling fingers, he swayed, painfully holding his balance, from side to side, drawn by the roar. Since he would have fallen with his first step, he didn't dare budge, but showed a miserable bravado, grasping the arm of anyone who approached him, slurring, winking, chuckling, raising his ringed and wrinkled index finger in silly jest and, in a vile and ambiguous manner, licking his lip with the tip of his tongue. Aschbach watched him with furrowed brows, and once again a feeling of dizziness overcame him, as if the world was inclined, in a slight but unbridled way, to distort itself into something strange and grotesque; a feeling, however, that the circumstances prevented him from following, since the stamping activity of the machine had just started again and the ship had resumed its interrupted journey through the San Marco Canal. And so he saw him once more, that most astonishing landing place, that dazzling composition of fantastical architecture which the Republic presented to the reverent gaze of approaching sailors: the palace's easy grandeur and the sighing bridge, the columns with lions and saints on the shore, the proudly advancing flank of the fairy-tale temple, the view into the square and the great clock, and contemplating, he thought that to come ashore in Venice, to enter a palace through a side door, would be no different than how he had now, like a ship, as if over the high sea, reached the most unlikely of cities.

An hour passed before he appeared. One had arrived, but not quite; one had no hurry, yet felt driven by impatience. The young Polensers, patriotically dressed and likely moved by the military bugle calls echoing from the direction of the public gardens across the water, had come up on deck, and, inspired by Asti, were shouting cheers at the Bersaglieri exercising on the opposite shore. But it was revolting to see in what state the old man's company with the young had reduced him. His aged brain had been unable to keep pace with the wine, he was pitifully drunk. With vacant, bewildered eyes, a cigarette between his trembling fingers, he stumbled, laboriously holding his balance, in both directions pulled by the noise. Had he taken the first step, he would have fallen, so he dared not budge from the spot; yet he showed a wretched excess, clutched at the buttons of anyone approaching him, mumbled, blinked, giggled, raised his ringed, wrinkled index finger to silly banter and licked his lips in a disgusting, ambiguous way with the tip of his tongue. Aschenbach watched him with dark eyebrows, and once again a feeling of dizziness overcame him, as if the world were inclining, albeit lightly, towards the strange and grotesque; a feeling which, however, the circumstances prevented him from pursuing, as the pounding activity of the machine resumed and the ship, interrupted in its approach to the goal, once more took up its course through the San Marco canal. So he saw him again, that extraordinary landing place, that dazzling composition of fantastical building, which the Republic presented to the reverent gaze of approaching sailors: the light splendor of the palace and the sighing bridge, the pillars with lions and the holy at the shore, the pompously advancing flank of the fairy-tale temple, the view of the piazza and the giant clock, and contemplating, he thought that to arrive on land, to enter a palace through a back door in Venice, would be like arriving, like ships, by way of the high sea to reach the most unlikely of cities.

An hour passed, but she didn't appear. They had arrived and yet weren't there; they had no hurry, yet felt driven by impatience. The young Poles, patriotically dressed, and no doubt also inspired by the military bugle signals echoing from the direction of the public gardens across the water, had come on deck, and, their faces flushed with excitement, were cheering on the Bersaglieri exercising on the opposite side. But it was repulsive to see in what state his false camaraderie with the youth had brought the festooned old men. His old head had not been able to keep pace with the wine, he was pitifully drunk. With a vacuous gaze, a cigarette between his trembling fingers, he swayed, painstakingly holding his balance, forwards and backwards, torn by the din. But as soon as some trouble arose with his wife, a failure in his work, or a run of bad luck at cards, he'd feel the full force of his illness; he could endure these setbacks, expecting that he would soon set things right, overcome them, and achieve success and success in great measure. But now every failure demoralized him and cast him into despair. He told himself: I was just starting to get better, and the medicine was already starting to take effect, and then this wretched misfortune or unpleasantness... He grew angry with the misfortune or with people who were making life difficult for him and killing him, and he felt how that anger was killing him; but he couldn't help it. It seemed he should have understood that his irritability towards circumstances and people was worsening his illness, and that therefore he should pay no mind to unpleasant incidents; but he made the opposite reasoning: he said he needed peace and quiet, kept track of everything that disrupted it, and became irritated at any slight disruption. It made his condition worse that he read medical books and consulted doctors. His deterioration was going on so steadily that he could deceive himself by comparing one day with another – the difference was slight. But when he consulted with doctors, it seemed to him that he was sliding downhill fast, even very quickly. And despite that, he kept consulting the doctors.

- Ah, no, you don't believe me, I see that, you think I'm just a jester, spinning you harmless yarns, Porphiry burst out laughing, - oh, you're right, of course; I'm just as the Almighty himself has seen fit to create me: only comedies in others make me laugh; I'm a buffoon! [56] But listen, and I'll repeat it, Rodion Romanovich, excuse me, sir, an old man, still a young man of the first youth, therefore I value human intellect above all, just as the whole young generation does. The keenness of mind and the detached reasoning bewitch you, sir. And it's just as that former Austrian general, [57] for example, whom I can only judge by military events: on paper they beat and captured Napoleon, and then, in their office, they cleverly calculated and got it all sorted out; and yet, General Mack surrenders with his entire army! Ha-ha-ha! I see, I see, sir Rodion Romanovich, you're laughing at me, because I, a respectable man, keep digging up examples from military history. Oh, what can I do, it's a weakness, I love military matters, and I love reading all these military reports... I could have made a career in the military, really, I could have been a major, ha-ha-ha! But, anyway, now I'll tell you, dear fellow, the whole truth about that particular case: reality and nature, sir, are important things, and they'll catch even the most calculating person off guard! Come, listen to an old man, I'm speaking seriously, Rodion Romanovich (Porphiry, now barely thirty-five, has suddenly become an old man; his voice has changed, and he seems all crooked), - I'm an honest man, I assure you... Am I really an honest man? What do you think? It seems I am: I'm sharing these things with you for free, and I'm not asking for any reward, ha-ha! Well, so, I'll continue: cleverness, in my opinion, is a wonderful thing; it's the beauty of nature and the comfort of life, and it can come up with such tricks that even a poor, enthusiastic young fellow, who's carried away by his own imagination, as he usually is, and also naturally entranced by nature - won't be able to guess, even if his life depended on it! But nature helps the poor fellow out, that's the problem! And the young people who are so carried away by cleverness and "jump over all obstacles" (as you have so aptly and cunningly put it) won't even think about it. He'll, well, tell a lie, that is, a private individual in disguise, and tell it magnificently, in a most ingenious way; and here, it seems, is the triumph, and he should enjoy the fruits of his cleverness; but he trips over his own feet and falls into a fainting spell right in the most interesting, most scandalous moment! Well, suppose it's illness, or heat, which sometimes occurs in a room, but still! Still, he came up with an idea! He lied superbly, but he failed to calculate human nature. There, that's the cunning part! Another time, carried away by the jesting nature of his cleverness, he'll start to play pranks on the person suspecting him; he'll pale, just for show, just to play along, but too convincingly pale, too much like the truth, and then - he'll come up with another idea! Although he might fool you at first, but by the end of the night, he'll come to his senses, if he's not a total fool. And it's like that all the time! And what's more, he'll start running ahead, rushing in, where he's not even invited, talking non-stop about things he shouldn't be talking about, making up all sorts of allegories, ha-ha-ha! And then he'll come and start asking: why are they taking so long with me? Ha-ha-ha! And this can happen to even the cleverest person, to a psychologist and a writer! Nature is a mirror, the most transparent one, look into it and admire it, that's it! But what's wrong, Rodion Romanovich, have you gotten too hot, perhaps, or should I open the window for you?

– Ah, no, you, I see you don't believe me, think I'm just joking you with harmless stories, – Porphiry took up again, becoming more and more merry and constantly chuckling with pleasure, and again starting to spin around the room, – of course, you're right; my appearance is made by God Himself in such a way that it only stirs up comical thoughts in others; a buffoon!; but I'll tell you, and I'll repeat it again, that you, dear Father Rodyon Romanych, please excuse me, old fellow, that I, a man still young, or rather, of the first youth, therefore value human reason above all, as is done by the whole young generation. The agile wit and detached arguments of reason entice you – and this is precisely how the former Austrian Hofkriegsrat, as I can judge from military events, drew up battle plans against Napoleon on paper: they defeated him, took him prisoner, and then, in their office, cleverly calculated and planned everything out, and look, General Mack surrenders with his entire army, ha-ha-ha! I see, I see, Father Rodyon Romanych, you're laughing at me for such a state official as I, pulling examples from military history. What can I do, I have a weakness for military affairs, and I just love to read all these military reports... I would have fared better in military service, I must say. Perhaps I wouldn't have become Napoleon, but I would have been a major, ha-ha-ha! Well, so I'll now, my dear fellow, tell you the detailed truth about that particular case: reality and nature, sir, are important things, and how the most perceptive calculation can be thwarted! Hey, listen to the old fellow, I'm speaking seriously, Rodyon Romanych (speaking, barely thirty-five-year-old Porphiry Petrovich seemed to age suddenly; even his voice changed, and he hunched up somehow), – besides, I'm an open person – am I an open person or not? As you see it? It seems to me that I am: I'm sharing these things with you for free, and I don't ask for any rewards, ha-ha-ha! Well, so I'll continue: wit, in my opinion, is a wonderful thing – it's a beauty of nature and a consolation in life, and it can pull off such tricks that, I think, it's difficult even for some poor investigator to guess what's going to happen to someone, especially when he's himself captivated by his own imagination, as is always the case, since he's a human being! But the nature of the poor investigator saves him – that's the trouble! But young people, captivated by their wit, 'striding over all obstacles' (as you so wittily and cleverly put it), wouldn't even think about this. He, let's assume, lies – that is, the person – is a private case – incognito – and lies wonderfully well, in the most ingenious way; there would be a triumph, and he would enjoy the fruits of his wit, but look! he trips and falls into an apoplexy right in the most interesting, the most scandalous spot. Perhaps it's an illness, or a faint from the stuffiness in the room, but still! Still, the thought is clear! He lied magnificently, but couldn't calculate human nature. That's the treachery – where is it? Another time, carried away by his own witticisms, he'll start to dupe a suspicious person; he'll turn pale on purpose, as if playing a game, but too convincingly pale – too natural – and he'll give away his thought! Though he manages to fool you at first, but by the next morning, he'll think better of it, if only he's not making a mistake. And that's always the case! And what's the matter with him? He'll start running ahead, and blurt out things he shouldn't, without being asked, and start talking non-stop about what he shouldn't be talking about, inventing various allegories, ha-ha-ha! He'll come and start asking: why, then, are they taking so long to take me? Ha-ha-ha-ha! And this can happen even to the most wittiest person, a psychologist and a writer! Nature is a mirror, a transparent mirror! Look into it and admire it – that's what I'm saying! But why are you so pale, Rodyon Romanych, are you short of breath, perhaps, and can I open a window for you?

-No, you, I see, don't believe me - I, it seems, keep telling you merry tales, harmless jokes - picked on you, I grabbed Porphiry, growing more and more cheerful and ceaselessly laughing with pleasure, and again beginning to spin around the room, - you are quite right - I, of course, you are right; my figure has been created by God himself in such a way that it only stirs up comical thoughts in others; a buffoon, I am; but I'll tell you, and repeat to you, Rodyon Romanych, forgive me, an old man, that you, a young fellow, still in the first flush of youth, you value human reason above all else, like the whole youth. The quick-wittedness of the mind and the detached arguments of reason seduce you - it is just like that old Austrian general of the General Staff, for instance, as far as I can judge about military events: they defeated Napoleon on paper, took him captive, and in their office, they had it all figured out and calculated in the most ingenious way, but look, General Mack himself surrenders with his entire army, ha-ha-ha! Maybe I wouldn't have been Napoleon, but I would have been a major, ha-ha-ha! Well, so now I'll tell you, my dear fellow, the whole truth about that particular case: reality and nature, sir, are important things, and how the most piercing calculation can sometimes be foiled! When just born, my horns had not yet eclipsed my brow, and my hair had not yet covered my shoulders. My sagacity was divine, and my features even more refined. I was indeed a heavenly elixir deer, a phoenix as beautiful as a being enchanted by the smoke and fog of the flowers. The dragon's stock was not common, nor did my youth conform to the mundane. I wore the six celestial weapons, and with them I soared and transformed in boundless variations. Now, having received the golden decree from the Jade Emperor, I was appointed to lead three cauldrons to the Sea Gathering. When I approached the Monkey King, he said, "Who are you, young master? You have knocked on my door, what business do you have?"

Natasha taunted: "Foolish monkey! Don't you recognize me? I am Nezha, the third son of the King of the Eastern Heavens. I am here on a mission from the Jade Emperor to capture you." The Monkey King laughed and said, "Young Prince, your baby teeth have not yet fallen out, your umbilical cord has not yet dried up. How dare you talk so big? I'll spare your life and not strike you. Look at my banner: the word on it is the title that the Jade Emperor has bestowed upon me. If it is as you wish, I will become a disciple; if it is not, I will not hesitate to report to the Imperial Court."

Natasha looked up and saw the characters "All-Heaven Great Sage". He exclaimed, "This monkey dares to call himself a title as grand as this, you should be terrified! I'll give you a taste of my sword!" The Monkey King replied, "I will just stand still and let you strike a few times." The enraged Nezha let out a loud roar, calling out, "Transform!" and transformed into three-headed six-armed figure, with an evil glint in his eyes, holding six sets of weapons: the cutting sword, the chopping knife, the binding rope, the submitting club, the embroidery ball, and the fire wheel. He leapt forward with a flash. The Monkey King saw this and was startled, exclaiming, "This young fellow is quite skilled in his art! No etiquette, watch me transform too!"

The Great Sage laughed and shouted, "Transform!" and transformed into a three-headed six-armed figure, too. He used his gold-banded staff to swing back and forth, and it also transformed into three rods. The six hands grasped the three rods and held them in place. This battle shook the ground and caused the mountains to tremble, truly a thrilling spectacle of swordplay:

Just as the cornrows veil the cranium, and the down is not yet covering the shoulders. Divine and sharp-witted, the bone is more refined and resplendent. It is indeed the heavenly unicorn child, and it must be the rainbow-colored Phoenix Fairy. A dragon's descendants naturally do not have ordinary appearances, and their youthful features are not like those of mortals. Wearing six kinds of divine and magical weapons, their flying and transformations have no bounds. Having received the edict of the Jade Emperor's golden mouth, the merit of shooting at the Sea Assembly has been three great halls bestowed. Wukong approaches near and comes to ask: "You are from which household's younger brother? Intruding on my gate, what business do you have?"

Nakai shouts: "Filthy monkey! Do not you recognize me? I am the Sanzang Third Prince Nakai. I have been sent by the Jade Emperor to come here and apprehend you." Wukong smiles and says: "Young prince, your baby teeth have not yet fallen out, and your natal hair has not yet dried. How dare you speak such great words? I'll spare your life and won't hit you. Just take a look at the characters on my flag, offer a petition to the Jade Emperor: if my official title is such, I will return; if it is not in line with my heart's desire, I will definitely strike at the Sacred Heaven Palace."

Nakai lifts his head to look and finds the four characters "Qitian Dasheng" (Emperor of Heaven's Great Sage). Nakai says: "This monkey thief is how mighty in his divine abilities that he dares to claim such a name! Don't be afraid! Eat my one sword!" Wukong says: "I'll only stand still and won't move; let you hack at me a few times."

Nakai becomes enraged, lets out a loud shout and calls out "Transform!" and immediately transforms into three heads with six arms, ferocious and sinister, holding six types of magical weapons: the Cutting Demons Sword, the Cutting Demons Knife, the Binding Demons Rope, the Suppressing Demons Mallet, the embroidered ball, and the fire wheel, ready to pounce forward, clashing. Wukong sees this and is shocked: "This young prince is indeed capable of a few tricks! You do not pay homage, look at my divine powers!" The Great Sage shouts "Transform" as well and also transforms into three heads with six arms; his Golden Stave also transforms into three. The six hands grasp the three staves and obstructs.

This battle is truly earth-shattering, good!

When his little horns first protruded and his fur first covered his shoulders, he was already very intelligent and perceptive, and his bones were perfectly fine and delicate. Truly, he was a celestial child of the Qilin, and it was no wonder that he was also called a fey phoenix. As he was born of dragon blood, he naturally didn't look ordinary, and his age seemed not to be that of a mortal being. He was endowed with the Six Divine Instruments, and could fly and transform in the most wondrous and boundless ways. As he received a decree from the Jade Emperor's golden mouth, he was appointed to participate in the Marine Assembly, shooting at three ceremonial targets. The Monkey King approached him and asked, "You are a young master of some household, who dares to enter my domain and what is your business here?" Nezha shouted, "You are a shameless monkey! Don't you recognize me? I am Nezha, the third prince of the Heavenly Lord of the Tower of the Azure Heaven! I have been sent by the Jade Emperor on a mission, come to apprehend you!" The Monkey King laughed and said, "Young prince, your baby teeth have not yet fallen out and your fetal hair has not yet dried, how can you speak such big words? I will spare your life for now and not strike you. Just look at the words on my banner and if they are a title that suits you, I will submit to the Jade Emperor and cease the assembly; if not, I will definitely report back to the Palace of the Supreme Ruler of the Palace of the Heavenly Spire!" Nezha looked up at it, and the words "Supreme Sage of Heaven" were there. Nezha said, "This monkey who dares to be so boastful, how could he have such great spiritual power and dare to call himself by that name? Don't be afraid! Take a bite of my sword!" The Monkey King said, "I just stand still, let you strike a few times." Nezha, enraged, let out a loud shout, and called out, "Transform!" and immediately transformed into three heads and six arms, holding the six types of instruments: the demonic-killing sword, the demon-slaying knife, the demon-binding cord, the demon-subduing club, the embroidered ball, and the fire wheel. With a flourish and a flutter, he charged forward. The Monkey King saw him, and was shocked, "This young master is quite skilled in his art! No ceremony, look at my spiritual powers!" The Great Sage then let out a shout, "Transform!" and also transformed into three heads and six arms; his Golden Hoop Staff was extended and became three of them. The six hands grasped the three staves, and the battle was so intense that it shook the earth and mountains and it was a wonderful sight:

At birth, eyebrows are barely formed, and hair is not yet covering the shoulders. Mysterious and exceedingly perceptive, with bone structures more resplendent and more beautiful than ever before. Truely it is a Sky-Phoenix from Heaven, or a Flower-Fairy of Inkstone-Colors. A dragon's lineage cannot be expressed by ordinary appearances; at this majestic age, it doesn't look like ordinary mortals. With six types of divine armory and equipment on its person, it swiftly changes and transforms without bounds. Now, having received a decree from the Jade Emperor's Golden Mouth, I have been appointed to preside over the Three Platform Meetings at the Sea. The Empty-Captain drew near, and asked, "You are someone's young master, how dare you come to my gate with business?" Nezha roared, "Foolish demonic monkey! Don't you recognize me? I am Nezha, the third prince of the Heavenly Lord of the West, now dispatched by the Jade Emperor to come and capture you." The Monkey laughed and said, "Little Prince, your baby teeth haven't fallen out and your fetal hair isn't dry, how dare you speak such great words? I'll spare your life, I won't strike you. Just look at the words on my banner, if I hold an official rank like that, I will submit to the Jade Emperor; if it does not meet my expectations, I will certainly go up to the Divine Palace of the Spirits." Nezha looked up to see "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven" written on the banner. Nezha said, "This demonic monkey dares to claim such a title and achievement! Don't be afraid! Take a blow from me with my sword!" The Monkey said, "I'll just stand here immobile, and let you strike a few times, that's all." That Nezha became enraged, and let out a loud roar, calling "Transform!" and immediately transformed into three heads and six arms, his hands gripping six types of martial equipment, including the Demon-Slaying Sword, Demon-Slaying Dagger, Demon-Tying Rope, Demon-Dumping Pestle, Decorative Ball, and Fire Wheel, waving wildly, striking the Monkey's face. The Monkey saw this and was taken aback, saying, "This young prince is quite skilled in his martial arts! No civility at all, I will show you my divine abilities!" Ah, Great Sage, let out a call of "Transform!" and also transformed into three heads and six arms; his Golden-Collar Staff changed into three rods, and six hands grasped the three rods, forming a formidable array. This battle was truly earth-shaking and heaven-stirring, it was a fight worthy of killing:

Just as the infant's hair brushes the fontanel, its fur has not yet covered its shoulders. It's mysterious, clever, and keenly perceptive, with bone structures more refined and elegant. It's indeed a creature from the heavenly realm, a true son of the mythic creature, Qilin. It's the dragon's breed, and its appearance is not of this mundane world. At six years old, it's at the prime of its youth and doesn't look like a common mortal. It wields six divine tools, soaring and changing without bounds. Now it's received the edict from the Jade Emperor's golden mouth, decreeing it to participate in the Sea Congress, and to shoot down the Three Platforms' Three Gates. At the time, the Monkey King drew near and asked, "You're someone's younger brother, right? How dare you enter my domain with such an intention?" Nezha shouted back, "You pestilential monkey! Don't you recognize me? I'm Nezha, the third son of the Heavenly King of Pillar. I'm here as the Jade Emperor's special envoy, to capture you." The Monkey King laughed and said, "Little Prince, your milk teeth have not yet fallen out, and your fetal hair has not yet dried. How dare you speak such grandiose words? I'll let you keep your life, and won't harm you. Just look at the characters on my flag. If you've recognized the title bestowed upon me by the Jade Emperor, then you won't need to use force; I'll convert. But if you don't meet my expectations, then I'll absolutely conquer the Palace of the Heavenly Spirits." Nezha raised his head to take a look, and he saw "Great Sage Equal to Heaven" written on it. Nezha exclaimed, "This pestilential monkey dares to assume this title! Don't be afraid! Take my sword!" The Monkey King said, "I'll just stand still and not move, and let you hack at me a few times." That Nezha, enraged, let out a loud shout and called, "Change!" Immediately transformed into a three-headed, six-armed creature, looking hideous and wicked, holding six kinds of tools of war: the Slash Devil Sword, the Butcher Knife, the binding Rope, the Taming Hammer, the Painting Ball, and the Fire Wheel. It let out a roar and attacked in a flurry of movement, its swords flashing towards the Monkey King's face. The Monkey King's heart was shocked, "This little prince is quite skilled with his movements! No respect for propriety, I'll display my supernatural powers!" The Great Sage, taking a mighty voice and shouting "Change!", transformed into a three-headed, six-armed creature as well; the Golden Horn Cudgel in his hand also transformed into three. He held the three staffs with his six hands. This confrontation was truly a world-shaking battle, a truly brutal one:

He didn't know why he was embracing her, he couldn't account for why he felt irresistibly drawn to kissing her, to kissing her all over, but he kissed her as he wept, wailing and drenched in his own tears, and swore passionately to love her, to love her eternally. 'Pour forth the earth with the joy of thy tears and love these thy tears...' – echoed in his soul. What was he crying about? Oh, he was crying out of sheer rapture even for these stars that shone out to him from the depths, and 'he wasn't ashamed of this ecstasy'. As if the threads of all these countless divine worlds had converged at once in his soul, and it was all quivering, 'touching other worlds'. He yearned to forgive everyone for everything and beg for forgiveness, oh, not for himself, but for everyone, for everything and for all, and 'for me, and for others they are asking', – echoed in his soul once more. But with every moment he felt all too clearly, as if it were something hard and unshakeable, like that vault of the heavens, descending into his soul. Some kind of idea seized his mind – and from that moment on, for all his life, for all eternity. He fell to the ground a weak youth, but stood up a resolute fighter for his whole life, and suddenly in that very moment of his rapture, he knew and felt it. And he could never forget it for the rest of his life. 'Someone visited my soul at that moment,' – he would say later with firm faith in his words...

He didn't know why he was hugging her; he gave no account to himself why he felt an irresistible urge to kiss her, to kiss her all over, but he was kissing her crying, sobbing, and bathing in his tears, and he swore passionately to love her, to love her for eternity. "Moor the land with the tears of joy and love these tears of yours...". Echoed in his heart. What was he crying about? Oh, he cried in his own raptures even about those stars that shone out from the abyss for him, and he didn't feel ashamed of this ecstasy. As if the threads from all those countless worlds of God's had converged at once in his soul, and it quivered, 'touched by other worlds'. He wanted to forgive everyone for everything and ask for forgiveness – not for himself, but for everyone, for everything, and for all, and 'they ask for forgiveness for me and for others', – echoed again in his heart. But with each instant he felt distinctly and tangibly, as if something hard and unshakeable, like this heavenly firmament, descended into his soul. Some idea came to power in his mind – and it was to last a lifetime, and for eternity. He fell to the ground as a weak youth, but rose up as a resolute warrior for life and suddenly in that very moment of his rapture, he realized and felt it. And he could never forget that moment for the rest of his life. 'Someone visited my soul in that hour,' he would say afterwards with a firm faith in his words...

He knew not for what purpose he embraced her; he could not account for why an unyielding desire to kiss her, to kiss her all over, had taken hold of him. As if all the countless threads from all these divine worlds had converged in his soul at once, and it trembled, "touching other worlds." He wanted to forgive everyone for everything and ask forgiveness, not for himself, but for everyone, for everything, and for all, and "others ask forgiveness for me," resounded once again in his soul. Some idea somehow seized his mind – and from that moment on, for all eternity. He fell to the earth as a weak youth, but rose as a steadfast warrior for life, and at that very moment of his ecstasy, he knew and felt this. He could never forget it for the rest of his life. Master Pixin said, "I live here and rely on catching wolves and tigers to make a living, and catching snakes and insects to sustain myself, so the beasts are afraid of me when I am around. If the wickedness of people infuriates you with irreconcilable indignation and sorrow, and you are even driven by a desire for revenge against the wicked, then fear this feeling above all. Immediately go and seek out your own torment, as if you were guilty of this wickedness yourself. Accept these torments, endure them, and your heart will be assuaged, and you will understand that you are also guilty, for you could have shone forth as an innocent and did not. If you had shone, you would have illuminated the path for others with your light, and the one who committed the wickedness may not have done it in your presence. Even if you shone, and yet you saw that people did not save themselves even with your light, remain firm and do not doubt the power of heavenly light; believe that if they were not saved now, they will be saved later. And if they are not saved later, their children will be saved, for your light will not perish, even if you yourself have already died. The righteous man departs, but his light remains. It is those who are saved by the one who saves who are always saved. The people do not accept their prophets and persecute them, but they love their martyrs and venerate those who have been tormented. You, however, work for the whole, you do for the coming age. Never seek rewards, for you already have a great reward on this earth: the spiritual joy of the righteous, which only the righteous attain. Do not fear the mighty or the powerful, but be wise and always be dignified. Know the measure, know the time, learn this. In solitude, remain and pray. Lie on the ground and kiss it. Kiss the earth and love it ceaselessly and inexhaustibly, love all, love everything, seek out this ecstasy and this rapture. Drench the earth with the tears of your joy, and love these tears of yours. Do not be ashamed of this ecstasy, cherish it, for it is a great gift of God, one that is given to few, and is reserved for the chosen.

Petr Ivanovich sighed even deeper and more sorrowfully, and Praskovya Fyodorovna thanked him with a grateful hand. Entering her pink silk-upholstered parlor with a dim lamp, they sat down at the table: she on the divan, and Petr Ivanovich on a worn, springless, and improperly fitted low ottoman. Praskovya Fyodorovna had wanted to warn him to sit on another chair, but found this warning out of place and thought better of it. As Petr Ivanovich sat down on this ottoman, he recalled how Ivan Ilyich had decorated this parlor and consulted with him about this very pink silk with green leaves. Sitting on the divan and walking past the table (the parlor was teeming with trinkets and furniture), the widow snagged her black lace shawl on the carving of the table. Petr Ivanovich got up to disentangle it, and the freed ottoman began to shift and nudge him. The widow herself started to disentangle her lace, and Petr Ivanovich sat down again, suppressing the rebellious ottoman. But she had not disentangled all of it, and Petr Ivanovich got up again, and the ottoman continued to be rebellious, even letting out a small click. When it was all over, she pulled out a clean linen handkerchief and began to cry. The episode with the lace and the struggle with the ottoman cooled Petr Ivanovich down, and he sat there, sulking. The awkward situation was interrupted by Soko-lov, the late Ilyich's butler, with a report that the plot of land at the cemetery, which Praskovya Fyodorovna had chosen, would cost two hundred rubles. She stopped crying and, with the look of a martyr, glanced at Petr Ivanovich and spoke in French that it was very difficult for her. Petr Ivanovich made a silent gesture expressing his certain conviction that it could not be otherwise.
