After passing three years, the patriarch once again sat on the throne, and his discourse was delivered to the assembly. He spoke of karmic cases and analyzed external appearances. Suddenly he asked, "Where is the Monkey?" The Monkey approached, kneeling down, and said, "Your disciple is here." The patriarch said, "You have been practicing what kind of method?" The Monkey replied, "Your disciple has recently developed a clear understanding of the dharma nature, and my root has also gradually stabilized." The patriarch said, "Although you have understood the dharma nature and grasped the root, you are still beware of the 'three calamities that bring harm'." The Monkey heard this and pondered for a long time, saying, "The words of my master are misguided. I have often heard it said that to cultivate the great dharma is to be as long-lived as heaven, and that when the Yang and Yin are in harmony, all illnesses will disappear. Why, then, are there three calamities that bring harm?" The patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary dharma: to steal the creation of heaven and earth, to seize the subtle principle of the sun and moon; after achieving the Great Perfection, the gods and demons will be hard to accommodate. Even though you will retain your youthful appearance and extend your lifespan, after five hundred years, heaven will send a calamity of thunder to strike you, and you must see into your true nature and illuminate your mind beforehand to avoid it. If you avoid it, your lifespan will be as long as heaven's; if you fail to avoid it, you will meet your death. After another five hundred years, heaven will send a calamity of fire to burn you. This is not the fire of heaven, nor is it ordinary fire, but is called the 'dark fire.' From your own Dantian it will rise and burn upward through the Muddy Pellet Palace, burning the Five Organs to ashes and turning your limbs to decay, undoing the thousand-year effort of your hard practice, reducing it to nothing. After another five hundred years, heaven will send a calamity of wind to blow you. This is not the wind of the four cardinal directions, nor is it the gentle breeze, nor the wind of the flowers and grass, but is called the 'Returning Wind.' From the crown of your head, it will blow into your six cavities, passing through the Middle Dantian and piercing the Nine Apertures, dissolving your flesh and bones, and causing your body to disintegrate. That's why you must avoid all three calamities." The Monkey heard this and was filled with dread, bowing his head in reverence and saying, "The Venerable One has taken pity on me and taught me how to avoid the three calamities. I shall never forget the debt of gratitude." The patriarch said, "It's not difficult to learn, but you are different from others, so it cannot be transmitted to you." The Monkey said, "I also have a round head that touches the sky, and a square foot that stands on the earth, and I have nine apertures and four limbs, and Five Organs and Six Cavity like a normal human being. What makes me different from others?" The patriarch said, "You may look like a human, but you are short one cheek." The Monkey's face is harelipped and his mouth is narrow. The Monkey stretched out his hand to feel it and laughed, saying, "My master is mistaken! I may be short one cheek, but I have a surplus of this fold of skin, which is also useful for me to twist and turn." The patriarch said, "Well, you want to learn the common techniques, don't you? There are thirty-six methods of the Heavenly General, and seventy-two methods of the Earthly Prison." The Monkey said, "I wish to learn how to cultivate these common techniques, starting with one of the methods of the Earthly Prison." The patriarch said, "Since you are willing, come forward and I will pass on the incantation to you." He then leaned in close and whispered some mysterious method, which the Monkey did not know what it was. The Monkey King also comprehended it all at once, and he immediately practiced and cultivated it, mastering all seventy-two methods of transformation.

It had been three years since the Old Master had ascended to his throne again and preached to the multitude, using parables and discussing the external form. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is the Awakened Monkey?" The Awakened Monkey came forward, kneeling down, and said, "I am your disciple." The Old Master asked, "What kind of doctrine have you been practicing lately?" The Awakened Monkey replied, "I have recently made progress in my understanding of the true nature and have also solidified my foundation." The Old Master said, "If you have achieved understanding of the true nature and mastered the source, why are you still worried about the three calamities and their misfortunes?" The Awakened Monkey pondered this for a long time and said, "Master's words are incorrect. I have always heard that the Way is elevated and virtuous, coequal with Heaven, and when the yin and yang have reached harmony, no sickness arises. So how can there be these three calamities and their misfortunes?" The Old Master said, "This is an extraordinary Way: it involves taking away Heaven and Earth's creative power and invading the subtle mechanisms of the sun and moon. After attaining enlightenment, it is difficult for ghosts and spirits to abide. Although you may maintain your youth and long life, after five hundred years, a thunder calamity will come and you must use your insight and wisdom to avoid it in advance. If you can avoid it, your life will be as long as Heaven's, but if you fail to avoid it, your life will come to an end. After another five hundred years, a fire calamity will descend and burn you. This fire is neither divine fire nor ordinary fire, and it is called '陰火' or 'dark fire'. It will arise from your 'mingmen' meridian, pass through the 'hudun' palace, burn the five viscera to ashes, and rot your limbs. After another five hundred years, a wind calamity will come and blow you away. This wind is not the east wind, south wind, west wind, or northwest wind, nor is it the gentle breeze or the dry wind; it is called '披风' or 'assailing wind'. It will blow into your fontanel, pass through the dantian, and pierce the nine apertures, dispersing your flesh and bones, and your body will dissolve. So you must avoid all of these calamities." The Awakened Monkey listened and was deeply frightened, bowed his head, and said, "Grand Old Man, take pity on me and teach me the method of avoiding the three calamities." The Old Master said, "This is not difficult, but you are different from others, so I could not pass it on to you." The Awakened Monkey said, "I also have a round head, a broad forehead, four limbs, nine orifices, five viscera, and six bowels. How am I any different from others?" The Old Master said, "You may look like people, but you have fewer cheekbones." In truth, the Awakened Monkey had a crooked face and a pointed chin. The Awakened Monkey reached out and touched his face, laughing and said, "Master, you have not calculated correctly! Although I have fewer cheekbones, I have this 'small bag' more than others, and I can still adapt to the changes." The Old Master said, "Well, what will you learn from the common people? There are thirty-six types of heavenly star gods and seventy-two types of terrestrial transformations. You want to learn one of the terrestrial transformations, do you?" The Awakened Monkey said, "I am willing to struggle and toil to learn one terrestrial transformation." The Old Master said, "If you are so willing, come forward and I will pass it on to you in a secret phrase." Thereupon, he whispered a mysterious phrase in his ear, of which he knew not the content. This Monkey King was suddenly enlightened and understood all at once, and when he learned the phrase, he practiced it and cultivated it, mastering all seventy-two types of terrestrial transformations.

Not long after, the Patriarch once again occupied his seat, and the assembly listened as he explained the principles of the doctrine. Using an analogy, he was discussing the process of cultivating the "flesh skin" outside the body. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is the Monkey?" The Monkey approached, kowtowing, and said, "Disciple is here." The Patriarch asked, "What have you been cultivating for the past few years?" The Monkey replied, "Recently, my understanding of the dharma nature has become clearer, and my fundamental root has become more solid." The Patriarch said, "You have achieved clarity of dharma nature and have grasped the fundamental root, and yet, you still have to be wary of the 'three calamities'." The Monkey listened, and after deliberating for a long time, said, "The Patriarch's words are in error. I often hear that the great virtuous ones abide by the heavenly virtue and coexist with heaven, that the water and fire are in harmony, and that all sicknesses are eliminated. How can there be the three calamities?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary path: it involves obtaining the creative power of heaven and earth, and secretly penetrating the profound principle of the sun and moon. Although one may possess an elixir body and a long lifespan, after five hundred years, a thunder calamity will be sent by heaven to strike you. You must cultivate awareness and discernment beforehand, and use them to avoid the calamity. If you can avoid it, your lifespan will be as long as heaven's, but if you fail to avoid it, you will meet your demise. Another five hundred years later, a fire calamity will be sent by heaven to burn you. This fire is not the fire of heaven, nor is it ordinary fire, but rather the 'yin fire.' It will begin to burn from the Moshan spring, right through the Muddy Palace, and reduce your five viscera to ashes, causing your four limbs to wither away. After another five hundred years, a wind calamity will be sent by heaven to blow you away. This wind is not the wind from the east, south, west, or north, nor is it the gentle, golden, or spring wind, but rather the 'assassin wind.' It will enter your skull through the fontanel, pass through your six cavities, go through the dan field, pierce the nine apertures, and consume your flesh and bones. This is why you must avoid them all." The Monkey listened, and his very bones trembled with fear. He kowtowed and prayed, "The venerable Patriarch, who is full of compassion, has transmitted to me the method to avoid the three calamities. I shall not forget your mercy." The Patriarch said, "This is not difficult. You simply differ from others, so I couldn't teach it to you." The Monkey said, "I also have a round head that touches the heavens, and feet that are square and plant firmly on the ground, with nine apertures and four limbs, and five viscera and six cavities, what's the difference?" The Patriarch said, "You may resemble people in appearance, but you lack a cheekbone." The Monkey's face was indeed misshapen, with a hollowed-out cheek and a pointed chin. The Monkey reached out to touch his cheek, laughing and said, "The Patriarch's words are not well-considered. I may lack a cheekbone, but I have a larger mouth, which can also accommodate more saliva." The Patriarch said, "Fine. What method of cultivation do you want to learn?" The Monkey said, "I want to learn one form of the general catastrophe method." The Patriarch said, "Since you want to learn, come closer and I will teach you the oral formula." He leaned in close and whispered something incomprehensible to the Monkey. This Monkey King also became enlightened at that moment, and when he mastered the oral formula, he practiced and cultivated himself, eventually mastering all seventy-two forms of catastrophe transformation.

Three years had passed, the Patriarch ascended to the throne again and preached to the assembly. His teaching focused on subtle affairs, analyzing the external appearance and inner reality. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is the Monkey King?" The Monkey King approached, bowing down: "Your disciple is here." The Patriarch asked, "What has your disciple been cultivating these days?" The Monkey King replied, "I have recently gained a deep understanding of the law of nature and my root is gradually solidified." The Patriarch said, "If you understand the law of nature and have grasped the root, yet still have the Buddha-nature within you, you only need to be wary of the 'three disasters that bring harm'." The Monkey King listened and pondered for a long time before saying, "Your words are wrong, venerable master. I often hear that a being with great virtue is long-lived and shares the lifespan of heaven, that water and fire are harmonized, and that all illnesses do not occur. How can there be the three disasters that bring harm?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary way: by depriving heaven and earth of their creative power, and invading the mysterious mechanism of the sun and the moon; after achieving the elixir, even the spirits find it hard to bear. Although you may remain youthful and long-lived, five hundred years will pass and heaven will send a calamity of thunder to strike you. You must first realize your true nature and be aware of your mind. If you can avoid it, your lifespan will be equal to heaven's, but if you cannot, you will meet your demise. Five hundred years later, heaven will send a fire that is not the fire of heaven nor the ordinary fire, known as the 'yin fire'. This fire will burn from the Cave of the Three Caverns and pass through the Palace of Dirt, turning the five viscera to ashes and reducing the four limbs to dust. Your thousand-year ascetic practice will all be illusions. Another five hundred years will pass and heaven will send a calamity of wind that is not the east, south, west, or north wind, nor the gentle breeze or the spring breeze, known as the 'absorbing wind'. This wind will blow into the cranial cavity and pass through the six orifices, then pierce the Dan field and the nine apertures, dissolving bone and flesh. That is why you must avoid them." The Monkey King heard this and his bones turned cold with fear. He bowed his head and said, "Grand Master, in compassion, teach me the method to avoid the three disasters." The Patriarch said, "This is not difficult, but because you are different from others, I am not permitted to teach you." The Monkey King said, "I also have a head that touches the sky and feet that stand on the ground, just like ordinary people, with nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six bowels. How am I different from others?" The Patriarch said, "Although you look like a human, you have fewer cheeks." The Monkey King indeed had a cheekless face and a pointed chin. He stretched out his hand to touch his face and laughed, saying, "Venerable master, you are mistaken! Although I have fewer cheeks, I have more of this pouch on my cheek, and it is enough to block the changes." The Patriarch said, "Fine, what will you learn from the ordinary world? There are thirty-six forms of the Heavenly Star, and seventy-two forms of the Earth Star." The Monkey King said, "I am willing to search through it all, let me just learn one form of the Earth Star." The Patriarch said, "Since you are determined, come forward and I will teach you the oral formula." He leaned in and whispered some mysterious method, and the Monkey King's one aperture was opened, at the same time understanding all hundred apertures. He immediately memorized the oral formula and practiced and refined himself, mastering all seventy-two forms of transformation.

But after three years had passed, the Venerable Master returned to his throne and taught the scriptures. His lecture was about analogies and cases, and he discussed the essence of one's external form. Suddenly he asked, "Where is the Monkey?" The Monkey drew near and bowed: "Your disciple is here." The Venerable Master said, "What practices have you been cultivating these days?" The Monkey replied, "Your disciple has recently achieved a certain degree of attainment in the Way and has gradually solidified his foundation." The Venerable Master said, "You have achieved the Way and have understood the root, yet your essence still contains the potential for three disasters." The Monkey listened and pondered for a long time before saying, "Your words, Master, are at fault. I've heard it said that one's virtue should be cultivated to the point where it equals that of Heaven, and one's lifespan should be equal to the heavens. When water and fire have reached harmony, one should not be susceptible to any illness. How can there be three disasters?" The Venerable Master said, "This is a transcendent practice: by usurping the creative power of Heaven and Earth, one invades the subtle principle of the sun and moon. Even though one may achieve a physical transformation and prolong one's lifespan, if one does not perceive one's true nature and avoid the disasters, one will be struck by a bolt of thunder after five hundred years and die. To avoid it, one must see through one's true nature and flee beforehand. If one can avoid it, one's lifespan will be equal to that of Heaven. If one cannot avoid it, one will die then and there. Five hundred years later, a disaster of fire will descend upon you. This fire is not the ordinary fire, but is called 'yin fire.' It will arise from your dantian and penetrate through to the crown of your head, reducing your flesh and bones to ashes and turning a thousand years of cultivation into an illusion. Another five hundred years later, a wind disaster will blow you away. This wind is not an ordinary wind, but is called 'ascended wind.' It will blow in through your fontanelle, pass through your dantian, and pierce through your nine orifices, causing your body to disintegrate and your flesh and bones to scatter. That's why you must avoid it." The Monkey listened and was deeply frightened, bowing his head in reverence and saying, "The Venerable Master is compassionate and has taught me how to avoid the three disasters. I will never forget your kindness." The Venerable Master said, "It is not difficult, but you are different from others, so it cannot be taught to you." The Monkey said, "I have a round head that touches the heavens and feet that stand firmly on the earth, just like other people. I have nine orifices, four limbs, five viscera, and six bowels, so how am I different from them?" The Venerable Master said, "You may look like other people, but you have fewer facial muscles." Indeed, the Monkey had a distorted face and a pointed chin. The Monkey reached out and touched his face, laughing and saying, "Master, you were mistaken! Although I have fewer facial muscles, I have a longer muzzle, which is just as good." The Venerable Master said, "Fine, you want to learn how to be like other people? You need to master the 36 transformations of the heavenly general and the 72 transformations of the earthly spirits." The Monkey said, "I wish to learn the 72 transformations of the earthly spirits." The Venerable Master said, "Since you are so determined, come closer and I will teach you the incantation." He then leaned in close and whispered some mysterious techniques. At that time, the Monkey was one-eyed and his intelligence was boundless. He memorized the incantation and practiced it on his own, eventually mastering all 72 transformations.

"The assembly would convene as planned; only after my emissaries retrieve the Great Vehicle Sutra, shall I, in utmost sincerity, carry out a good deed." All the officials uniformly obeyed. At the time, within the temple, someone asked, "Who dares to carry out the emperor's intention and go up to the West to offer incense to the Buddha to seek the true scripture?" Before the question could be finished, a monk suddenly appeared beside them and, bowing to the emperor, said, "This humble monk is of no ability, and I wish to offer the service of a dog or a horse to assist the emperor in seeking the true scripture, and pray that the kingdom of our emperor may forever remain secure." The Tang emperor was overjoyed, walked forward, and grasped the monk's hand with his imperial hand, saying, "If the monk is capable of this loyalty and virtue, no distance is too far, no road too perilous, I am willing to enshrine you as my brother." Xuanzang bowed his head in gratitude. The Tang emperor truly was a paragon of virtue, went to the temple and before the Buddha, bowed four times and called out, "Your Imperial Brother, Holy Monk." Xuanzang expressed heartfelt thanks, saying, "Your Majesty, this humble monk has no virtue or ability, yet has been blessed by the heavens to receive such grace and favor. When I depart, I shall with my life, toil and strive until I reach the West. If I do not reach the West, and do not obtain the true scripture, I dare not return to the country, lest I fall into the abyss of the hells forever." He then took incense at the Buddha's feet, vowing thus. The emperor was delighted and ordered his attendants to return, waiting for a propitious day to depart, and issued an edict sending him on his way, and so the imperial retinue dispersed.

"The great assembly was convened, awaiting the arrival of the great sutra with the envoy. Then, following the imperial decree, all officials took it upon themselves to abide by it. Meanwhile, inside the temple, someone asked, 'Who is willing to execute the emperor's will, to ascend to the Western Heavens to seek the sutra?' Before the question could be completed, a monk rushed over and paid homage to the emperor, saying, 'I am but a humble monk, willing to take on the tasks of a dog or a horse, to accompany Your Majesty in seeking the true sutra, to pray for the perpetuation of the kingdom and the dynasty.' The king of Tang was greatly delighted and approached to help the monk up with his imperial hand, saying, 'If you can fulfill this noble intent, I shall not be afraid of the distant road, traversing mountains and rivers, and I wish to acknowledge you as my brother.' Xuanzang bowed in gratitude. 

The king of Tang truly was extremely virtuous, and he went to the temple in front of the Buddha, and bowed four times to Xuanzang, calling him 'the imperial brother sage-monk.' Xuanzang expressed his thanks without end, saying, 'Your Majesty, what virtue or abilities could I have, to be regarded with such imperial favor and benevolence? If I were to go, I would surely give up my life in my efforts, until I reach the Western Heavens. If I were to fail to reach the Western Heavens, and fail to obtain the true sutra, I dare not return to my country, and risk being trapped in the hells of endless suffering.' He took incense in front of the Buddha, vowing with it. The king of Tang was greatly delighted, and ordered them to return to the palace, to select a propitious day and hour, and to issue an imperial edict to send them out. Thus, the imperial entourage dispersed in all directions."

"Gather your distinguished colleagues, wait for my messenger to obtain the sacred sutras from the West, and then carry out a thorough revision of the good deeds. All officials obey my instructions accordingly. At that time, when inquired by me in the temple, 'Who among you is willing to carry out my intentions and journey to the West to pray to the Buddha to obtain the sutras?' Nobody replied. Just as the inquiry was about to be dropped, a monk walked past and bowed before the emperor, saying, 'I am an unworthy monk, willing to exert myself like a horse or dog and accompany Your Majesty to seek the true sutras and pray for the perpetual stability of the kingdom.' The Tang emperor was overjoyed, approached him and took his hand, saying, 'This monk truly displays filial piety and loyalty, and is not afraid of a long journey or traversing mountains and rivers. I am willing to make him my brother.' Xuanzang bowed his head in gratitude. The Tang emperor was truly a wise and virtuous king and, together with Xuanzang, bowed to the Buddha four times, and addressed him as 'Holy Monk, imperial brother.' Xuanzang expressed his heartfelt gratitude, saying, 'Your Majesty, I have no virtues or abilities, how could I be so fortunate as to have Your Majesty bestow such benevolence upon me? I am going to the West, determined to sacrifice my life and body, and will not return unless I have obtained the true sutras. If I do not obtain them, I dare not return to the country, and will be forever damned to the hell of transmigration.' He then held incense in front of the Buddha, taking an oath in this manner. The Tang emperor was overjoyed, ordered him to return to the palace, and selected auspicious days and hours for the expedition. He then issued a decree, and the emperor's retinue dispersed to prepare for the journey."

"The imperial decree says to bring the sacred scriptures here, and then I shall truly cultivate good deeds," all the officials were to carry out in accordance with it. At that time, in the temple, someone asked, "Who dares to fulfill my will, to go to the west to the Buddha to request the scriptures?" The question was not yet finished when a monk walked over from the side and bowed in front of the emperor, saying, "This humble monk is unrefined, I wish to exert the effort of a dog or a horse, and beg Your Majesty to seek the true scriptures with me, and pray for the permanent stability of the empire." The King of Tang was overjoyed, he went forward and held the emperor's hand to help him up, saying, "The venerable monk indeed truly acts with virtue, not afraid of the distant journey, to traverse mountains and rivers, I am willing to enlist you as my brother." Xuanzang bowed to express his gratitude. The King of Tang truly was very virtuous, so he went to the temple in front of the Buddha and bowed to him four times, calling him "Imperial younger brother, holy monk." Xuanzang expressed his boundless gratitude, saying, "Your Majesty, this humble monk has what virtue, what ability, dare to be favored by Heaven's benevolence, such as this? When I go, I must cast my body and life, persist until I reach the west. If I do not reach the west, and do not get the true scriptures, I dare not return to the country, forever to be submerged in the hells." He took incense in front of the Buddha, with this as his vow. The King of Tang was greatly pleased, and immediately ordered the imperial decree to be returned, waiting for a propitious day and time, to issue the imperial edict to dispatch him, and thus the imperial carriage returned, the guests dispersed.

Thus, the victoriously assembled assembly awaits my dispatched representative to obtain the great vehicle sutra. When the chosen one returns, I will take it seriously, carefully cultivate good deeds. All officials abide by this in observance. At the time, someone asked inside the temple, "Who is willing to carry out my edict, go to the western heavens to pray to the Buddha for the sutra?" No one replied. A Buddhist master beside him suddenly flashed by, bowed before the emperor and said, "I am a poor monk, I wish to perform the humblest of tasks, and, with your majesty's benevolence, seek the true sutra together." The king of Tang was very pleased, walked forward and, with his imperial hand, helped the Buddhist master to rise. "The Buddhist master indeed upholds such loyalty and virtue; he is not afraid of the long journey, braving mountains and rivers; I wish to consider him as my brother." Xuanzang bowed to thank him. The king of Tang was truly virtuous, so he went to the temple in front of the Buddha, and, with Xuanzang, performed four prostrations, calling him "Your brother, the saintly monk." Xuanzang was deeply grateful and said, "Your Majesty, your subject has what virtues or abilities to deserve such imperial favor and benevolence? If I go, I shall devote my life and struggle until the western heavens. If I do not obtain the true sutra, I dare not return to the country and suffer eternal degradation in the hell." He then raised incense in front of the Buddha, using this as an oath. The king was very pleased, and thus ordered to return to the palace, awaiting a propitious day and time to send off the official dispatch, so all the attendants dispersed.

Carefree and easy, I drink and sing to my heart's content, and long songs and sighs follow the twists and turns of the wind. I invite my elder brother to join me, and call out to my younger brother to gather our boat companions. We bring our friends and acquaintances together to visit an elderly friend. We frequently play at guessing hands and exchange cups, we play cards and speak in riddles, and the sound of the drums resonates through the temple bell. We boil shrimp and steam crab every morning, and stir-fry duck and cook chicken every day. My foolish wife brews tea and scatters her emotions, while my mountain wife cooks with intention and composure. In the morning, I lift my staff and go fishing in the shallow waters, and when the day breaks, I carry firewood over the great slope. After the rain, I wear a cloak and catch the lively carp, and in the wind, I wield an axe to fell dry cedars. I hide my tracks and avoid the world, and don the mask of a fool. 

Zhang slightly said, "Li brother, I've taken the lead in starting a sentence. Now, brother, please compose a couplet to respond. And the younger brother should follow suit." "I am a wild man of the mountains and forests, under the influence of the moon and wind; I am a wandering vagabond of the rivers and lakes, and I take refuge in the leisure of an old pensioner. I have my share of leisure, and I spend it in carefree ease; I have no reputation or fame, and no noise or news comes to my ears. On moonlit nights, I sleep in a thatched hut; on cloudy days, my body is shaded by the water buffalo hat. I forget all cares and friendships with the friends I've made, and I delight in associating with herons and wild geese. I don't concern myself with profit or loss; I hear no sound of war drums or battle drums by my side. Whenever the mood strikes, I take a sip of fragrant wine; and I spend my days eating wild greens. Two bundles of firewood are my livelihood, and a fishing line is my means of sustenance. I call my young son to grind steel on the anvil, and quietly summon my simple-minded daughter to mend old cloth. When spring arrives, I enjoy seeing the green willows, and when the season is warm, I delight in seeing the emerald rushes. In the summer, I escape the heat to repair new bamboo; in June, I take a break from the heat by harvesting tender lotus roots. When the frost comes, I often cook chickens and slaughter crabs; on the Double Ninth Festival, I cook crabs that are strong and plentiful at the time. When winter arrives, I spend the day on the house, and in the ninth month, I do not have to worry about cooking.

I indulge in unrestrained singing, letting out carefree long songs, surrendering to the wind and rain. I call my friends and invite them to set sail, gather my colleagues and gather together in the countryside. We play the exchange-gift game and frequently pass the wine cups, discard the cards and casually gossip about the fortune-telling masters. We grill shrimp and boil crabs, singing and feasting every day, the foolish wife brews tea, and my wife prepares the meal with a composed mind. By daybreak, I lift my walking stick and fish in the shallow waters, by sunrise, I carry firewood and cross the great river. After the rain, I put on my hat and catch live fish, in the wind, I play with an axe, cutting down the dead pines. I keep a low profile, avoiding the world, pretending to be a fool. I hide my name and fade into obscurity, a deaf mute. 

Zhang asked, "Li Brother, I have just started a line, now I'll let my brother go first, little brother also has to continue." Li said, "A mountain man who fakes madness under the wind and moon, a rascal who registers as a retired veteran on the rivers and lakes. He is leisurely and free-spirited, with no trouble in his mouth, and his talk is always about enjoying a peaceful life. Under the moonlight, I sleep in a thatched hut, and when the sky is foggy, I cover myself with a reed mat. I've forgotten my desires and gotten to know my friends, the pine and the plum. I'm happy to form an alliance with the seagull and the heron. I don't care about fame or fortune, I don't hear the sound of armor and halberds. At any time, I take a cup of fragrant wine, and every day, I eat wild vegetable soup. The two bundles of firewood are my living, and the fishing line is my livelihood. At leisure, I call my young child to sharpen his axe, quietly I call my foolish child to mend his old fabric. When spring comes, I love to watch the green willows, and when the seasons blend, I enjoy watching the green reeds. In the summer, I avoid the heat and cultivate new bamboo, in June, I take a mid-day rest and pick the tender lotus roots. In autumn, I hunt and kill fat geese often, on the Double Ninth Festival, I boil the crabs in time. In winter, I go back to my room and sleep through the day, and in the ninth month, I stay up late, not even steaming rice.

To wander at will, and freely pour out one's passions, letting the wind blow and the world spin. I call out to my elder brother, and invite my friends to join me on a wild expedition. We take a boat, accompanied by fellow travelers, to gather wild mushrooms. We engage in rowdy games of chance, and exchange coins as we drink from the cup. We break open cards and announce each's fortunes, as they freely circulate around the clock. We grill shrimp and boil crab in the morning, and cook duck and chicken every day. My foolish wife brews tea and puts me in a lighthearted mood; my mountain wife carefully prepares meals with serene intentions. When morning comes, I take up my walking stick to wade through the waves; by day I carry firewood over the big hills. After the rain, I wear my raincoat and catch the living carp; before the wind, I hack at withered pines with my axe. I stealthily avoid the world, and wear a mask to conceal my foolishness; I hide my name and abandon my fame. 

Zhang Shi said, "Lee brother, I just came up with the first line, now it's your turn to come up with a pair, my little brother should also join in." Lee said, "The wild mountain man feigns madness under the wind and moon, the wandering merchant casts off the burden of age. I have leisure time, but I deliberately live carefree, and I disdain the quarrels that would bring me fame. At night I sleep in a thatched hut, my body wrapped in a reed mat. When the world is dark and the body is covered with a reed mat, I forget my worries and recall the friendships of a long time past. I enjoy meeting fellow travelers who share my love for the friendships of swans and herons. I don't calculate the value of fame or wealth, nor do I hear the sounds of war drums in my ears. Whenever I have a chance, I enjoy drinking fragrant wine, and live the simple life of eating wild vegetables for the three meals. My livelihood depends on two bundles of firewood, and my means of survival is one fishing line. In my leisure time, I call my little son to sharpen the steel axe; in my quiet moments, I call my foolish child to mend the old quilt. When spring arrives, I enjoy watching the green willows; when the seasons merge, I like to see the green stalks of the reeds. In the summer, I avoid the heat to plant new bamboo; in June, I use a fan to escape the heat and pick the tender lotus. After the frost comes, I enjoy eating roasting chicken daily; on the autumn equinox, I cook crabs at the right time. In the winter, I go back to sleep all day; by the ninth month, I am not steamed.

I play the flute freely, singing long songs and sighing carelessly, letting the winds and tempests blow. I call my brother over with a whistle, gather my companions and summon an old fellow to join us on the field. We order cups of ale and pass them around, our guesses flying like hands exchanging fortunes at the board of chance. We boil shrimp and steam crabs for our daily feasts, sauté ducks and roast chickens for our every meal. The foolish woman brews tea for us with a carefree heart, while the mountain wife cooks meals with an easy mind. When the morning comes, I take up my walking stick to fish for the gentle ripples, and when the day breaks, I carry a bundle of firewood to cross the big river. After the rain, I wear a waterproof mat and catch a living carp, and in front of the wind, I swing my axe to chop a withered pine. I hide my traces, withdraw from the world, and disguise my foolishness. I hide my name and conceal my identity, living a mute and deaf life. 

Zhang Zhongmou said, "Li brother, I'll start with a line, and now it's my brother's turn, and my younger brother should also follow suit." Li said, "The wild man in the mountains poses as crazy, and the old outcast enjoys the leisure of the winding streams. He has a share of leisure to idle about carefree, and no one spreads rumors about him with a tongue that longs for peace. Under the moonlit night, he sleeps in a grass hut securely, and when the heavens are dark, he covers himself lightly with a reed hat. He forgets his emotions and becomes friends with the fir and the plum blossoms, and he's happy to associate with the seagulls and the sandpipers in an oath of friendship. He doesn't count on fame or profit, and he doesn't hear the clanging of the spears in his ears. He drinks wine at any time and sips fragrant liquor, living from day to day on vegetable soup. He makes a living by selling two bundles of firewood and fishes with a single fishing rod. In leisure, he calls his little boy to grind steel axes, and in quiet, he summons his foolish child to mend his old clothes. When spring arrives, he likes to watch the green willows, and at the right time, he enjoys seeing the green reeds. When summer comes, he escapes the heat to fix new bamboo, and in June, he takes a siesta and picks the fresh water caltrops. When the frost arrives, he kills fat chickens every day, and on the Double Ninth Festival, he cooks the fresh crabs. When winter comes, he stays in bed all day, and when the ninth month arrives, he doesn't steam anything."

He sings, he toasts, and makes merry without a care, his long songs and sighs carried away by the wind. He calls his friend, invites his companion, and invites the villagers to gather together. The wine jar is passed and the cups are raised, the cards are shuffled and the dice are cast. Fresh shrimp and steamed crabs are savored daily, and stir-fried duck and roasted chicken are enjoyed every day. The foolish wife brews tea with a carefree heart, while the mountain wife cooks with a calm mind. When morning comes, he wields his staff to catch the morning waves, and at dawn he carries firewood over the great dam. After the rain, he dons a rain hat and catches a lively carp, and in the wind, he hews at a withered pine. He conceals his tracks and avoids the world, disguising himself as a fool.

Zhang Jian said: "Brother Li, I'll take the lead and start with a couplet; now it's my brother's turn to start a couplet, and the younger brother will follow suit."

"Wind and moon mock the rustic mountain man, the wanderer on the riverbank gazes at the retired old fellow. Leisurely he separates the fine from the coarse, carefree, he indulges in peace. At night, his body sleeps soundly in the thatched hut, and under the gloomy sky, his body is covered with a reed mat. He forgets the world and makes friends with pine and plum trees, and he's happy to form a bond with herons and egrets. He doesn't worry about reputation or wealth, and he doesn't hear the din of battle. He drinks a cup of fragrant liquor at will, and enjoys a simple meal of wild greens. Two bundles of firewood are his livelihood, and a fishing line is his daily occupation. When he's idle, he has his young boy sharpen his steel axe, and when quiet, he calls his foolish child to repair his old quilt. When spring arrives, he delights in watching the green willows, and in the warm breeze, he enjoys seeing the green lotus. When summer comes, he escapes the heat to plant new bamboo, and in the sixth month, he takes refuge in the cool shade to pick the tender lotus. When the frost descends, he often kills chickens at dawn, and on the Double Ninth, he cooks the fat crabs in time. When winter comes, he stays in bed all day, and by the ninth day of the ninth month, he cooks for himself without needing to be told."

The Russian heart can distinguish a great man even in the enemy of his homeland. That is to say, I don't remember if I literally expressed myself that way... I was a child, but I think that's what I meant! Napoleon was taken aback, he thought and said to his suite: "I love the pride of this child! But if all Russians think like this child, then..." – he didn't finish and entered the palace. I immediately intervened in the suite and ran after him. The suite parted to let me through and looked at me as a favorite. But all of that only flashed by... I remember only that, entering the first hall, the Emperor suddenly stopped in front of the portrait of Empress Catherine, looked at it thoughtfully for a long time, and finally said: "She was a great woman!" – and passed on. In two days, everyone already knew me in the palace and in the Kremlin, and they called me "le petit boyard". I only went home to sleep. At home, I almost went mad. Two days later, Napoleon's chamberlain, Baron de Bazancourt, who couldn't withstand the campaign, died. Napoleon remembered me; I was taken, led without explaining the matter, tried on the uniform of the deceased, a boy of twelve years old, and when I was brought to the Emperor in the uniform, he nodded at me with his head, and then announced to me that I was honored by his majesty's favor and was promoted to chamberlain of his majesty. I was happy, I indeed felt a warm sympathy for him... well, and apart from that, a brilliant uniform is a lot for a child... I went in a dark-green tailcoat, with long and narrow folds; gold buttons, red cuffs with gold embroidery, a high, standing, open collar with gold embroidery, embroidery on the folds; white striped breeches, a white silk waistcoat, silk stockings, shoes with buckles... and during the Emperor's horseback ride, and if I participated in the suite, high boots. Although the situation was not brilliant and the enormous misfortunes were already being foreseen, etiquette was observed as much as possible, and even more so, the more these misfortunes were foreseen.

They had hardly reached the top when the painter tore the door open completely and, with a deep bow, invited K to enter. He refused to let any of the girls in, no matter how much they begged and how hard they tried to sneak in, either without or against his permission. Only the hunchbacked one managed to slip through under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, spun her around once, and then set her back down in front of the door with the other girls, who, while the painter had left his post, hadn't dared to cross the threshold. K didn't know how to assess the whole thing, as it seemed to be happening in a friendly agreement. The girls by the door stretched their necks one after the other, called out joking phrases to the painter that K couldn't understand, and the painter laughed while the hunchbacked one almost flew out of his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed again to K, held out his hand, and introduced himself: "I am the artist Titorelli." K pointed to the door behind which the girls whispered and said, "It seems you're very popular in this house." "Oh, those creatures!" said the painter, futilely trying to fasten his nightshirt at the neck. He was barefoot and only wore a wide, yellowish linen pant that was secured by a strap whose long end swung back and forth. "These creatures are a true nuisance," he went on, abandoning the nightshirt whose last button had just come undone, fetching a chair, and forcing K to sit down. "I once painted one of them – she's not even here today – and since then they've been persecuting me. If I'm here myself, they only come in if I let them, but if I'm gone for even a moment, at least one of them is always here. They've even had a key to my door made and lend it to each other. One can hardly imagine how annoying it is. For example, I come home with a lady I'm supposed to paint, open the door with my key, and find the hunchbacked one at the little table, coloring her lips with a brush while her little siblings, whom she's in charge of, roam around and dirty up the room in every corner. Or, as it happened to me yesterday evening – excuse me, please, considering my state and the disorder in the room – I come home late at night and want to get into bed, and then something nips at my leg; I look under the bed and pull out another of those things. I don't know why they're pushing themselves on me; it's certainly not because I'm trying to lure them. You could probably notice that I'm not interested in them. This studio would be made available to me for free, and I would have moved out long ago if it weren't for it." Just then, a tiny voice whispered behind the door, "May we come in now?" "No," the painter replied. "Not even me?" asked the voice again. "Not me either," said the painter, went to the door, and locked it.

The evening was fresh, warm, and clear; the weather had been wild and untrammeled since morning. Raskolnikov was hurrying to his apartment; he was in a hurry to finish everything before sunset. As long as possible, he would not have wanted to encounter anyone. As he climbed up to his apartment, he noticed that Nastasya, torn away from the samovar, was intently watching him and following him with her eyes. "Is someone there?" he thought to himself. The image of Porfiry repelled him. But having reached his room and opened the door, he saw Dunya. She was sitting all alone, plunged in thought, and, it seemed, had been waiting for him for a long time. He stopped at the threshold. She leapt up from the sofa in fright and straightened up before him. Her gaze, fixed immobile on him, expressed horror and an unquenchable grief. "Please, the two venerable monks, please sit on the horse platform for a while and wait for me to go in and report to the master." Monkey King released Gao Cai and let the horse go, and the old master and the other monks waited outside the door.

You would lose all your respect for the judges if you heard the curses with which I greet him when he gets in over my bed. I could take the key away from him, but it would only make things worse. You can open any door in this place with the slightest effort." As the painter was speaking, K. was thinking whether he should take off his coat; he eventually realized that he wouldn't be able to stay here any longer if he didn't do so, so he took off the coat and draped it over his knees, so he could put it on again if the conversation ended. As soon as he had taken off his coat, one of the girls cried out, "He's taken off his coat!" and everyone rushed to the joints to see the spectacle for themselves. "The girls believe," said the painter, "that I'm going to paint you and that you're undressing as a result." "Yes," said K., not particularly amused, as he felt no better than before, although he was now sitting in his shirt sleeves. Almost gruffly, he asked, "What were the two other options called?" He had already forgotten the expressions.

"The apparent acquittal and the kidnapping," said the painter. "It's up to you which one you choose. Both can be achieved with my help, of course, but the difference lies in the fact that the apparent acquittal requires more effort, and more of it is temporary, while the kidnapping requires less but more enduring effort. First, let's discuss the apparent acquittal. If you wish for that, I'll write a statement on a piece of paper certifying your innocence. The text for such a statement was passed down to me by my father and is completely unassailable. With this statement, I'll go on a round of visits to the judges I know. I'll start by presenting the statement to the judge I'm currently painting, who comes to the session tonight. I'll show him the statement, explain that you're innocent, and vouch for your innocence. That's not just a superficial but a real and binding guarantee." There was a hint of accusation in the painter's eyes that K. was asking him to bear the weight of such a guarantee. "That would be very kind of you," said K. "And the judge would believe you and still not acquit me in reality?" "As I said," replied the painter. "Moreover, it's not even certain that everyone would believe me; some judges might, for example, ask me to bring you to see them. Then you would have to come with me. In that case, the matter would already be half won, especially since I would instruct you in advance on how to behave in front of that particular judge. It's worse with judges who – and that will happen – reject me from the outset. We can and must do without them, since individual judges can't make the final decision. If I collect a sufficient number of signatures from the judges with my statement, I'll take the statement to the judge who's handling your case. I might even have his signature; then everything would develop a bit faster. In general, there are no more significant obstacles, and it's then that the defendant feels the most hopeful. It's strange, but true, that people are more hopeful at this time than after the acquittal. There's no need for special effort now. The judge has the assurance of a number of judges in the statement, and he can acquit you without a care, and he certainly will, once the formalities have been completed, to please me and other acquaintances. You, on the other hand, can leave the court and be free." "So I'm free then," said K., hesitantly. "Yes," said the painter, "but only apparently free or, to put it more accurately, temporarily free. The lowest judges, to whom my acquaintances belong, don't have the power to acquit definitively; this power belongs only to the highest court, which is completely inaccessible to us, and which we don't even want to know about. Our judges have the power to release you from the charge, but not to exonerate you. That means that if you're acquitted in this way, you're still not truly acquitted; you're only temporarily relieved. I've already told you this, but you didn't listen."

This ordered arrangement astonished K at first, then however he said just as quietly as the painter: "I believe you contradict yourselves." "How so?" asked the painter patiently, leaning back with a smile. This smile gave K the feeling that he was now looking for inconsistencies not in the painter's words but in the trial itself. Despite this, however, he did not retreat and said: "You mentioned earlier that the court is inaccessible to evidence, later you limited this to the public court, and now you're saying that the innocent don't need any help at the court. Already there's a contradiction there. Besides, you've said before that one can influence the judges personally, but now you're denying that the real acquittal, as you call it, can ever be achieved through personal influence. There's a second contradiction there." "These contradictions are easily cleared up," said the painter. "It's about two different things here, what is in the law and what I've personally experienced; don't confuse the two. In the law, I haven't read it myself, of course, but it says on the one hand that the innocent are acquitted, on the other hand it doesn't say that the judges can be influenced. But I've just experienced the opposite of that. I know of no real acquittal, but I do know of many cases of influence. It's possible, of course, that in all the cases I've known there was no innocence at all. But isn't that improbable? In so many cases not a single one of innocence? I used to listen carefully to my father when I was a child, when he would tell stories about court cases at home, and the judges who came to his studio would tell him about the court too; we talk about nothing else in our circles; as soon as I got the chance to go to court myself, I always made use of it, I've listened to and observed countless cases at crucial stages, and – I have to admit – not a single real acquittal."

"None at all," said K., as if he were speaking to himself and his hopes. "That confirms the opinion I already have of the court. So it's useless from this side as well. One hangman could replace the whole court." "You mustn't generalise," said the painter discontentedly, "I was only speaking from my own experience." "That's enough," said K., "or have you heard of acquittals from earlier times?" "There were such acquittals, I think," replied the painter. "It's hard to establish whether they actually happened, though. The court's final decisions aren't published, they're not even accessible to the judges, so we only have legends about old cases. These legends do include real acquittals, but you can believe them if you like; they're not verifiable. Still, we shouldn't dismiss them entirely, they probably contain some truth, and they're very beautiful, I've even painted some pictures that deal with such legends."

"They're just legends and won't change my mind," said K. "Can you even rely on those legends in court?" The painter laughed. "No, you can't," he said. "Then it's pointless to talk about them," said K., he wanted to accept the painter's views for now, even if he found them unlikely and at odds with other reports. He didn't have the time to check everything the painter said for its truth or to refute it; it was already a big enough achievement to persuade the painter to help him in some way, no matter how insignificant. So he said: "Let's set the real acquittal aside then, you mentioned two other possibilities."

"The apparent acquittal and the abduction," said the painter. "That's what it must be," said K. "But, before we discuss those, don't you think you should suggest we open a window? It's almost unbearable." The painter nodded as if he understood K's discomfort very well. "Can't we open the window?" asked K. "No," said the painter. "It's just a fixed glass pane, you can't open it." K. then realised he had been hoping that the painter or he himself would suddenly get up and break the window open. He was ready to take a deep breath of fresh air with his mouth open. The feeling of being completely shut off from the air made him dizzy. He tapped gently on the feather bed next to him and said in a weak voice: "It's rather uncomfortable and unhealthy."

"Oh no," said the painter in defence of his window, "because it can't be opened, it holds the heat better in here, even though it's just a simple pane, than a double window would. If I wanted to ventilate, which isn't really necessary since air is getting in through the joints in the beams, I could open one or both of my doors." K., comforted a little by this explanation, looked around to find the second door. The painter noticed this and said: "It's behind you, I had to move it out of the way of the bed."

Now K. saw the small door in the wall for the first time. "It's just that everything here is too small for an atelier," said the painter, as if he wanted to forestall K's criticism. "I had to set it up as best I could. The bed in front of the door is naturally in a very poor position. The judge I'm painting now comes in through that door, while I'm asleep, and I've given him a key to this door so he can come in and wait for me in the atelier if I'm not at home. But he usually comes early in the morning, when I'm still asleep, and it naturally wakes me up. You'd lose all respect for the judges if you heard the curses I hurl at him when he climbs over my bed. I could take the key away from him, but it would just make things worse. One can break all the doors out of their hinges with the least effort."

As the painter talked, K. was thinking about whether he should remove his rock, but he eventually saw that if he didn't do it, he wouldn't be able to stay here any longer, so he took off his rock and put it over his knees, so he could put it on again when the conversation was over. As soon as he took off his rock, one of the girls called out: "He's already taken off his rock!" and one heard the others pushing to get a look at the spectacle. "The girls think, of course," said the painter, "that I'm going to paint you and that's why you're taking off your clothes."

"So," said K., only slightly amused, since he didn't feel much better off than before, even though he was now sitting in his undershirt. "How did you call the two other possibilities?" he asked gruffly. He had already forgotten the phrases. "The apparent acquittal and the abduction," said the painter. "It's up to you to choose which one. Both are possible through my help, of course, not without effort, the difference is that the apparent acquittal requires a more considerable, a collected temporary effort, while the abduction requires a much smaller but more lasting effort. Let's start with the apparent acquittal then. If you'd like to go for that, I'll write a certificate of your innocence on a piece of paper. The text for such a certificate has been passed down to me from my father and is unassailable. I'll then go around to the judges I know, with this certificate, and start with the judge I'm painting now. I'll bring the certificate to him this evening when he comes to the session, explain to him that you're innocent, and act as a guarantor for your innocence. This is not just an external but a real, binding guaranty."

There was a hint of accusation in the painter's eyes that K. was making him bear the burden of such a guaranty. "That's very kind of you," said K. "And the judge will believe you and still not really acquit me?" "As I said," replied the painter. "Besides, it's not even certain that everyone will believe me; some judges might ask to see you in person. In that case you'd have to come with me. But in that case, the situation is already half won, especially since I'd make sure to brief you on how to behave in front of that particular judge. The worst part is when judges turn me down outright. We'll avoid those, of course, if I can help it, but we can also afford to do that, since individual judges can't decide the outcome here. If I collect a sufficient number of signatures from the judges with this certificate, I'll go to the judge who's currently handling your case. I might even get his signature, which would speed things up a bit. Otherwise, things will usually go pretty smoothly from there. There won't be much to hold things up then; for the accused, it's a time of utmost optimism. It's strange, but true: people are more optimistic in this phase than after the acquittal. There's no need for any special effort now. The judge has the guarantee of a number of judges in his hands, he can acquit you freely and will do so, of course, after formalities have been completed, to please me and my friends. And you'll leave the court a free man."

"Then I'm free," said K. hesitantly. "Yes," said the painter, "but only apparently free or, more accurately, temporarily free. The lower judges, who are my friends, don't have the right to acquit you finally; only the highest court has that right, which is unattainable for us. As for how things are there, we don't know and don't want to know. The higher court has the right to acquit you from the indictment, but not to absolve you. That means that even if you're acquitted in this way, you're not entirely off the hook; you'll still be tied to the indictment, which can be pulled out at any time."

It was a very rainy, stormy morning when K. came to the office, already full of troubles about the day ahead of him, at seven o'clock in order to finish at least some work before the visit would take him away from it. He was very tired because he had spent half the night studying an Italian grammar to prepare a bit; the window, which he had often sat at lately, lured him more than the desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately, the servant just then entered and announced that the Director had sent him to inquire if the Procurator was there yet; was he here, then he should be so kind as to go over to the reception room, since the gentleman from Italy was already there. "I'm coming," said K., stuffed a small dictionary into his pocket, took an album of the city's sights, which he had prepared for the visitor, under his arm, and went through the office of the Deputy Director into the directors' room. He was pleased that he had come to the office so early and could be available, which was probably not seriously expected of anyone. The Deputy Director's office was, of course, just as empty as in the depth of night; probably the servant should also have called him into the reception room, but it had been unsuccessful. As K. entered the reception room, the two gentlemen stood up from the deep armchairs. The Director smiled pleasantly, clearly he was very pleased about K's arrival, and immediately made the introductions; the Italian shook K's hand firmly and, smiling, called someone a "dawn riser." K. did not quite understand whom he meant; it was also a strange word, the meaning of which K. only slowly comprehended. He answered with some flat sentences, which the Italian laughed at again, while he several times stroked his grayish-blue, bushy beard with a nervous hand. This beard was apparently scented, one was almost tempted to approach and smell it. When they had all sat down and a small, introductory conversation began, K. noticed with great discomfort that he could only understand the Italian in snippets. When he spoke completely calmly, he could almost understand him completely; but this was only a rare exception, most of the time his words poured out of his mouth; he shook his head with pleasure. At times like these, he would get himself entangled in some dialect, which had nothing Italian about it for K., but which the Director understood and spoke as well, which K. could have foreseen since the Italian came from southern Italy, where the Director had also been for several years. In any case, K. recognized that the possibility of understanding the Italian had been taken away from him to a large extent; his French was only barely understandable as well; also, the beard covered his lip movements, whose sight might have helped with understanding. K. began to foresee many troubles, but for the time being, he gave up trying to understand the Italian – in the Director's presence, who easily understood him, it would have been unnecessary effort –, and he limited himself to begrudgingly observing the Italian, how he rested deeply yet lightly in the armchair, how he often tugged at his short, sharply cut jacket, and how he once tried to convey something with his raised arms and loose joints, which K. did not understand, although he kept his eyes fixed on the hands as he bent forward. Eventually, K. who otherwise remained idle, only mechanically followed the conversation with his eyes, made aware of his earlier fatigue, and caught himself in his alarm, fortunately just in time, in the moment that he had been about to get up, turn around, and leave. Finally, the Italian looked at his watch and sprang up. After he had bid farewell to the Director, he pushed himself close to K., so tightly that K. had to push his armchair back in order to move. The Director, who certainly recognized the need in K. against the Italian, intervened in the conversation, and did so cleverly and delicately, so that it seemed as if he was only giving small advice, while in reality he clarified everything the Italian, who spoke tirelessly, said, in short for K. The Director told him that the Italian would first have to attend to some business matters, that he would unfortunately have only little time, and that he by no means intended to rush through all the sights; rather, he had made up his mind – provided K. agreed, and with K., the decision lay – to only visit the cathedral, but to explore it thoroughly. He was extremely happy about the opportunity to do this, accompanied by a scholar and amiable man – that was K., who was engaged in nothing but ignoring the Italian and quickly taking in the Director's words – and he asked him, if the hour suited him, to meet him in the cathedral in about two hours, perhaps around ten o'clock. He himself hoped to be there at that time for certain. K. answered in a suitable manner, the Italian first shook the Director's hand, then K.'s, then the Director's again, and left, with both of them following, but still half-turned towards them, still talking, to the door. K. then stayed a little while with the Director, who looked particularly pale today. He thought he had to apologize to K. in some way and said – they stood close together in confidence –, first he had intended to accompany the Italian himself, then, however, had decided to send K. instead – he gave no further reason –. If he did not understand the Italian at first, he should not be shocked by it; understanding would come quickly enough; and even if he understood nothing at all, it was not so bad, since for the Italian it was not so very important to be understood. By the way, K.'s Italian was quite astonishingly good, and he would certainly make his way with this matter. That was how K. was dismissed. The time that was still free to him, he spent in extracting rare vocabulary, which he needed for guiding him in the cathedral, from the dictionary. It was a very tedious job; servants brought the post, officials came with various requests and stayed, since they saw K. occupied, by the door, not moving until K. had listened to them; the Deputy Director did not let it pass, and came in to disturb K. often, took the dictionary from him, and flipped through it apparently quite meaninglessly himself; parties even emerged, whenever the door opened, in the half-darkness of the anteroom and hesitantly bowed – they wanted to draw attention to themselves, but were not sure if they had been seen –, all this moved around K. as if it were his center, while he himself gathered the words he needed, then looked them up in the dictionary, then wrote them out, practiced their pronunciation, and finally tried to memorize them. However, his earlier good memory seemed to have completely left him; sometimes he got so angry at the Italian, who was causing him this exertion, that he buried the dictionary under papers with the firm intention of not preparing any further, but then he saw that he could not remain silent before the Italian before the artworks in the cathedral, and he pulled the dictionary out with even greater fury.

He was extremely tired, for he had spent half the night studying an Italian grammar in preparation; the window, which he had spent far too much time at in recent days, was tempting him more than the desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. "I'm coming," said K., tucked a small dictionary into his pocket, took a brochure of the town's sights that he had prepared for the visitor under his arm, and went through the office of the Deputy Director into the Director's office. He was happy to have come to the office so early and to be available right away, a thing that no one would have taken seriously. The Deputy Director's office was, of course, still empty as in the dead of night, and probably the servant should have summoned him to the waiting room as well, but it had been unsuccessful. As K. entered the waiting room, the two gentlemen rose up from their deep armchairs. The Director smiled kindly, clearly he was delighted that K. had come; he immediately made the introductions, the Italian shook K.'s hand firmly and, smiling, referred to someone as an early riser. K. did not understand exactly who he meant, and besides it was a strange word whose meaning K. only understood a little while later. He replied with a few smooth sentences, which the Italian took laughing, while he stroked his grey-blue, bushy mustache with a nervous hand several times. This mustache was apparently perfumed, one was almost tempted to go closer and smell it. As they all sat down and a small, introductory conversation began, K. noticed with great discomfort that he only understood the Italian in patchy bits. When he spoke quietly, he understood almost completely, but those were only rare exceptions, mostly his words poured out of his mouth, and he shook his head with joy. In such conversations, however, he regularly got entangled in some dialect that had nothing Italian about it any more, but which the Director understood and spoke, which K. could have foreseen, for the Italian was from Southern Italy, where the Director had also spent a few years. In any case, K. realized that the possibility of understanding the Italian had been taken from him to a large extent, for his French was also only poorly understood, and besides, the mustache covered the lip movements, whose observation might have helped understanding. K. began to foresee a lot of trouble, for the time being, he gave up trying to understand the Italian – in the presence of the Director, who understood him so easily, it would have been unnecessary effort –, and he restricted himself to grudgingly observing the Italian, how he lay deep and yet lightly in the armchair, how he often patted his short, sharply cut jacket, and how he once attempted to show something with raised arms and loose, loose joints in his hands, which K. did not understand, even though he followed the hands with his gaze from under his eyebrows. Eventually, K. – who otherwise remained unoccupied and only mechanically followed the coming and going of the conversations with his gaze – made himself realize, to his fright, that he had been on the verge of getting up, turning around and leaving, in his distraction. Finally, the Italian looked at his watch and jumped up. After he had bid farewell to the Director, he pushed his way up to K., so tightly that K. had to push his armchair back in order to be able to move; the Director, who certainly saw the distress in K.'s eyes at not understanding the Italian, intervened in the conversation, and did it so cleverly and delicately that it seemed as if he was only providing minor advice, while in reality he explained to K. everything the Italian was constantly pouring into the conversation, in short order. K. learned from him that the Italian would have to attend to some business, that unfortunately he would only have a little time, that he by no means intended to hurry through all the sights, but rather – although only if K. agreed, for he, the Director, had the decision – had made up his mind to visit only the cathedral, and that in particular to explore it thoroughly. He was delighted to be able to carry out this visit with the accompaniment of a learned and charming gentleman – that was meant to be K., who was busy doing nothing else but trying to tune out the Italian and quickly catching the words of the Director –, and he asked him to come to the cathedral at ten o'clock, two hours from then, and hoped to be there himself at that time. K. replied with a corresponding answer, the Italian shook hands first with the Director, then with K., then again with the Director, and went, accompanied by both, but only half-turned towards them, still talking, to the door. K. then stayed a while with the Director, who looked particularly suffering today. He thought he had to apologize to K. somehow and said – they were standing intimately close to each other – that he had originally intended to accompany the Italian himself, but then – without giving a particular reason – had decided to send K. instead. If the Italian did not understand him right from the start, then K. should not let himself be taken aback, for understanding would come quickly, and if he did not understand anything at all, then it was also not so bad, for it was not so important for the Italian to be understood. Anyway, K.'s Italian was surprisingly good, and he would certainly make do with the situation. With that, K. was dismissed. The time still available to him he spent writing down rare vocabulary he needed for guiding the Italian through the cathedral from his dictionary. It was a very tedious task; servants brought the mail, officials came with various requests and stood by the door, not moving until they had spoken to K., the Deputy Director did not let the opportunity slip to disturb K., came in often, took the dictionary from him and leafed through it, seemingly quite senselessly, and in the dimly lit anteroom, parties would emerge, if the door was opened, and hesitantly bowed – they wanted to attract attention, but were not certain if they were seen –, everything moved around K. as around his center, while he himself collected the words he needed, looked them up in the dictionary, wrote them down, practiced their pronunciation, and finally tried to memorize them. However, his earlier good memory seemed to have abandoned him altogether; at times, he became so angry with the Italian for causing him this exertion that he buried the dictionary under papers, with the intention of not preparing himself any further; but then he saw that he could not stand silently walking with the Italian in front of the cathedral's artworks, and with even greater fury, he pulled the dictionary out again.

It was a very rainy and stormy morning when K. came to the office at seven, full of trouble for the day that lay ahead, to get at least some work done before the visitor would take it away from him. As soon as he finished greeting him - after inviting him to sit down in the armchair, which he had no time to do - he asked K. for a brief conversation in private. "It is necessary," he said, struggling to swallow, "it is necessary for my peace of mind." K. immediately dismissed the servant from the room with the instruction not to admit anyone. "What did I hear, Josef?" the uncle cried out as soon as they were alone, sat on the table, and stuffed various papers under himself without looking up, in order to sit more comfortably. K. was silent, he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the exertion of the past few days, as he was, he first gave himself over to a pleasant lassitude and gazed out the window at the opposite side of the street, from where only a small, triangular section was visible from his seat, a piece of empty wall between two shop facades.

"You're looking out the window!" the uncle cried out with raised arms, "For goodness' sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true, can it be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K. and shook himself out of his distraction, "I don't know what you want from me." "Josef," said the uncle warningly, "you've always spoken the truth as far as I know. Should I take your last words as a bad sign?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "So it is," replied the uncle, slowly nodding, "I've heard about your trial." "From whom?" K. asked. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have any contact with you, you don't pay much attention to her, despite that, she found out. I received the letter today and naturally came right away. Not for any other reason, but it seems like a sufficient reason. I can read you the part of the letter that pertains to you." He pulled the letter out of his wallet. "Here it is." It reads: "Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time, last week I was once in the bank, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I waited almost an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak with him, perhaps an opportunity will arise soon. On my name day he sent me a big box of chocolate, it was very sweet and considerate. I had forgotten to write about it to you then, only now, when you asked me, did I remember. Chocolate, by the way, disappears in the pension immediately, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been given chocolates, it's already gone. But what concerns Josef, I wanted to tell you. As mentioned, I wasn't allowed into the bank because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After waiting for a while, I asked a servant if the negotiation would last long. He said it probably would be, because it was likely to be the trial against the prokurist. I asked what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, he replied that he wasn't mistaken, it was a trial, and a serious one, but he knew no more. He would have liked to help the prokurist, because he is a good and just man, but he didn't know how to begin, and he wished that influential gentlemen would take an interest in him. This would certainly happen, and it would ultimately have a good outcome, but for the time being it doesn't seem to be going well, as he could gather from the prokurist's mood. I didn't pay much attention to this, tried to calm down the simple-minded servant, forbade him to talk about it to others, and considered the whole thing to be idle chatter. Nevertheless, it might be good if you, dear father, would look into this matter on your next visit, it will be easy for you to find out more and, if necessary, use your influential connections to intervene. But if it's not necessary, which is probably the most likely, then your daughter will soon have the opportunity to hug you, which she would be happy about." - "A good child," said the uncle, when he finished reading, and wiped away some tears from his eyes. K. nodded, he had completely forgotten about Erna due to the various disturbances of the past few days, even her birthday had slipped his mind, and the story about the chocolates was apparently invented just to protect him from the uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and certainly not enough rewarded with the theater tickets he would regularly send her from now on, but he didn't feel suitable for visits to the pension and conversations with an 18-year-old gymnasium student. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten his haste and excitement due to the letter and was reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" cried the uncle.
