I asked what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, but he said he wasn't mistaken, it was a serious trial, but he didn't know any more. He himself would like to help the head of the administration, since he's a good and just man, but he didn't know how to start, and he only wished that influential gentlemen would take an interest in him. This will probably happen, and it will ultimately have a good outcome, but for now it looks, as he gathered from the head of the administration's mood, not good at all. I didn't pay much attention to this chatter, tried to calm the simple-minded servant down, forbade him from talking about it to others, and considered the whole thing to be nonsense. Nevertheless, it might be a good idea if you, dear father, were to look into the matter on your next visit, it will be easy for you to get more information, and if it really is necessary, you can intervene through your powerful connections. But if it's not necessary, which is probably the most likely thing, then your daughter will soon have an opportunity to hug you, which would make her happy." – "What a good child," said the uncle as he finished reading, and wiped away some tears from his eyes. K. nodded; he had completely forgotten Erna due to the various disturbances of the past few days, even her birthday had slipped his mind, and the story about the chocolates was apparently invented just to defend him in front of the uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theater tickets he would now send her regularly, he was certainly not sufficiently rewarded, but he felt unsuitable for visits to the pension and conversations with a young eighteen-year-old student. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten the haste and agitation in the letter and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" cried the uncle.

He dozed off on the bench, but his anxiety continued even in his sleep. Just before falling asleep, he remembered that Hippolytus would kill ten people, and he smiled at the absurdity of the assumption. Around him was a beautiful, clear silence, with only the rustling of leaves, from which it seemed that the silence became even quieter and more isolated. He dreamed a lot of restless dreams, and every moment he would shudder. Finally, a woman came to him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could always call her by name and point her out – but strangely, she had a completely different face from the one he had always known, and it was agonizingly hard for him not to recognize her as that woman. In her face there was so much remorse and horror that it seemed she was a terrible criminal and had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned him with her hand and pressed a finger to her lips, as if warning him to go after her more quietly. His heart stopped; he wanted to recognize her as no criminal, no matter what; but he felt that something terrible would happen immediately, for the rest of his life. It seemed to him that she wanted to show him something nearby, in the park. He stood up to follow her, and suddenly someone's bright, fresh laughter sounded next to him; someone's hand suddenly found itself in his hand; he grabbed this hand, tightly clenched it, and woke up. And in front of him stood Aglaya, laughing loudly.

Said the Monkey King attacked the door, but could not open it. He had to return to the Guanyin Temple. The monks in the temple had already buried the old monk, and were all attending Master Tang in the abbot's quarters. After finishing the morning repast, they laid out the noon repast. Just as they were about to add soup and change the water, the Monkey King descended from the void. The monks bowed down in reverence, ushered him into the abbot's quarters, and greeted Master Tang. Master Tang said, "The Monkey King has come. What about your robes?" The Monkey King said, "I've got a reason for it. This morning, I didn't wrong these monks after all. It was the black demon from Black Wind Mountain who stole them. Old Sun went quietly to search for him. He saw him and an elegant white-robed gentleman, as well as an old Taoist priest, sitting on a slope with grasses and flowers, discussing something. He was another one who wouldn't reveal himself. He suddenly said, 'Tomorrow is his mother's birthday, and he has invited all the demons to attend the celebration. Tonight he obtained a precious silk robe of the Buddha, which he wants to use for the occasion, to make a grand feast, which he calls the Celestial Tribute of the Buddha's Robe.' Old Sun seized the opportunity and struck him, causing the black demon to disperse into the wind. The Taoist priest disappeared as well, leaving only the white-robed gentleman, who was none other than a white snake with flowers transformed. I was in a hurry to follow him to his cave entrance and demand that he come out to fight with him. He admitted it, but said he took it back. We've been fighting for half a day, with neither side giving way. The demon retreated back into his cave and locked the stone door, not daring to come out. Old Sun returned to see his master, to report this news, and now the location of the robe is known. We're no longer afraid of him taking it." The monks heard the news, and all clasped their palms together and bowed their heads, murmuring "Amitabha Buddha! Today we've found the location, and we're finally safe!" The Monkey King said, "Don't be so elated, I still haven't got it in my hands yet, and Master hasn't left the temple yet. Let's just wait until I have the robe, and then I'll make sure Master leaves the temple safely and sound. Then and only then will you be truly safe. If there's the slightest risk, the Monkey King will not be trifled with! Has Master had a good meal and some good tea? Has Master's horse been fed some good grass?" The monks all eagerly agreed, saying, "Yes, yes, yes! We've never been remiss in serving the old master."

It is said that as Pilgrim did not succeed in breaking open the door, he could only return to the Guanyin Temple. The temple monks had already buried the old monk and were attending Master Tang in the Abbot's quarters. After completing the early meal, they then set up the midday meal, and as they were adding soup and changing the water, they suddenly saw Pilgrim descending from the sky, whereupon the monks bowed and welcomed him into the Abbot's quarters, where they greeted Master Tang. Master Tang said, "Monkey, you're here; how's your robes?" Pilgrim said, "I've found the reason. Originally, I hadn't wronged these monks at all; it was that black fiend from Black Wind Mountain who had stolen it. Old Sun went to search for him in secret, and saw him and a white-robed scholar and an old Daoist sitting in front of a grassy slope, talking to each other. He was also one of those unrepentant fiends, and he suddenly blurted out that the day after tomorrow was his 'Mother's Day,' and he had invited various evil spirits to come and celebrate his birthday, and at night he had obtained a silken Buddha robe, which he wanted to use to celebrate his birthday, and so he called it the 'Celebration of the Buddha Robe Assembly.' Just then, Old Sun had snatched it from him and struck him with a staff, whereupon the black fiend was blown away by the wind and disappeared. The old Daoist also vanished, but I killed the white-robed scholar, who turned out to be a white snake that had become a human. I then rushed to the cave entrance, calling for him to come out and fight with me. He had already acknowledged it was him who had taken it, and the two of us fought for half a day without either of us gaining the upper hand. The fiend went back into his cave, intending to eat, and locked the stone door, and was afraid to come out. But Old Sun returned to report to his master, and informed him that he had already found the whereabouts of the robes, so he wasn't afraid that he wouldn't return it to me."

The monks listened to this and clasped their palms together, and those who bowed bowed, all chanting the phrase "Namo Amitabha!" "Today I've found it, and we have our lives back!" Pilgrim said, "You shouldn't be too jubilant yet; I haven't gotten it yet, and Master hasn't even gone out the door yet. It's only when I've gotten the robes and Master has left the temple safely that it will be your haven of peace; but if there's even the slightest sign of trouble, I'm a master not to be trifled with! Has Master had some good tea and food? Has he been given some good fodder for his horse?" The monks all replied with one voice, "Yes, yes, yes, and we haven't neglected him in the slightest."

Said the Monkey King, I couldn't break open the gate, so I only returned to Guanyin Temple. The monks there had already buried the old monk and were attending the Tang Monk in the chief abbot's quarters. Having finished the early morning meal, they prepared the midday meal and were just refilling the pot and changing the water when I suddenly appeared from empty space. The monks bowed in reverence, ushered me in to the chief abbot's quarters, and I saw the Tang Monk. The Tang Monk said, "You've arrived, Monkey, how is your cassock?" I replied, "I've found the reason. Initially, it wasn't those monks who were at fault – it was actually the wicked demon from Black Wind Mountain who stole it. The old master went secretly in search of him and found him conversing with a white-clad gentleman and an old Taoist on the hillside amidst the wild grass. He was another one who didn't invite trouble – he suddenly said that the day after tomorrow was the anniversary of his mother's passing, and he would invite all the devils to come and celebrate his birthday. At night, he obtained a silk Buddhist robe, which he wanted to use for the celebration and host a grand feast, calling it the Celebrating the Buddhist Robe Assembly. The old master blocked his path and struck him with a fist, causing the Black Wind to disperse, and the Taoist also disappeared. However, the white-clad gentleman was a white snake that had become a demon and was killed by me. I then hastily chased him to his lair, calling out for him to come out and fight me. He had already confessed to taking it, and we fought for half a day without anyone emerging victorious. The demon then retreated into his lair, closed the stone door and was too afraid to come out. I returned to report to my master and informed him of the cassock's whereabouts, so I'm not afraid that he won't return it to me."

The monks heard this and all clasped their hands together, bowing their heads and reciting, "Namo Amitabha Buddha! Today we've found where it is, and our lives are saved!" I said, "Don't be so happy and carefree yet – I still haven't obtained the cassock and my master hasn't left the temple yet. Let's wait until I've got the cassock before sending my master off safely – that will be the time for you all to enjoy peace. If there's the slightest bit of delay, I'm not an easy person to provoke! Have you all prepared good tea for my master to drink and good fodder for my horse to eat?" The monks all replied with one voice, "Yes! Yes! Yes! We haven't neglected my lord even a little!"

Speaking of it, when the Monkey King attacked the gate without succeeding, he could only go back to the Guanyin Temple. The monks at the temple had already buried the old priest and were all attending the Grand Master Tang in the Chamber of the Chief Priest. Having finished the early meal, they set out the noon meal, and just as they were about to serve soup and change the water, the Monkey King appeared out of thin air. The monks all bowed down to greet him and escorted him into the Chamber of the Chief Priest, where he saw the Grand Master Tang. The Grand Master Tang said, "Monkey, you've arrived. How's your robes?" The Monkey King replied, "It's got something to do with that. In the first place, I didn't wrong these monks at all. It was those demons from Black Wind Mountain who stole it. The old monk went secretly to search for it and found him with a white-robed young scholar and an old Daoist sitting in front of a grassy slope, talking to each other. This is also a kind of monstrous being who doesn't offer any justification for his actions. He suddenly said that it was the day when his mother was suffering, and he invited all sorts of wicked creatures to join him in a feast, calling it the celebration of the Buddha's robe. He also got hold of a piece of silk from the Buddha's robes that night, and he wanted to use it to celebrate his birthday. But I struck him with my iron rod and the Black Wind Mountain demon turned into a gust of wind and ran away. The old Daoist was nowhere to be seen, but I killed the white-robed young scholar who turned out to be a white snake with magical powers. I hurriedly rushed to the entrance of his cave and called for him to come out to fight me. He admitted his guilt, saying he took it back. We fought for half a day without determining who was in the lead. The monster, however, retreated to his cave and wanted to have his meal. He shut the stone door and wouldn't come out of fear. The Monkey King then returned to report to his master. He told him the news before he had the sacred robes in hand, saying he didn't fear that they would not be returned to him. The monks heard the news and clasped their hands, bowed their heads, and all recited in unison: "Namu Amida Buddha! Today, we have found the location of the robes, and now we have our lives back!" The Monkey King said, "Just don't be too elated and joyful yet; I haven't taken the robes back in my hand, and the Grand Master hasn't yet left the Chamber. Wait until I get the robes back, and I'll make sure the Grand Master sets out safely, then you monks can live in peace. If there's even the slightest danger, the Monkey King is the one who'll be in trouble! Have you prepared some fine tea and food for my master? Have you prepared some fine grass for the horse to eat?" The monks all eagerly replied in unison: "Yes, yes, yes! And not a single time have we neglected the old monk."

But it is said that Tripitaka attempted to open the door, but was unable to do so. He was forced to return to the Guanyin Temple. The monks at that temple had already buried the old Patriarch, and were attending to Tripitaka. After morning alms, they prepared the noon meal. As they were adding soup and changing the water, just then Monkey King descended from the void and was greeted by the monks. He was ushered into the Abbot's quarters, where he saw Tripitaka. "You've arrived, Monkey," said Tripitaka, "what happened to your garment?"

"I've found the reason," replied Monkey. "I hadn't laid a trap for those monks earlier, only that black demon of Mount Black Wind had stolen it. The Old Master went to secretly search for him, and saw that he and a young scholar dressed in white and an old Taoist were sitting on the grassy slope discussing matters. He was a sly monster and suddenly revealed the secret that the next day was the anniversary of his mother's passing, and he invited all evil spirits to attend a birthday feast. He had received a fine silk Buddha robe and was going to use it as a pretext for a grand feast, calling it the celebration of the Buddha's robe. I quickly subdued him and struck him with a stick, and he fled in the shape of a gust of wind. The Taoist had disappeared, but I had killed the young scholar who was a white snake that had transformed into a being. I then hastily ran to the cave mouth and called out to him to come out and challenge me to a duel. He admitted his guilt and said he had taken it back. They fought for half a day without either side gaining the upper hand. But the monster retreated into the cave and locked the stone door behind him, too afraid to come out. I went back to see my Master and told him this news, and now that I know where the garment is, there's nothing to fear about it being returned to me."

The monks all listened and clapped their hands, bowed their heads, and chanted "Namo Amitabha Buddha!" "Today we've found where it is, and now our lives are secure!"

Monkey said, "Don't rejoice prematurely, I haven't yet recovered it, and the Master hasn't yet come out. We must wait until I've got the garment and then we can let the Master set out safely. It will only be a place of peace and comfort for you all then. But if there's the slightest bit of danger, the Old Master is a master you don't want to annoy! Has Master been given good tea and food? Has Master's horse been given good fodder?"

The monks all eagerly replied, "Yes! Yes! Yes! We haven't neglected the Old Master in the least."

"Master, here is the saddle and bridle," said Tripitaka after seeing them.  Tripitaka was overjoyed, received them, and handed them over to the pilgrim, who tried them on his back to see if they fitted. The pilgrim got off and took the things one by one to look at, and they were indeed some wonderful articles. To authenticate this, a poem was recited:

The saddle has intricate carvings flashing in the sun and shining with silver decorations, and the seat gleams with threads of gold. The cover has many layers of plush, folded in neat rows, and the reins are held by a cord of purple silk. The headstall has a leather cover with designs of flowers, while the fan has gold lines painting a beautiful animal. The bit is made of wrought iron, and the ends are reinforced with ends dipped in water, with a cord tied at the base. The pilgrim's heart was full of delight as he put the saddle and bridle on the horse, and it felt as if they had been made to order.

Tripitaka bowed to the old man, who hurried to help him up, saying, "No, no, it's nothing to thank for!" The old man did not wait for him to finish thanking, but invited him to mount. When the monk came out of the gate, he mounted his horse, and the pilgrim carried his luggage. The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, a leather whip with a handle of fragrant creeper and a tip with tiger muscle silk, and offered it to him on the roadside, saying, "Holy monk, I've still got one whip left to present to you before you leave."

The monk on horseback took the whip and said, "Many thanks, many thanks!" Just as they were saying their goodbyes, the old man had disappeared from view, and when they looked back, they saw that the ground was empty. They heard a voice from the air saying, "Monk, don't be slow! I am the spirit of the mountain god of Mount Luofu, sent by the Bodhisattva to present the saddle and bridle to you two. You two should make good speed on your journey, but don't waste any time."

Tripitaka was so startled that he nearly fell off his horse. He dismounted, looked up in the air, and paid his respects, saying, "I, a disciple, am a mere mortal, do not recognize the holy spirit's face, and beg forgiveness for my offense. Please convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva for their kindness and blessings."

The monk kept bowing until he lost count, and at the roadside, the living Sun Wukong and the Monkey King were laughing and pleased, running up to grab Tripitaka's horse halter and say, "Master, get up! He's gone far away, you can't see or hear your prayers and prostrations. What's the point of bowing?" 

The old monk said:

The master said, "The saddle and reins are presented." Three catties saw him, happy to receive them, and instructed Tripitaka to take them, to look at whether they fitted. Tripitaka walked forward, taking one thing after another to look at, and indeed they were some fine items. To prove it, it is said:

Carved saddle shines with rainbow lights, tassels of silver stars.
Treasure seat glitters with golden thread.
A layer of padding on the stool is filled with wool.
The ropes of three purple strings are tied.
The headstall is stitched with teaming flowers, a cloud fan painted with gold dancing beasts.
The rings are beaten from iron and polished to a shine, with two hangings drenched with water, and the hair-string decorations tied.
Tripitaka was secretly delighted, and placed the saddle and reins on the horse as if they had been made for him. 
Tripitaka bowed to thank the old man, the old man hurriedly helped him up, saying, "I was worried! I was worried! No need to trouble yourself to thank!"

The old man didn't stay to see Tripitaka get on the horse, and said to Tripitaka, "Come on!" 
The two old men came out of the door, mounted their horses, Tripitaka carried his luggage. The old man took out a whip from his sleeve, it was made of the bark of a fragrant vine, wrapped with tiger cord, and handed it over respectfully on the side of the road saying, "Holy monk, I have one more thing to give you, I'll give it to you on your way."

Tripitaka took the whip in his hand on the horse, saying, "Thank you for your generosity! Thank you for your generosity!"

Just as they were about to exchange greetings, the old man had already disappeared. When they looked back, the temple grounds were empty. Suddenly, they heard someone speaking from the air, saying, "Holy monk, don't hurry. I am the spirit of Mount Luofu, sent by the Bodhisattva to give you the saddle and reins. You two can proceed with your journey, but don't be slow. "

The three of them were frightened and fell off the horse. They looked up and bowed, saying, "The disciple is but a human being with mortal flesh, and does not know the respect of the divine. I beg you to pardon me. Please convey this to the Bodhisattva, and bestow your blessings on me."

He just kept bowing, but didn't count the number of times. Just by their side, the Sun Wukong was laughing out loud, the Monkey King was delighted, and ran up to Tripitaka, grasping his robes, saying, "Teacher, get up, he's gone far away and can't hear you, he can't see you bowing. Just keep bowing like that."

Tripitaka said:

"Why are you laughing, my dear Sun Wukong? What are you laughing at? 

"Have you come to mock the laws of the monastery and to provoke the Bodhisattva? Then perhaps you won't get the monkey power after this journey. I'll be offended and won't save you.

"Your Reverence the Great Sage, let's get going, we have a long way to go.

"You know, when a mandarin duck flew to the skies, it's not just to soar, but also to sweep the waters below. If the fish and the birds see it, they'd know that the waters are sweet, so they'd come to live there. It's the same with you, Sun Wukong. You have the power of the Eight Lotus Flowers, why don't you just use it for your own benefits?

"As for me, I have promised the Bodhisattva to return to the capital, bring back the scriptures and spread the Buddhist teachings. My body is worn out, and I have a hundred thousand strands of silk that are far from rich.

"Please Sun Wukong, think about it with your great intelligence. When will we arrive in the Western Heavens? How will the world welcome the sacred scriptures? Don't forget the crowd of demon spirits and the various troubles on the road. Think with your wise head and decide on a plan. Why should we fly about without a thought?"

"Master, I present the saddle and bridle." The Three Caverns Master saw them and happily accepted them, teaching the Pilgrim to take them, and after mounting the horse, he looked and found them to be a suitable match. The Pilgrim walked up and one by one examined them, and indeed, they were fine things. There is a poem to attest to it, saying: 
The carved saddle gleams with vibrant colors, like stars in the silver moon.
The decorated stool radiates light, with golden threads shining bright.
A soft cloth draped on the tray, in several layers, tied with purple rope.
The rein head is made of a block of leather, with patterned flowers intricately crafted.
The cloud fan, with golden designs, depicts beasts dancing in the wind.
The metal ring clinks against the anvil, making the leather straps crisp.
The tips of the straps are dipped in water, with decorative hairs tied at the end.
The Pilgrim felt joy in his heart, and when he put the saddle and bridle on the horse, it looked as if they were made for him.

The Three Caverns Master bowed in gratitude, but the old man hurried to help him up and said, "Please, don't mention it! Please don't mention it!" The old man didn't invite him to stay, but instead bid the Three Caverns Master to mount his horse. The venerable monk left the gate, climbed onto his horse, and the Pilgrim carried the luggage. The old man took out a whip from his sleeve, a whip with a leather handle wrapped in scented cloth, with a piece of tiger sinew thread tied at the end, and offered it to the Three Caverns Master, saying, "Saintly monk, I still have one more gift for you, so please take it with you."

The Three Caverns Master was grateful and said, "Your benevolence is boundless! Your benevolence is boundless!" Just as he was about to ask for news, the old man had already disappeared, and when he looked back, the shrine was gone, and it was just a vast expanse of open land. Only then did he hear someone speaking from mid-air, saying, "Saintly monk, don't dawdle! I am the deity of the Mountain of Falling Flowers, sent by the Bodhisattva to present the saddle and bridle to you. You are to continue your journey to the West, but please don't delay."

The Three Caverns Master hastily got off his horse and bowed to the empty air, saying, "A disciple's ordinary mortal body cannot recognize the face of the noble deity, I beg your forgiveness. Please pass on my gratitude to the Bodhisattva, may they bestow their blessings upon me." He just kept bowing to the sky, without counting the number of bows, and on the side of the road, a living, laughing Sun Wukong and a delighted Monkey King appeared, and they came up to pull the Three Caverns Master up and said, "Master, get up! He's already gone far away, you can't hear your prayers and you can't see your bowing. Why keep bowing like that?"

The venerable monk said:

The Master, I present to you the saddle and bridle. Three Cavern Saw Monks saw it and was overjoyed, accepting it and instructing the Practitioner to take it. The Practitioner mounted his horse and looked at it to see if it was a good fit. The Practitioner walked forward and one by one, took up the pieces to look at them, and it indeed was some fine items. There was a poem as evidence, a poem that said:

The saddle carves, colors shining like stars, decorated with silver thread. 
The ornate bench shines, its gold lines radiant. 
A silken rug, layered like furs, folded and piled up. 
Three silk ropes, tightly tied with purple threads. 
The head of the bridle, a bundle of leather straps, adorned with colorful flowers. 
A fan, drawn in the image of cloud and beasts, is drawn with gold. 
The iron jawbiters, ground and polished, are suspended and hung with water-wet ends. 
The Practitioner's heart was secretly delighted, and he put the saddle and bridle on the horse as if they were custom-made. 

Three Cavern Saw Monks bowed to thank the old man, but the old man hastily helped him up and said, "Oh no, don't trouble yourself to thank me!" 
The old man didn't wait any longer, invited Three Cavern Saw Monks to mount his horse. Three Cavern Saw Monks came out of the door and mounted the horse, and the Practitioner carried his luggage. 
The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, a whip made from a piece of fragrant vine with a handle of leather strings and a tip of tiger's sinew, and handed it over to him, saying, "Saintly Monk, I have one more thing to give you, to send you off." 
Three Cavern Saw Monks in the horse replied, "I'm deeply grateful! I'm deeply grateful!" 

Just as he was about to ask a question, the old man had already disappeared. Upon looking back, the shrine was just a patch of empty land. 

Only to hear someone speaking from the air, "Saintly Monk, please don't be slow. I am the Land Deity of Luofa Mountain, sent by the Bodhisattva to give you the saddle and bridle. You should hurry on your journey, but don't be too slow." 

The Practitioner was frightened and rolled down from the horse, looked up and kowtowed, saying, "Disciple, a mere mortal, didn't recognize the divine face, begging to be pardoned. Please ask the Bodhisattva to transmit my gratitude." 

He just kept banging his head against the ground, and did not count how many times. On the side of the road, the Monkey King and the Sun Wukong were alive, laughing and losing their joy, and came forward to grab hold of Three Cavern Saw Monks and said, "Father, get up, he's already gone far away, you can't hear your prayers or see you kowtowing. What are you still kowtowing for?"

The Practitioner said:

"What can be seen with the eyes can be reported with the mouth, if you speak of it it is like dust in the wind. 
If you only speak of it, it will be a false report, a mere story, and it cannot be related to the true state of things. 
If you say it, then it is like seeing smoke in the sky. 
If you don't say it, then it is like not seeing anything. 
Therefore, if I speak of it, it will be false, and if I don't speak of it, it will be empty, so I'll just kowtow instead."

The Master, I present the saddle and reins. Upon seeing him, the pilgrim expressed his joy and received them, then handed them over to the Traveller to carry. The Traveller looked at them on the horse and examined them one by one to see if they matched. The pilgrim walked up in front to inspect them, one by one, and, sure enough, they were some good things. There is a poem to attest to it, a poem that says:

The saddle shines with carved designs that sparkle like silver stars,
The upholstered cushions beam with light, with golden thread shining bright.
The covering has multiple layers of woolen cloth piled up, 
The three straps are made of purple silk threads.
The rein head is made of quilted leather with flowers embroidered on it,
The cloud fan has golden decorations depicting beasts in motion.
The iron jawbone is hammered into shape, the two tassels are dipped in water, tied with horsehair.
The pilgrim was secretly delighted, and as he put the saddle and reins on the horse, it was just like they were made to fit.

The pilgrim bowed to thank the old man, but the old man hastily helped him up and said, "No need to thank me, no need to thank me, it's no trouble at all!" The old man no longer lingered, and invited the pilgrim to mount his horse. The venerable monk then left the gate, mounted his horse, and the Traveller carried his luggage. The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, it was made of a strip of aromatic cinnamon bark about an inch thick, with tiger tendon strings tied at the end, and handed it to him with a bow, saying, "Holy monk, I still have a gift for you, please accept it as a parting gift."

The pilgrim on horseback accepted it and said, "I am grateful, I am grateful!" Just as they were about to bid farewell, the old man was gone, and when they looked back, the temple was empty. They could hear someone speaking in mid-air saying, "Holy monk, please hurry along, do not tarry! I am the land god of Mount Luofu, sent by the Bodhisattva to give you the saddle and reins. Please hurry along on your journey, do not tarry."

The pilgrim rolled off his horse in a hurry, gazing upwards to pay his respects and saying, "I, a humble disciple, am blind to the majesty of the gods and do not recognize your divine visage, I beg for your pardon. Please pass on my thanks to the Bodhisattva and bestow your benevolence upon me." The pilgrim went on, not counting how many times he bowed, and, to the side, a living figure of the Monkey King was laughing out loud and a smiling Sun Wukong was grinning, they both came up and pulled at the pilgrim's sleeves saying, "Father, please get up, he has already gone far away, you can't hear your prayers and can't see your bows, just stop bowing like this!"

The pilgrim said, "Old Master, why did the land god of Mount Luofu come to bless us and give us the saddle and reins?"

As K. passed the corridor that separated his office from the main staircase on one of the next evenings – he was almost the last one to go home, only two servants were still working in the small glow of a lamp in the expedition – he heard sighs coming from behind a door that he had always suspected to be a storage room, without ever having seen it himself. He stopped in amazement and listened again to see if he wasn't mistaken – it was quiet for a while, then the sighs came back. – At first, he wanted to call one of the servants, maybe a witness was needed, but then an insatiable curiosity overcame him, and he burst the door open. It was just as he had suspected, a storage room. Old, unusable printing types, overturned empty clay ink bottles were behind the threshold. But in the room itself, three men stood, bent in the low space. A candle glued to a shelf lit them. "What are you doing here?" K. asked, rushing with excitement, but not loudly. The man who clearly dominated the others and who first caught K.'s attention, was dressed in a sort of dark leather outfit, which left his neck down to his chest and his entire arms bare. He didn't answer. But the other two cried out: "Sir! We are to be flogged because you complained to the investigating judge about us." And now K. realized that it was really Franz and Willem, the guards, and that the third one held a whip to flog them. "Well," said K. and stared at them, "I haven't complained, I just said what happened in my apartment. And you didn't behave yourself either, anyway." "Sir," said Willem, while Franz sought to secure himself behind the third one, "if you only knew how poorly we are paid, you would judge us better. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to get married, people seek to enrich themselves, as it goes, through hard work alone does not suffice, even the most arduous; your fine laundry has tempted me, it's of course forbidden for the guards to act this way, it was wrong, but it's a tradition that the laundry belongs to the guards, it's always been that way, believe me; it's only understandable what these things mean for someone who is unfortunate enough to be arrested. If he brings it up publicly, then the punishment must follow." "What you're saying, I didn't know, I wasn't asking for their punishment, it was a matter of principle for me." "Franz," Willem turned to the other guard, "didn't I tell you that the sir wasn't asking for our punishment? Now you see that he didn't even know we had to be punished." "Don't let yourself be swayed by such speeches," said the third one to K., "they've become a little feeble-minded from the fear of the whips. What this one here is saying about his possible career is downright laughable. Look at him, how fat he is – the first few whip strokes will be completely lost in the fat. – Do you know why he's so fat? He has the habit of eating the breakfast of all the arrested men. Didn't he also eat your breakfast? I told you so. But a man with such a belly can never, ever become a flogger, that's out of the question." "There are such floggers," claimed Willem, who was just unfastening his belt. "No," said the flogger, striking him with the whip so that he recoiled, "you should not listen, but take off your clothes." "I would reward you if you let them go," said K. and, without looking at the flogger again – such deals are best handled with downcast eyes – pulled out his wallet. "You want to get me to report you too, and get me whips as well?" said the flogger. "No, no!" "Be reasonable," said K., "if I wanted those two to be punished, I wouldn't want to buy them off now. I could simply close the door here, see nothing and hear nothing, and go home. But I'm not doing that, I'm actually interested in setting them free; if I had suspected they were to be punished or could be punished, I would never have mentioned their names. I don't think they're guilty, the organization is guilty, the high officials are guilty." "That's it!" cried the guards, and immediately they got a slap on their already bare backs. "If you had a high judge under your whip," said K. and pressed the whip back down, which was about to rise again, "I wouldn't hinder you, on the contrary, I would give you more money so you can whack it out for the good cause." "What you're saying sounds believable," said the flogger, "but I won't be bribed. I'm here to flog, that's what I was appointed for." The guard Franz, who had been fairly restrained so far in the expectation of a favorable outcome of K.'s intervention, now, only wearing his pants, approached the door, hugging K.'s arm and whispering: "If you can't get us both off scot-free, at least try to get me out of this. Willem is older than I, he's less sensitive in every way, he's even been given a light punishment a few years ago, I on the other hand am not yet disgraced, and I was led astray by Willem in both good and bad. My poor bride is waiting for me below by the bank, I'm so ashamed, I'm so ashamed." He dried his face, which was completely drenched with tears, with K.'s coat. And K. really did want to save the wardens; if he had already started to fight against the corruption of this judicial system, so he was at it now.

As K. passed the corridor on one of the next evenings, which separated his office from the main staircase - he was almost the last to go home, only two servants were still working in the little light of a lamp in the expedition - he heard sighs coming from behind a door that he had always suspected to be a broom closet, but had never seen himself. He stood frozen in amazement and listened again to make sure he wasn't mistaken - it became quiet for a bit, then the sighs started again. - At first, he wanted to call one of the servants to fetch, they might need a witness, but then a most uncontrollable curiosity overcame him, so he virtually flung the door open. It was exactly as he had suspected, a broom closet. Irreplaceable, old printing sorts, overturned empty earthen ink bottles lay behind the threshold. But in the room itself, three men stood huddled in the low space. A candle stuck to a shelf gave them light. "What's going on here?" K. asked, getting worked up, but not loudly. The man, who appeared to be in charge of the others and was the first to catch K.'s attention, was dressed in a sort of dark leather garb that left his neck all the way down to his chest and his arms bare. He didn't answer. But the other two exclaimed: "Sir, we're to be flogged because you complained about us to the investigating judge." And now it was only then that K. realized that it was really Franz and Willem, the guards, and that the third one had a rod in his hand to flog them. "Well," said K., staring at them, "I didn't complain, I only said what happened in my apartment. And you two, by the way, didn't behave impeccably." "Sir," said Willem, while Franz hid behind him, apparently securing himself to the third man, "if you only knew how poorly we're paid, you would judge us better. I have a family to support, and Franz here wanted to get married; we want to make a living, but by mere work it doesn't work, not even with the utmost diligence. Your fine clothes tempted me; it's, of course, forbidden for the guards to act like this, it was wrong, but it's a tradition that the clothes belong to the guards; it's always been like this; it's understandable, after all, what do such things mean for the one who's been unlucky enough to get arrested? But if one brings it up publicly, then the punishment follows." "What you're saying now, I didn't know," said K., "I didn't demand their punishment at all, it was about a principle for me." "Franz," Willem turned to the other guard, "didn't I tell you that the Herr didn't demand our punishment? Now listen, he didn't even know we were to be punished." "Don't let that move you," said the third one to K., "the punishment is as just as inevitable." "Don't listen to him," said Willem, interrupting himself only to quickly press the hand he had just received a whip lash to, "we're only punished because you reported us. If you hadn't done that, nothing would have happened to us, even if they'd known what we'd done. Can that be called justice?" We two, especially I, have proven ourselves as guards for a long time," said Willem. "We had prospects of advancement and would have probably become floggers like that one, who was lucky enough not to have been reported on; a complaint like that comes rarely enough. And now, sir, everything is ruined, our careers are over, we'll have to do much lower work than the duty of a guard, and to boot we're now getting these terribly painful floggings." "Can a rod really inflict such pain?" asked K., and he examined the rod that the flogger held. "We'll have to undress completely," said Willem. "Oh," said K., looking closely at the flogger, "he's as brown as a sailor and has a wild, fresh face." "Is there no way to spare the two floggings?" he asked him. "No," said the flogger, shaking his head with a smile. "Strip!" he ordered the guards. And to K. he said, "You don't have to believe everything they say, they've become a little mad from fear of the floggings. What this one, for example," he pointed to Willem, "tells about his possible career is downright laughable. Look, how fat he is – the first floggings will get lost in the fat altogether. – Do you know how he became so fat? He has the habit of eating the breakfast of the arrested men. Haven't you noticed him eating your breakfast too? Well, I said it. But a man with such a belly can never and never become a flogger, that's out of the question." "There are such floggers," insisted Willem, who was unfastening his belt. "No," said the flogger, and he struck Willem across the neck with the rod so hard that he winced, "don't listen to him, but undress." "I'd pay you well if you spared them," said K. and took out his wallet without looking at the flogger again – such dealings are best done with downcast eyes. "You want to report me too and bring me floggings?" said the flogger, "and now you're trying to bribe me? No, no!" "Be reasonable," said K., "if I had wanted the two to be punished, I wouldn't want to buy them off now. I could simply shut the door, not see or hear anything and go home. But I don't do that; on the contrary, I'm genuinely concerned about freeing them; if I'd known they were to be punished or could be punished, I wouldn't have mentioned their names. I don't think them guilty at all, the organization is to blame, the high officials are to blame." "So it is!" cried the guards and immediately received a blow across their already stripped backs. "If I had you under my rod, I'd really not hold you back from flogging, on the contrary, I'd give you money to beat hard for the good cause." "What you say sounds plausible," said the flogger, "but I won't be bribed. I'm hired to flog, so I flog." The guard Franz, who had hitherto been rather restrained, expecting a favorable outcome of K.'s intervention, now stepped forward, only in his trousers, to the door, knelt down to K.'s arm and whispered, "If you can't secure leniency for both of us, at least try to free me. Willem is older than I, less sensitive in every way, and he's had a light flogging a few years ago; but I'm not dishonored yet and was only led astray by Willem, my teacher in good and evil. Downstairs, my poor fiancée is waiting for the outcome, I'm ashamed to the point of desperation." He dried his face with K.'s coat, which was soaked with tears. "I'm waiting no more," said the flogger, grasped the rod with both hands and struck Franz, while Willem cowered in a corner and watched without even daring to turn his head. Then the scream that Franz let out was unbroken and unchangeable; it didn't seem to come from a human being, but from a tortured instrument, the whole corridor echoed with it, the whole house had to hear it. "Don't scream," shouted K., unable to hold back, and while looking intently in the direction from which the servants must have come, he pushed Franz, not hard, but hard enough for him to fall down and frantically search the floor with his hands; the blows, however, were not avoided; the rod found him on the ground; as he writhed under it, its tip moved regularly up and down. And already, in the distance, a servant appeared, and a few steps behind him another one. K. quickly closed the door, went to one of the windows and opened it. The screaming had completely stopped. In order not to let the servants come in, he called out, "I'm it!" "Good evening, Mr. Procurator!" it was called back. "Is something happened?" "No, no," replied K., "it's just a dog barking in the yard." As the servants didn't move, he added, "You may stay at work." In order not to engage in conversation with the servants, he leaned out the window. When he looked again into the corridor after a little while, they were already gone. K. now stayed by the window, he didn't dare to go into the broom closet and wanted to go home neither. It was a small quadrangular yard, into which he looked down; there were office rooms all around, all windows were already dark, only the topmost ones caught a moonlit glow. K. searched anxiously with his eyes to penetrate the darkness of a corner of the yard, where some hand-carts had been driven into each other. It was tormenting him that he hadn't managed to prevent the flogging, but it wasn't his fault that he hadn't managed to prevent it; if Franz hadn't screamed, it would have been different, he would have probably found some way to persuade the flogger in the decisive moment; if the whole lower stratum of officials was scum, why should the flogger, who had the most inhumane job, be an exception? K. had also noticed how the flogger's eyes had sparkled at the sight of the banknote, he had only pretended to flog seriously in order to increase the bribe amount. And K. would not have spared, it was genuinely his intention to free the guards; if he had started to combat the corruption of this judicial system, he would not be able to stop now.

It cannot be said that the hero's nature was so harsh and heartless, and that his feelings were dulled to the point where he did not know either pity or compassion. He felt both, and he even wanted to help, but only if it wouldn't involve a considerable amount, and not touch the money that was not meant to be touched; in short, the father's advice: be thrifty and save a coin – it'll pay off in the end. But it wasn't a particular fondness for money for its own sake that motivated him; miserliness and greed did not possess him. No, it was something else that drove him: a vision of a life in abundance, with all sorts of comforts; carriages, a well-furnished home, and delicious meals – these were constantly whirling in his head. So that he could finally enjoy all this later, when the time came, he carefully saved every kopeck, stingily withholding it from himself and others for the time being. Whenever a wealthy man rode past in a sleek carriage, with well-groomed horses harnessed in a fine harness, he would stop dead in his tracks, frozen to the spot, and then, waking up, as from a long sleep, would say: "And he was once a clerk, with his hair combed in a ringlet!" And whatever reminded him of wealth and comfort left an indelible impression on him. Having graduated from school, he did not even want to rest: his desire to start work and serve was so strong. Nevertheless, despite his excellent diplomas, it was with great difficulty that he secured a position in the government office. And in the provinces, one needs patronage! He got a small post, with a salary of thirty or forty rubles a year. But he resolved to tackle his work with great zeal, to overcome all obstacles. And indeed, he showed an unprecedented self-denial, endurance, and self-restraint. From early morning till late evening, without tiring his mind or body, he would write, completely covered in office paperwork, not going home, sleeping on office tables, sometimes eating with the night guards, and yet managing to maintain his dignity, dress neatly, and even exhibit something noble in his movements. It must be said that the officials in the office were particularly ugly and unprepossessing. Some of them had faces that looked like poorly baked bread: one cheek was puffed out to one side, their chin was askew to the other, and their upper lip was blown out in a pimple, which, in addition to that, cracked. In short, they looked very unattractive. They all spoke in a stern tone, with a voice as if they were about to hit someone, and they often made offerings to Vakh, thus showing that there are still remnants of paganism in the Slavic nature. They even arrived at meetings, as they say, after getting drunk, and the atmosphere was unpleasant and not at all aromatic. In such a company, Chichikov, presenting a complete opposite in his appearance, voice, and sobriety, could not remain unnoticed. However, his path was a difficult one; he fell under the authority of a very elderly provator, who was like a stone statue of insensitivity and unshakeability: he was always the same, impenetrable, never showing a smile on his face, never greeting anyone, not even with a query about their health. Nobody saw him ever be anything other than what he always was, neither on the street nor at home; never did he show any sign of weakness, nor did he get drunk and laugh; never did he give in to wild revelry, as a bandit does in a drunken fit, but even a shadow of such a thing was absent in him. He was precisely nothing: neither villainous nor good, and something frightening appeared in this absence of all qualities. His stony face, without any sharp irregularities, did not hint at any similarity; the features of his face were strictly proportional to each other. Only the many wrinkles and creases that lined them made people look at him as if he was a face that the devil used to shape in the dead of night. It seemed there were no human powers that could overcome this man and win his favor, but Chichikov decided to try. At first, he began to fawn on him in small, imperceptible ways: he examined the quill with which he wrote and made a few similar ones to give to him every time; he blew and swept off the sand and tobacco from his table; he brought a new cloth for his inkwell; he found his old, wretched hat, which was the ugliest in the world, and always placed it next to him a moment before his departure; he cleaned his back for him, if he had gotten it dirty with paint on the wall – but all this was met with complete indifference, as if nothing had been done at all, as if nothing had been noticed. Finally, he inquired about his family life and discovered that he had a grown-up daughter, with a face that was similar in its appearance to a face shaped by the devil in the dead of night. From this side, he came up with an idea. He found out which church she attended on Sundays, and always stood opposite her, neatly dressed, with a stiffly starched cravat, and the business was successful: the stern provator shifted in his seat and invited him for tea! And in the office, they didn't have time to look around before it became arranged that Chichikov moved into his house, became a necessary and important person, bought flour and sugar for him, treated his daughter like a fiancée, called the provator "old man," kissed his hand; everyone in the office thought that by the end of February, before the Great Lent, there would be a wedding. The stern provator even began to lobby for him with the authorities, and not long after, Chichikov himself was appointed provator on a vacant position. It seemed that this was the main purpose of his connections with the old provator, because he secretly sent his trunk home and the next day was already on a new apartment. He no longer called him "old man" or kissed his hand, and the wedding plans were forgotten as if they had never happened. However, when they met, he would always affectionately shake his hand and invite him for tea, and the old provator, despite his eternal immobility and frozen indifference, would every time shake his head and say to himself: "He's duped me, he's duped me, that scoundrel!"

It cannot be said that the hero of our tale was as coarse and unfeeling as is often represented, and that his sentiments were dulled to the point where he felt neither pity nor compassion; he felt both, and would have liked to help, but only on condition that it wouldn't be a significant expense, wouldn't disturb the funds that were not to be touched; in short, his father's advice: "save and pin a kopeck for a rainy day" seemed sensible. But in him it was not a genuine fondness for money for money's sake; neither parsimony nor avarice had control over him. No, it was not they that moved him: a life of comfort and plenty, with all its luxuries, haunted his imagination; carriages, a well-appointed home, and delicious meals were the things that constantly danced in his head. In order to taste all these eventually, in time, it was the kopeck that was saved, stingily refused to himself and others at the time. When a wealthy merchant passed by on his stylish sleigh, riding horses in a fine harness, he would stop in his tracks, frozen, and then, waking up, as from a long sleep, would say: "And yet he used to be a clerk, he used to wear his hair in a queue!" And anything related to wealth and comfort would make a profound impression on him, one that he himself could not fathom.

Having left school, he didn't even want to rest; his desire to start work and service was so strong. However, despite his praiseworthy diplomas, he struggled hard to get a position in the government office. Out in the provinces, it's all about patronage, after all! He got a tiny posting, with a salary of thirty or forty rubles a year. But he was resolute, and he devoted himself to his service with dedication, determination, and self-restraint, showing an unheard-of ability to resist. From early morning till late evening, without tiring either his physical or mental strength, he wrote, drowning in government papers, not going home, sleeping on office tables, sometimes eating with the nightwatchmen, and yet, he managed to keep his dignity, dress properly, maintain a pleasant expression on his face, and even exhibit something noble in his movements. It's worth noting that government clerks stood out for their dullness and lack of refinement. Some of them had faces that looked like bad bread: one cheek was puffed up, the chin slanted the other way, the upper lip was swollen, and to top it off, it was cracked; in short, they were not exactly attractive. They all spoke in a stern tone, as if gathering to give someone a thrashing; they made frequent sacrifices to Vakh (a nod to paganism in the Slavic psyche); they even sometimes came to their posts after drinking, which made things unpleasant in the office, and the air was not exactly fragrant.

Among such officials, Chichikov naturally stood out, representing a perfect opposite in the matter of a refined face, and a friendly voice, and complete abstention from strong drink. However, his path was difficult; he had to deal with an old, stubborn prosecutor, who embodied a sort of granite indifference and impassivity: he was always the same, impenetrable, never showing a smile on his face, never greeting anyone, even with a query about their health. No one ever saw him be anything but what he was, either on the street or at home; he never showed a spark of humor, never got drunk and laughed in his cups; he never gave in to unbridled revelry, as a robber does in a drunken moment, but even the faintest hint of such a thing was absent in him. He was precisely nothing: neither good nor bad, and it was this complete lack of anything that was frightening. His granite face, without any sharp irregularities, hinted at no similarity to anything; his features were so evenly proportioned. Only the frequent wrinkles and furrows that etched them made people think of him as one of those faces on which, as the saying goes, the devil came to beat the flax at night. It seemed that there was no way to win him over and gain his favor, but Chichikov tried. At first, he began to ingratiate himself in small, imperceptible ways: he carefully examined the quill pens the prosecutor used, made a few similar ones, and placed them before him every time; he dusted and swept the sand and tobacco off his desk; he introduced a new blotting pad for his inkwell; he found his old hat, a hat more hideous than any that had ever existed, and placed it beside him every time before the meeting; he cleaned his back for him if he got it dirty with wall paste – but all this went completely unnoticed, as if nothing had been done. Eventually, he discovered the prosecutor's family life, learned that he had a grown daughter with a face that, as if by a miracle, also resembled the image of a face on which the devil comes to beat the flax at night. From this side, he thought up a plan. He learned which church she attended on Sundays, and every time he stood outside it, dressed neatly, with his shirtfront starched, and the thing took effect: the stern prosecutor wavered and invited him for tea! Before long, things had arranged themselves so that Chichikov moved in with him, became a necessary and welcome person, buying flour and sugar for him, treating his daughter like a fiancée, calling the prosecutor "father," kissing his hand; everyone in the office was convinced that at the end of February, just before Lent, there would be a wedding. The stern prosecutor even started making a fuss for him with the authorities, and soon Chichikov got promoted to the position of a prosecutor in a vacancy that had opened up. In this, it seemed, lay the main purpose of his connections with the old prosecutor, because he secretly sent his trunk home and the next day he was already in a new apartment. He stopped calling the old prosecutor "father" and stopped kissing his hand, and the matter of the wedding was quietly dropped, as if nothing had happened. However, whenever he met him, he would always warmly shake his hand and invite him for tea, so that the old prosecutor, despite his perpetual impassivity and cold indifference, would shiver his head every time and mutter to himself: "He's taken me for a fool, he's taken me for a fool, that devil's son!"

It is impossible to say, however, that his nature was so harsh and hard, and that his feelings were so numbed, that he did not know how to feel compassion or pity; he felt both, and even wanted to help, but only not in any way that involved a significant amount, not to touch the money that should not be touched; in other words, a father's instruction: save and store up a coin – it will come in handy. But he was not fond of money for its own sake; he was not driven by stinginess or miserliness. No, it was not these things that moved him: ahead of him was a life of all comforts, with all the essentials; carriages, a well-settled home, delicious meals – this was what was constantly whirling in his head. So that he might finally enjoy all this at some point, after a time, the coin was carefully saved, sparingly refused even to himself and others. When a rich man would ride by in his fancy coaches, on fine horses in a rich harness, he would come to a stop as if rooted to the spot and, coming to, as from a long sleep, would say: "And he used to be a clerk, with his hair combed into a circle!" And whatever related to wealth and comfort produced in him an impression he could hardly grasp himself. 

Leaving school, he did not even want to rest: his desire to start work and serve was so strong. However, despite the commendable certificates, he was barely placed in the government office. And in remote outposts, connections are needed! A minor position was given to him, with an annual salary of thirty or forty rubles. But he resolved to work with passion, to overcome and conquer everything. And indeed, he showed an unheard-of self-discipline, patience, and self-restraint. From early morning to late evening, without tiring his mental or physical strength, he wrote, buried up to his neck in bureaucratic papers, did not go home, slept in the office on desks, often ate with the watchmen, and yet was able to maintain his tidiness, dress neatly, have a pleasant expression on his face, and even some nobility in his movements. It is necessary to say that the office clerks were particularly distinguished by their plainness and lack of comeliness. Some had faces that looked like poorly baked bread: one cheek was puffed out to one side, the chin was twisted to the other, the upper lip was blown out like a bubble, and on top of that, it was cracked; in short, they were quite ugly. Among such officials, Chichikov could not help but stand out and be noticed, representing in all respects the perfect opposite of plainness of face, and the politeness of voice, and the complete absence of any strong drink.

However, his road was difficult; he fell under the jurisdiction of an already old procurator, who was a kind of embodiment of insensibility and impassiveness: he was always the same, impenetrable, never showing a smile on his face, never greeting anyone, not even with a request about their health. His marmoreal face, without any sharp irregularities, did not hint at any similarity; his features were in a stern proportion to each other. It seemed there was no human strength to overcome such a man and win his favor, but Chichikov tried. At first, he started to please him in minor ways: he carefully examined the pen nibs he used and, preparing several like them, laid them in his hand every time; he blew and brushed off the sand and tobacco from his table; he brought a new cloth for his inkwell; he found his wretched hat, a hat that had ever existed in the world, and every time he placed it near him just before the end of the meeting; he cleaned his back for him if he had marked it with white chalk on the wall; but all this remained absolutely without any notice, as if nothing had been done at all. Finally, he sniffed out his domestic, family life, learned that he had a grown daughter with a face that looked as if the devil was threshing grain on her at night. From this side he came up with a plan. He stopped calling him "old fellow" and no longer kissed his hand, and the matter of the wedding was just dropped as if it had never happened. But when they met, he would always pat him on the hand and invite him for tea, and the old attorney, despite his perpetual immobility and coldheartedness, would every time shake his head and mutter to himself: "Cheated, cheated, that scoundrel!"

It cannot be said, however, that the hero's nature was as harsh and cruel, and that his feelings were so dulled, that he did not know either pity or compassion; he felt both, he would even have liked to help, but only to the extent that it did not involve a considerable sum, so as not to touch the money that was not to be touched; in a word, the paternal advice: save and store up a copper – it will come in handy. But in him, there was no attachment to money for its own sake; thriftiness and stinginess did not rule over him. No, it was not they that motivated him: a life full of pleasures, with all the amenities, appeared before him; carriages, a well-settled home, delicious meals – these were the things that constantly whirled in his head. To taste all this, eventually, at some time, that's why the copper was saved, sparingly withheld from himself and others alike. When a wealthy man passed by in a sleek sleigh, driven by fine horses in a rich harness, he would stop dead in his tracks, and then, waking up as from a long sleep, would say: 'And he was a clerk, he used to wear his hair in a queue!' And everything that was connected with wealth and comfort made an indescribable impression on him.

Leaving school, he did not even want to rest: his desire to start working and serve was so strong. However, despite the excellent certificates, it was with great difficulty that he got assigned to a government office. And in remote areas, you need influence! A tiny post was assigned to him, with a salary of thirty or forty rubles a year. But he resolved to throw himself into his work with passion, to overcome everything. And, indeed, he showed incredible self-denial, patience, and self-restraint. From early morning to late evening, without exhausting his spiritual or physical strength, he wrote, buried in official documents, did not go home, slept in the office, often had meals with the janitors, and yet managed to keep himself tidy, properly dressed, and with a pleasant expression on his face, and even a certain nobility in his movements. It should be noted that the office officials stood out for their dullness and lack of amiability. Some of them had faces that looked as if bad bread had been made of them: one cheek had been puffed up, the chin had been pulled to one side, the upper lip had been blown out like a bubble, and, on top of that, it had cracked – in short, they looked very ugly. They all spoke in a stern tone, with a voice as if they were trying to intimidate someone; they often made sacrifices to Vakh, thus showing that in the Slavic nature there are still many remnants of paganism; they would even come to the meeting drunk, which made things unpleasant in the presence and the air was not at all fragrant. Among such officials, Chichikov could not fail to stand out, presenting a complete contrast in the smoothness of his face, the friendliness of his voice, and the complete lack of any strong drinks. But despite this, his path was difficult; he fell under the authority of an elderly and long-serving prosecutor who was some kind of monument to indifference and unyieldingness: forever the same, impassive, never showing a smile on his face, never greeting anyone, even with a query about their health. No one had ever seen him in a state that was different from what he always was, either on the street or at home; he had never shown any change, never gotten drunk and laughed in his drunkenness; he had never indulged in wild revelry, as a robber might, but even a shadow of such a thing was not in him. There was nothing in him either purely evil or purely good; something terrifying revealed itself in this absence of everything. His granite-like face, without any sharp irregularities, did not hint at any resemblance; the features of his face were in strict harmony with each other. Only the frequent wrinkles and unevenness of his skin made him look like one of those people, as the saying goes, on whom the devil comes to thrash corn at night. It seemed that there were no human powers that could overcome him and win his favor, but Chichikov tried. At first, he started to win him over in small, unnoticed ways: he carefully examined the pencils with which the prosecutor wrote, and, making a few copies of them, he would leave them by his side every time; he would brush off and sweep the sand and tobacco from his table; he introduced a new cloth for his inkwell; he found the prosecutor's old, wretched hat somewhere, and every time would put it next to him just a moment before the end of the meeting; he would clean his back if he had gotten it dirty with chalk – but all this was met with complete indifference, as if nothing had been done. Finally, he got wind of the prosecutor's home life, learned that he had a grown daughter with a face that looked as if she was also the one the devil came to thrash corn at night. From that angle, he came up with a plan. He learned which church she attended on Sundays, stood every time in front of her, neatly dressed, with his cravat tucked in strongly – and it worked: the stern prosecutor wavered and invited him to tea! And before the officials in the office could even turn around, things had arranged themselves so that Chichikov moved into the prosecutor's house, became a necessary and important person, bought flour and sugar, treated his daughter like a fiancée, called the prosecutor 'papa', kissed his hand; everyone in the office thought that in February, at the beginning of the Great Lent, there would be a wedding. The stern prosecutor even started lobbying for him with the authorities, and after some time, Chichikov himself became a prosecutor in a vacant position. In this, it seemed, lay the main goal of his connection with the old prosecutor, because there, secretly, he sent his trunk home and the next day found himself already on another apartment. The prosecutor was no longer called 'papa' and was no longer kissed on the hand, and the wedding plans just faded away, as if nothing had happened. However, whenever they met, he would affectionately shake his hand and invite him to tea, and the old prosecutor, despite his eternal immobility and cold indifference, would every time shake his head and mutter to himself: 'He's fooled me, he's fooled me, that scoundrel!'

It was he who told me about his emotional state in the last days of his stay in his master's household, explained Ippolit Kirillovich. Other witnesses as well attest to the same: the defendant himself, his brother, and even their servant, Gregory – all those who must have known him very well. Add to this the fact that Smerdyakov was utterly depressed by his illness and "afraid as a chicken." "He would fall at my feet and kiss my feet," reported the defendant, when he was still unaware of the negative consequences of such a revelation, "he was a chicken in a convulsive fit," he expressed it in his own peculiar way. And it was this same defendant who chose him as his trusted informant and terrified him to such an extent that he finally agreed to become his spy and messenger. In this capacity as a household watchdog, he betrayed his master and informed the defendant about the existence of a package with money and the signs by which it was possible to get to his master – and he might just as well have told him everything. "They'll kill me, I saw it right there, they'll kill me," he said during the investigation, shaking and trembling even before us, despite the fact that the one who had terrorized him was already under arrest and could no longer come to punish him. "I was suspected all the time," he added, "I was in a state of fear and tremors, and I rushed to tell them every secret in order to prove my innocence to them and to have them pardon me and let me live." These are his own words, which I noted down and remembered: "As soon as he would shout at me, I would fall to my knees before them." A young man of high moral principles, who had gained the trust of his master, who had returned the money he had lost to him, the unfortunate Smerdyakov, presumably, was horribly tormented by remorse for his betrayal of his master, whom he loved as his benefactor. As medicine says, people severely suffering from epilepsy are always inclined to continuous and, of course, painful self-reproach. They suffer from their "guilt" in something or to someone, suffer from pangs of conscience, often even without any foundation, exaggerate and even invent for themselves various sins and crimes. And it is this very subject who becomes guilty and criminal due to fear and intimidation. In addition, he strongly felt that from the unfolding circumstances something unpleasant might arise. When Feodor Pavlovich's eldest son, Ivan Fyodorovich, was leaving for Moscow just before the catastrophe, Smerdyakov implored him to stay, but, being a coward by nature, he did not dare to express his concerns to him in plain and categorical terms. He was content with hints, but they were not understood. It should be noted that Smerdyakov regarded Ivan Fyodorovich as a kind of protection, a kind of guarantee that as long as he was at home, no harm would come to him. Recall the expression in Dmitri Karamazov's "drunken" letter: "I'll kill the old man if only Ivan leaves." So it was as if Ivan's presence in the house was a guarantee of peace and order. And so, he leaves, and Smerdyakov immediately, almost an hour after Ivan's departure, falls into a convulsive fit. But this is quite understandable. It is worth noting that, being overcome by fear and a kind of despair, Smerdyakov in the last days had felt within himself the possibility of approaching convulsive fits, which had always occurred in him in moments of emotional tension and shock. The day and hour of these fits could not be predicted, of course, but an epileptic can feel the predisposition to a fit in advance. This is what medicine says. And only just as Ivan Fyodorovich is leaving the estate, Smerdyakov, under the impression of his own loneliness and helplessness, goes to do some household chores in the cellar, goes downstairs by the stairs and thinks, "Will there be a fit or won't there be one, and what if it happens now?" And it is precisely this mood, this apprehension, these questions that give him a throat spasm, which always precedes a convulsive fit, and he flies down to the bottom of the cellar without a consciousness. And it is exactly in this very natural accident that they try to find some suspicion, some indication, some hint that he intentionally pretended to be ill! But if he intentionally did so, the question arises: for what purpose, with what calculation, and with what goal?
