The discussion had just reached that point when the master of the Xianyuan residence busied himself, and asked Master Sun to take a vegetarian meal. However, the Traveler took some sesame seeds and got onto a cloud to go in search. Just as they were traveling, they saw a small strange creature carrying a camphor wood box strapped to its left armpit, coming along the main road. The Traveler estimated that the box must contain some letter of introduction, so he raised his staff to strike, but alas, he couldn't help himself and gave a fatal blow, which left the creature floundering on the ground, resembling a meat pie, yet still dragging along beside the road. He then lifted the lid of the box to take a look, and lo and behold, it was a formal invitation. The invitation read: "Shengsheng Xiong Bian (Bear-but) kowtows and addresses: The venerable Elder of the Golden Pool, Big Master of the Dan Hall: I have received your numerous kindnesses and am deeply grateful. Last night, I witnessed the difficulty of the return of the prosperity, and failed to offer any assistance. Assuming the divine machines have no other malice. I, by chance, obtained a piece of Buddhist robes, and would like to hold a feast. I shall prepare wine and delicacies, and respectfully wait for the Elder to drop by for an enjoyment. I beg the Elder to kindly grant me an audience on that day. Sincerely, Shengsheng Xiong Bian. Two days prior to that date." 

The Traveler having seen this, burst out laughing loudly, "What a pitiful old fellow, how he died so miserably! He had obviously conspired with the demon maid! It's no wonder he lived to the age of two hundred and seventy. I suppose that demon maid must have taught him some subtle art to extend his lifespan. Old Sun remembers his appearance and will disguise himself as a monk to pay him a visit to his cave. If he succeeds, he can just retrieve my cassock, which would be a great convenience."

Just as they were speaking, the master of the mansion on the second floor, once again, got ready the vegetarian food and invited Mr. Sun to a fast. The monk, however, ate some of the required portion, and then rode on a cloud again to search. While he was on his way, he suddenly saw a small monster, with a cherry wood box stuck under his left arm, coming from the main road. The monk guessed that the box must contain some invitation, so he raised his staff and struck the monster on the head. Unfortunately, he couldn't resist hitting him, and the monster was hit so hard that he was flattened like a pancake and left lying on the road. The monk opened the box to take a look, and sure enough, it contained an invitation. The invitation read: "Kumang (i.e., the monster) Hong bows respectfully, pays homage to the great Immortal, Elder Gold Pool, of the Dan Pavilion: Your goodness has been bestowed upon me many times, and I deeply feel grateful. Observing the difficulties in receiving official appointment, I have lost the opportunity to receive your protection, and I believe the reason is that I must have offended you somehow. I have obtained a Buddhist robe and wish to hold a literary gathering. I have carefully prepared the tea and am eager to receive your visit and enjoy a friendly chat together. I invite you to come at your convenience. I bid you farewell two days in advance. Respectfully, Kumang." The monk saw this and burst out laughing loudly, "That old wretch is scoundrel enough to live for two hundred and seventy years! He has been making friends with demons all along! That's why he has lived so long. I remember his appearance, and now I will change into a monk and go into his cave to see where my Buddhist robe is kept. If I get my hands on it, I will bring it back, and it will save me a lot of trouble."

Just as they were talking, the courtyard host prepared a vegetarian meal and invited Master Sun to take his leave. The monk, however, only took a snack, and, riding his cloud, went off to look for him. While on the way, they chanced upon a small demon, who was carrying a intricately crafted flower-pine wood box tucked under his left armpit, approaching from the main road. The monk suspected that there must be some invitation inside the box and lifted his staff to strike. Alas, he was so taken aback by the demon's looks that he could not help but hit him, and the demon was beaten to a pulp, just like a pancake, and dragged along the road. The monk then opened the box to take a look and indeed found an invitation inside. The invitation read: "The Junior Fellow Student He Shao Fang sincerely bows to the Grandmaster of the Golden Pool's Tower of Elixir: You have graciously bestowed your benevolence on me repeatedly, and I am deeply grateful. Tonight, observing the hardships of this scholar, I fear that I may have done him harm inadvertently. However, I suspect that it was just a matter of your divine intervention, and that there must have been no other reason for it. The other day, I happened to obtain a Buddhist robe, and I would like to use it as an opportunity to hold a refined gathering. I shall provide some wine and flowers and await your esteemed presence. Please arrive at the appointed time and let us get together. I look forward to it. Sincerely. I will send word in two days in advance." The monk laughed heartily upon reading it and said: "That old scoundrel won't have lost a single thread of his life! It seems that he has made a pact with a fairy! I've often thought it strange that he has lived to be two hundred and seventy years old. I suspect that that fairy must have taught him some kind of elixir technique, which has given him this longevity. Old Sun remembers his appearance, so let me just transform into a monk and go to his lair to see where he has put my cassock. If I can get my hands on it, I'll just take it back without exerting myself."

The old sage just said this, and the chief of the house in the upper mansion once again went to prepare the offerings, inviting Mr. Sun to a vegetarian meal. The Great Sage then ate a bit, and, riding his auspicious cloud, went to search again. Just as he was on his way, he saw a small demon, with a small box of jujube wood under his left armpit, coming from the main road. The Great Sage surmised that there must be some invitation card inside the box, raised his staff, and struck with all his might, alas, he couldn't help but spare him, and struck him instead with such force that he was flung to the side of the road like a fried pancake. As he opened the box to take a look, lo and behold, it was indeed an invitation. The invitation read: "Servant Bear-gem kowtows nine times, submits to Elder Patriarch of the Golden Pool, Golden Robes: Time and again, I have received your kindness, deeply grateful. Observing the change in my fortune, I have suffered loss, and, considering the workings of the divine, there must be no other mishap. I obtained a Buddha's robe, and wish to hold a gathering, carefully preparing the elegant cups, to present and savour the purities. At the appointed hour, I humbly request that you deign to come and exchange courtesies. With gratitude. Two days in advance. Bring it along." The Great Sage saw this and burst out laughing, "That scoundrel, won't regret it one single hair! He's clearly allied himself with the fiend! No wonder he's lived for 270 years! I reckon that fiend must have passed on some deceitful tricks to him, and that's why he's got this long life. The Great Sage still remembers his face, I'll just transform into the monk, and go to his lair to look for where my robes are. If I succeed, I'll just take them back, and it will save me the trouble."

Just then, the Tathagata and others returned and the abbot of the Shangfang yuan summoned the monk to take his afternoon meal. The priest finished a few bites, then mounted the celestial cloud and went out again to search. As he was traveling, he saw a small strange being with a silken box tucked under his left armpit, coming along the main road. The priest thought that there must be a letter or notice inside the box, so he raised his staff to strike. Alas, he couldn't help but strike first, and struck him so hard that the creature fell to the ground like a meat pie. The staff left him sprawled out on the road, so he opened the box to take a look, and sure enough, it was an invitation inside. The invitation read: "Respectfully presented by Assistant Graduate Xiong Ma, on bended knees I bow, sir Grand Sage Jinchi Lao Dasheng of the Danfang hall: your numerous benevolences I have received, my gratitude is profound. Watching the difficult return of the Eight Trigrams in the night, I failed to offer any aid, yet I reckon that your supernatural abilities would not lead to any other consequence. I happened to get hold of a Buddhist robe, and wanted to host a festive gathering, and took the liberty of preparing a floral cup to present it to you for your noble enjoyment. I await your divine visit. I beg to trouble you to be present at the appointed time, a day in advance. Respectfully, beforehand, I invite." The priest saw this, and laughed loudly: "That old scoundrel won't die even an inch! He has formed an alliance with the demon, that's why he's lived for 270 years. He must have gotten some small secret from the demon to prolong his life. The priest remembers his appearance, so I'll change into that monk and go to his cave to take a look, see where I've left my dhyotis robes. If I manage to get it, I'll just take it back, and that would save me a lot of trouble."

So, that's where people come to live, I'd rather say it's where people come to die. I've been there. I've seen hospitals. I saw a person stumbling and sinking. People gathered around him, so I didn't have to. I saw a pregnant woman. She made her way slowly along a high, warm wall, sometimes feeling it, as if to convince herself that it was still there. Yes, it was still there. Behind it? I looked at my map: Maternity House. Good. They will deliver her— they can do that.

Good. They'll deliver her – you can do that.

I was so struck by his proposal that I couldn't help but weep. He took my tears for gratitude and said that he had always been convinced that I was a kind, sensitive, and learned young woman, but that until he had gathered all the particulars about my current behavior, he had not dared to take such a step. He inquired about you, stating that he had heard everything about you and that you are a man of noble principles, and he said that from his side, he did not want to be in your debt and that five hundred rubles would be enough to repay you for everything you have done for me. When I explained to him what you have done for me, which cannot be repaid in any amount of money, he said it was all nonsense, that it was mere fantasy, that I am still young and that reading novels is bad for young girls, that books corrupt virtue, and that he utterly despises any kind of books; he advised me to live for many years and then speak of people; "then," he added, "you will get to know people." 

Then he said I should carefully consider his proposal, that he would be very annoyed if I were to make such an important decision rashly, adding that rashness and infatuation destroy inexperienced youth, but that he greatly desires a favorable response from me, and that, finally, in the opposite case, he is forced to marry a wealthy merchant's daughter in Moscow, because, as he says, he has pledged to a villainous nephew that I shall be disinherited. He forcibly left five hundred rubles with me, as he said, for pastries; he said that in the village I was plump as a pancake, that I would be with him like butter in oil, that he has a lot of troubles now, that he spent the whole day on affairs, and that now, between tasks, he came to me. Then he left. I thought a lot, I changed my mind many times, I tormented myself, thinking, dear friend, and finally I decided. Dear friend, I will marry him; I must agree to his proposal. If anyone can rescue me from my shame, restore my good name, ward off poverty, hardships, and future misfortunes, it is he alone. What can I expect from the future, what can I ask of fate? Fedor says that one shouldn't lose one's happiness; he asks – what then is happiness? At least I do not find any other way out for myself, dear and precious friend. What am I to do? I have already ruined my health through work; I cannot work constantly. Go out into society? – I would perish from longing; besides, I would not suit anyone. I am sick by nature, and so I would always be a burden to others. Of course, I am not going to heaven now, but what am I to do, dear friend, what am I to do? What choice do I have?

There were, nonetheless, moments of holding back and half-consciousness. He thought about it in consternation. On what paths! He had, like every man in whom natural virtues instilled an aristocratic interest in his ancestry, become accustomed to recalling his forebears in the achievements and successes of his life, to assure himself of their consent, their approval, their necessarily begrudging respect. He was thinking of them now, here, entangled in such an inappropriate experience, lost in such exotic indulgences of feeling; recalling their staid reserve, their manly character, and smiling wistfully. What would they say? But, after all, what would they have said to his entire life, which had diverged from theirs to the point of degeneration, to this life under the spell of art, about which he had once, in the middle-class values of his fathers, expressed a mocking youth's insight and which, at its core, was so similar to theirs! He too had served, he too had undergone hard discipline; he too was a soldier and a man of war, just like many of them—for art was a war, a grueling struggle for which one did not last long today. A life of self-overcoming and defiance, a harsh, resolute and abstinent life, which he had fashioned into a symbol of a delicate and timely heroism—it was surely manly, surely brave to name it thus, and it seemed to him as if the Eros he had mastered was suited to such a life in some way and inclined towards it. Had he not held a special place of esteem among the bravest of peoples, yes, was it not said that he had flourished through bravery in their cities? Many warriors of old had willingly borne the yoke, for no degradation was considered worthy of a god, and actions that would have been censured as marks of cowardice if done for other purposes: bowing, oaths, heartfelt entreaties and servile nature—these did not bring shame to the lover, but rather earned him praise for it.

The Bodhisattva led the multitudes into the hall and after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, he met with the Old Lord and the Queen Mother, and each of them took their seats. "How will the Peony Feast turn out?" the Bodhisattva asked. The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year we invite the meeting with great joy and festivity. But this time it was marred by the mischief of the mischievous monkey. It was indeed an empty invitation." The Bodhisattva inquired, "What is the origin of the mischievous monkey?" The Jade Emperor said, "The mischievous monkey is the product of Flower Fruit Mountain in the Blossoming County of the Eastern Victory Heaven. When he was first born, he emitted golden light with his eyes. He did not initially provoke any concern, but later on he became refined, subdued dragons and tigers, and even killed some people. The Dragon King and the King of the Underworld reported to me. I intended to seize him, but the Long Cheng star intervened and said, 'In the three realms, any creature with nine orifices can become immortal.' I then bestowed upon him teachings, invited him to the Upper Realm, and appointed him as the Official of the Stables and the Steed. However, he detested the humble post and rebelled against the heavenly court. I then dispatched Li the Heavenly King and Nezha the Prince to coax him into submission. I also issued a decree, summoning him to the Upper Realm and appointed him as the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' but without any rank or stipend. He, having nothing to do, wandered east and west, and I again feared that he might cause trouble, and so I assigned him to oversee the Peach Blossom Garden. But he disregarded the laws and regulations, and even ate the big peaches of the ancient trees. When the meeting was set up, I did not invite him, but he devised a plan to entice the shoeless Sage of the Red Foot, impersonating him and entering the meeting. He stole the divine dishes and divine liquor, and also stole the Old Lord's elixir and a considerable amount of imperial liquor, taking it away to share with the crowd of monkeys on the mountain. My heart is troubled by this, so I dispatched a million heavenly troops, deploying the heavenly net to capture him. This day has passed without any report of the outcome, and I do not know how the matter will turn out."

The Bodhisattva led the multitude inside, and, upon greeting the Jade Emperor, they all took their seats. Then they asked, "What was the occasion of the Peach Banquet this year?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, we hold the banquet in celebration, but this year, the mischievous Monkey Spirit created chaos. It was a mere pretence." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where did the Monkey Spirit originate?" The Jade Emperor said, "The Monkey Spirit was born from the rocks of Flower Fruit Mountain in the Beak Hill Country of the Eastern Golden Island. When he was first born, he emitted golden light from his eyes and shot it into the Imperial Authority. Initially, I didn't pay much attention to him. He subsequently refined his form, subdued the dragon and tamed the tiger, and, to my knowledge, he caused people to die of fright. Then the Dragon King and the King of the Underworld both reported him to me. I ordered to apprehend him. But the Long Yang Star intervened saying, 'In the three realms, any creature with nine openings can become a transcendental being.' So, I promoted him, making him the Principal Official in charge of the Imperial Stables, and let him go to the upper realms. But he despised the humble rank, rebelled against the heavenly court. I then entrusted Li the King of Heaven and Nezha the Prince to subdue him, and also issued a decree to pacify him, and sent him to the upper realms, and appointed him the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' However, he had no wages to manage, and just wandered about, doing nothing. I feared he might cause more troubles, so I entrusted him to manage the Garden of the Peach Banquet. He didn't follow regulations, and ate all the great peaches from the old trees. When the banquet was set, he, as a man without any wages, was not invited. So, he disguised himself as the appearance of the Barefoot Immortal and deceitfully deceived the guests, stole all the delicacies and sacred wine, and also stole some of the old sage's elixir and some of the royal wine, and took it all to share with the monkeys on the mountain. I was troubled by this, so I ordered ten million heavenly soldiers and the net of heaven and earth to capture him. This day, I see no sign of his capture, and do not know the outcome."

Buddha invited the multitude to enter, and, upon arriving, he performed ceremonial rites with the Jade Emperor, after which he met with Laojun and Wangmu, and they all sat down. He then asked, "What about the Peaches of Immortality banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Each year I host a banquet in celebration, filled with joy and festivity. This year, however, the mischievous monkey caused a commotion, and it was a futile invitation indeed." 

Buddha asked, "Where did the mischievous monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The mischievous monkey originated from the Flawless Mountain on the Eastern Ocean's Proudness Country, and was born from a rock egg. At the time of its birth, it emitted golden light and shot upwards, piercing the Heaven of Effulgence. Initially, I did not take it seriously, but it later became refined and conquered dragons and tigers, and even self-exterminated its own register. The Dragon King and King of the Underworld then reported to me. I wanted to apprehend it, but Long Geng Star interceded, saying, 'In the Three Realms, any being with nine apertures may become a transcendent.' I then granted it education and promoted it to the heavens, appointing it the Marquis of the Stables and the Protégé of the Heavenly Steeds. It, however, grew tired of its humble position and rebelled against the heavenly court. I then dispatched Li Tian Wang and Nezha, the Prince, to pacify it, and released a proclamation to soothe its resentment, and promoted it to the heavens, enfeoffing it as the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' However, it held no office but no stipend. As a result, it had no occupation and indulged in carefree wandering. I was again concerned that it might cause more trouble, so I appointed it to manage the Peach Garden. But it did not follow the law and ate all the large peaches from the old trees. When the banquet was finally set, I did not invite him, but it devised a ruse to entice the barefoot Great Immortal, and it changed its appearance to enter the banquet, where it stole all the delicacies and sacred wine, and even stole Laojun's elixir and a substantial quantity of imperial wine to take back and share with its fellow monkeys on the mountain. My heart is vexed with worry because of this, and I mobilized the ten million heavenly soldiers, and with the net of the heavens and the earth, we subdued it. On this day, there has been no report of the outcome, and I do not know whether we were victorious or not."

The Bodhisattva led the assembly in, after paying homage to the Jade Emperor.  They sat down, then asked, "How was the Peaches banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, I would hold the banquet, and it was filled with joy and pleasure. But this year, the mischievous monkey caused trouble, making it utterly futile." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where does this monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The monkey was born from the stone egg of the Flower Fruit Mountain in the Outshining God's Land of Pride." It was born with its eyes shining like gold, shooting out light into the palace of the seven luminaries. At first, I didn't pay much mind, but it later refined itself, taming dragons and subduing tigers. Then, the Dragon King and the King of the Underworld reported the matter. I wanted to capture it, but the long-eng heavenly star said, "In the three realms, anyone who has nine openings can become an immortal." So I made it my teacher and enlightened it, promoting it to the upper realm, and appointed it as the Master of the Stables and the Marshal of the Divine Steeds. But it complained of the position being small, and thus it turned against the heavenly palace. I then ordered Li the Heavenly King and Nezha the Crown Prince to pacify it, and I issued a decree to calm it down, promoting it to the upper realm, and appointing it as the "Great Sage Equal to Heaven." It still had no wealth, and so I instructed them to help manage the Peaches banquet. But it didn't follow the rules, and it ate all the big peaches from the old trees. When the banquet was set, I didn't invite it, but it designed to deceive the Naked Immortal, entering the assembly disguised as him, and ate all the divine food and divine drinks, also stealing the Elder's elixir and some imperial liquor to take back to the mountain and enjoy with the other monkeys. I was worried sick about this, so I mobilized the ten million heavenly soldiers and the Heavenly net to trap it. But as I have not yet received any news, I don't know the outcome of the battle.

The Bodhisattva brought all the guests into the hall, and, after paying his respects to the Jade Emperor, sat down with the Immortal Master and the Queen Mother. He then asked, "What about the Grand Peaches Banquet this year?" The Jade Emperor replied, "We always hold the banquet annually, and it's always filled with joy and festivity. But this year, a mischievous monkey caused trouble, making the invitation empty and hollow." The Bodhisattva inquired, "Where did the mischievous monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor replied, "The mischievous monkey was born from an egg on Flower Fruit Mountain in the Flower Fruit Country of the Eastern Continent of Victory, and at the moment of birth, it emitted a golden light that pierced the Jade Bureau. Initially, we didn't pay much attention to it. As it grew stronger, it became powerful and could tame dragons and subdue tigers. But then it claimed to be self-deified and erased its name from the official register. The Dragon King and the Lord of the Underworld reported this to me. I wanted to capture it, but the Long Geng star advised me that 'anyone with nine orifices can become an immortal.' So I taught it the Way and promoted it to the Heavenly Region, making it the official in charge of the Stable of Magical Horses. It grew dissatisfied with its low rank and rebelled against the Heavenly Palace. I then dispatched Li the King of Heaven and the Prince Zhi of Great Hero to pacify it and summon it back to the Heavenly Region, and I appointed it as the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven' without assigning it any official salary. As it had nothing to do, it went off east and west, causing trouble wherever it went. Fearing that it might create more trouble, I appointed it to oversee the Grand Peaches Garden. But it disobeyed the rules and stole the large peaches from the old trees. When the banquet was set up, it didn't receive any invitation, so it disguised itself as the red-haired Immortal Sage, stole all the delicacies and wine, and also stole the Immortal Elixir and the Supreme Wine in great quantities, to enjoy with the other monkeys on the mountain. I was deeply distressed by this, so I deployed ten million heavenly soldiers and the Heaven and Earth nets to capture it. I haven't seen any results yet, and I'm still unsure if I'll succeed."

The copper snake and iron dog fought over their meals, yet were forever trapped in the river with no escape. The poem says: When I heard the ghosts cry and the gods howl, the blood-red waves rose as high as a thousand feet. Countless ox heads and horse faces appeared, ferociously guarding the bridge of Nai River. Just as I was speaking, the bridge officials had already gone away. Emperor Taizong was startled and worried, nodded his head in secret, and murmured with sorrow, accompanying the judge and the Grand Marshal, they had already crossed the Nai River's cruel water and reached the painful threshold. They then arrived at the Void City, and they only heard the tumultuous crowds shouting, clearly saying, "Li Shimin has arrived! Li Shimin has arrived!" Emperor Taizong heard the cries, and his heart trembled with fear. He saw a group of ghosts with arms severed at the waist and feet missing, approaching to stop him, all shouting, "Return our lives! Return our lives!" Emperor Taizong was frightened, hiding and dodging, only calling out, "Crivensir, save me! Crivensir, save me!" The judge said, "Your Majesty, these people are the ghosts of the sixty-four different bandits and the seventy-two different rebels, and all the prince-ghosts and the ghostly leaders; they are all wronged in life and have no one to avenge them. They have no prospect of ascending, nor any money and goods to redeem themselves; they are all starving ghosts." Your Majesty has some money and goods, if you give them to them, I can only save them now." Emperor Taizong said, "I, a humble monarch, come empty-handed, how could I have any money and goods?" The judge said, "Your Majesty, in the daylight world, there is a person, with gold and silver in abundance, kept by me in this underworld. Your Majesty can make a promise and write an oath, I can act as guarantor, and you can borrow from him one treasury to give to these starving ghosts, so you can pass through." Emperor Taizong asked, "Who is this person?" The judge replied, "He is a native of Henan, Kaifeng Prefecture, surname Xi, given name Liang. He has thirteen treasuries of gold and silver here. If you, Your Majesty, borrow from him and repay it when you return to the daylight world, that will be fine." Emperor Taizong was delighted and willing to make a promise. He thus drew up a document with the judge, borrowing one treasury of gold and silver, ordering the Grand Marshal to distribute it to the ghosts. The judge then instructed the Grand Marshal, "You can divide this gold and silver evenly to help the ghosts, so the great Tang Emperor can pass through, and his longevity is still long. I will take the instructions of the Ten Kings and return their souls to them, and instruct them to hold a water and land ritual in the daylight world, to help them transcend and be reborn. From then on, they should no longer cause any trouble." The ghosts heard the words, and after receiving the gold and silver, all retreated. The judge ordered the Grand Marshal to swing the spirit banner to guide Emperor Taizong out of the Void City, and they ran up the broad road of Pingyang, drifting and fluttering away. Ultimately, I do not know which road they took to escape, and I shall continue the story in the next chapter.

Copper serpents and iron dogs squabble over their meals; one and all fall into the canal without an exit. A poem says: "When listening to the wails of ghosts and the cries of spirits, the bloody water churns to a height of ten zhang." Countless ox heads and horse faces glared fiercely as they guarded the bridge over the canal.

As he was speaking, the several bridge officers had already departed. Emperor Taizong's heart was filled with terror and alarm; he nodded and let out a low sigh, his heart heavy with sorrow. He walked together with the judge and the Grand Prefect, having long crossed the canal's evil waters and the lake of suffering. Before long, he arrived at the Capital of the Wrongly Executed, where he only heard the din of the masses crying out, clearly saying, "Li Shimin has come! Li Shimin has come!" The emperor was startled by the calls, his heart trembling with fear. He saw a group of ghostly apparitions with arms severed at the waist and legs but no heads, who stood in front of him, blocking the way, all shouting, "Give us back our lives! Give us back our lives!"

The emperor was frightened and called out, "Cui Mr. (xiansheng) rescue me! Cui Mr. rescue me!" The judge said, "Your Majesty, those people are the spirits of the 64 provinces' calamities and the 72 type of rebellious bandits, the spirits of princes and commanders; they were all wrongfully put to death and have no way to ascend to the heavens, and they also have no silver or gold to dispose of, and so they are wandering as destitute spirits. If Your Majesty lends them some silver or gold, I shall be able to save them." The emperor said, "The emperor has come empty-handed to this place, where can I possibly get silver or gold?" The judge said, "Your Majesty, in the world above, there is a man who has a large quantity of gold and silver, which is deposited here in the underworld. Your Majesty may draw up a document and make an oath, I, the judge, shall be responsible, and borrow a storehouse of his gold and silver, to give them to these spirits so that they may pass on."

The emperor asked, "Who is this man?" The judge said, "He is from the prefecture of Kaifeng in Henan province, surname Xiang, given name Liang. He has thirteen storehouses of gold and silver deposited here. Your Majesty, if you borrow from him, you may return it to him in the world above." The emperor was delighted and readily agreed to make an oath. He thus drew up a document with the judge, borrowing a storehouse of his gold and silver, ordering the Grand Prefect to dispense it evenly to the spirits. The judge then instructed, "These gold and silver, you all divide them fairly to use, send the emperor's old grandfather (Taizong) on his way, his lifespan is still early, and I shall lead the spirits to the world above to make a large assembly of Buddhist ceremonies, and to let you all attain rebirth, and then have no more troubles."

The spirits heard this and, having received the gold and silver, all retreated. The judge ordered the Grand Prefect to shake the spirits' banners and lead the emperor out of the Capital of the Wrongly Executed and to hurry up the Plain Bright Road, floating and swaying away. It remains uncertain which road he took, let alone how he escaped, to be told in the next installment.

When the iron dog and bronze snake went for their daily meals, they all fell into the unending waters of the unpassable river. The poem said: 'The sound of ghosts crying and spirits calling could be heard over ten thousand feet; countless ox heads and horse faces blockaded the river bridge.' Just as Emperor Taizong was saying this, the messengers of the bridge had already returned. Emperor Taizong's heart grew anxious and fearful, and he nodded in sorrow, moving silently alongside the judge and the grand commander as they quickly crossed the evil waters of the blood pond and entered the Border of Great Suffering.

Upon arriving at the City of Wrongful Death, they heard the commotion of countless people shouting. They were clearly saying, 'Li Shimin has come! Li Shimin has come!' Emperor Taizong heard the cries and his heart trembled with fear. Seeing a group of ghosts with no heads and one arm, their feet still intact, blocking his path, they called out, 'Return our lives! Return our lives!' Emperor Taizong panicked and hid, calling out, 'Master Cui, save me! Master Cui, save me!' The judge said, 'Your Majesty, these are the ghosts of the 64 types of land bandits and the 72 types of grassland rebels, the spirits of countless kings and leaders; they were wronged in their past lives and had no chance to be reborn. Emperor Taizong said, 'As for me, I have no wealth. Where could I possibly find it?' If you borrow from him and return it in the world above, it will be fine.' Emperor Taizong was extremely delighted and agreed to make a solemn oath, so they drew up a contract with the judge and borrowed a storehouse, instructing the grand commander to distribute the gold and silver. The judge instructed them, 'You can divide the gold and silver equally among yourselves to use as you see fit, and let the big Tang emperor go, for his lifespan is still long.' The judge took the letter of the ten kings' decree and sent Xiang Liang's spirit back to the world above to have a great Water and Land Assembly to help the ghosts achieve rebirth, and to not have any more troubles. The ghosts, having received the gold and silver, all retreated in unison. The judge ordered the grand commander to wave the spirit beckoning banner and led Emperor Taizong out of the City of Wrongful Death, and they hastily ran up the broad Plain Road, fluttering and floating away. But ultimately, it is unknown which path they took, and we will continue in the next chapter.

Copper serpents and iron dogs, disputing over food, are forever trapped in the Nai River without escape. Your Majesty can write your name and seal a promise, and I, as surety, will lend it to you. Then you can give it to these hungry ghosts, and you can pass on."

Your Majesty, if you borrow from him, you can return it to him in the world above." So they wrote a contract with the judge, to borrow one chest of gold and silver, and ordered the Chancellor to distribute it among the ghosts. The judge further instructed, "You ghosts, take this gold and silver, use it in proportion, and let our great Tang emperor pass through, for his life span is still early. I have received ten warrants of the Ten Kings, to send him back to his soul, and to hold a Water and Land Assembly in the world above to help you ghosts transcend, and to have no more troubles."

The ghosts heard the instructions, and received the gold and silver, all nodded in agreement and retreated. The iron dogs and copper snakes quarreled for food, doomed to fall into the endless river with no escape. This recent case gave me a lot of trouble. The wretched young man, returning home, shot himself that very night; I was with him until the last moment... As for those confessional Jesuit taverns, it's truly my most enjoyable pastime during sad moments in life. Here's another case, just a few days ago. A blonde Norman girl, a girl of twenty, comes to the old father pater. Beauty, body, nature – my salivation's running. She leans in, whispers to the pater her sin. "What, my daughter, haven't you fallen again already?..." – exclaims the pater. – "O Sancta Maria, what I'm hearing: it's not the same. But how long will this continue, and how can you feel no shame?" – "Ah, my father," the sinner replies, her eyes full of penitent tears. – "It gives him so much pleasure and so little trouble for me!" Nature, the truth of nature, took its toll. You're about to wrinkle your nose, you're about to scowl again? I don't know what to do to please you...

That Zen Master transmitted scriptures and tread on cloud light, intending to leave for the Uatter Nest, when the Tang Sanzang caught hold of him and begged him to tell the route to the West beforehand. The Zen Master smiled and said, "The path is not hard to travel; listen to my instructions. Over thousands of mountains and rivers, there are many noxious places and demons. If you encounter a precipice touching the heavens, fear not the terror. When passing by the Ears of the Hear Rocky Peak, tread with the edge of your foot and step carefully. Be cautious in the dark pine grove, where there are many fox demons and fragmented paths. In the kingdom's city, there are many spirits, and the demon lord lives in the mountains. The tiger sits in the zither hall, and the gray wolf is the head clerk. The lion and elephant are at the helm, the tiger and leopard are officials, the wild boar carries a load, and the water spirit is ahead. The aged stone monkey does not harbor resentment or anger. You ask those acquaintances of yours, they will know the way to the West." The Traveler heard these words, and with a cold smile said, "We'll go; there is no need to ask him; I will tell you myself." The Tang Sanzang did not understand his meaning, and the Zen Master transformed into golden light and went straight up to the Uatter Nest. The elder went up to thank him, and the Traveler's heart was filled with great anger; he brandished his iron staff and scattered it wildly up above, but saw that lotus flowers bloomed in ten thousand numbers, and sacred mist shielded a thousand layers. The Traveler with all his might, could not possibly pull a single strand of the Uatter Nest's vines. The Tang Sanzang saw this and caught hold of the Traveler and said, "A Bodhisattva such as you, how can you strike at someone's nest?" The Traveler said, "He cursed my brothers and me." The Tang Sanzang said, "He spoke of the path to the West, how could he be cursing you?" The Traveler said, "You do not know? He said the wild boar carried a load, it was cursing my brother Eight Rules; he said the ancient stone monkey was old, it was cursing my brother Sandy. How can you understand his meaning?" Eight Rules said, "Elder brother, calm down. The Zen Master knows of past and future events, but let's not verify whether the water spirit being ahead of us is true or not, let's just let him be." The Traveler, seeing the lotus flowers and sacred mist, approached the nest's edge, and could only request his master to mount his horse and depart for the West down the mountain. That day: it so happened that they made clear the West's bliss for many people, but caused disaster to the demons of the mountain. But in the end, it remains unknown how the path ends, let's hear the continuation in the next chapter.

The monk transmitted the scriptures and stepped into the clouds, heading towards the place of Uxaccha. Tang Sanzang caught hold of him and said he must be told the path to the west. The monk smiled and said, "The road is not difficult to traverse. Listen to my instruction: there are a thousand mountains and a thousand waters, many hidden treacherous paths, and numerous demons. If you encounter the heavenly cliff, fear not the dangers. When you come to the peak of Mo'er Rock, tread with caution. When you enter the black pine forest, beware of fox spirits cutting off the path. In the National Spirit City, spirits abound, and the demon king resides in the mountains. The old tiger sits in the Court of the Lute, and the grey wolf is the Chancellor. The lion and elephant have taken their thrones, the tiger and leopard are the attendants. The wild boar carries his burden, and the water spirits lead the way. The old monkey has held a grudge for years. Ask him who is familiar with the westward path." 

The Great Sage listened and coldly laughed, saying, "We will not need to ask him; just ask me." Tang Sanzang was puzzled by his words, but the monk transformed into a golden light and ascended to Uxaccha directly. The Patriarch bowed and paid his respects, while the Great Sage's heart grew angry and he raised his iron staff to throw it wildly. But all he saw was a sea of lotus flowers and a myriad layers of auspicious mist. The Great Sage had the strength to stir the sea and overturn the rivers, yet he could not even capture a thread of the Uxaccha tree's vine. 

Tang Sanzang saw this and caught hold of the Great Sage, saying, "Sage, this Bodhisattva, why did you disturb his nest?" The Great Sage replied, "He has cursed my two brothers." Tang Sanzang said, "He spoke of the path to the West, not of cursing you." The Great Sage said, "You don't understand? He said the wild boar carries the burden, meaning he cursed Monkey King. He said the old monkey holds a grudge for years, meaning he cursed Sun Wukong." Tang Sanzang said, "You misunderstand." 

The Monkey King saw the lotus flowers and the auspicious mist, and drawing close to the nest, he had no choice but to invite the Patriarch to mount his horse and set off towards the west. The farther away they went, the more they encountered hardships and disasters, and the more calamities they encountered in the demon mountain. Ultimately, the path ahead was unknown, and we shall continue with the next chapter.

The Patriarch transmitted scriptures, stepped on radiant clouds, and aimed to go to the place of the Crow's Nest. Let me give you some instructions.  A thousand mountains, a thousand rivers are deep.  There are many rugged places and many places with demons.  If you encounter a precipitous cliff, be fearless and unafraid.  When you reach the Cave of the Earl of Music, proceed with caution and tread lightly.  Be careful when passing through the dark cypress grove, for there are many fox spirits.  The national spirits are plentiful in the Country City, and the demon master inhabits the Mountain City. The wild boar carries the luggage, and the water spirits are ahead.  The old stone monkey is without anger.  You can ask anyone you meet who knows the road to the West."  When the pilgrim heard these words, he coldly laughed and said: "We are going, we do not need to ask him.  Let me tell you instead." Tripitaka saw this and pulled the pilgrim and said:  "Great Sage, a bodhisattva such as you, how could you attack his nest?"  The pilgrim replied:  "He cursed my two brothers."  Tripitaka said:  "What he spoke of was the path to the Western Heaven, why did he curse you?"  The pilgrim said:  "You do not know?  He said that the wild boar carried the luggage, that was a curse on you, brother Eight.  He said the old stone monkey was of long years, that was a curse on you, brother Sun.  How can you not understand his meaning?"  Brother Eight said:  "Brother, calm down.  This Chan Master knows of past and future events. The pilgrim saw the lotus flowers and auspicious fog, and nearing the cave, he got on his horse and descended the mountain to go to the West.  This is how the Clear-fortune people in the world become fewer, and the calamity demons multiply in the mountains.  In the end, the outcome of the journey is unknown, and we shall continue in the next chapter.

Only just as this thought flashed, they all, without exception, at once began to state what had long been seen and what had long been foreseen; all of it had been clear even since "the poor knight," but at the time they had refused to believe in such absurdity. So the sisters maintained; of course, Elizabeth Prokofievna had foreseen it all and known it long before anyone else, and her heart had been troubled for a long time, but whether this had been for a long time or not - now the thought of the prince suddenly became unbearable to her, specifically because it befuddled her. There stood the question, which had to be resolved immediately, but not only could it not be resolved, but poor Elizabeth Prokofievna herself was unable to pose it to herself in complete clarity, no matter how she strained. The matter was difficult: "Is the prince good or not good? Is all this good or not good? If it's not good (which is undoubtedly the case), then what is not good? And if, perhaps, it might be good (which is also possible), then what is good?" The family's patriarch, Ivan Fyodorovich, was, naturally, first of all astonished, but then suddenly admitted that, "good heavens, the very same thing had been plaguing him for a long time; no, no, it had been plaguing him all the time, and as if it would suddenly appear to him again!" He fell silent at once under his wife's stern gaze, but he fell silent in the morning, while in the evening, alone with his wife, and forced to speak again, he suddenly expressed a few unexpected thoughts with a certain verve: "Well, what's the point, after all?..." (Silence). "Of course, it's all very strange, if it's true, and he doesn't argue with it, but... " (Again, silence). "On the other hand, if one looks at things straight on, then the prince, I swear, is an extraordinary young man, and... and... well, in the end, our family name will have a certain sort of support from the name of our noble family, which is in decline, in the eyes of the world, that is, looking at things from that angle, that is, because... of course, one has to take the light into account; light is light; but still, the prince is not without some estate, though only a certain one. He has... and... and... and... " (A prolonged silence and a decisive stumbling block). Having listened to her husband, Elizabeth Prokofievna stepped out of her usual boundaries.

As it turned out, however, the Epanchin family suddenly came to one and the same and agreed opinion that something of great importance had happened to Aglaya, and that her fate was being decided – it is very difficult to recount this in sequence. But just as soon as the thought flashed in all of them, they immediately became unanimous in what they had long already seen and clearly foreseen; what had been clear even with "the poor knight" from the very beginning, but then they had not wanted to believe in such absurdity. The sisters maintained; of course, Lizaveta Prokofievna had seen and understood everything before all the others and had been grieved for a long time; but – long ago or not long ago – the thought of the prince had suddenly become too unsettling for her, precisely because it had shaken her off her balance. There was a question that needed to be resolved immediately; not only could it not be resolved, but poor Lizaveta Prokofievna herself could not clearly formulate the question to herself, despite her effort. The situation was difficult: "Is the prince good or not good? Is everything good or not good? If not good (which is in no doubt), then what is not good? And if maybe it is good (which is also possible), then what is good?" 

Their father, Ivan Fyodorovich, was, of course, initially amazed, but then suddenly admitted that, by God, the same kind of thing had been haunting him for a while, and would sometimes even pop into his head uninvited. He immediately fell silent under the stern glance of his wife, but remained silent until evening, when he was alone with his wife and compelled to speak again. He then suddenly expressed several unexpected thoughts as if with renewed energy: "Well, what's the point, after all?" (pause). "Of course, it's all very strange, if only it's true, and he's not disputing it, but..." (pause again). "But on the other hand, if we take a closer look, the prince is, by God, a most wonderful young man, and... and... well, finally, our family name will have a certain backing from a member of our family name that is in a lower status in the eyes of the world, that is, from this perspective, it will mean... light; light is light; but, still, the prince is not without means, at least a certain amount. He has... and... and... and..." (prolonged pause and a decisive cough). After listening to her husband, Lizaveta Prokofievna left the boundaries.

Li Dingdao said: "Your water is clear, but not as green as my mountains. The evidence lies in a ci poem: 'Cloud forest is one stretch, filled with blossoming pines, listening to the oriole's song in silence, like a skilled flute player. The red is thin and green is plump, spring is warm, the moment summer arrives time turns quickly. It's also a time when autumn arrives, easily exchanging the beauty of flowers, like the fragrance of yellow flowers, suitable to be enjoyed. Winter comes swiftly, like grasping it with a finger, free and carefree through the four seasons without any constraint.'"

The fisherman said: "You have mountains that are green but not as clear as my water, and being able to enjoy many good things, with a ci poem as evidence: 'Xian Jiang cloud and water is a lifetime's abundance, rowing the horizontal boat and it's like being at home. Living fresh fish, roasting green turtle, steaming purple crab, boiling red shrimp. Lotus rhizome, watercress sprouts, lotus seed stalk, and chicken head – all of them can be boasted about. Delicate lotus, old water lily, young celery leaves, white cress, and bird's eye flowers.'"

The woodsman said: "You have clear water but not as green as my mountains, and being able to enjoy many good things, also with a ci poem as evidence:
