— This is just how it is, Prince, — Rogozhin said gloomily, scowling. — Just like Zalyezhev used to say. Then, I was running across Nevsky in my father's worn-out boots and in my stockings, and she comes out of the shop, gets into her carriage. That's when I felt a burn inside. I run into Zalyezhev; the fellow looks like a shop assistant from a barber's, and he's got a monocle in his eye. Back then, when I was still a kid and wore my family's broken-down boots and woolen stockings, we were nothing alike. He says, 'No, you're not him; that's the Princess,' — 'Her name is Nastasya Filipovna Barashkova,' he says, 'and she lives with Tozky, but Tozky has been completely in the dark about her, because he's now a man of fifty-five years old, and he wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all of Petersburg.' He tells me that I should go see Nastasya Filipovna today at the Bolshoi Theatre, at the ballet, in her box, in the orchestra. 'You'd better try to go to the ballet, Prince,' my mother says, 'it's one way to get back at her!' I slipped out and, however, I saw Nastasya Filipovna again; I didn't sleep the whole night. Next morning, the deceased gives me two five percent bonds, each worth five thousand roubles. 'Sell them, he says, pay off the debt to the Andreikovs for seven thousand five hundred, and I'll keep the change, without going anywhere, just bring it to me.' I sold the bonds, took the money, but didn't go to the Andreikovs; instead, I went to the English shop and bought two hatpins, each with a diamond the size of an oak kernel. I was left with a debt of four hundred roubles, gave them my name, and they believed me. I took the hatpins to Zalyezhev: 'This is it, brother, we're off to see Nastasya Filipovna!' We set off. I don't even remember what was under my feet, what was before me, what was beside me. We walked straight into her box, and she came out to meet us. I didn't introduce myself as myself; 'It's from Partjenka, Prince Rogozhin, a token of our meeting yesterday,' Zalyezhev says. 'Do do us the honor of accepting it.' She unfolded it, took a glance, smiled, 'Thank your friend, Mr. Rogozhin, for his courteous attention,' and took her leave. Well, I should have died on the spot right then! I only went because I thought, 'I won't be coming back alive, anyway!' But what hurt me most was that Zalyezhev had taken all the credit for himself. I'm short, and I'm dressed like a lackey, and I stand there in silence, ogling her, and I'm ashamed, while he's done up like a proper gentleman, in powder, with curls and a striped cravat, and he's pouring it all out, showing off, and I reckon she must have taken him for me! 'So, I say, let's get out of here,' I say as we exit. 'Don't even think about coming back to me now, understand?' He laughs, 'What account are you going to give to Semen Partjenka?' I thought of throwing myself into the water then and then not going home, but I thought, 'It's all the same anyway,' and I went back home like a scoundrel.

— That's exactly how it is, said Rogauchin, gloomily and furrowed-browed, — the same old fooler that Zalezhin was talking about. Then I, Your Highness, was crossing over the Nevsky Prospect in my father's beshmet coat, and she comes out of the store, gets into her carriage. That lit a fire in me right there. I run into Zalezhin, that cad, dressed like a shop assistant from a barber, with a monocle in his eye, and we used to wear smutty boots and spectacles. This, he says, isn't you, this is, he says, the Countess, and her name is Nastasya Philippovna Barashkova, and she lives with Totsky, and Totsky can't shake her off now, because he's getting on in years, over fifty, and he wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all of St. Petersburg. He goes and tells me that I can see Nastasya Philippovna at the Bolshoi Theatre today, in the ballet, in her box, in the loge, she'll be sitting. Come on, I say to you, go to the theatre, just try; my parents will kill you! But I managed to sneak out and see Nastasya Philippovna again, that very same night I couldn't sleep. The deceased gives me two five-percent bonds, each for five thousand roubles, go, he says, sell them, take the seven thousand five hundred to the Andreyevs, pay it off, and give me the rest, without setting foot outside, I'll be waiting for you. I sold the bonds, took the money, but didn't go to the Andreyevs' office, instead I went to the English shop and picked out two tie-pins, each with a diamond almost as small as a nut, I was left with four hundred roubles, gave my name, they believed me. With the tie-pins I went to Zalezhin: that's the way it is, brother, let's go see Nastasya Philippovna. We set off. I don't remember what was under my feet, what was in front of me, what was on my sides – nothing. We walked straight into her box, she came out to us. I didn't say I was me, who I really was, but Zalezhin says, "From Parfen, to Nastasya Philippovna, from Rogauchin, as a souvenir from yesterday's meeting; please accept it." She opened it, took a look, smiled: "Thank your friend, Mr. Rogauchin, for his kind attention," she said, and bowed and left. I almost wish I had died right there and then. If I did go, it was because I thought to myself, "I'll never come back alive!" The most humiliating thing for me was that that scoundrel Zalezhin had already taken it upon himself to steal the show. I'm short, dressed like a fop, standing there, mute, ogling at her, because I'm ashamed, and he's all dressed up, with powder on, his hair curled, a striped cravat – he's bursting with pride, he's pouring it on, and I'm sure she's taken him for me! "You know, I say, as we leave, you mustn't even think about her, do you understand?" He laughs: "How are you going to account for yourself to Semen Parfenovich?" I almost went in the water right then and there, without going home, but I think to myself: "Well, it's all the same anyway," and as a wretched soul, I went back home.

— That's it, just as it is, Rostanev muttered, his face dark and scowling, — exactly what Zalëzhëv said then. I was then crossing Nevsky Prospect in the same old caftan my father used to wear, and she comes out of the shop, gets into her carriage. That set my blood on fire at the time. I run into Zalëzhëv, that swaggering poseur, wearing a monocle and dressed like a hairdresser's assistant, and we were once quite different, you know, in worn-out boots and a worn-out coat. 'It's not you,' he says, 'it's the princess, and her name is Nastasya Fëdorovna, the Barashkova, and she lives with Tozsky, and Tozsky's stuck to her for dear life, being already over fifty-five and wanting to marry the most beautiful woman in St. Petersburg.' He whispered to me that I could see Nastasya Fëdorovna in the theatre today, at the ballet, in the imperial box, in the loge. Why don't you go and take in the ballet at our place? — it's one way to get rid of me! I snuck out for an hour, and I saw Nastasya Fëdorovna again, and I didn't sleep that whole night. The old fellow gave me two five-percentage theatre tickets, each for five thousand, saying, Go, sell them, take seven thousand five hundred to the Andreyevs' office, pay it off, and keep the rest, without going anywhere, I'll be waiting for you. I sold the tickets, took the money, and didn't go to the Andreyevs' office, but went straight to the English shop and bought two pairs of earrings with diamonds, one diamond in each, almost like cherries, and owed 400 rubles, and I gave my name, and they believed me. With the earrings, I went to Zalëzhëv: all right, come on, brother, let's go to Nastasya Fëdorovna. We went. I have no idea what was under my feet, what was in front of me, what was beside me — nothing. We went straight into the imperial box, and out came she herself. I didn't say who I was, that it was me; Zalëzhëv says, 'From Parfen, the Rostanev fellow, for your memories of yesterday's meeting; would you be so kind as to accept?' She opened it, took a look, smiled: 'Thank your friend Mr. Rostanev for his kindness,' she says, 'and goodbye,' and off she went. Ah, why didn't I kill myself right then! And if I did go, it was because I thought, 'I'll never come back alive!' And what was most galling was that that rascal Zalëzhëv took all the credit to himself. I'm so short, and dressed like a lackey, and I stand there, silent, gazing at her, and I'm ashamed, and he's all dressed up to the nines, in powder and pomade, rosy-cheeked, with a striped cravat, so fancy, so effusive, and she probably took him for me! 'You see, I say to him as we leave, you're never to think of this again, understand?' He laughs: 'And how will you account to Semen Parfenych for all this?' I was ready to jump into the water right then, not go home, but I thought, 'It's all the same,' and like a scoundrel, I went back home.

— That's just the way it is, Prince, — Rogozhin growled, frowning — the very same thing Zalezhov was saying. I was then crossing Nevsky in my father's old valise, when she comes out of the store and gets into her carriage. That's how I got burned that time. I bump into Zalezhov, and he's no gentleman, he's dressed like a barber's assistant, and he's wearing glasses, and we, my father and I, used to walk around in old boots and patched trousers. 'This is not you,' he says, 'this is Princess, her name is Nastasya Filippovna Barashkova, and she lives with Totsky; Totsky is absolutely under her thumb now, because he's over fifty-five years old, and he wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all of Petersburg.' He whispered to me that I could see Nastasya Filippovna at the Bolshoi Theatre that very day, at the ballet, in her own box, in the bénéfice; she'd be sitting there. Come on, my parents say, try to go to the ballet, one punishment is enough, and she'll kill me! However, I slipped out for an hour, quietly, and saw Nastasya Filippovna again; I didn't sleep that whole night. The dead man gave me two five-per-cent stocks for five thousand each, saying, 'Go, sell them, take seven thousand five hundred to the Andreys' office, pay up, and give me the remaining nine hundred without going anywhere; I'll be waiting for you.' I sold the stocks, took the money, but didn't go to the Andreys' office, but instead went to the English shop and bought a pair of brooches and two diamonds, about as big as hazelnuts, and was left with four hundred rubles; they believed me and gave them to me. With the brooches I went to Zalezhov, and that's how it is, come on, brother, let's go to Nastasya Filippovna. We set off. I don't even remember or know what was under my feet, what was in front of me, what was beside me. We walked straight into her box, and she came out to us. I didn't say who I was, but Zalezhov said, 'This is from Parfen, from Rogozhin; it's a gift, a reminder of our meeting the day before; kindly accept it.' She unfolded it, looked at it, smiled: 'Thank your friend, Mr. Rogozhin, for his kind attention,' she said, and bowed and went away. And that's why I didn't die on the spot! If I did go, it was because I thought, 'Anyway, I won't be coming back alive!' And what was most humiliating for me was that this rogue Zalezhov had taken all the credit for himself. I'm small, I'm dressed like a dandy, I stand there, mute, with my eyes fixed on her, and it's humiliating, while he's there, dressed in all the latest fashion, with powder, curled hair, and a checked cravat, and he's bursting with laughter, cracking jokes, and I'm sure she must have taken him for me instead! 'You'd better not even think about me,' I said, as we were leaving. 'How will you give an account to Semen Parfenovich?' she laughed. I really wanted to jump into the water at the time, go home without going in, but I thought, 'Well, what does it matter anyway,' and like a scoundrel, I went back home.

— That's how it is, — said Rogozhin with a sullen expression, — just what Zalyazin was talking about. At that time, Your Highness, I was crossing the Nevsky Prospekt in my father's caftan, and she stepped out of the shop and got into a carriage. It all left a burn on me. I run into Zalyazin, the fellow, and he's not at all like me, walks like a barber's lackey, and has a lorgnette in his eye, while we used to wear muddy boots and stockings with big patches. This, he says, isn't you, it's Princess, and her name is Nastasya Filipovna, surname Barashkova, and she lives with Tozky, and Tozky can't now part with her, having reached the ripe age of fifty-five, and he wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all Petersburg. He whispered to me that you might see Nastasya Filipovna today at the Bolshoi Theatre, in the ballet, in her own loge, in the bower, that she'll be sitting in. Our father says, try to get to the ballet, he'll kill you! But I, however, quietly slipped out for an hour and saw Nastasya Filipovna again; I didn't sleep that whole night. Next morning, the deceased hands me two five percent bonds, each for five thousand roubles, says, sell them, deliver seven thousand five hundred to the Andreys to their office, pay it in, and bring me the remaining change, without setting foot anywhere, I'll be waiting for you. I sold the tickets, took the money, but didn't go to the Andreys' office, but instead went straight to the English store and picked out a pair of diamond studs, almost like grains of sesame, and I still owed four hundred roubles, and I gave my name, they believed me. I went to Zalyazin with the studs: well, well, let's go, brother, to Nastasya Filipovna. We set out. I don't remember, I don't know what was under my feet, in front of me, on the sides – we walked straight to her box, and she came out to meet us herself. I didn't say I was the one, that it was me; Zalyazin says, 'From Partenny, to Rostanev, as a token of our meeting yesterday; with your permission, please accept it.' She unfolded it, looked at it, smiled: 'Thank your friend, Mr. Rostanev, for his kind attention,' – and took her leave and left. Oh, I should have died right then and there! If I did go, it was because I thought: 'I'll never come back alive!' What was most humiliating for me was that this scoundrel Zalyazin claimed it all for himself. I'm short and dressed like a lackey, standing there in silence, gazing at her, and I'm ashamed, while he's stylish, in powder and curls, rosy, with a checkered cravat, and he bursts out laughing and is so self-assured, and I'm sure she took him in for me! 'Listen, I said, as we left, you'll never think of me now, understand?' He's laughing: 'How are you going to give an account to Semen Parfenich then?' I thought of jumping in the water and not going home, but I thought: 'What difference does it make?' – and as a wretched man, I returned home.

– You won't believe it, you can't even imagine, Polenka, – she said, pacing around the room, – how well and lavishly we lived in Papa's house and how that drunkard ruined me and will ruin all of us! Papa was a dignified colonel and was almost a governor; he only needed one more step and everyone would come to him and say: 'We consider you, Ivan Mikhailovich, to be our governor.' When I... keh! when I... keh-keh-keh... oh, accursed life! – she exclaimed, coughing up mucus and clutching her chest, – when I... ah, when at the governor's ball... I was seen by Princess Bezsemelnaya, – who later blessed me when I married your father, Pavel, – she immediately asked: 'Isn't that the lovely girl who danced in a shawl during the graduation?' (She should sew up that hole; I would have taken up the needle and threaded it, and now... keh! ...tomorrow... keh-keh-keh... it will tear to pieces again! – she cried out, sobbing...)... Prince Schegolsky had just arrived from Petersburg, a chamberlain... he danced the mazurka with me and the very next day wanted to come with a proposal; but I thanked him in lofty expressions and said that my heart belongs to another. That other was your father, Pavel; Papa was extremely angry... Is the water ready? Alright, give me a shirt; and stockings? – she turned to the little daughter, – you go to sleep without a shirt this night, you can just... put the stockings nearby... wash them... As for this ragsameller, this drunkard! He took the shirt and tore it like a rag, completely destroyed it... I wish he would ruin us all at once and for good! God! Keh-keh-keh-keh-keh! Oh, again! What's that? – she shrieked, glancing at the crowd in the hallway and at people carrying some sort of bundle into her room. – What is it? What are they bringing? God!

– You won't believe it, you can't even imagine, Polly, – she said, pacing around the room, – how joyfully and lavishly we lived in Papa's house and how this drunkard has ruined me and will ruin all of you! Papa was a high-ranking colonel and almost a governor; it was just one step away, so everyone came to visit him and say: 'We already consider you, Ivan Mikhailovich, to be our governor.' When I... khe! when I... khe-khe-khe... Oh, cursed life! – she exclaimed, coughing up phlegm and clutching her chest, – when I... ah, when at the last ball... at the host's... the Princess Bez zemel'naya saw me – the same one who blessed me when I married your father, Paul – she immediately asked: 'Is that the lovely young lady who danced in a shawl at the graduation?..' (There's a run to sew up; I would have taken my needle and patched it up right now, just as I taught you, and tomorrow... khe!... tomorrow... khe-khe-khe... it will tear all the more apart! – she cried out, sobbing)... Then the cameral counselor Prince Shchegolsky had just arrived from St. Petersburg... he danced a polka with me and the next day wanted to come with a proposal; but I myself thanked him with flattering words and said that my heart belongs to another man. This other man was your father, Paul; Papa was furious... Is the water ready? Okay, hand me the shirt; and stockings?.. Lida, – she turned to the little daughter, – you just, without a shirt, sleep tonight; somehow... just lay out the stockings by... Get it washed... What this ragamuffin won't leave, this drunkard! He tore the shirt to shreds, as if it were some rag to wipe his face with... We should have gotten it all over with, to suffer through two nights in a row! Lord have mercy! Khe-khe-khe-khe-khe! What's this? – she screamed, looking at the crowd in the hallway and at the people pushing through with some sort of litter into her room. – What's this? What's this they're carrying? Lord have mercy!

– You wouldn't believe, you can't even imagine it, dear Polenka, she said, pacing around the room – how we lived so joyfully and lavishly in Papa's house, and how this drunkard ruined me and will ruin you all! Papa was a dignified colonel and almost a governor; he was only one step away from it, so everyone came to see him and said: 'We already consider you, Ivan Mikhailych, as our governor.' When I... kh-ee! when I... kh-ee-ee-ee... oh, cursed life! – she screamed, coughing up phlegm and clutching her chest – when I... ah, when at the last ball... at the leader's... I was seen by Princess Bezumelna, – who blessed me when I was marrying your father, Pavel – she immediately asked: 'Isn't that the lovely young woman who danced with a shawl at the graduation party?..' (The tear needs to be mended; I'd take my needle and thread right now and sew it up, just like I taught you, or else tomorrow... kh-ee! tomorrow... kh-ee-ee-ee... it'll tear even more! – she cried out in anguish…)... Then, the kammerjunker Prince Shchegolsky, who had just arrived from St. Petersburg, danced a mazurka with me and the next day wanted to come with a proposal; but I thanked him in flattering words and said that my heart has long belonged to someone else. This other person was your father, Pavel; Papa was terribly upset... Is the water ready? Give me the shirt; and the stockings?... Lidochka, – she turned to her little daughter – you can go to bed tonight without the shirt; just... put the stockings nearby... wash... And this drunkard won't leave me be! He tore the shirt, as if it were some kind of rag; he ruined the whole thing... I wish it was over with, to stop suffering like this for two nights in a row! God! Kh-ee-ee-ee-ee! What's this? – she screamed, looking at the crowd in the corridor and the people pushing into her room with some sort of litter – What's this? What are they bringing? God!

– You won't believe, you can't even imagine, little Polly, – she said, pacing in the room, – how joyfully and lavishly we lived in our father's house and how that drunkard has ruined me and will ruin you all! Our father was a state colonel and nearly a governor, with just one step left, and everyone would come to see him and say, "We consider you, Ivan Mikhailovich, our governor." When I... khe! when I... khe-khe-khe... oh, cursed life! – she exclaimed, spitting phlegm and clutching her chest – when I... ah, when at the final ball, at the host's... the Countess Bezzezmeal was present, who blessed me when I married your father, Polly, – she immediately asked: "Isn't that the pretty girl who danced with a shawl at the ball?" (The rip in my dress needs to be mended; if I'd only had a needle and thread, I'd have sewn it up just like I taught you, and tomorrow... khe!... tomorrow... khe-khe-khe... it would have ripped even more!)... Then a chamberlain, Prince Shchegol'sky, had just arrived from Petersburg... he danced a mazurka with me, and the next day he intended to come with a proposal; but I myself thanked him in polite terms and said my heart belonged to someone else a long time ago. That someone was your father, Polly; my father was furious. Is the water ready? Let's get your shirt; the stockings?... Lida, – she turned to her little daughter, – you can sleep without a shirt tonight, just put the stockings alongside... and wash it too... Why this rags? This drunkard tore the shirt like a dirty rag. I'd rather, for my own sake, not to have to go through this again for two nights in a row! Oh Lord! Khe-khe-khe-khe! Again! What's this? – she shrieked, glancing at the crowd in the hallway and at the people pushing with some sort of burden into her room. What is it? What are they carrying? Oh Lord!

– You won't believe it, you can't even imagine, Polenka, she said, pacing around the room – to what extent we lived joyfully and lavishly in father's house, and how that drunkard destroyed me and will destroy all of you! Father was a titled colonel, already almost a governor; he was just one step away from it, so everyone came to see him and said: 'We count you, Ivan Mikhailych, as our governor already.' When I... khe! when I... khe-khe-khe... oh, cursed life! – she shrieked, clearing her throat and clutching her chest – when I... ah, when at the final ball... with the leader... I was spotted by Princess Bez zemel'ny, – who blessed me when I married your father, Polya, – that very moment she asked: 'Isn't that the lovely young woman who danced in a shawl at the graduation?' (I should have mended that tear; I could have taken my needle now and sewn it up, just like I taught you, and tomorrow... khe! tomorrow... khe-khe-khe... it would have ripped all the more! – she wailed, straining.)... Then Prince Shchegolev had just arrived from Petersburg, still, a chamberlain... he danced a mazurka with me, and the very next day he wanted to come with a proposal; but I myself thanked him in lofty terms and said that my heart belonged to someone else long ago. That someone was your father, Polya; father was utterly enraged... Is the water ready? Here, take the shirt; and stockings?... Lida, – she turned to her small daughter – you sleep like that, without a shirt, tonight; just somehow... lay out your stockings beside... wash the ones that were dirty... This rag of a man won't stop drinking, a drunkard! He tore the shirt, like some old cloth to be torn up; if only he would just stop causing us to suffer for two nights in a row! God! Khe-khe-khe-khe-khe! Oh no! What's that? – she shrieked, glancing at the crowd in the hallway and at the people carrying some sort of burden into her room – What's that? What's being brought in? Oh, God!

In days of old, when the drums sounded and the bells rang out, it indeed roused the Three Sea Dragon Kings. A moment later, all three arrived simultaneously outside, and Ao Qin said: "Elder brother, is there something urgent that calls for beating the drums and striking the bell?" The Old Dragon said: "Wise brother, it's not something to be said! A Heavenly Saint from Fruitful Mountain, came to visit me this morning, claiming to be my neighbor, and later requested a certain type of armor, refusing the steel trident as too small, and the painted halberd as too light. He then took a piece of Heavenly River- decreeed treasure iron, took it out with his own hands, and discarded some techniques. Now that he is seated in the palace, he is again asking for some new armor. I have none to give him, that's why the drums are beating and the bells are ringing; come, wise brother, let us summon him here and see if you have any armor to give him. We'll then send him out the door and let him leave." Ao Qin heard this and his face turned red with anger: "My brothers, mobilize the troops, let's deal with him!" The Old Dragon said: "No need to act! That piece of iron is so strong that if you wrap it, you'll die; if you knock into it, you'll be destroyed; you'll bruise your skin, and crack your bones!" The Western Sea Dragon King, Ao Jun, said: "Second brother, don't meddle with him; just prepare a suit of armor for him and send him out the door. We'll then draft a memorial to Heaven, and Heaven itself will deal with him." The Northern Sea Dragon King, Ao Shun, said: "That's right. I have a pair of lotus-silk Cloud-slipper boots here." The Western Sea Dragon King, Ao Jun, said: "I have a golden coat-of-mail armor with lock-plates." The Southern Sea Dragon King, Ao Qin, said: "I have a purple-golden crown with phoenix wings." The Old Dragon was overjoyed, and led him into the crystal palace for an audience. With the crown, the coat-of-mail armor, and the Cloud-slipper boots, Monkey King donned them properly and brandished the magical rod with ease. As he left, he shouted: "Make a commotion! Make a commotion!" The four Sea Dragon Kings were enraged and began discussing a memorial to be submitted to Heaven.

Back when we were young, the beat of drums and the chime of bells would indeed stir up the Three Sea Dragon Kings. Before long, they all came together, and Ao Qin said, "Brother, is there some pressing matter that requires the beating of the drums and the striking of the bells?" The Old Dragon replied, "It's not worth mentioning, brother. There's a sage from the Peach Blossom Mountain who came to see me early in the day, and then asked me for a weapon. I presented him with a steel trident, but he thought it was too small, and I offered him a painted halberd, but he thought it was too light. He then produced a block of Iron from the Bottom of the Heaven River and took out some divination numbers. Now that he's sitting in the palace, he's asking for something to wear. Since I don't have any armor, I beat the drums and strike the bells, and asked you, brother, to come. Do you have any armor to give him, so we can just send him off?" Ao Qin heard this and flew into a rage, saying, "My brothers, let's mobilize our troops and apprehend him!" The Old Dragon said, "Don't talk about apprehending him! That block of iron is bound to kill him with just a scratch, wound him with just a touch, or bruise him with just a tap, and wound his tendons with just a rub!" Ao Xu, the Dragon King of the Western Sea, said, "Brother, don't do anything to him. Let's just provide him with some armor, send him out the door, and then we'll submit a memorial to heaven to let heaven handle it." Ao Shun, the Dragon King of the Northern Sea, said, "That makes sense. I have a pair of silk lotus cloud slippers here." Ao Xu said, "I brought a golden suit of armor with a breastplate." Ao Qin said, "I have a purple gold crown with phoenix feathers." The Old Dragon was overjoyed, led him into the Crystal Palace to see him, and presented the armor and accessories to him. Monkey King put on the crown, the golden armor, and the cloud slippers, made some moves with the rod of wonders, and beat it out of there, saying, "Don't make a noise! Don't make a noise!" The Four Sea Dragon Kings were displeased, and began to discuss submitting a memorial to heaven on the matter.

In olden times, when the drums sounded and the bells rang out, it indeed disturbed the three Dragon Kings of the Ocean, who arrived shortly, all gathering outside. Ao Qin said: "Big Brother, what's the hurry, to beat the drums and ring the bells?" The Old Dragon replied: "Esteemed brother, it's not a good thing to say! A Holy Man from the Heavenly Peach Mountain came to recognize me as a neighbor early this morning, and later requested a piece of armor. He thought a steel fork was too small and a painted halberd too light. He took out a piece of divine iron from the Heavenly River's bed, and wasted some techniques. Now he's sitting in the palace, asking for more equipment. I have nothing, so I'm ringing the bells and beating the drums to call on you, esteemed brother. Do you have some equipment, let's give him a set, and send him off at the door." Ao Qin heard the words and was enraged: "My brothers, assemble the troops and take him on!" The Old Dragon said: "Don't even think about it! That piece of iron is so hard that if you hug it a little, you'll die; if you knock against it a little, you'll be injured; if you scrape against it a little, you'll break your skin; if you rub against it a little, you'll hurt your tendons!" Ao Ju, the Dragon King of the Western Sea, said: "The Second Brother should not handle this matter himself; let's just get him a set of armor, send him out the door, and report to the Heavenly Throne. Heaven will surely deal with him." Ao Shun, the Dragon King of the Northern Sea, said: "That's a good idea. I have a pair of Lotus Silk Cloud Step Boots here." Ao Ju said: "I have a set of golden steel armor here." Ao Qin, the Dragon King of the Southern Sea, said: "I have a Purple Gold Phoenix Crown here." The Old Dragon was delighted, took him into the Crystal Palace, and presented them to him. Monkey King put on the crown, the armor, and the cloud step boots, and with his Invincible Staff, he set off and left, saying: "Clamor! Clamor!" The four Dragon Kings were not pleased, and on one side, they made plans to submit a report to the Heavenly Throne.

In the past, when the drums beat and the bells rang, the three Dragon Kings of the Sea were indeed roused, and soon came to meet at the outside of the hall. Ao Qin said, "Big brother, what's the urgent matter, beating the drums and clanging the bells?" The Old Dragon said, "Dear brother, it's not a good thing to say. Later, he requested an armament from me, but I offered him the steel trident, thinking it too small, and the painted halberd, thinking it too light. Ao Jun, the Dragon King of the Western Sea, said, "Second brother, don't engage him; let's just gather a set of armor for him and send him out, and then submit a memorial to Heaven. The Old Dragon was overjoyed, brought him into the crystal palace, and presented it to him. Sun Wukong dressed in the golden crown, golden armored breastplate, and Cloud Stepping Shoes, made himself comfortable, waved the Iron Flute, and headed out, saying to the dragons, "Make a ruckus! Make a ruckus!" The four Dragon Kings were not pleased, on one side discussing how to submit a memorial to Heaven.

Long ago, when the drums and bells resounded, as expected, the three sea dragons were startled, and soon arrived. All of them met outside and Ao Qin said, "Elder brother, is there some urgent business that has caused the drums to beat and the bells to ring?" The eldest dragon said, "Honorable younger brother, it's not good to talk about it! Ao Qin heard this and became enraged, saying, "My brothers, we should set up our troops and give him a lesson!" The middle dragon, Ao Xun, said, "Don't mention setting up troops! That block of iron, if you wrap it around your body, you'd be killed; if you tap it with your head, you'd be extinguished; if you catch the glancing blow, your skin would be broken; and if you scrape against it, your tendons would be injured!" The eldest dragon was overjoyed and led him into the crystal palace for an audience. Monkey King put on the crown, the breastplate, and the cloud-walking boots and, with his moveable staff, set off on the road, shouting, "Clatter! Clatter!" The four sea dragons were indignant and on one side discussed submitting a memorial to Heaven.

After midday, he left the beach, returned to the hotel, and let himself be taken upstairs to his room. He spent a long time there inside, in front of the mirror, contemplating his grey hair and his weary yet sharp face. At that moment he thought about his fame and the fact that many people on the streets knew him and regarded him with reverence, owing to his talent for precisely and elegantly phrased words,—called to mind all the external successes of his talent that came to mind, and even his ennoblement. He then made his way down to the dining hall for lunch and dined at his little table. As he entered the lift after finishing his meal, a group of young people, who had also come from breakfast, pressed in behind him into the swinging compartment, and Tadzio also stepped in. He stood quite close to Aschenbach, closer than before, so that he perceived and recognized him not in abstract distance, but precisely, with the details of his humanity. The boy was addressed by someone, and while he replied with a sweetly indescribable smile, he already stepped out again in the first-floor area, backward, with downtrodden eyes. Beauty is modest, thought Aschenbach and pondered the reason. However, he had noticed that Tadzio's teeth were not particularly pleasing: somewhat jagged and pale, lacking the sheen of health and having an unusual, glassy transparency like that sometimes found in anemic people. He is very delicate, he is sickly, thought Aschenbach. He will probably not grow old. And he refrained from giving account of a feeling of satisfaction or consolation that accompanied this thought.

After the completion of the task, the emperor was overjoyed. However, he again gathered a multitude of officials, issued an imperial decree, summoning monks, to construct a grand Buddhist assembly for the salvation of souls in the underworld. The decree was posted throughout the empire, instructing officials in every place to recommend outstanding monks to the capital for the assembly. Before the time of the assembly, which was set for a month, monks from all over the country arrived. The Tang emperor issued a decree, ordering the imperial recorder, Pu Yi, to elect outstanding monks to construct Buddhist affairs. Pu Yi, upon receiving the edict, immediately presented a memorial to stop the construction of the Buddhist hall, arguing that there was no Buddha. The memorial read: "The law of the West Regions has no sovereign-subject relationships of fathers and sons, yet it uses the Three Paths and Six Paths to deceive the ignorant and foolish, to pursue past crimes and peek at future blessings, and to recite Sanskrit phrases in order to cheat one's way out of punishment. Moreover, life and death, as well as long or short lifespans, are all matters of nature; morality, righteousness, authority, and blessings depend on the ruler. Nowadays, the ignorant multitude feigningly attribute everything to Buddhism. From the Five Emperors and Three Kings up until the present, there has never been the Buddhist doctrine. A wise and loyal minister, with a long dynasty, is the hallmark of a ruler. It was not until Emperor Ming of Han that he established the cult of foreign deities, and the only one who did so was the West Regions' Shanmen, who was actually a barbarian who disturbed China, and his teachings are not worthy of belief."

The emperor heard the memorial and then handed it to the court officials for discussion. At the time, there was a prime minister, Xiao Yu, who stepped forward and bowed his head to speak:

Having finished submitting his report, the Emperor was extremely pleased.  He then gathered many officials and issued a summons to call forth the monks, to construct a water and land convention for the deliverance of souls in the underworld.  The edict was circulated throughout the land, requiring officials from all places to recommend virtuous monks to proceed to Chang'an to participate in the convention. Within a month, monks came from all over the country.  The Emperor issued an edict ordering Grand Historian Shi Yupu to hold an election to choose the high-ranking monks and to oversee the construction of the Buddhist ritual.  Upon hearing the edict, Shi Yupu immediately submitted a memorial to banish the image of Buddha, saying that there is no Buddha.  The memorial stated: "In the Western Regions, there is no sovereign and subject, father and son, who do not lure the stupid and foolish into the three paths and six destinations, making them seek their past transgressions and contemplate their future blessings by reciting the sounds of the heavens.  Moreover, birth and death, longevity and fate, are all naturally determined; punishments, virtue, and blessings are all bound to the ruler.  I have heard that common people deceive themselves by claiming to follow the Buddha's teachings.  From the time of the Five Emperors and the Three Kings, there has never been the Buddha's law, only the loyalty of the ruler and the ministers, and a long-lasting dynasty.  Even Emperor Mingdi first established the deities of the Western Regions, and only the Western Regions' Shangmen transmitted their teachings.  In reality, it was the barbarians who disobeyed China, and it is not worthy of trust."  Emperor Taizong heard this memorial and then discarded it among the discussions of the ministers.  At that time, Chancellor Xue Ju came forward, bowed and said:

After the report was presented, the Emperor was overjoyed. He then assembled a multitude of officials and issued an edict to summon monks, ordering the construction of a grand ceremony to liberate the spirits in the underworld. The edict was sent throughout the empire, instructing officials in various places to recommend worthy monks, who would come to Chang'an to preside over the ceremony. Within a month, monks from all over the empire arrived. The Emperor issued a decree, instructing Cui Yi, the Imperial Secretary, to recommend worthy monks and oversee the construction of the Buddha's works. Cui Yi heard the edict and promptly drafted a memorial to oppose the construction of a Buddhist pagoda, stating that there is no Buddha. His memorial read:

"In the lands of the West, they have no notion of royalty, nobility, or kinship. They lead people astray with the three paths and six destinies, coaxing the ignorant and foolish to incur the guilt of past transgressions and covet the good fortune of the future. They mouth nonsensical Sanskrit phrases in the hope of securing an easy reprieve. Moreover, the cycle of birth and death, the span of life and fate, are determined by nature itself; the command of benevolence and righteousness, and the blessings and curses, are under the control of the ruler. Now, I hear that the common folk are twisting the facts and claim that it is all due to Buddhism. Since the time of the Five Emperors and the Three Kings, there has never been a Buddhist doctrine. Only Emperor Hui of the Han Dynasty first established the worship of foreign gods, and even then, it was only the monk from the West, Shandao, who introduced their teachings to China. But in fact, it was a barbarian invasion, and it is hardly worth believing."

The Emperor heard his words and then tossed the memorial to the assembled officials to deliberate upon it. At the time, the Prime Minister, Xiao Yu, stood forward and kowtowed to the throne, saying:

Upon completion of the work, Emperor Taizong was greatly pleased. He then gathered many officials, posted edicts across the land, and recruited monks to build a grand Buddha hall for rescuing the souls of those in the underworld. The edict covered the entire empire, instructing local officials to recommend wise monks to attend in Chang'an. By the end of the month, many monks had arrived. When Fu Yi received the edict, he promptly submitted a memorial advising against erecting a Buddhist scripture tower, stating: 

"The laws of the Western Regions have no emperor-subject relationships of parent-child. They preach the Three Paths and Six Realms to entice the ignorant and foolish to pursue rewards for past mistakes and benefits in the future, relying solely on reciting Sanskrit to seek an easy escape. It was only Emperor Wu of the Han who first established the worship of foreign deities. However, even in the Western Regions, it was only the monks of the Sangha Gate who transmitted their teachings, which in fact were a foreign invasion of China, not worthy of trust."

When Emperor Taizong heard these words, he eventually handed the memorial to his officials to deliberate. At the time, there was a grand councillor, Xiao Yu, who stood forward, bowed low, and said:

The Prince of Tang dispatched an edict to have the Censor, Beidi Fu, hold elections for virtuous monks to construct Buddhist affairs. When Fu Beidi received the edict, he immediately presented a memorial to abolish the heavenly bridge, saying that there was no Buddha. The memorial read: "In the West, the laws have no monarch and subject, father and son; they use the Three Ways and Six Paths to delude the ignorant and foolish, in pursuit of the crimes of the past and the blessings of the future, and recite Sanskrit words in the hopes of escaping punishment. Furthermore, life and death, longevity and early demise, are all matters of natural destiny; the ruler's benevolence, virtue, and blessings, are all attached to the monarch. Now, I have heard that the common people pervert the truth and all claim it is due to the Buddha. From the Five Emperors and the Three Kings, there has never been a Buddhist law; a wise ruler and a loyal minister, with a long reign, are the most crucial factors. Until Emperor Ming of Han first established the cult of foreign deities, but the only place where Buddhism originated was in the West, at the foot of the hemp tree, and it was actually a case of the barbarians invading China; it is not a matter worthy of being believed." Emperor Taizong, upon hearing these words, thus threw the memorial among his officials to discuss it. As the bamboo knocks against the fallen moon, and the rooster sings with the rising mists, the monks rise, gathering tea and water for morning alms. Xuanzang then donned his saffron robes, ascended to the main hall, and paid respects before the Buddha, saying, "I, Chen Xuanzang, a humble disciple, shall journey to the West in search of scriptures. Though with my mortal eyes I am blind to the true form of the living Buddha, I swear to perform this vow: whenever I encounter a temple, I shall burn incense; upon meeting a Buddha, I shall bow to the Buddha; and when I come upon a pagoda, I shall sweep it clean. May the merciful Buddha graciously bestow upon me the golden body six feet tall, grant me the true scriptures, and allow me to bring them back to the Eastern lands." After making this prayer, he returned to the main hall to break his fast. The two attendants led out the horses, hastening their pace. Xuanzang emerged from the mountain gate, bid farewell to the crowd of monks. The monks, reluctant to part, followed him as far as ten li, then turned back, weeping; Xuanzang continued on westward. It was the season of autumn, and everywhere he saw: in several villages, the willow trees had shed their lotus flowers, and the few maple and elm trees had shed their crimson leaves. The road was shrouded in mist and rain, and the people were scarce. Yellow chrysanthemums bloomed, and the tree branches were slender. The water was cold, and the lotus flowers were broken and wilted. The piling up of frost and snow in the pinyin and red water lilies, the setting sun, the lone wild geese soaring into the sky, their cries shattered the night's silence. The distant and dark clouds drifted by, and the wild geese departed, the solitary cranes arrived, and their plaintive cries and melancholy songs shattered the night's silence.

As morning dawned again, the bamboo tapping broke through the broken moon, and the cock's chanting woke the rising clouds. The multitude of monks arose and tidied up the tea and water for the pre-dawn vegetarian meal. Xuanzang, donning his saffron robes, ascended to the main hall, prostrated before the Buddha, and said: "I am Xuanzang's disciple, going to the Western Heaven to acquire the scriptures. With mortal eyes, I am blind and ignorant, not knowing the true form of the living Buddha. Now, I make a vow: wherever I encounter a temple, I will burn incense; wherever I meet a Buddha, I will worship the Buddha; and wherever I see a tower, I will sweep it. I implore the merciful Buddha to reveal the thirty-six-inch gold body to me early, to grant the true scriptures, and to leave behind a legacy in the East." After finishing his vow, Xuanzang returned to the monastery and entered the hall for the vegetarian meal. After finishing the meal, his two attendants put their horses in order and urged them on. Xuanzang exited the mountain gate and bid farewell to the multitude of monks. The monks, unable to bear the separation, escorted him as far as ten li before returning, and Xuanzang continued on his journey westward. It was autumn, and all that could be seen were: scattered willow branches and broken pendent flowers, red maple and willow leaves falling, sparse villagers and wild geese on the winding path, golden chrysanthemums, the skeletons of mountains, the icy water, and the broken lotus leaves. The ground was covered with frost, and snow. The setting sun cast a lonely glow, and a solitary goose flew across the sky, and the night-breaking sounds of various birds filled the air.

It was dawn once more with the sound of bamboo tapping the fallen moon and the rooster singing in the growing light of day. The monks all arose and prepared for the morning meal. Xuanzang donned his saffron robes and went up to the main hall to pay homage to the Buddha, saying, "I, Dharma Master Xuanzang, am setting out for the Western Heaven to fetch scriptures, but my eyes are dim and I don't recognize the true form of the living Buddha. I now take a vow: as I journey on, I will burn incense at every temple I encounter, bow to every Buddha I meet, and sweep the floors of every stupa. I humbly beseech the Buddha to show me His six-foot golden body at an early date, grant me the true scriptures, and transmit them to the East. After finishing my prayer, I returned to the Main Building to take my meal. After completing my meal, my two attendants busied themselves tightening the saddles and urging on the horses. The Tripitaka Master went out of the mountain gate, bade farewell to the monks, who could not bear to part and sent him off as far as ten li, with tears in their eyes, and then returned. The Tripitaka Master thus set off straight for the West. It was the season of autumn, and on the road, one saw: the villages were scattered with autumn cabbages, and the numerous lotus flowers were shattered, the maple and willow leaves had fallen, and the smoke and rain scattered the lonely traveler, the autumn chrysanthemums were beautiful, the mountain bones were slender, the water was cold, the lotus leaves were broken, and the people were gaunt. The camellia and red salvia frost covered the sky, the setting sun, a lone heron plunged into the empty space, the far-off and hazy clouds flew by, the quail left, and the geese arrived, their plaintive, mournful cries shattered the night.

Early again, the bamboo struck the fallen moon, the chickens sang the rising dawn mist. The monks arose, gathered to clean up the tea and breakfast. Xuanzang donned his monk's robes, went up to the main hall, bowed before the Buddha, and said: "Disciple Xuanzang, going to the west to fetch scriptures, my mundane eyes are dim, unable to discern the true form of the living Buddha. Now I vow: wherever I encounter a temple, I will burn incense; where I meet a Buddha, I will bow to the Buddha; where I see a stupa, I will sweep the stupa. May the merciful Buddha show me the golden body, give me the true scriptures, and leave a legacy in the East." Having finished the blessing, he returned to the abbot's quarters to take breakfast. After finishing breakfast, the two attendants tightened the horse's saddle and hastened the journey. Xuanzang left the mountain gates, bid farewell to the monks. The monks could not bear to part, and followed him for ten li before returning, Xuanzang then continued on his westward journey. It was that autumn season, and all he saw were: many villages had fallen willows and scattered pampas grass; a few trees had red maples and willows, with leaves falling. The road was dusty from the rain, and few people were seen; chrysanthemums were beautiful, the mountains were rugged, the water was cold, and the lotus had broken. The pixie grass was red, the lotus was red with frost; the fallen colors of the setting sun filled the sky. Faint and indistinct, the wild clouds flew by, the willow birds flew away, the migrating geese arrived, and the night was broken by the clear, melancholic sounds.

The morning was once again the bamboo drumming at the falling moon, the chicken singing in the rising dawn clouds. Those monks arose, tidying up the tea and water for the early morning meal. Xuanzang then donned his robe, went up to the main hall, and paid respects before the Buddha, saying, "I am Xuanzang, a disciple, bound for the West to seek the scriptures, but my eyes are dull and stupid, and I do not recognize the true form of the living Buddha. Now I take an oath: On the road, if I come across a temple, I will burn incense; if I meet a Buddha, I will pay my respects; if I encounter a pagoda, I will sweep it clean. I hope that the Buddha will have mercy on me, manifest his thirty-six-foot golden body, bestow the true scriptures, and leave behind a transmission to the Eastern land." After the vow, he returned to the abbot's quarters to partake in the meal. After the meal, the two attendants tightened their saddles and hastened their journey. Xuanzang left the mountain gate, bid farewell to the monks, who, unable to bear the separation, followed him for ten li and then returned, tears in their eyes. Xuanzang thus proceeded westward. It was the time of autumn, and one could see: In several villages, willow branches were withered, cattails were scattered, and a few maple and poplar trees had shed their red leaves. The road was shrouded in haze and rain, and fewer travelers appeared. The chrysanthemums were beautiful, the mountain peaks were slender, the water was cold, and the lotus flowers were crushed and wilted. The plum blossoms were like coral, the sun was a snowy sky, and the falling light was solitary and desolate. Faint and dull clouds drifted, the crows departed, and the geese arrived, their mournful cries piercing the night.
